lessons.title: Janapadas and Mahājanapadas

activities.prompt: Why did some small kingdoms join together to become bigger, stronger lands?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Places and Bigger Places
activities.body: A janapada is a place where people have settled down. Each clan was linked with its own janapada. As trade networks grew, janapadas were linked together. By the 8th or 7th centuries BCE, some early states had merged. The bigger merged units were called mahājanapadas. Your book's most common list names 16 of them. They stretched from Gandhāra in the northwest to Anga in the east.
keyPoints: A janapada is a settled place linked with a clan.
Trade networks linked the janapadas together.
Some early states merged into bigger units called mahājanapadas.
Your book names 16 mahājanapadas in its most common list.
activities.explanation: Janapadas were the settled places, and mahājanapadas were the bigger merged units.

activities.prompt: A trader compares the Ganga plains with hills containing iron ore. Why could mahājanapadas grow in both?
steps: Many mahājanapadas were in the Ganga plains because agriculture grew well there.
Good farming therefore gave plains states a reason to grow.
Iron ore in the hills gave states another reason to grow.
Thus, farming and iron ore both helped explain mahājanapada growth.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does the word janapada mean?
options: A large group of traders on the move
A king's army that marched to war
A place where people have settled down
A kind of coin used in the markets
activities.explanation: The word janapada means a place where people have settled down. Each clan was linked with a janapada like this.

activities.prompt: Mahājanapadas were small single villages formed by one clan.
activities.explanation: Mahājanapadas were bigger units. They were made when early states merged together.

activities.prompt: Each clan was linked with a territory called a ______.
activities.hint: It means a place where people have settled down.
activities.explanation: A janapada is the settled territory linked with a clan. Well done for remembering the word.

activities.prompt: Match each word to what it describes in your book.
pairs: A place where people have settled down
A bigger unit made when early states merged
The northwest end of the mahājanapadas
The eastern end of the mahājanapadas
activities.explanation: A janapada is a settled place. Mahājanapadas were bigger merged units that stretched from Gandhāra to Anga.

activities.prompt: Why did many mahājanapadas grow up in the Ganga plains?
options: Farming grew well there
Most of their capitals were soon abandoned
The plains were far away in the south
Iron ore was never found in the hills
activities.explanation: Agriculture grew well in the Ganga plains, so many states grew there. Iron ore in the hills was a different reason for growth.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the order your book describes them.
items: Each clan was linked with its own janapada
Trade networks linked the janapadas together
The bigger merged units were called mahājanapadas
activities.explanation: First each clan had its janapada. Trade then linked them. Later, early states merged into mahājanapadas.

activities.prompt: Which four states does your book name as among the most powerful new states?
options: Iron, gold, silver and copper
Kings, traders, clans and farmers
Rivers, hills, plains and forests
Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti
activities.explanation: Your book names Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti as among the most powerful new states. Remember these four names from this lesson.

activities.prompt: One new mahājanapada grows in the Ganga plains. Another grows near hills with iron ore. Why could both grow?
options: The plains grew through farming; the hills grew through iron ore.
The plains grew through iron ore; the hills grew through farming.
The plains grew through trade; the hills grew through mergers.
Both grew because their capitals remain cities today.

why.The plains grew through iron ore; the hi: This mistake swaps farming and iron ore.
why.The plains grew through trade; the hills: This mistake uses general events instead of local growth reasons.
why.Both grew because their capitals remain: This mistake uses later city survival as the earlier cause.

activities.explanation: This is right because farming helped plains states and iron ore helped hill states.

activities.prompt: A teacher calls a settled clan’s territory a janapada. What must be true?
options: People have settled down in that territory.
Several early states have merged in that territory.
Trade networks have linked that territory.
A living city stands in that territory.

why.Several early states have merged in that: This mistake confuses a mahājanapada with a janapada.
why.Trade networks have linked that territor: This mistake confuses a settled territory with a trade network.
This mistake confuses an ancient capital with a clan’s territory.

activities.explanation: This is right because janapada means a place where people settled.

lessons.title: Kings and Assemblies

activities.prompt: Who decides how a kingdom is run, and can the people help?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Kings and Assemblies
activities.body: Some states had a king, called a rājā. In a monarchy, the rājā was the final authority. Usually, a rājā became ruler by being the son of the previous one. The king collected taxes and kept law and order. Many states also had an assembly, called a sabhā or samiti. Most members of the assembly were elders. A good ruler was supposed to take advice from these assemblies.
keyPoints: A rājā usually became ruler by being the previous ruler's son.
The assembly was called a sabhā or samiti, and most members were elders.
In Vajji and Malla, the assembly had more power than the ruler.
activities.explanation: Some states had kings, while others had assemblies with more power.

activities.prompt: A king ignores his janapada's assembly. People wonder whether he is a good ruler. Why?
steps: Each janapada had an assembly called a sabhā or samiti.
A good ruler was supposed to take advice from these assemblies.
Therefore, the king should hear the assembly before making a decision.
Ignoring it means he is not following the rule for a good ruler.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What was a sabhā or samiti in your book?
options: A royal tax paid to the rājā
A group of guards at the palace
An assembly or council in each state
A ruler chosen by the king's son
activities.explanation: Each state had an assembly or council called a sabhā or samiti. The other choices are not about assemblies.

activities.prompt: A rājā usually became ruler by being the ______ of the previous one.
activities.hint: Think of a family member.
activities.explanation: Usually, a rājā was the son of the ruler who came before.

activities.prompt: Match each word to its meaning from the lesson.
pairs: the final authority in a monarchy
activities.explanation: A rājā was the final authority in a monarchy. A good ruler listened to the assemblies.

activities.prompt: Why did a good ruler take advice from the assemblies?
options: The assembly collected all the taxes for the king.
A good ruler was supposed to take advice from them.
The rājā had no law or order to keep.
Only the king's sons could sit in the assembly.
activities.explanation: Your book says a good ruler was supposed to take advice from the assemblies. The other choices do not match the lesson.

activities.prompt: According to some texts, what could the assembly do to an incompetent ruler?
options: Give the ruler more land
Lower the taxes
Build a new palace
Remove the ruler from power
activities.explanation: Some texts say an incompetent ruler could be removed. Your book adds that these mentions do not prove it was an official law.

activities.prompt: Scholars often call the gaṇas and sanghas early ______.
activities.hint: The word starts with R.
activities.explanation: Scholars often call these states early republics. They were called gaṇas or sanghas.

activities.prompt: Most assembly members were elders. A king must follow the rule for a good ruler. What should he do?
options: Listen to the assembly before making his decision.
Ignore the assembly and make the decision alone.
Wait for the assembly to choose the next ruler.
Ask the assembly only after making his decision.

why.Ignore the assembly and make the decisio: This mistakes the king's own decision for his required duty to seek advice.
why.Wait for the assembly to choose the next: This confuses giving advice with choosing the ruler.
why.Ask the assembly only after making his d: This seeks advice too late to guide the king's decision.

activities.explanation: Taking advice from assemblies was the rule for a good ruler.

activities.prompt: In a monarchy, the rājā was the final authority. In Vajji and Malla, how did rule work?
options: Their assembly had more power and chose the ruler.
Their rājā kept more power than their assembly.
Their rulers always inherited power from the previous king.
Their assemblies collected taxes and kept law and order.

why.Their rājā kept more power than their as: This reverses the difference because their assembly had more power.
why.Their rulers always inherited power from: This confuses chosen rulers with the usual rule of hereditary succession.
why.Their assemblies collected taxes and kep: Taxes and law and order are listed as the king's duties.

activities.explanation: Their assembly had more power, and its members chose the ruler.

activities.prompt: Some texts say an incompetent ruler could be removed by an assembly. What can we say without claiming too much?
options: Removal was mentioned, but it was not proved to be law.
Every ruler was certainly removed by an established law.
Assembly removals happened regularly in every janapada.
Texts prove that assemblies could never remove rulers.

why.Every ruler was certainly removed by an: This turns one mention into a certain law for every ruler.
why.Assembly removals happened regularly in: This turns a possibility in some texts into a regular rule everywhere.
why.Texts prove that assemblies could never: This turns a possible mention into proof that removal never happened.

activities.explanation: The mention does not prove that removal was an established law.

activities.prompt: Rājās usually became ruler as sons of the previous ruler. In a monarchy, what is most likely after a king's death?
options: His son will probably become the ruler.
The assembly will certainly choose his son.
His son will become ruler after paying extra taxes.
An elder will probably become the ruler instead.

why.The assembly will certainly choose his s: This confuses monarchy with Vajji and Malla, where assemblies chose rulers.
why.His son will become ruler after paying e: This confuses collecting taxes with the rule for choosing a successor.
why.An elder will probably become the ruler: This assumes an elder's position makes him the usual successor.

activities.explanation: This matches the usual rule that a rājā succeeded as the previous king's son.

activities.prompt: A map marks several janapadas but does not show assemblies. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Each marked janapada probably had an assembly.
Only one janapada probably had an assembly.
Every janapada was ruled by a chosen assembly.
No janapada had an assembly at all.

why.Only one janapada probably had an assemb: The fact applies to each janapada, not just one.
why.Every janapada was ruled by a chosen ass: Having an assembly does not mean that it ruled the janapada.
This mistakes a map's missing symbols for missing assemblies.

activities.explanation: Each janapada had an assembly, so the marked janapadas likely did too.

lessons.title: Iron, Coins and Trade

activities.prompt: Why did people first start using coins to buy and sell things?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Iron, Coins and Trade
activities.body: In this period, iron was a major shift in technology. Iron made better weapons than bronze, which were lighter and sharper. Cities need technology to grow, and iron helped with that. Trade was growing too. So people needed coins. The first Indian coins were silver. They are called punch-marked coins. Each mahājanapada, or state, usually made its own coins.
keyPoints: Iron made lighter and sharper weapons than bronze.
Coins were needed because trade was growing.
The first Indian coins were silver punch-marked coins.
activities.explanation: Iron and coins are two big ideas in this lesson.

activities.prompt: A mahājanapada faces nearby warfare and growing trade. What should it use for tools, weapons, and money?
steps: The mahājanapada should use iron tools because cities need technology to grow.
Iron weapons were lighter and sharper, so they suited nearby wars.
Coins were needed because trade was growing, so traders needed money.
It should issue its own silver punch-marked coins because mahājanapadas usually did.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Why were coins needed in India?
options: Because iron tools were no longer used
Because trade was growing
Because bronze weapons were too sharp
Because the first coins were made of iron
activities.explanation: The lesson says coins were needed because trade was growing. Trade was the reason.

activities.prompt: The first Indian coins were made of ______.
activities.hint: It starts with the letter s.
activities.explanation: The lesson says the first Indian coins were made of silver.

activities.prompt: Iron weapons were heavier than bronze weapons.
activities.explanation: The lesson says iron weapons were lighter and sharper than bronze. Read that part again to be sure.

activities.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: The name for the first Indian coins
What the first Indian coins were made of
A state that usually made its own coins
activities.explanation: Each word matches one idea from your book.

activities.prompt: Put these in the order the lesson describes.
items: The first Indian coins were made of silver
activities.explanation: Trade grew first, and that made people need coins. The first coins were then made of silver.

activities.prompt: Why might iron weapons matter in warfare?
options: They were the same as punch-marked coins
They were used to pay for goods in trade
They were lighter and sharper than bronze
They were the first coins used in India
activities.explanation: The lesson says iron weapons were lighter and sharper than bronze. It also mentions warfare between neighbouring mahājanapadas.

activities.prompt: Cities need technology to grow. Iron was the major technology shift. What could help a city grow?
options: The city could use iron technology to support growth.
The city could stop using bronze and change everything.
The city could avoid technology and still grow well.
The city could use bronze in place of iron technology.

why.The city could stop using bronze and cha: This wrongly assumes one metal must replace everything.
why.The city could avoid technology and stil: This mistakes staying unchanged for helping cities grow.
why.The city could use bronze in place of ir: This ignores that iron was the major technology shift.

activities.explanation: This connects iron technology with the growth cities need.

activities.prompt: Early in the 2nd millennium BCE, iron techniques were perfected. Late in it, iron tools were common. What does this show?
options: The techniques took time to become widely used.
The techniques spread as soon as they were perfected.
Iron tools were common before techniques were perfected.
The later period had no iron tools at all.

why.The techniques spread as soon as they we: This assumes spreading happened immediately after perfection.
why.Iron tools were common before techniques: This reverses the order of techniques and common use.
why.The later period had no iron tools at al: This ignores that iron tools were common by the later time.

activities.explanation: Centuries were needed for the perfected techniques to spread widely.

activities.prompt: Iron weapons were lighter and sharper than bronze weapons. Some mahājanapadas fought nearby. Why might rulers want iron weapons?
options: Iron weapons could give fighters lighter and sharper weapons.
Iron weapons were heavier and less sharp than bronze.
Iron weapons were useful only for peaceful trade.
Iron weapons could make fighting less likely nearby.

why.Iron weapons were heavier and less sharp: This reverses what iron weapons were like.
why.Iron weapons were useful only for peacef: This confuses weapons with peaceful trade.
why.Iron weapons could make fighting less li: This assumes better weapons would stop fighting.

activities.explanation: The right weapons were lighter and sharper than bronze.

activities.prompt: Trade was growing in India. Coins were a new innovation. Why were coins needed for traders?
options: Growing trade created a need for money.
Shrinking trade created a need for money.
Coins were needed because tools became sharper.
Coins were needed because warfare always increased.

why.Shrinking trade created a need for money: This reverses the link between trade and coins.
why.Coins were needed because tools became s: This mixes the need for coins with sharper tools.
why.Coins were needed because warfare always: This treats some warfare evidence as always increasing warfare.

activities.explanation: Coins were needed because trade was growing.

lessons.title: Varṇa and Jāti

activities.prompt: Why did people in India once belong to different groups, and how did those groups work?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Ways to Group People
activities.body: A complex society often divides itself into groups. In India, two ideas help you understand these groups: varṇa and jāti. Varṇa came from Vedic texts and has four parts. A jāti is a community with one professional occupation, which supports its livelihood. Skills of a jāti were passed on from generation to generation.
keyPoints: Varṇa came from Vedic texts and has four parts.
A jāti is a community tied to one professional occupation.
Skills of a jāti were passed on from generation to generation.
activities.explanation: Varṇa and jāti help you see how Indian society grouped people.

activities.prompt: A child sees communities doing different work and passing skills to the next generation. How should this be understood?
steps: A jāti links a community to one occupation, because that work supports its livelihood.
Skills pass between generations, so communities can continue their occupations.
Varṇa came from Vedic texts and had four groups, so it helps explain social organisation.
Such divisions often create inequality, so equality remains an unachieved ideal.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Shudras were the artisans, craftspeople, workers or servants.
activities.explanation: The lesson lists Shudras as artisans, craftspeople, workers or servants. So this statement is true.

activities.prompt: Match each varṇa to its main job.
pairs: defending the society and the land
increasing wealth through trade, business or farming
activities.explanation: Each varṇa was expected to do a different kind of work in society.

activities.prompt: Skills of a jāti were passed on from one ______ to the next.
activities.hint: Think of a family line: parents, then children, then the next family line.
activities.explanation: Skills were handed down from one generation to the next. That is how a jāti kept its work alive.

activities.prompt: Which of these best describes a jāti?
options: A group of people who defend the land and the society.
A kind of ancient text that came from Vedic writings.
A community with a specific professional occupation tied to its livelihood.
A place where people go to trade goods and produce wealth.
activities.explanation: A jāti is a community linked to one job that supports its livelihood. Varṇa is a different idea.

activities.prompt: Which statement matches what the lesson says about equality?
options: Most societies have already reached perfect equality.
Equality happens by itself when a society has many groups.
Equality is a rule that all societies must follow by law.
Equality is an ideal that very few societies have ever achieved.
activities.explanation: The lesson says equality is an ideal. Very few societies have reached it, so it is rare.

activities.prompt: Groups in a complex society can form only by class.
activities.explanation: The lesson says groups can form by class, occupation or other criteria. So the word 'only' makes this false.

activities.prompt: A community depends on making tools. Its members pass tool-making skills to the next generation. What does this show?
options: Skills pass between generations in a jāti.
Jātis have no connection to professional work.
Varṇa comes only from later inventions.
Social groups never keep inequalities.

why.Jātis have no connection to professional: This mistake ignores the close link between jātis and work.
This mistake treats varṇa as a later invention instead of a Vedic concept.
This mistake denies that divisions can create inequalities.

activities.explanation: This is right because jātis pass occupational skills between generations.

activities.prompt: A Vedic text lists four varṇas. Another source shows four social groups with different duties. What can we understand?
options: Indian society's varṇa idea had four groups with distinct duties.
Every society must use exactly four groups with different duties.
Jātis mean only individual jobs, not whole communities.
Equality was common in every society.

why.Every society must use exactly four grou: This mistake assumes that every society must have four groups.
why.Jātis mean only individual jobs, not who: This mistake confuses a whole community with one person's job.
This mistake forgets that very few societies have achieved equality.

activities.explanation: This is right because there were four varṇas with different duties.

activities.prompt: Community A preserves knowledge. Community B increases wealth through farming and trade. How should we compare their work?
options: Community A fits Brahmin work, while B fits Vaishya work.
Community A fits Vaishya work, while B fits Brahmin work.
Community A fits Shudra work, while B fits Kshatriya work.
Both communities fit only servant work in society.

why.Community A fits Vaishya work, while B f: This mistake swaps the duties of Brahmins and Vaishyas.
why.Community A fits Shudra work, while B fi: This mistake gives both communities duties that do not match their work.
why.Both communities fit only servant work i: This mistake ignores the different duties of Brahmins and Vaishyas.

activities.explanation: This is right because Brahmins preserved knowledge and Vaishyas increased wealth.

lessons.title: Roads and Cities Beyond the North

activities.prompt: How did people travel and trade across the vast lands and seas of ancient India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Roads and Cities Beyond the North
activities.body: Your book tells how roads and cities grew beyond the north. The Uttarapatha linked the northwest with the Ganga plains, which are wide, flat lands. The Dakṣhiṇapatha began at Kauśhāmbī and crossed the Vindhya hills to reach the far south. Cities began to appear in the south around 400 BCE. Ports on the coasts became busy centres of trade.
keyPoints: The Uttarapatha linked the northwest with the Ganga plains.
The Dakṣhiṇapatha began at Kauśhāmbī and crossed the Vindhya hills.
Ports on the western and eastern coasts were busy centres of trade.
activities.explanation: Roads and ports link places together, so keep these names in mind.

activities.prompt: A traveller starts at Kauśhāmbī and wants to reach the far south. Which road can help?
steps: Because Kauśhāmbī was the Dakṣhiṇapatha's starting point, this road fits the journey.
The Dakṣhiṇapatha crossed the Vindhya hills to go all the way south.
So it can help the traveller reach the far south.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which road linked the northwest with the Ganga plains?
options: Dakṣhiṇapatha road
Śhiśhupalgarh city
Uttarapatha road
Kauśhāmbī city
activities.explanation: Your book says the Uttarapatha connected the northwest with the Ganga plains. The other names are a road and cities, but not this link.

activities.prompt: Match each road or city to what it did or was.
pairs: Linked the northwest with the Ganga plains
Crossed the Vindhya hills and went south
activities.explanation: Each road and city has its own job in your lesson. Reading the words slowly helps you spot the match.

activities.prompt: Ports on the western and eastern coasts were vibrant centres of ______.
activities.hint: Think about goods being bought and sold.
activities.explanation: Your book says these ports were busy centres of trade. Ports were places where goods moved in and out.

activities.prompt: Why did people in the southern regions trade so widely?
options: They had no roads that led to them.
They were rich in stones, gold and spices.
They had no ports on any coast.
Their people never traded with anyone.
activities.explanation: Your book says the southern regions were rich in stones, gold and spices. Because of these riches, they traded widely.

activities.prompt: Put the Dakṣhiṇapatha journey in order, from start to finish.
items: It went all the way south.
activities.explanation: Your book says the road began at Kauśhāmbī and crossed the Vindhya hills to go all the way south.

activities.prompt: Cities began to appear in the south about 400 BCE. The mahājanapadas stopped existing around 300 BCE. Which is true?
options: The mahājanapadas ended before cities began in the south.
Cities began in the south before the mahājanapadas ended.
Both happened at the same time, around 300 BCE.
activities.explanation: 400 BCE is earlier than 300 BCE, so the southern cities came first. The mahājanapadas ended later, around 300 BCE.

activities.prompt: A southern region had stones, gold and spices. What would you predict?
options: It would trade widely with other regions.
It would stop trading because of its wealth.
It would lose all its roads quickly.
It would have no southern cities.

why.It would stop trading because of its wea: Wealth encouraged trade here, so it did not stop trading.
The facts do not say that rich regions lost their roads.
The facts do not say that rich regions lacked southern cities.

activities.explanation: These riches explain why the region traded widely.

activities.prompt: Southern cities appeared around 400 BCE. What might change by 300 BCE?
options: The mahājanapadas might stop existing around then.
Southern cities might disappear from the map.
Ports might replace all southern cities.
Square plans might be forgotten by then.

why.Southern cities might disappear from the: Nothing says southern cities disappeared by 300 BCE.
Nothing says ports replaced the southern cities.
Nothing says square city plans ended by 300 BCE.

activities.explanation: The mahājanapadas stopped existing around 300 BCE.

activities.prompt: By 300 or 200 BCE, the land was nearly connected. Which roads help?
options: The Uttarapatha and Dakṣhiṇapatha linked distant regions.
The ports alone connected every region.
The square plans connected northern and southern cities.
The southern kingdoms ended all long roads.

This ignores the roads and overstates what ports could do.
why.The square plans connected northern and: A city's square shape did not connect distant regions.
why.The southern kingdoms ended all long roa: The kingdoms emerged around 400 BCE, but no fact says they ended roads.

activities.explanation: These roads joined distant areas and helped make wider connection possible.

activities.context: A museum exhibit shows urban phases in India. It identifies the Harappan civilisation as the First Urbanisation. Around the early 2nd millennium BCE, it came apart: some cities were left empty, while people who remained in others returned to village life. The exhibit says urban life returned in the 1st millennium BCE in the Ganga plains and parts of the Indus basin. It says historians use archaeological digs and ancient texts, including Late Vedic, Buddhist and Jain texts.
activities.prompt: If one Harappan city had kept its busy markets when the civilisation came apart, what might have happened?
options: That city might have retained some urban life earlier.
Every Indian city would have stayed urban for the next millennium.
The Second Urbanisation would have begun in every region at once.
Village life would have vanished from the Indus basin.

why.Every Indian city would have stayed urba: One city would not show that every Indian city remained urban.
why.The Second Urbanisation would have begun: One city would not make the later urban phase begin everywhere at the same time.
why.Village life would have vanished from th: Continued activity in one city would not remove village life throughout the Indus basin.

activities.explanation: Keeping a busy market could have allowed some urban activity to continue earlier.

activities.context: A museum exhibit shows urban phases in India. It identifies the Harappan civilisation as the First Urbanisation. Around the early 2nd millennium BCE, it came apart: some cities were left empty, while people who remained in others returned to village life. The exhibit says urban life returned in the 1st millennium BCE in the Ganga plains and parts of the Indus basin. It says historians use archaeological digs and ancient texts, including Late Vedic, Buddhist and Jain texts.
activities.prompt: A site has archaeological remains of new cities, and Late Vedic, Buddhist and Jain texts also mention such cities. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: The site has both material and written evidence for the Second Urbanisation.
The site must belong only to the First Urbanisation.
The archaeological finds are useful, but the written references add no useful evidence.
The site proves that urban life continued without any break.

why.The site must belong only to the First U: The remains and text references point to the later urban phase.
why.The archaeological finds are useful, but: Texts mentioning the cities are also useful evidence and should not be dismissed.
why.The site proves that urban life continue: A whole millennium without urban life separated the two urban phases.

activities.explanation: Archaeological finds and references in the texts together support the conclusion.

activities.prompt: Explain why the Harappan civilisation is called India's First Urbanisation, and what happened after it came apart.
activities.answer: The Harappan civilisation is called India's First Urbanisation because it was the first phase of urban life in India. After it came apart, some cities were left empty. People who remained in others returned to village life, while big buildings, crowded streets and busy markets disappeared from the cities.
points: The Harappan civilisation is called the First Urbanisation.
It represents India's first phase of urban life.
Some cities were left empty after it came apart.
Remaining people returned to village life, and city features disappeared.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A class project compares two clan territories in north India. Traders travel between the settlements, so their trade connections become stronger. Towards the end of the 2nd millennium BCE, regional cultures reorganise in north India. By the 8th or 7th centuries BCE, some early states merge. The class also studies a territory in the Ganga plains and a hill territory with iron ore, and asks what helped the merged states grow there.
activities.prompt: The traders keep making journeys between the two territories. What is the most likely result?
options: Their growing trade links make a merger into a mahājanapada more likely.
The territories will remain separate because each clan must stay in its own janapada.
The territories can merge only if the usual list of mahājanapadas grows beyond sixteen.
The territories will become separate mahājanapadas because stronger trade links remove the need for larger states.

why.The territories will remain separate bec: A clan’s link with a janapada did not prevent such mergers.
why.The territories can merge only if the us: Sixteen is the number in the most common list, not a merger condition.
why.The territories will become separate mah: Stronger trade links encouraged connection rather than making larger states unnecessary.

activities.explanation: Expanding and connected trade helped some early states merge into bigger units.

activities.context: A class project compares two clan territories in north India. Traders travel between the settlements, so their trade connections become stronger. Towards the end of the 2nd millennium BCE, regional cultures reorganise in north India. By the 8th or 7th centuries BCE, some early states merge. The class also studies a territory in the Ganga plains and a hill territory with iron ore, and asks what helped the merged states grow there.
activities.prompt: A map shows one mahājanapada in the Ganga plains and another in a hill area. Which comparison gives the best explanation for their growth?
options: Good farming in the plains and iron in the hills both aided expansion.
The plains benefited from hill iron ore, while the hills benefited from Ganga-style farming.
The plains benefited because they reached Anga, while the hills benefited because they lay in Gandhāra.
The plains benefited from having sixteen mahājanapadas, while the hills benefited from weaker clan ties.

why.The plains benefited from hill iron ore,: Iron ore in the hills was another reason for mahājanapada growth.
why.The plains benefited because they reache: Gandhāra and Anga mark the wider span of the mahājanapadas, not causes of growth.
why.The plains benefited from having sixteen: The usual number sixteen and the clan-territory link do not explain geographical growth.

activities.explanation: Agriculture grew well in the Ganga plains, helping many mahājanapadas develop there.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between a janapada and a mahājanapada?
activities.answer: A janapada was a territory linked with a clan, and the word meant a place where people had settled down. A mahājanapada was a bigger merged unit made when some early states combined. The most common list names 16 mahājanapadas.
points: A janapada was linked with a clan.
Janapada means a place where people had settled.
A mahājanapada was a bigger merged unit.
Some early states had merged into mahājanapadas.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A rājā of a mahājanapada is deciding how to govern. The janapada has an assembly whose members are mostly elders, and the rājā must decide whether to follow their advice. Some texts say that an assembly could remove an incompetent ruler, although this does not prove that removal was an established law. Vajji and Malla had a different system: their assemblies had more power, and assembly members chose the ruler.
activities.prompt: The rājā wants to follow the expectation for a good ruler. What should he do?
options: Consider the assembly's advice before deciding.
Make the decision alone because the rājā was the final authority.
Ask the assembly to collect the taxes instead.
Treat the elders' status as proof that the ruler had to obey every decision.

why.Make the decision alone because the rājā: Final authority in a monarchy did not remove the expectation of taking advice.
why.Ask the assembly to collect the taxes in: The rājā collected taxes; this task was not assigned to assemblies.
why.Treat the elders' status as proof that t: Being mostly elders did not prove that assembly decisions were legally binding.

activities.explanation: Correct: a good ruler was supposed to take advice from assemblies.

activities.context: A rājā of a mahājanapada is deciding how to govern. The janapada has an assembly whose members are mostly elders, and the rājā must decide whether to follow their advice. Some texts say that an assembly could remove an incompetent ruler, although this does not prove that removal was an established law. Vajji and Malla had a different system: their assemblies had more power, and assembly members chose the ruler.
activities.prompt: A student finds a text saying that an incompetent ruler could be removed by an assembly. What is the safest conclusion for a school report?
options: The source records a claim, but it does not establish a binding legal rule.
Removal was definitely the law in every janapada.
The assembly had greater authority in every mahājanapada.
The ruler had no final authority in any mahājanapada.

why.Removal was definitely the law in every: Some texts mentioned removal, but this did not establish a law for every janapada.
why.The assembly had greater authority in ev: Only Vajji and Malla are identified as having assemblies with more power.
why.The ruler had no final authority in any: In mahājanapada monarchies, the rājā was the final authority.

activities.explanation: Correct: the mention does not prove that removal was an established law.

activities.prompt: Explain why advice from assemblies and removal of an incompetent ruler should be understood as two different ideas.
activities.answer: A good ruler was supposed to take advice from the assembly. Most members were elders. This advice expectation is different from the claim in some texts that an incompetent ruler could be removed. Such mentions do not prove that removal was an established law.
points: Assemblies were part of each janapada's government.
Most assembly members were elders.
Good rulers were expected to take their advice.
Removal was mentioned in some texts but was not proved to be law.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In a growing city of a mahājanapada, a craft worker now uses iron tools because the city needs technology to grow. Iron techniques were perfected centuries earlier, but their spread took centuries. A merchant uses silver punch-marked coins when paying for goods, as trade grows. Each mahājanapada usually issues its own coins. Nearby mahājanapadas may also fight, and iron weapons are lighter and sharper than bronze ones.
activities.prompt: The merchant visits a neighbouring mahājanapada to trade. What should the merchant expect about the coins there?
options: The neighbouring mahājanapada will probably have its own coins.
The merchant can use only the coins from the first mahājanapada.
All mahājanapadas will use exactly the same coin design.
Silver coins will no longer be accepted because each area issues coins.

why.The merchant can use only the coins from: The first mahājanapada's coins might not be the local coins.
why.All mahājanapadas will use exactly the s: Separate coin issues do not mean every area used an identical design.
why.Silver coins will no longer be accepted: Silver coins were the first Indian coins, so metal alone does not remove the local coin system.

activities.explanation: Each mahājanapada usually issued its own coins.

activities.context: In a growing city of a mahājanapada, a craft worker now uses iron tools because the city needs technology to grow. Iron techniques were perfected centuries earlier, but their spread took centuries. A merchant uses silver punch-marked coins when paying for goods, as trade grows. Each mahājanapada usually issues its own coins. Nearby mahājanapadas may also fight, and iron weapons are lighter and sharper than bronze ones.
activities.prompt: If warfare occurs between two neighbouring mahājanapadas, what advantage would iron weapons give their users?
options: They would be easier to carry and able to cut more precisely than bronze weapons.
They would be heavier but sharper than bronze weapons.
They would have the same weight and sharpness as bronze weapons.
They would be lighter but unable to cut as precisely as bronze weapons.

why.They would be heavier but sharper than b: Iron was not described as heavier than bronze.
why.They would have the same weight and shar: Iron weapons were better, not equal to bronze weapons.
why.They would be lighter but unable to cut: Iron weapons were sharper, not less precise, than bronze weapons.

activities.explanation: Iron weapons were lighter and sharper than bronze ones.

activities.context: In a growing city of a mahājanapada, a craft worker now uses iron tools because the city needs technology to grow. Iron techniques were perfected centuries earlier, but their spread took centuries. A merchant uses silver punch-marked coins when paying for goods, as trade grows. Each mahājanapada usually issues its own coins. Nearby mahājanapadas may also fight, and iron weapons are lighter and sharper than bronze ones.
activities.prompt: Why did the merchant need to use silver punch-marked coins while buying goods?
options: Trade was increasing, so a new way of making payment had become necessary.
The merchant wanted weapons that were lighter and sharper than bronze ones.
Iron tools had reached the city and therefore silver coins were compulsory.
Every mahājanapada had issued the same coins for its soldiers.

why.The merchant wanted weapons that were li: Weapon quality is not the reason given for using coins.
why.Iron tools had reached the city and ther: Iron tools and coins were separate developments.
why.Every mahājanapada had issued the same c: Each mahājanapada usually issued separate coins, not one shared system.

activities.explanation: Coins were needed because trade was growing.

activities.prompt: Explain how iron weapons were better than bronze weapons.
activities.answer: Iron weapons were better than bronze weapons because they were lighter and sharper. Their lighter weight made them different from heavier bronze weapons, while their sharper cutting quality gave them another advantage. Therefore, iron offered clear improvements in both weight and sharpness for warfare.
points: Identifies iron weapons as the better choice.
Explains that they were lighter.
Explains that they were sharper.
Connects the improvements to warfare.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A village has occupational jātis linked with the four varṇas described in Vedic texts. An artisan jāti teaches its craft to children, while a farming jāti continues to work in farming. The community regards these inherited skills as the proper way to earn a livelihood. Although the different groups provide services needed by others, some groups receive greater respect or wealth. The village therefore shows how the two-fold varna-jāti system can bring occupational divisions and inequalities.
activities.prompt: An artisan’s child learns the family craft instead of choosing a different occupation. What does this mainly show?
options: The jāti is preserving its occupational livelihood through inherited skill.
The child has entered a varṇa because all village occupations are interchangeable.
The jāti has stopped passing knowledge to the next generation.
The child’s occupation is unrelated to the village’s varna-jāti organisation.

why.The child has entered a varṇa because al: The other choices do not explain the transmission of occupational skill.
why.The jāti has stopped passing knowledge t: The varna-jāti system is relevant because it organises groups by occupation.
why.The child’s occupation is unrelated to t: Inherited skills connect a jāti with its livelihood.

activities.explanation: The child is learning the skill of the jāti’s occupation.

activities.context: A village has occupational jātis linked with the four varṇas described in Vedic texts. An artisan jāti teaches its craft to children, while a farming jāti continues to work in farming. The community regards these inherited skills as the proper way to earn a livelihood. Although the different groups provide services needed by others, some groups receive greater respect or wealth. The village therefore shows how the two-fold varna-jāti system can bring occupational divisions and inequalities.
activities.prompt: After the artisan jāti gains greater respect and wealth, another occupational group loses some benefits. What is the most likely result?
options: The village’s occupational divisions are creating inequality between groups.
The village has achieved complete equality because every group has a duty.
The two-fold system no longer includes occupational communities.
The four varṇas must now be replaced by new occupations.

why.The village has achieved complete equali: Equality is an ideal, not something this case demonstrates.
why.The two-fold system no longer includes o: The case still clearly includes jātis.
why.The four varṇas must now be replaced by: Nothing in the case suggests replacing the varṇas.

activities.explanation: Different outcomes between groups show inequality.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between varṇa and jāti?
activities.answer: Varṇa was the four-part idea that came from Vedic texts and concerned the broad duties of four groups. A jāti was a community connected to a specific occupation and livelihood. The skills of a jāti were passed from generation to generation, so occupation and inherited skill were also closely connected.
points: Varṇa is linked with the four groups in Vedic texts.
Jāti is an occupational community.
Jāti skills pass between generations.
Varṇa and jāti are related but not the same.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Ravi is preparing a school exhibition on cities and trade. The Uttarapatha connected the northwest with the Ganga plains, while the Dakṣhiṇapatha began at Kauśhāmbī and crossed the Vindhya hills to reach far south. Southern cities appeared from about 400 BCE, when the Cholas, Cheras and Pānḍyas emerged. Stones, gold and spices supported wide trade through vibrant coastal ports. The mahājanapadas stopped existing around 300 BCE. By 300 or 200 BCE, almost the entire Subcontinent was one connected land.
activities.prompt: Ravi must show a road leading travellers into the far south. Which route should he select?
options: For the southern journey, use the road beginning at Kauśhāmbī and crossing the Vindhya range to reach the far south.
For the southern journey, use the road joining the northwest directly to the Ganga plains.
For the southern journey, choose a road that stays in Kauśhāmbī and never crosses the Vindhya range.
For the southern journey, use a road that begins on a western coastal port and runs only northward.

why.For the southern journey, use the road j: This describes the northern connection made by the Uttarapatha, not the southern route.
why.For the southern journey, choose a road: This leaves out the Vindhya crossing needed to continue into the far south.
why.For the southern journey, use a road tha: Ports were trade centres, but they were not the stated starting point of this southern road.

activities.explanation: This correctly matches the starting point, hill crossing and southern destination of the Dakṣhiṇapatha.

activities.context: Ravi is preparing a school exhibition on cities and trade. The Uttarapatha connected the northwest with the Ganga plains, while the Dakṣhiṇapatha began at Kauśhāmbī and crossed the Vindhya hills to reach far south. Southern cities appeared from about 400 BCE, when the Cholas, Cheras and Pānḍyas emerged. Stones, gold and spices supported wide trade through vibrant coastal ports. The mahājanapadas stopped existing around 300 BCE. By 300 or 200 BCE, almost the entire Subcontinent was one connected land.
activities.prompt: Which timeline best fits the southern part of Ravi's exhibition?
options: Southern cities and the Chola, Chera and Pānḍya kingdoms emerged around 400 BCE, while the mahājanapadas ended around 300 BCE.
Southern cities appeared around 400 BCE, but the three kingdoms emerged only after 300 BCE, when the mahājanapadas ended.
The three kingdoms emerged around 400 BCE, but southern cities did not appear until around 300 BCE.
Southern cities and all three kingdoms appeared around 400 BCE, and the mahājanapadas continued after 300 BCE.

why.Southern cities appeared around 400 BCE,: This places the kingdoms' emergence after the mahājanapadas had ended.
why.The three kingdoms emerged around 400 BC: This reverses the timing because southern cities appeared from about 400 BCE.
why.Southern cities and all three kingdoms a: This incorrectly suggests that the mahājanapadas continued after they had stopped existing.

activities.explanation: This correctly matches the emergence of southern cities and kingdoms with the disappearance of the mahājanapadas.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: New Beginnings: Cities and States

activities.prompt: What name does the lesson give to the Indus or Harappan civilisation?
options: The Second Urbanisation
Early republics
India's First Urbanisation
The mahājanapadas
activities.explanation: The lesson calls the Indus or Harappan civilisation India's First Urbanisation. The Second Urbanisation came later.

activities.prompt: The Harappan civilisation came apart around the early 2nd millennium BCE.
activities.explanation: The lesson says this happened around the early 2nd millennium BCE.

activities.prompt: People who stayed in the old cities went back to ______ life.
activities.hint: Think of small settlements, not big cities.
activities.explanation: Once the parts of the city had disappeared, people went back to village life.

activities.prompt: Match each word from your book to its meaning.
pairs: a place where people have settled down
a bigger unit made by merging early states
the first Indian coins, made of silver
a community with a set professional occupation
activities.explanation: Each word has its own meaning in the lesson. Learning them helps you follow the story of the cities and states.

activities.prompt: In every mahājanapada, the assembly chose the ruler.
activities.explanation: Some mahājanapadas were monarchies, where the rājā was the final authority. Only some states let the assembly choose the ruler.

activities.prompt: Why were many mahājanapadas in the Ganga plains?
options: Because iron ore was dug from its plains
Because ports were built on its coasts
Because its rivers dried up each year
Because farming grew well in that land
activities.explanation: Farming grew well in the Ganga plains, so many states grew there. Iron ore was found in the hills, not the plains.

activities.prompt: The first Indian coins were made of ______.
activities.hint: It is a shiny metal, and the word starts with S.
activities.explanation: The lesson says the first Indian coins were silver. They are called punch-marked coins.

activities.prompt: What was the major shift in technology in this period?
options: Iron
Bronze
Silver coins
Gold
activities.explanation: Iron was the major technology shift of this time. Iron made lighter and sharper weapons than bronze.

activities.prompt: How did a rājā usually become ruler?
options: By being chosen by the assembly
By paying the most taxes
By being the son of the previous rājā
By winning a war in the south
activities.explanation: A rājā usually became ruler as the son of the previous one. In some states, the assembly chose the ruler instead.

chapters.title: The Rise of Empires
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what is an empire?; building and ruling an empire; trade, trade routes and guilds; the rise of magadha.

lessons.title: What is an Empire?

activities.prompt: How can many separate kingdoms become one great empire?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is an empire?
activities.body: An empire is a large land made of many smaller kingdoms or territories. The word comes from the Latin word imperium, which means supreme power. The emperor rules the whole land from a capital city. Smaller kingdoms in the empire pay tribute to the emperor. They are called tributaries. Tribute can be money, gold, grain, livestock or elephants. Smaller territories still have their own rulers.
keyPoints: An empire is a large land made of many smaller kingdoms or territories.
The emperor rules the whole land from a capital city.
Smaller kingdoms pay tribute to the emperor and are called tributaries.
activities.explanation: Think of an empire as one big land that holds many smaller lands inside it.

activities.prompt: Small kingdoms join under one ruler. Is their land an empire?
steps: The kingdoms form one large land because smaller kingdoms share a ruler.
One capital serves the whole empire because the emperor rules from it.
Their land is an empire because it joins smaller kingdoms under a ruler.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which of these is an empire, according to your book?
options: A small village with one leader
A single city with a busy market
A large land made of many smaller kingdoms
A river that flows through a valley
activities.explanation: An empire is a large land. It is made up of many smaller kingdoms or territories.

activities.prompt: Smaller kingdoms in an empire pay ______ to the emperor.
activities.hint: Think about what smaller kingdoms give the emperor.
activities.explanation: Smaller kingdoms pay tribute. Because of this, they are called tributaries.

activities.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: A smaller kingdom that pays tribute
The city from which the emperor rules
activities.explanation: Imperium comes from Latin. Samrāj is an ancient Sanskrit word for emperor, meaning lord of all.

activities.prompt: Which of these can tribute be, according to your book?
options: Only gold coins and silver cups
Only land and big stone houses
Only paintings and very old books
Money, gold, grain, livestock or elephants
activities.explanation: Your book lists money, gold, grain, livestock and elephants as tribute. The other choices are not on that list.

activities.prompt: Which idea matches what your book says about emperors and wars?
options: Wars have no effect on empires at all
Emperors often grew their empires after fighting wars
Wars always make empires smaller and weaker
Empires never change their size at all
activities.explanation: Your book says emperors often grew their empires after fighting wars against smaller kingdoms.

activities.prompt: Put the stages of an empire's story in order.
activities.explanation: Your book says empires rise, then expand, and then decline.

activities.prompt: War expands an empire. A smaller kingdom joins it. What happens next?
options: Its ruler may stay, but it must send tribute.
Its ruler may stay, but tribute must stop.
Its ruler must leave for the emperor's capital.
Its ruler may become the new emperor.

why.Its ruler may stay, but tribute must sto: This wrongly thinks local rule cancels the duty to pay tribute.
why.Its ruler must leave for the emperor's c: This wrongly thinks the emperor replaces every smaller ruler.
This wrongly makes a tributary the ruler of the whole empire.

activities.explanation: The smaller land can keep its ruler while paying tribute to the emperor.

activities.prompt: A map shows one capital and smaller territories. What might it show?
options: It may show an empire ruled from one capital.
It may show many empires ruled from separate capitals.
It may show a tribute list of smaller kingdoms.
It may show one small kingdom with no other territories.

why.It may show many empires ruled from sepa: The map shows one capital, not a capital for each land.
why.It may show a tribute list of smaller ki: A map of places does not show a list of tribute payments.
why.It may show one small kingdom with no ot: The map shows smaller territories as well as one capital.

activities.explanation: One capital and smaller territories fit the structure of an empire.

activities.prompt: A small kingdom keeps its ruler. It sends grain to the emperor. Why?
options: Its ruler keeps local power while the emperor receives tribute.
Its ruler keeps all power while the emperor receives tribute.
Its ruler loses local power while the emperor receives tribute.
Its ruler keeps local power while the emperor gives tribute.

why.Its ruler keeps all power while the empe: This wrongly gives the smaller ruler power over the whole empire.
why.Its ruler loses local power while the em: This wrongly removes the smaller territory's own ruler.
why.Its ruler keeps local power while the em: This wrongly makes the emperor pay tribute to smaller rulers.

activities.explanation: The smaller ruler can remain while the emperor receives tribute.

activities.prompt: A Latin source says imperium means supreme power. A Sanskrit source says samrāj means lord of all. What can both sources show?
options: Different words can describe the highest power over many lands.
Different words describe the rule of one small kingdom.
Both sources name the same capital city in different ways.
Both sources show that smaller kingdoms paid tribute.

why.Different words describe the rule of one: Supreme power and lord of all do not mean rule of one small kingdom.
why.Both sources name the same capital city: Neither word means the name of a capital city.
why.Both sources show that smaller kingdoms: The word meanings concern rule and power, not payments of tribute.

activities.explanation: Both words point to total rule, which belongs to an emperor.

activities.prompt: An emperor grows his land through war. Smaller rulers keep their posts. Why might this system continue?
options: The emperor gains tribute while smaller rulers keep local power.
The emperor gains all local power while smaller rulers lose their posts.
The emperor gains tribute while smaller rulers control his capital.
The emperor gains land while smaller rulers reject every tribute.

why.The emperor gains all local power while: This wrongly removes the smaller rulers' power and posts.
why.The emperor gains tribute while smaller: This wrongly gives smaller rulers control of the emperor's capital.
why.The emperor gains land while smaller rul: This wrongly says smaller rulers reject the tribute they must pay.

activities.explanation: The emperor receives tribute while smaller rulers keep their own power.

lessons.sceneCaption: A map of the Vijayanagara Empire highlighting its tributary states.

lessons.title: Building and Ruling an Empire

activities.prompt: How did rulers build mighty empires and keep everyone together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is an empire?
activities.body: An empire covers a large area. Many different kinds of people live inside it. These people often speak different languages and follow different customs. Emperors often let regional kings keep ruling their own lands. In return, those kings pay tribute, which means a payment of wealth, and show loyalty. Kings wanted wealth and power for themselves and for the empire.
keyPoints: An empire covers a large area with many kinds of people.
Regional kings often kept ruling in return for tribute and loyalty.
Kings wanted wealth and power for themselves and the empire.
activities.explanation: Tribute is a payment that shows loyalty to a stronger ruler.

activities.prompt: An emperor controls faraway lands, but his army is costly. Should he let regional kings rule?
steps: The emperor wants tributary states controlled, so he needs to keep an army.
Soldiers, horses, and elephants need care, so keeping the army costs a lot.
Regional kings can keep ruling, so the emperor can gain tribute and loyalty.
He should let regional kings rule in return for tribute and loyalty.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Why did emperors often let regional kings keep ruling?
options: They wanted tribute and loyalty to stop.
In return for their tribute and loyalty.
So the kings could leave the empire.
They wanted the kings to stop ruling.
activities.explanation: The kings paid tribute and showed loyalty, so the emperor let them keep their lands. Well done for spotting this!

activities.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: A large area with many kinds of people
A king who keeps ruling part of an empire
activities.explanation: Each word describes a part of how empires worked. Great matching!

activities.prompt: An empire keeps an army to control its ______ states.
activities.hint: These states pay tribute to the empire.
activities.explanation: Tributary states pay tribute, so the empire keeps an army to control them.

activities.prompt: Why did rulers try to control rivers and trade routes?
options: To stop all trade on the rivers.
To give the rivers away to neighbours.
To get resources and tax from them.
To remove every army from the land.
activities.explanation: Rivers and trade routes brought resources and money from tax. Rulers wanted both for their empire.

activities.prompt: A kingdom wanted to become the overlord. What might it do first?
options: Give away all tribute to neighbouring kings.
Stop keeping any army at all.
Wage war on neighbouring territories to conquer them.
Let every neighbour keep its land for free.
activities.explanation: A kingdom might first fight neighbours to win their land. Then it could grow strong enough to become the overlord.

activities.prompt: A kingdom with stronger ______ power and surplus resources became the overlord.
activities.hint: Think about the strength of its soldiers and armies.
activities.explanation: Military power means the strength of an army. A kingdom with strong armies and spare resources could become the overlord.

activities.prompt: A king controls tributary states. Soldiers, horses, and elephants all need care. What happens to the king's money?
options: It falls because keeping the army costs a lot.
It rises because soldiers must give the king tribute.
It stays because only soldiers need regular care.
It grows because horses and elephants need less care.

why.It rises because soldiers must give the: This confuses who pays tribute; tributary states pay the ruler.
why.It stays because only soldiers need regu: This wrongly ignores the care needed by horses and elephants.
why.It grows because horses and elephants ne: No fact says these animals need less care or bring in income.

activities.explanation: An army is costly because soldiers, horses, and elephants all need care.

activities.prompt: An empire covers large areas. People speak different languages and follow different customs. How can the emperor rule them?
options: Let regional kings rule, if they give tribute and loyalty.
Make every language group follow one local custom.
Ask each language group to lead the emperor's army.
Move all language groups to one central town.

why.Make every language group follow one loc: This wrongly assumes one custom should replace all others.
why.Ask each language group to lead the empe: This wrongly treats language groups as army leaders instead of governed peoples.
why.Move all language groups to one central: This wrongly assumes moving people is how an emperor gains control.

activities.explanation: Regional kings can keep ruling while the empire receives tribute and loyalty.

activities.prompt: A map shows two forts. One is on a border beside a trade route. The other is far from both. Which fort helped the ruler more?
options: The border fort, because it controlled an important trade route.
The far fort, because distance makes every place strategic.
The border fort, because routes never bring resources or tax.
The far fort, because borders do not need strong settlements.

why.The far fort, because distance makes eve: The map does not show the far fort as strategic.
why.The border fort, because routes never br: This wrongly says trade routes cannot bring resources or tax.
why.The far fort, because borders do not nee: This wrongly treats borders as unimportant for control.

activities.explanation: Borders were strategic, and trade routes brought resources and tax.

activities.prompt: Two neighboring kingdoms fight. One has stronger military power and extra resources. What may happen next?
options: The stronger kingdom may become the overlord.
The weaker kingdom may become the overlord.
Both kingdoms may stop fighting because wars are free.
The stronger kingdom may lose because resources do not matter.

why.The weaker kingdom may become the overlo: This overlooks the advantage of stronger military power and surplus resources.
why.Both kingdoms may stop fighting because: This wrongly treats war as free, although armies are costly.
why.The stronger kingdom may lose because re: This wrongly ignores that surplus resources help a kingdom conquer.

activities.explanation: With greater military power and surplus resources, a kingdom could become overlord.

activities.prompt: People in one region speak another language and follow another custom. The emperor lets local kings keep ruling. Why would local kings accept?
options: They can keep power while giving the emperor tribute and loyalty.
They can change every local language and custom quickly.
They can stop paying anything because the emperor lives far away.
They can replace the emperor with a stronger local ruler.

why.They can change every local language and: This wrongly assumes rulers can remove language and custom differences by force.
why.They can stop paying anything because th: Distance does not remove the emperor's need for tribute and loyalty.
why.They can replace the emperor with a stro: This wrongly suggests the emperor's authority can simply be replaced.

activities.explanation: Keeping local rule was the benefit; tribute and loyalty were the exchange.

lessons.sceneAlt: A map of the Mughal Empire at its greatest extent shows Rajputana divided into semi-autonomous and fully autonomous regions.
lessons.sceneCaption: Map of the Mughal Empire at its peak, including Rajput regions with varying degrees of autonomy.

lessons.title: Trade, Trade Routes and Guilds

activities.prompt: How did ancient India’s traders connect people, places, and communities?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Trade and Guilds
activities.body: Long ago, traders moved goods across India. Goods like textiles (cloth), spices, gems and animals were traded. Some goods travelled to distant countries by land or sea. Important trade routes existed from about 500 BCE. More trade meant more income for producers, the people who made goods. Guilds were powerful groups of traders, craftsmen, moneylenders and farmers. They shared market information and made their own rules.
keyPoints: Goods like textiles and spices were traded across India.
Guilds were powerful groups that shared information and made their own rules.
A guild had an elected head and executive officers to help.
activities.explanation: Trade helped goods travel far, and guilds helped traders work together.

activities.prompt: A king needs more money and workers for his army. How can more trade help?
steps: Large armies need money, workers and resources.
Growing trade can give producers more income.
More income can also give the ruler more tax.
More trade can therefore help meet the army's needs.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which people could belong to a guild?
options: Only kings, soldiers and royal servants
Traders, craftsmen, moneylenders and farmers
Only children, teachers and school helpers
Only priests, sailors and village headmen
activities.explanation: Your lesson says guilds were groups of traders, craftsmen, moneylenders and farmers.

activities.prompt: Goods like textiles and spices were traded across India.
activities.explanation: Your lesson says traders moved textiles, spices, gems and animals across India.

activities.prompt: Important trade routes existed from about ______ BCE.
activities.hint: It is a three-digit number.
activities.explanation: Your lesson says important trade routes existed from about 500 BCE.

activities.prompt: The king was supposed to make all the rules for guilds.
activities.explanation: Guilds could make their own rules, and the king was not supposed to interfere with them.

activities.prompt: Why did guild traders share market information?
options: So everyone in the guild could benefit
To keep good ideas hidden from members
So that only the head could earn money
To stop members from trading at all
activities.explanation: Traders shared resources and market news so that everyone gained. Working together helped the whole guild.

activities.prompt: What happened when more trade took place?
options: Producers earned less; the ruler got less tax
Producers stopped making goods to sell
The ruler had to pay the traders instead
Producers earned more; the ruler got more tax
activities.explanation: More trade brought more income for producers and more tax for the ruler. Trade helped both sides.

activities.prompt: A kingdom's army needs more money, workers and resources. More trade may help. How?
options: It can bring more income and more tax for the ruler.
It can remove the army's need for workers.
It can stop producers from earning any income.
It can give the army fewer trading routes.

why.It can remove the army's need for worker: This wrongly thinks more trade removes the army's needs.
why.It can stop producers from earning any i: This wrongly thinks more trade takes income away from producers.
why.It can give the army fewer trading route: This wrongly connects more trade with fewer trade routes.

activities.explanation: This is right because more trade brings more income and tax.

activities.prompt: Guild members make a rule for their own group. A king dislikes it. What should happen?
options: The king should not interfere with the guild's rule.
The king should replace it with a different rule.
The guild should cancel all its internal rules.
The king should choose every guild officer himself.

why.The king should replace it with a differ: This wrongly gives the king power over guild rules.
why.The guild should cancel all its internal: This wrongly treats guild rules as harmful rather than useful.
why.The king should choose every guild offic: This wrongly gives the king control over guild leadership.

activities.explanation: This is right because the king should not interfere in guild rules.

activities.prompt: A guild needs a head and executive officers. Two members want the head. What should they follow?
options: The guild's usual process of electing its head.
The king's usual choice of the guild head.
The first member's right to become the head.
The guild's choice to have no guild head.

why.The king's usual choice of the guild hea: This wrongly makes the king responsible for choosing the head.
why.The first member's right to become the h: This wrongly assumes that the first member must become head.
why.The guild's choice to have no guild head: This wrongly believes that guilds did not need heads.

activities.explanation: This is right because a guild head was usually elected.

lessons.title: The Rise of Magadha

activities.prompt: How did Magadha grow so powerful so quickly?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Strong Kingdom Called Magadha
activities.body: Long ago, between the 6th and 4th centuries BCE, north India changed deeply. One strong kingdom was Magadha. It covered modern south Bihar and some nearby areas. Magadha sat in the Ganga plains. These plains had fertile land and many resources. Fertile means good for growing crops. That helped Magadha grow strong. Its kings were powerful and important.
keyPoints: Magadha was a strong kingdom in north India.
It lay in the fertile Ganga plains.
Its land and its kings helped it grow powerful.
activities.explanation: Magadha grew strong because of its good land and its powerful kings.

activities.prompt: A farmer wants to know why Magadha grew stronger. How did its land and iron help?
steps: Magadha's fertile Ganga plains gave farmers land for growing food.
Nearby iron ore was used to make iron ploughs, so farmers grew more food.
The extra food created a surplus, so more people could work on arts and crafts.
Lighter, sharper iron weapons strengthened the army, so Magadha became stronger.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Nanda Dynasty
activities.body: Around the 5th century BCE, Mahāpadma Nanda rose to power in Magadha. He founded the Nanda dynasty. A dynasty is a line of rulers from one family. As the economy grew, he started issuing coins. The economy means how people make, use and trade goods and money. Issuing means making coins and sending them out.
keyPoints: Mahāpadma Nanda rose to power around the 5th century BCE.
He founded the Nanda dynasty.
He started issuing coins as the economy grew.
activities.explanation: The Nanda dynasty grew strong and started making its own coins.

activities.prompt: What kind of land was in the Ganga plains where Magadha lay?
options: Dry land with almost no water
Ice-covered mountain peaks
Fertile land full of resources
Deep, salty sea water
activities.explanation: Your lesson says the plains had fertile land and many resources. Well done!

activities.prompt: Magadha's iron ore came from faraway islands across the sea.
activities.explanation: Your lesson says the iron ore came from nearby hills, not faraway islands.

activities.prompt: Match each thing to what it did for Magadha.
pairs: Let more people focus on arts and crafts
activities.explanation: Iron tools helped farming and the army. Extra grain gave people time for crafts.

activities.prompt: Lighter and sharper iron weapons made Magadha's army stronger.
activities.explanation: Your lesson says lighter, sharper iron weapons made the army stronger. Great thinking!

activities.prompt: Surplus grain let more people focus on arts and ______.
activities.hint: Think of making beautiful things with your hands.
activities.explanation: Surplus means extra. Extra grain let people spend time on arts and crafts.

activities.prompt: Why was the Nanda empire conquered and absorbed into the Maurya empire?
options: Dhana Nanda was kind and fair to people
Dhana Nanda oppressed and exploited his people
Dhana Nanda had no money to rule
Dhana Nanda never ruled Magadha
activities.explanation: Oppressed means treated people very unfairly. Because of this, the Nanda empire was conquered.

activities.prompt: A farmer uses an iron plough and grows more food. What can this extra food help Magadha do?
options: Support more artists and crafts workers.
Make every farmer use an iron weapon.
Move Magadha away from the Ganga plains.
Stop the kingdom from becoming stronger.

This confuses extra food with iron weapons for the army.
More food did not make Magadha leave its fertile plains.
More food helped Magadha grow rather than stop growing.

activities.explanation: This is right because the food surplus let more people focus on arts and crafts.

activities.prompt: Map A shows fertile plains and nearby iron ore. Map B shows poor land and no iron ore. Which map better explains Magadha's growth?
options: Map A, because fertile land and iron ore helped growth.
Map B, because poor land made iron tools stronger.
Map A, because fertile land removed the need for iron.
Map B, because nearby iron ore reduced the food supply.

why.Map B, because poor land made iron tools: This wrongly treats poor land as a cause of Magadha's growth.
why.Map A, because fertile land removed the: This wrongly says fertile land made iron unnecessary.
why.Map B, because nearby iron ore reduced t: This wrongly says iron ore reduced food production.

activities.explanation: This is right because Magadha had fertile land and nearby iron ore.

activities.prompt: Ajātaśhatru helped make Magadha strong. Around the 5th century BCE, Mahāpadma Nanda rose to power. What happened next?
options: He founded the Nanda dynasty and began issuing coins.
He ended the use of coins and left Magadha weaker.
He moved Magadha away from the Ganga plains.
He gave up iron tools because farming had improved.

why.He ended the use of coins and left Magad: This turns coin use backwards, since coins began as the economy grew.
why.He moved Magadha away from the Ganga pla: This wrongly imagines a move away from Magadha's fertile plains.
why.He gave up iron tools because farming ha: This wrongly assumes improved farming made iron tools unnecessary.

activities.explanation: This is right because Mahāpadma Nanda founded the dynasty and began issuing coins.

activities.prompt: A source shows coins appearing while Magadha's economy was growing. What does this suggest?
options: Mahāpadma Nanda issued coins as the economy grew.
Magadha's economy grew because Dhana Nanda oppressed people.
Coins appeared before farmers produced a food surplus.
Coins replaced iron ploughs in Magadha's fields.

why.Magadha's economy grew because Dhana Nan: This confuses later oppression with the earlier growth of the economy.
why.Coins appeared before farmers produced a: This reverses the link between food surplus, growth, and coins.
why.Coins replaced iron ploughs in Magadha's: This confuses coins with tools used for farming.

activities.explanation: This is right because Mahāpadma Nanda issued coins as the economy grew.

activities.prompt: Dhana Nanda is rich but treats his people harshly. People dislike him. What is likely to happen next?
options: The Maurya empire will conquer and absorb the Nanda empire.
The Nanda empire will stay strong because Dhana Nanda is rich.
People will support Dhana Nanda because rich rulers are liked.
His wealth will stop the Maurya empire from becoming stronger.

why.The Nanda empire will stay strong becaus: This mistakes personal wealth for popular support.
why.People will support Dhana Nanda because: This confuses being rich with treating people fairly.
why.His wealth will stop the Maurya empire f: This assumes wealth could prevent a conquest.

activities.explanation: This is right because oppression and exploitation led to the conquest.

activities.prompt: A blacksmith has iron ore from nearby hills. The kingdom needs more food and a stronger army. What should the blacksmith make?
options: Iron ploughs for farmers and lighter, sharper weapons for soldiers.
Iron weapons for farmers and iron ploughs for soldiers.
More iron ploughs for farmers but no weapons for soldiers.
Only weapons for soldiers because farms already had enough.

why.Iron weapons for farmers and iron plough: This swaps the needs of farmers and soldiers.
why.More iron ploughs for farmers but no wea: This forgets that iron weapons also strengthened the army.
why.Only weapons for soldiers because farms: This forgets that iron ploughs helped farmers grow more food.

activities.explanation: This is right because ploughs helped farmers and weapons strengthened the army.
