lessons.title: The Greeks and the Mauryas

activities.prompt: How did Greece and India become connected through kings, battles, and wise advisers?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Alexander and the Mauryas
activities.body: Alexander was a young Greek king from Macedonia. He campaigned against Persia and conquered the Persian Empire. His empire spread over three continents. He brought his campaign to India and defeated Porus. After his death, his empire was divided. Around 321 BCE, Chandragupta Maurya founded the Maurya Empire. A campaign is a military journey. An empire is a large land with many people under one ruler.
keyPoints: Alexander was a young Greek king who conquered the Persian Empire.
After Alexander died, his empire was divided.
Chandragupta Maurya founded the Maurya Empire around 321 BCE.
activities.explanation: Alexander's story and the Maurya Empire are both part of your book's history.

activities.prompt: Alexander’s soldiers are tired and homesick in India. What should Alexander expect?
steps: Alexander’s campaign reached India after fighting Persia.
His soldiers became tired and homesick, so they refused to go farther.
Therefore, Alexander should expect the advance into India to stop.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who was Alexander?
options: An Indian sage who taught in the forests
A Greek historian who lived at a royal court
A young king from Macedonia who campaigned against Persia
A mentor who helped a young Indian ruler
activities.explanation: The lesson says Alexander was a young Greek king from Macedonia who campaigned against Persia.

activities.prompt: Alexander died in Babylon at the age of 32.
activities.explanation: Your book says Alexander died in Babylon when he was 32 years old.

activities.prompt: Match each name to what you learned about them.
activities.explanation: Each name belongs to a different part of the story of Alexander and the Mauryas.

activities.prompt: Why did Alexander's soldiers refuse to go further into India?
options: They were rested and keen to march on
They were tired and homesick
They had already conquered all of India
activities.explanation: Your book says the soldiers were tired and homesick, so they would not go on.

activities.prompt: Megasthenes was a Greek ______ and diplomat who lived at Chandragupta's court.
activities.hint: Someone who writes about the past.
activities.explanation: Your book calls Megasthenes a Greek historian and diplomat.

activities.prompt: Why did Alexander spare all the Indian sages?
options: He was impressed by them
He was angry with them
He was tired and wanted to go home
activities.explanation: The lesson says Alexander was impressed by the sages, so he spared every one of them.

activities.prompt: A young king built one large empire. After he died, local leaders received separate parts. Which past change matches?
options: Alexander’s empire was divided after his death.
Alexander’s soldiers refused to march farther into India.
Alexander met Indian sages and spared them.
Chandragupta founded the Maurya Empire around 321 BCE.

why.Alexander’s soldiers refused to march fa: This is about soldiers refusing to march, not dividing an empire.
why.Alexander met Indian sages and spared th: This is about meeting and sparing sages, not dividing rule.
why.Chandragupta founded the Maurya Empire a: This is about founding an empire, not dividing one after a king’s death.

activities.explanation: This matches the division of Alexander’s empire after his death.

activities.prompt: A map shows Alexander’s conquered lands across three continents. What can the map support?
options: His empire reached far beyond one region.
Every region used the same local government.
Alexander lived in each conquered land.
The empire ended when he entered India.

why.Every region used the same local governm: A map of territory does not show how each region was governed.
The map shows territory, not where Alexander lived.
The map gives no reason to think his empire ended in India.

activities.explanation: Three continents show that his empire covered a wide area.

activities.prompt: Megasthenes lived at Chandragupta’s court and watched its work. What can his account best support?
options: Greek and Mauryan leaders had direct contact.
Every part of India followed Chandragupta’s court.
Megasthenes himself founded the Maurya Empire.
Greek people knew nothing about the Mauryan court.

why.Every part of India followed Chandragupt: One court cannot prove that every part of India obeyed it.
why.Megasthenes himself founded the Maurya E: He was a visitor at the court, not the empire’s founder.
why.Greek people knew nothing about the Maur: His stay shows that Greeks could know about the Mauryan court.

activities.explanation: A Greek diplomat living at the court shows direct contact.

activities.prompt: After Alexander died, his empire was divided among generals and satraps. A satrap received one region. Which rule fits?
options: The satrap governed only his divided region.
The satrap governed every continent alone.
The satrap shared every region equally.
The satrap obeyed only Indian sages.

why.The satrap governed every continent alon: The empire was divided, so one leader did not govern all.
The facts do not say that every region was shared equally.
The rulers were generals and satraps, not Indian sages.

activities.explanation: A divided empire gave each leader a part to govern.

lessons.title: Aśhoka and Life in the Mauryan Period

activities.title: Aśhoka and Life in the Mauryan Period
activities.body:
Aśhoka was a Maurya king and Chandragupta's grandson, who ruled from 268 to 232 BCE.

Aśhoka expanded the empire to cover almost all of the subcontinent.

Aśhoka waged a fierce war at Kalinga, which is modern Odisha.
keyPoints: After seeing the death at Kalinga, Aśhoka chose the path of peace.
Aśhoka sent emissaries to Sri Lanka, Thailand and Central Asia.
activities.explanation: Now try some questions.

activities.prompt: How did Aśhoka’s choices change the way people lived?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.prompt: A king’s empire covers almost the whole subcontinent. How can he keep it together?
steps: His empire now covers almost the whole subcontinent.
A bigger empire is harder to hold together.
He can send orders from place to place by couriers.
This message system can help him hold the empire together.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did Aśhoka choose after seeing the death at Kalinga?
options: The path of peace
The path of hunting
The path of endless war
The path of trade
activities.explanation: Seeing the suffering at Kalinga made Aśhoka choose peace instead of more war.

activities.prompt: Aśhoka was the grandson of Chandragupta.
activities.explanation: Your book says Aśhoka was Chandragupta's grandson, a Maurya king.

activities.prompt: Aśhoka called himself 'Devanampiya Piyadasi', which means Beloved of the ______.
activities.hint: The word starts with G.
activities.explanation: Devanampiya Piyadasi means Beloved of the Gods, so Gods is the missing word.

activities.prompt: Match each word to its meaning or place.
activities.explanation: Each pair links a name from your book to what it means or where it is.

activities.prompt: Why were famines rare in the Mauryan period?
options: Only one crop was grown each year.
Two crops were grown each year.
Couriers ate the extra food.
Animals were hunted for food.
activities.explanation: Two crops each year meant there was usually enough food, so famines were rare.

activities.prompt: A bigger empire is always easier to hold together.
activities.explanation: Your book says a bigger empire is harder to hold together, not easier.

activities.prompt: What is the main problem when an empire grows very big?
options: It becomes easier to rule every village.
It stops needing any messages at all.
It becomes harder to hold together.
It no longer needs any couriers.
activities.explanation: A bigger empire has more land to control, so it is harder to keep it united.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: Aśhoka waged a fierce war at Kalinga.
Aśhoka saw the death caused at Kalinga.
Aśhoka chose the path of peace.
activities.explanation: He saw the death after the war, and only then did he choose peace.

activities.prompt: Aśhoka saw death at Kalinga. What best explains his later peace?
options: He rejected war and cruelty after seeing death.
He wanted more war and hunting after seeing death.
He rejected hunting but wanted more war.
He wanted war but decided to keep hunting.

why.He wanted more war and hunting after see: This mistake thinks death made him seek more suffering.
This mistake understands the animal ban but not his peace.
why.He wanted war but decided to keep huntin: This mistake understands the war but not his animal ban.

activities.explanation: The death at Kalinga led him to choose peace.

activities.prompt: A map shows Aśhoka’s empire covering almost the whole subcontinent. What should the king expect?
options: Keeping this bigger empire together may be hard.
Growing two crops each year may be hard.
Sending emissaries to three lands may be hard.
Using one script for all places may be hard.

This confuses empire size with the yearly crop system.
why.Sending emissaries to three lands may be: This confuses empire size with sending emissaries.
why.Using one script for all places may be h: This confuses empire size with the shared script family.

activities.explanation: A bigger empire is harder to hold together.

activities.context: A visitor arrives at the capital city of a large empire. The emperor rules the whole land from this city. Many smaller kingdoms lie within the empire. Each has its own ruler, but pays tribute to the emperor and is therefore called a tributary. The visitor wonders how territories with their own rulers can belong to one large land. The word imperium is a Latin word meaning supreme power.
activities.prompt: Which description of the smaller kingdoms in the empire is correct?
options: They are tributaries, but each territory still has its own ruler.
They are tributaries, but the emperor has replaced each territory's own ruler.
They are independent lands, because having a ruler prevents them from belonging to an empire.
They are capital cities, because the emperor rules the whole land from each one.

why.They are tributaries, but the emperor ha: Wrong: the emperor does not replace the rulers of smaller territories.
why.They are independent lands, because havi: Wrong: territories with their own rulers can still belong to an empire.
why.They are capital cities, because the emp: Wrong: the emperor rules the whole land from one capital city.

activities.explanation: Correct: paying tribute makes each smaller kingdom a tributary.

activities.context: A visitor arrives at the capital city of a large empire. The emperor rules the whole land from this city. Many smaller kingdoms lie within the empire. Each has its own ruler, but pays tribute to the emperor and is therefore called a tributary. The visitor wonders how territories with their own rulers can belong to one large land. The word imperium is a Latin word meaning supreme power.
activities.prompt: A ruler in a tributary territory asks why he must pay tribute while still keeping his own ruler. Which response best explains the case?
options: The emperor holds supreme power over the whole empire, while the territory remains ruled by its own ruler.
The word imperium gives each smaller territory supreme power over the emperor.
A territory cannot remain a tributary once it has its own ruler.
Tribute is payment only for changing the capital city of the empire.

why.The word imperium gives each smaller ter: Wrong: imperium supports the emperor's authority over the empire.
why.A territory cannot remain a tributary on: Wrong: a tributary territory can have its own ruler.
why.Tribute is payment only for changing the: Wrong: tribute does not change where the emperor rules from.

activities.explanation: Correct: imperium means supreme power, and smaller territories may keep their own rulers.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between an empire and a tributary.
activities.answer: An empire is a large land containing many smaller kingdoms or territories. A tributary is a smaller kingdom that pays tribute to the emperor. It is one part of the empire, but it may keep its own ruler. Having its own ruler does not make a territory separate from the empire.
points: An empire is a large land made up of smaller kingdoms or territories.
A tributary is a smaller kingdom that pays tribute to the emperor.
A territory can be a tributary and still have its own ruler.
Having a ruler does not mean a territory lies outside the empire.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A kingdom with strong military power and surplus resources attacked nearby lands and became their overlord. The king allowed regional kings to keep ruling, receiving tribute and loyalty in return. He kept an army to control these tributary states and built a fortified settlement on the border. He also guarded a river and a trade route so that the kingdom could obtain resources and collect tax. However, caring for the army’s soldiers, horses and elephants used much money.
activities.prompt: After conquering the nearby lands, what should the king do to strengthen the overlord’s power?
options: Keep the conquered king as a local ruler, provided the overlord receives payment and allegiance.
Remove the local king and let the overlord rule every settlement directly.
Keep the local king but ask for neither payment nor allegiance.
Use all tribute to replace the army with fortified settlements alone.

why.Remove the local king and let the overlo: It follows the practice of keeping regional rulers in place.
why.Keep the local king but ask for neither: Removing payment and allegiance weakens the arrangement.
why.Use all tribute to replace the army with: Fortified settlements cannot fully replace the army.

activities.explanation: This arrangement gives the overlord payment and allegiance.

activities.context: A kingdom with strong military power and surplus resources attacked nearby lands and became their overlord. The king allowed regional kings to keep ruling, receiving tribute and loyalty in return. He kept an army to control these tributary states and built a fortified settlement on the border. He also guarded a river and a trade route so that the kingdom could obtain resources and collect tax. However, caring for the army’s soldiers, horses and elephants used much money.
activities.prompt: What should the king do to increase the empire’s resources and tax?
options: Control the river and trade route.
Let the regional kings keep all the taxes from the trade route.
Close the river and trade route to keep resources inside.
Leave the routes uncontrolled and use all surplus resources for the army.

why.Let the regional kings keep all the taxe: Keeping trade-route taxes from regional kings reduces the empire’s wealth.
why.Close the river and trade route to keep: Closing the routes would prevent trade and tax income.
why.Leave the routes uncontrolled and use al: Ignoring the routes misses a way to gain resources and tax.

activities.explanation: Controlling these routes helps the kingdom obtain resources.

activities.prompt: Explain why an emperor might allow regional kings to continue ruling after conquering nearby territories.
activities.answer: Allowing regional kings to continue ruling lets the emperor keep control through tribute and loyalty instead of ruling every area directly. This helps the empire gain wealth and power while regional rulers remain in place.
points: Regional kings continue ruling their areas
The emperor receives tribute and loyalty
The arrangement helps the emperor maintain control
The empire gains wealth and power
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A guild of traders and craftsmen prepared to send Indian goods to markets by land and sea. Members planned to pool resources and exchange market information before using routes such as Uttarapatha and Dakṣhiṇapatha. The guild had an elected head and executive officers. It followed internal rules that the king was not supposed to change. One trader wondered whether the ruler should make trading decisions. Another worried that the guild should stop sharing information even though it helped everyone.
activities.prompt: Before sending goods to distant countries, what should a guild member do to follow guild practice?
options: Pool supplies and exchange market news with other members
Keep all supplies private and withhold market news
Ask the king to control every trading decision
Let one member make all decisions without being elected

why.Keep all supplies private and withhold m: Keeping resources and news private denies shared benefits.
why.Ask the king to control every trading de: The king was not supposed to interfere in guild affairs.
why.Let one member make all decisions withou: Decisions were guided by an elected head and officers.

activities.explanation: Sharing resources and information follows guild practice.

activities.context: A guild of traders and craftsmen prepared to send Indian goods to markets by land and sea. Members planned to pool resources and exchange market information before using routes such as Uttarapatha and Dakṣhiṇapatha. The guild had an elected head and executive officers. It followed internal rules that the king was not supposed to change. One trader wondered whether the ruler should make trading decisions. Another worried that the guild should stop sharing information even though it helped everyone.
activities.prompt: If more trade brought producers more income, what would likely happen to the ruler's tax income?
options: The tax income would increase
The tax income would decrease
The tax income would remain unchanged
The tax income would be collected only from the guild head

why.The tax income would decrease: A decrease would not follow increased trade.
why.The tax income would remain unchanged: Increased trade changed the amount of tax income.
why.The tax income would be collected only f: Tax income was connected to trade, not only to the guild head.

activities.explanation: More trade meant more tax for the ruler.

activities.prompt: Explain how sharing resources and market information helped guild members.
activities.answer: Guild members shared resources and market information so that everyone in the association could benefit. Resources helped members carry out their work, while market information helped them plan their trading. Sharing both followed the guild's cooperative purpose and supported traders, craftsmen, moneylenders and farmers together.
points: Resources were shared among members.
Market information was exchanged.
The sharing benefited the whole guild.
Different guild members worked together.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: King Ajātaśhatru, one of Magadha’s powerful early kings, used the kingdom’s location in the fertile Ganga plains and nearby iron ore to strengthen it. Iron ploughs helped farmers produce more food, while sharper weapons strengthened the army. Surplus grain freed some people to practise arts and crafts. Later, Mahāpadma Nanda founded the Nanda dynasty and began issuing coins as the economy grew. Dhana Nanda’s wealth and cruel rule eventually led to the empire’s conquest.
activities.prompt: Suppose farmers in Magadha could no longer obtain iron ore from the nearby hills. What would most likely happen?
options: Food production and weapon-making would both decline, slowing Magadha’s growth.
Farmers would grow more food because the fertile plains would work better without iron.
The army and farming would remain strong because the Ganga plains alone were sufficient.
Surplus grain and arts would increase because fewer iron weapons would be needed.

why.Farmers would grow more food because the: Iron was also needed for stronger weapons.
why.The army and farming would remain strong: Without iron, both farming and military strength would be affected.
why.Surplus grain and arts would increase be: Fertile land alone could not remove the importance of iron.

activities.explanation: Iron ploughs helped farmers grow more food.

activities.context: King Ajātaśhatru, one of Magadha’s powerful early kings, used the kingdom’s location in the fertile Ganga plains and nearby iron ore to strengthen it. Iron ploughs helped farmers produce more food, while sharper weapons strengthened the army. Surplus grain freed some people to practise arts and crafts. Later, Mahāpadma Nanda founded the Nanda dynasty and began issuing coins as the economy grew. Dhana Nanda’s wealth and cruel rule eventually led to the empire’s conquest.
activities.prompt: Dhana Nanda is very rich, but his oppression and exploitation have made him unpopular. What should he do to reduce the danger that the Nanda empire will be conquered?
options: Stop oppressing and exploiting the people.
Increase the oppression so that he can become even richer.
Use all the surplus grain to produce more iron ploughs.
Issue more coins while continuing to exploit the people.

why.Increase the oppression so that he can b: His oppression helped create the conditions for conquest.
why.Use all the surplus grain to produce mor: A ruler should avoid mistreating the people.
why.Issue more coins while continuing to exp: Wealth alone did not protect Dhana Nanda’s empire.

activities.explanation: His exploitation made him unpopular among the people.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between the contributions of King Ajātaśhatru and Mahāpadma Nanda to Magadha.
activities.answer: Ajātaśhatru was an early king who helped make Magadha strong by using its fertile plains, iron ore, iron ploughs, and weapons. Mahāpadma Nanda came later and founded the Nanda dynasty. He also began issuing coins as Magadha’s economy grew.
points: Ajātaśhatru was a powerful early king.
He helped strengthen Magadha.
Mahāpadma Nanda founded the Nanda dynasty.
He began issuing coins as the economy grew.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A group of classmates is preparing a class debate about the Greek and Mauryan worlds. They learn that Alexander conquered Persia and defeated Porus in Punjab, but his tired, homesick soldiers refused to go farther into India. They also learn that Alexander's death led generals and satraps to divide his empire. The debate then turns to Chandragupta Maurya, who founded the Maurya Empire with Kauṭilya's help, and Megasthenes, who lived at his court.
activities.prompt: If Alexander's soldiers had not been tired and homesick, what should the classmates predict about his campaign in India?
options: The advance would probably have continued beyond Punjab.
The advance would probably have stopped after the battle with Porus.
The army would probably have moved back toward Macedonia.
The campaign would probably have shifted back to Persia.

why.The advance would probably have stopped: A battle with Porus did not completely end the campaign.
why.The army would probably have moved back: The soldiers were unwilling to travel farther from home.
why.The campaign would probably have shifted: Persia had already been conquered, so the campaign was no longer directed there.

activities.explanation: The soldiers' refusal was what prevented the advance from continuing.

activities.context: A group of classmates is preparing a class debate about the Greek and Mauryan worlds. They learn that Alexander conquered Persia and defeated Porus in Punjab, but his tired, homesick soldiers refused to go farther into India. They also learn that Alexander's death led generals and satraps to divide his empire. The debate then turns to Chandragupta Maurya, who founded the Maurya Empire with Kauṭilya's help, and Megasthenes, who lived at his court.
activities.prompt: The classmates want a sentence that correctly identifies Megasthenes's connection to the Mauryan Empire. Which sentence should they use?
options: He was a Greek historian and diplomat who lived at Chandragupta's court.
He was a Greek general who led Alexander's army into India.
He was an adviser to Porus during the battle in Punjab.
He was a Mauryan general who served under Chandragupta.

why.He was a Greek general who led Alexander: Alexander's army was commanded by Alexander, not Megasthenes.
why.He was an adviser to Porus during the ba: Megasthenes lived at Chandragupta's court, not with Porus.
why.He was a Mauryan general who served unde: Megasthenes was Greek rather than a Mauryan general.

activities.explanation: Megasthenes was a Greek historian and diplomat at Chandragupta's court.

activities.prompt: How did Alexander's experience in India differ from Chandragupta Maurya's role in the Maurya Empire?
activities.answer: Alexander brought his campaign to India, defeated Porus in Punjab, met Gymnosophists, and spared them. His soldiers then stopped because they were tired and homesick. Chandragupta Maurya founded the Maurya Empire around 321 BCE with Kauṭilya's help, while Megasthenes lived at his court.
points: Alexander campaigned in India and defeated Porus.
He met Gymnosophists and spared them.
His soldiers refused to continue because they were tired and homesick.
Chandragupta founded the Maurya Empire with Kauṭilya's help.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between the work of emissaries and couriers in Aśhoka's time?
activities.answer: Emissaries were people Aśhoka sent to Sri Lanka, Thailand and Central Asia. Couriers carried messages from place to place. Thus, emissaries helped Aśhoka make contact beyond his realm, while couriers helped communication reach different parts of the empire. One role concerned other lands; the other concerned carrying messages within the empire.
points: Emissaries were sent to Sri Lanka, Thailand and Central Asia.
Couriers carried messages from place to place.
Emissaries helped make contact beyond the empire.
Couriers helped communication within the empire.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: The Rise of Empires

activities.prompt: What is an empire?
options: A small kingdom with one ruler and no neighbours
A city where traders sell goods in a market
A large land made up of many smaller kingdoms or territories
A group of guilds that make their own rules
activities.explanation: An empire is a large land with many smaller kingdoms or territories inside it. The word imperium means supreme power.

activities.prompt: Smaller territories in an empire always lose their own rulers.
activities.explanation: Smaller territories still had their own rulers, even inside an empire. Read that part of your book again to check.

activities.prompt: Smaller kingdoms in an empire paid ______ to the emperor.
activities.hint: Money, gold or grain given to a ruler.
activities.explanation: Smaller kingdoms paid tribute and were called tributaries. Tribute could be money, gold, grain, livestock or elephants.

activities.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: a smaller kingdom that pays tribute to the emperor
a powerful group of traders, craftsmen, moneylenders and farmers
activities.explanation: Imperium means supreme power, and samrāj means lord of all. A guild was a powerful group that shared resources and market information.

activities.prompt: Why did an empire keep an army?
options: To make the guilds follow the king's rules
To control its tributary states
To ban hunting and cruelty to animals
To build the emperor's capital city
activities.explanation: An army helps an empire control the smaller kingdoms that pay it tribute. Guilds were meant to make their own internal rules.

activities.prompt: Keeping an army costs a lot, because soldiers, horses and elephants need care.
activities.explanation: Soldiers, horses and elephants all need care, so an army is expensive to keep. Well done for thinking about why.

activities.prompt: Megasthenes, a Greek historian and diplomat, lived at Chandragupta's ______.
activities.hint: The royal place where a king lives and rules.
activities.explanation: Megasthenes was a Greek historian and diplomat. He lived at Chandragupta's court.

activities.prompt: Put these events from the Nanda story in the order they happened.
items: Mahāpadma Nanda rose to power in Magadha.
He started issuing coins as the economy grew.
The Nanda empire was absorbed into the Maurya empire.
activities.explanation: The Nanda king rose to power first, then began issuing coins. Much later, the Nanda empire was absorbed into the Maurya empire.

activities.prompt: Why was the Nanda empire conquered and absorbed into the Maurya empire?
options: Dhana Nanda oppressed and exploited his people
Dhana Nanda was loved by all his people
Dhana Nanda was poor and had no coins
activities.explanation: Dhana Nanda was rich, but he was unpopular because he oppressed his people. Because of this, the Nanda empire was conquered.

activities.prompt: What made the army of Magadha stronger?
options: Heavy weapons that were slow to use
Lighter and sharper iron weapons
Weapons made from gold coins
activities.explanation: Lighter and sharper iron weapons made Magadha's army stronger. Iron ore from nearby hills helped the kingdom grow.

boss.sceneCaption: A map of the Vijayanagara Empire highlighting its tributary states.

chapters.title: The Age of Reorganisation
chapters.summary: In this chapter: the break-up of the maurya empire; the surge of the śhungas; the sātavāhanas; the chedis and kingdoms in the south.

lessons.title: The Break-up of the Maurya Empire

activities.prompt: Why did one mighty empire split into so many kingdoms, and what happened next?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: After the Maurya Empire
activities.body: The large Maurya empire broke up into many pieces. Many new kingdoms appeared across this large land. Some scholars call this time the age of reorganisation. Reorganisation means arranging things in a new way. Old regions were turned into new kingdoms, so the map of India changed a lot.
keyPoints: The Maurya empire broke up into many pieces.
Many new kingdoms appeared across the land.
The age of reorganisation means old regions became new kingdoms.
activities.explanation: Once one big empire split apart, many smaller kingdoms took its place.

activities.prompt: Two neighbouring kingdoms want the same border area. How might each king gain control?
steps: The border area matters because controlling it helps a kingdom stay safe.
One king may use a marriage alliance to gain control peacefully.
Another king may use force because kings also gained control that way.
Both methods are possible, but gaining the border helps keep the kingdom safe.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What happened to the Maurya empire, according to your book?
options: It grew bigger and stronger every year.
It stayed as one single empire forever.
It broke up into many pieces.
It joined together with a far-away land.
activities.explanation: Your book says the empire broke up into many pieces. The other choices do not match what happened.

activities.prompt: The break-up of the empire happened barely fifty years after Aśhoka.
activities.explanation: Your book says the break-up came barely fifty years after Aśhoka. That was a very short time.

activities.prompt: The north-west became strong, so outsiders could not invade it.
activities.explanation: Your book says the north-west became weak. A weak area was easier for outsiders to invade.

activities.prompt: Why was control over border areas important for a kingdom?
options: It made the kingdom easy for outsiders to invade.
It helped keep the kingdom safe.
It ended every competition between kingdoms.
It stopped art and literature from growing.
activities.explanation: Your book says control over border areas was important to keep a kingdom safe. The other choices go against what your book says.

activities.prompt: What might happen if the north-west became weak?
options: Outsiders could invade it more easily.
The north-west would become safer.
Outsiders would leave the land at once.
The map would stop changing.
activities.explanation: A weak north-west was open to invasion, as your book says. The other choices do not follow from a weak border.

activities.prompt: Along with politics, what else grew in this age?
options: Only the kings' palaces were built.
Literature stopped completely.
No new kingdoms appeared.
Art, architecture and literature also grew.
activities.explanation: Your book says art, architecture and literature also grew in this time. Many new kingdoms did appear, so the other choices are wrong.

activities.prompt: The north-west became weak when the Maurya Empire broke up. What could outsiders do next?
options: Invade the area because weakness gave them a chance.
Stay away because weak areas had strong defenders.
Make the north-west strong because it stayed whole.
Keep the same map because outsiders could not enter.

why.Stay away because weak areas had strong: This mistake treats weakness as strong defence.
why.Make the north-west strong because it st: This mistake assumes weakness can make an area strong.
why.Keep the same map because outsiders coul: This mistake assumes outsiders could not enter weak areas.

activities.explanation: This is right because weakness allowed outsiders to invade.

activities.prompt: One map shows the Maurya Empire. A later map shows many kingdoms. What does the change tell us?
options: The empire broke apart and new kingdoms appeared.
The empire stayed whole but moved farther north.
New kingdoms appeared but the empire still ruled them.
The map changed because art and literature grew.

why.The empire stayed whole but moved farthe: This mistake thinks a changed map means the empire moved.
why.New kingdoms appeared but the empire sti: This mistake thinks the old empire still ruled the new kingdoms.
why.The map changed because art and literatu: This mistake links map changes to cultural growth.

activities.explanation: This is right because the empire broke into new kingdoms.

activities.prompt: Control over border areas helps keep a kingdom safe. Which place should a king protect first?
options: The border area, because attacks may come through it.
The royal palace, because all attacks start there.
The art centre, because buildings can fight attackers.
The centre, because outsiders always begin inside.

why.The royal palace, because all attacks st: This mistake assumes every attack begins at the palace.
why.The art centre, because buildings can fi: This mistake thinks buildings can fight away attackers.
why.The centre, because outsiders always beg: This mistake thinks outsiders begin inside instead of at borders.

activities.explanation: This is right because border control helps keep a kingdom safe.

activities.prompt: Two new kingdoms compete for the same land. One king makes a marriage alliance. Why might he choose this?
options: Marriage alliances can gain control without using force.
Marriage alliances always end every fight between kingdoms.
A marriage alliance makes border control unimportant.
A marriage alliance forces the other king to leave.

why.Marriage alliances always end every figh: This mistake assumes an alliance always ends every fight.
why.A marriage alliance makes border control: This mistake assumes an alliance removes the need for borders.
why.A marriage alliance forces the other kin: This mistake assumes marriage always forces another king to leave.

activities.explanation: This is right because kings gained control through marriage alliances.

activities.prompt: New kingdoms appeared across the subcontinent in this age. What can a study of art, buildings and books show?
options: Art, architecture and literature also grew in this age.
Only new kingdoms appeared, while all culture stayed still.
Art and literature grew, but architecture did not change.
Culture grew only after every kingdom became one.

why.Only new kingdoms appeared, while all cu: This mistake thinks culture stayed still during political change.
why.Art and literature grew, but architectur: This mistake leaves architecture out of the cultural growth.
why.Culture grew only after every kingdom be: This mistake wrongly links cultural growth to one united kingdom.

activities.explanation: This is right because art, architecture and literature also grew.

lessons.title: The Surge of the Śhungas

activities.prompt: Why did one ruler's rule bring back ancient rituals and encourage new art?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Śhunga Dynasty
activities.body: A dynasty is a family of rulers who govern a land for a long time. Puṣhyamitra Śhunga founded the Śhunga dynasty. Its rulers controlled parts of north and central India. Puṣhyamitra's empire was smaller than the Maurya empire. He kept it safe from possible invaders. Vedic rituals came back, and Sanskrit became a favourite language. The Śhungas also supported literature, art and architecture.
keyPoints: Puṣhyamitra Śhunga founded the Śhunga dynasty.
The Śhungas ruled parts of north and central India.
Vedic rituals were revived, and the Śhungas supported literature, art and architecture.
activities.explanation: Your book describes how the Śhungas ruled, protected their empire and supported learning.

activities.prompt: A king wants to be the most powerful ruler and fears invaders. What should he do?
steps: He should perform a Vedic ritual because Puṣhyamitra used one to gain power.
He should protect the empire because Puṣhyamitra kept it safe from possible invaders.
After early fighting, he can become friendly with the Greeks because Puṣhyamitra did this.
His plan is to gain power, protect the empire, and build friendly ties.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who founded the Śhunga dynasty?
options: Patañjali
The Greeks
Puṣhyamitra Śhunga
Sanskrit
activities.explanation: Puṣhyamitra Śhunga founded the dynasty. Patañjali compiled the Yoga Sūtras instead.

activities.prompt: Match each name or word with its meaning in the lesson.
pairs: A favourite language for philosophy and literature
activities.explanation: Each name or word matches one clear idea in your book. Read each pair slowly.

activities.prompt: The Śhunga dynasty ruled parts of north and central India.
activities.explanation: Your book says the Śhunga rulers controlled parts of north and central India.

activities.prompt: Sanskrit became a favourite language for philosophy and ______.
activities.hint: It is about books, poems and stories.
activities.explanation: Your book says Sanskrit was a favourite for philosophy and literature.

activities.prompt: Why did Puṣhyamitra keep his empire safe?
options: He wanted to make it bigger than the Maurya empire.
He wanted to protect it from possible invaders.
He wanted to stop all other schools of thought.
He wanted to end the Vedic rituals.
activities.explanation: He kept the empire safe from possible invaders. The other choices go against what your book says.

activities.prompt: What happened after the early fighting between Puṣhyamitra and the Greeks?
options: He stayed at war with the Greeks.
He gave his whole empire to the Greeks.
He became friendly with the Greeks.
He forgot the Greeks ever existed.
activities.explanation: After some early fighting, he became friendly with the Greeks. Friendship came after the fighting, not the war.

activities.prompt: A map marks north and central India. What history fact fits?
options: Puṣhyamitra founded the Śhunga dynasty ruling these areas.
Patañjali founded the Śhunga dynasty ruling these areas.
Sanskrit founded the Śhunga dynasty ruling these areas.
Puṣhyamitra's Śhunga dynasty ruled every part of India.

why.Patañjali founded the Śhunga dynasty rul: This wrongly treats Patañjali, who compiled the Yoga Sūtras, as a founder.
why.Sanskrit founded the Śhunga dynasty ruli: This wrongly treats Sanskrit, which was a language, as a founder.
why.Puṣhyamitra's Śhunga dynasty ruled every: This wrongly changes the words 'parts' into 'every part'.

activities.explanation: This is right because Puṣhyamitra founded the Śhunga dynasty.

activities.prompt: After fighting with Greeks, what should a king do next?
options: Become friendly with the Greeks and keep the empire safe.
Keep fighting the Greeks and keep the empire safe.
Become friendly with the Greeks and trust the empire's size.
Perform a Vedic ritual and trust the empire's size.

why.Keep fighting the Greeks and keep the em: This wrongly assumes that continued fighting was his chosen path.
why.Become friendly with the Greeks and trus: This wrongly treats empire size as a replacement for real protection.
why.Perform a Vedic ritual and trust the emp: This wrongly treats a ritual and empire size as protection from invaders.

activities.explanation: This is right because Puṣhyamitra became friendly and kept his empire safe.

activities.prompt: A map shows Śhunga and Maurya; Śhunga art appears. What is true?
options: The Śhunga empire was smaller, and the Śhungas supported art.
The Śhunga empire was larger, and the Śhungas supported art.
The Śhunga empire was smaller, but the Śhungas rejected art.
The Śhunga empire was equal in size, and the Śhungas supported art.

why.The Śhunga empire was larger, and the Śh: This wrongly reverses the size shown by the two empires.
why.The Śhunga empire was smaller, but the Ś: This wrongly reverses the Śhungas' support for art.
why.The Śhunga empire was equal in size, and: This wrongly claims that the two empires had equal sizes.

activities.explanation: This is right because the Śhunga empire was smaller and the dynasty supported art.

lessons.title: The Sātavāhanas

activities.prompt: Who ruled the Deccan long ago, and how did they grow so rich?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Sātavāhana kingdom
activities.body: The Sātavāhanas ruled large parts of the Deccan, which is a wide area of land, from the 2nd century BCE onward. Their empire mostly covered today's Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Maharashtra. Their famous capitals were Amrāvatī and Pratiṣhṭhāna, also called Paithan. Many of their coins show ships, so sea trade mattered to them. Their trade networks even reached the Roman Empire.
keyPoints: They ruled large parts of the Deccan from the 2nd century BCE onward.
Their empire mostly covered today's Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Maharashtra.
Sea trade was so important that ships appear on their coins.
activities.explanation: Knowing where and when they ruled helps you remember their story.

activities.prompt: A coin shows a ship. Why did the Sātavāhanas earn money?
steps: Many coins show ships, so sea trade mattered to the Sātavāhanas.
Their trade reached the Roman Empire, so trade did not stay nearby.
The kingdom earned tolls and taxes, so trade could bring it money.
Therefore, trade and its taxes helped the kingdom earn money.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which of these was one of the Sātavāhanas' most famous capitals?
options: Gautamī Balaśhrī
Indra
Amrāvatī
Sūrya
activities.explanation: Amrāvatī was one of their most famous capitals. Indra and Sūrya are Vedic gods, and Gautamī Balaśhrī was a queen.

activities.prompt: Match each clue to the right answer.
activities.explanation: Ships on coins, trade with Rome and money from tolls all show that trade was big for them.

activities.prompt: The Sātavāhanas started ruling parts of the Deccan in the 2nd century CE.
activities.explanation: Your book says they ruled from the 2nd century BCE onward, not CE.

activities.prompt: The Sātavāhanas were very devoted followers of ______.
activities.hint: Look at the part of your book about their religion.
activities.explanation: Your book says they were devout followers of Vāsudeva, so they were very faithful to him.

activities.prompt: Which queen gave land to Buddhist monks?
options: Indra
Sūrya
Chandra
Gautamī Balaśhrī
activities.explanation: Your book says the powerful queen Gautamī Balaśhrī gave land to Buddhist monks. The other names are Vedic gods.

activities.prompt: Why did wealth and peace matter for art and writing?
options: Wealth and peace stopped culture from growing.
Wealth and peace helped literature, art and culture grow.
Art only grew when the kingdom was at war.
Wealth had no effect on art or writing.
activities.explanation: Your book says wealth and peace helped literature, art and culture grow. Well done for thinking it through!

activities.prompt: Many Sātavāhana coins show ships. What can a child learn from this?
options: Sea trade mattered to them.
Land trade mattered most.
They did not value ships.
They only traded nearby.

This wrongly ranks land trade without enough evidence.
This mistakes showing ships for disliking them.
This ignores trade reaching the Roman Empire.

activities.explanation: This is right because many coins show ships.

activities.prompt: Sātavāhana trade reached the Roman Empire. What can we say about their trading links?
options: They connected places across great distances.
They stayed inside only one Deccan city.
They reached no place outside the Deccan.
They traded only with Buddhist communities.

This mistakes one capital for the whole trading area.
why.They reached no place outside the Deccan: This ignores the trade links reaching Rome.
why.They traded only with Buddhist communiti: This confuses religion with the reach of trade.

activities.explanation: This is right because their trade reached the Roman Empire.

activities.prompt: The map covers today's Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Maharashtra. What does it show?
options: The Sātavāhana empire's area.
The main Sātavāhana trade routes.
The places where Buddhist monks lived.
The gods named in Sātavāhana inscriptions.

This confuses the covered area with trade routes.
This confuses the empire's area with monks' homes.
why.The gods named in Sātavāhana inscription: This confuses the empire's area with religious names.

activities.explanation: This is right because these places mostly formed the empire's area.

activities.prompt: Within the Sātavāhana kingdom, Buddhist monks received land. A widowed queen performed Vedic rituals. What does this show?
options: Only Buddhist practices existed there.
No religious practices existed there.
Only Vedic practices existed there.
Different religious practices existed there.

This ignores the Vedic rituals performed by the widowed queen.
This ignores both Buddhist land grants and Vedic rituals.
This ignores the Buddhist monks who received land.

activities.explanation: This is right because Buddhist and Vedic practices both appear.

lessons.sceneCaption: This intricately carved Amravati Stupa casing reflects the Buddhist art flourishing during the Sātavāhana period.

lessons.title: The Chedis and Kingdoms in the South

activities.prompt: Who ruled the south of India long ago, and how did they grow so strong?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Three Kingdoms of the South
activities.body: Three powerful kingdoms rose in the south of India: the Cheras, Cholas and Pānḍyas. Their rise happened between the 2nd or 3rd century BCE and the 3rd century CE. They stayed independent, even when Mauryan power was at its height. The Cholas ruled parts of south India from the 3rd century BCE to the 13th century CE. The Cheras traded widely with the Roman Empire and West Asia.
keyPoints: The Cheras, Cholas and Pānḍyas were three powerful southern kingdoms.
They stayed independent, even when Mauryan power was at its height.
The Cheras traded widely with the Roman Empire and West Asia.
activities.explanation: Remember the three names: Cheras, Cholas and Pānḍyas.

activities.prompt: How could Chola rulers protect their kingdom and help farmers in the Kāveri delta?
steps: Karikāla beat a joint force of Cheras and Pānḍyas, because the Cholas defended their power.
The Grand Anicut diverted Kāveri water to delta farmland, because farmers needed water for their fields.
So the Cholas could defend their kingdom and support farming in the Kāveri delta.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which people traded widely with the Roman Empire and West Asia?
options: The Chedi kings
The Jain monks
The Cheras
The Mauryas
activities.explanation: Your book says the Cheras traded widely with the Roman Empire and West Asia. Look back at that line.

activities.prompt: The Cholas ruled parts of south India from the 3rd century BCE to the 13th century CE.
activities.explanation: Your book gives these dates for the Cholas. Dates like these show how long a kingdom ruled.

activities.prompt: Match each name to what your book says about it.
pairs: Ruled western parts of Tamil Nadu and Kerala
Beat a joint force of the Cheras and Pānḍyas
activities.explanation: Each name has its own place or story in your book. Read each line again if you need to.

activities.prompt: The Chola king Karikāla beat a joint force of the Cheras and ______.
activities.hint: Think of the third crowned kingdom in your book.
activities.explanation: Your book says the Cheras and Pānḍyas joined forces against Karikāla. He still beat them.

activities.prompt: What did the Grand Anicut do for the farmers in the delta?
options: It took water away from the farmland in the delta.
It sent water from the Kāveri to farmland in the delta.
It stopped the Kāveri from flowing into the delta.
It moved the farmland up into the hills.
activities.explanation: Your book says the Grand Anicut diverted water from the Kāveri to farmland. Diverted means turned away to another place.

activities.prompt: What might happen if the Grand Anicut did not divert water from the Kāveri?
options: The Cheras would stop trading with the Roman Empire.
The Kāveri would carry more water to the farmland.
The Jain monks would move into the delta fields.
Farmland in the delta would get less water from the Kāveri.
activities.explanation: The Grand Anicut sent water to the farmland. Without it, the farmland would get less water.

activities.prompt: A Mauryan ruler wants Cheras to obey. What should the ruler expect?
options: the Cheras would obey, because Mauryan power was at its height
the Cheras would stay independent, because they kept their own kingdom
the Cheras would support Chedi kings, because Kalinga became powerful
the Cheras would leave south India, because Mauryan power was strong

why.the Cheras would obey, because Mauryan p: This confuses Mauryan strength with control over the Cheras.
why.the Cheras would support Chedi kings, be: This wrongly connects independent Cheras with rising Chedi power.
why.the Cheras would leave south India, beca: This assumes Mauryan strength forced the Cheras to leave.

activities.explanation: The Cheras stayed independent even when Mauryan power was at its height.

activities.prompt: A visitor sees the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves. Why might the visitor expect Jain monks?
options: The caves were probably made for Jain monks, because Khāravela followed Jainism.
The caves were probably made for Chedi kings, because they ruled Kalinga.
The caves were made for Jain monks, because Chera traders lived there.
The caves were made for Jain monks, because Roman traders stayed there.

why.The caves were probably made for Chedi k: This wrongly treats Chedi kings as the cave makers.
why.The caves were made for Jain monks, beca: This mistakes Chera traders for Jain monks.
This mistakes Roman trade for the caves' purpose.

activities.explanation: Khāravela followed Jain teachings, and the caves were probably made for Jain monks.

activities.prompt: Two southern armies join against the Cholas. Which past action fits best?
options: Karikāla beat the joint force, showing Cholas could defend their kingdom.
Cheras traded widely, showing trade could defeat the joint army.
Cholas stayed independent, showing they never faced other armies.
The Grand Anicut diverted water, showing it defeated the joint army.

why.Cheras traded widely, showing trade coul: This wrongly thinks trade could defeat the joint army.
why.Cholas stayed independent, showing they: This wrongly thinks the Cholas never faced other armies.
why.The Grand Anicut diverted water, showing: This wrongly treats a water work as a military weapon.

activities.explanation: Karikāla beat a joint force of the Cheras and Pānḍyas.

activities.prompt: A map shows Chola rule in south India. It spans the 3rd century BCE to the 13th century CE. What does this show?
options: the Cholas ruled parts of south India for a very long time
the Cholas ruled only during the Mauryan period and nowhere else
the Cheras ruled all of south India throughout this long period
the Pānḍyas replaced the Cholas during this long period

why.the Cholas ruled only during the Mauryan: This wrongly limits Chola rule to Mauryan power.
why.the Cheras ruled all of south India thro: This confuses the Cholas with the Cheras.
why.the Pānḍyas replaced the Cholas during t: This wrongly says the Pānḍyas replaced the Cholas.

activities.explanation: The Cholas ruled parts of south India from the 3rd century BCE to the 13th century CE.

activities.prompt: A map marks Chera land in western Tamil Nadu and Kerala. Another source says they traded with the Roman Empire and West Asia. What can we combine?
options: the Cheras had a western homeland and traded widely with two regions
the Cheras lived in eastern Tamil Nadu and traded only locally
the Cheras lived in Kalinga and traded only with Jain monks
the Cheras traded with the Roman Empire but never with West Asia

why.the Cheras lived in eastern Tamil Nadu a: This changes their western homeland to the east and limits their trade.
why.the Cheras lived in Kalinga and traded o: This mixes Chera trade with Chedi and Jain facts.
why.the Cheras traded with the Roman Empire: This leaves out one of the two trading regions in the source.

activities.explanation: The map gives their western homeland, and the source gives their wide trade.

lessons.sceneCaption: The Udayagiri and Khandagiri Caves were probably made for Jain monks.

lessons.title: Invaders from Outside: Indo-Greeks, Śhakas and Kuṣhāṇas

activities.prompt: Who were the foreign rulers who came to India and became part of its story?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Rulers From Outside Arrive
activities.body: Alexander left behind regional rulers called satraps when he retreated. Later, these rulers set up independent domains, which means their own lands. After the Mauryas declined, the north-west was an easy target for the Indo-Greeks. Their contact with India mixed Greek and Indian elements in daily life. Later, the Śhakas and the Kuṣhāṇas also came to power in parts of India.
keyPoints: Alexander left behind regional rulers called satraps.
Indo-Greek contact mixed Greek and Indian elements in daily life.
The Śhakas and Kuṣhāṇas later ruled parts of India.
activities.explanation: Keep the names in mind, because each group comes from a different place and time.

activities.prompt: Why did life in the north-west change after Alexander retreated and Mauryas declined?
steps: Alexander left satraps behind because he was retreating.
These regional rulers formed independent domains because they controlled their regions.
After the Mauryas declined, the north-west became an easy target for Indo-Greeks.
Indo-Greek contact mixed Greek and Indian elements, so daily life changed.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What were satraps?
options: Kings who came from central Asia
Regional rulers left behind by Alexander
Sailors who carried silk to Greece
activities.explanation: Alexander left satraps behind when he retreated. Well done for spotting the regional rulers.

activities.prompt: Alexander's satraps later set up independent domains of their own.
activities.explanation: Your book says these rulers later set up their own domains. Remember the word later.

activities.prompt: Alexander left behind regional rulers called ______ when he retreated.
activities.hint: Think of the word for a regional ruler, and it starts with s.
activities.explanation: Satraps were regional rulers. Alexander left them behind when he went back.

activities.prompt: Match each group to its story.
pairs: Found the north-west an easy target after the Mauryas declined
Ruled from the latter part of the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE
Came from central Asia into India, probably in the 2nd century CE
activities.explanation: Each group has its own place and time in your book. Matching them helps you remember.

activities.prompt: Which ruler supported art and culture, which led to new artistic styles?
options: Heliodorus
Alexander
King Kaṇiṣhka
activities.explanation: King Kaṇiṣhka supported art and culture. This led to new artistic styles in India.

activities.prompt: Some Indo-Greek coins showed Vāsudeva-Kṛiṣhṇa and Lakṣhmī. What does this show?
options: Only Greek gods appeared on Indo-Greek coins
Indian gods were banned on all coins
Lakṣhmī was a Kuṣhāṇa king
Indo-Greek rulers put Indian gods on some coins
activities.explanation: Some coins showed Indian deities, which shows a mix of ideas. Think about what the coins actually showed.

activities.prompt: Kuṣhāṇas came from central Asia into India. Their empire reached much of northern India. They controlled important Silk Route parts. King Kaṇiṣhka supported art and culture. What do these facts suggest about Kuṣhāṇa power?
options: They combined wide power, Silk Route areas, and royal support for art.
They combined narrow power with no Silk Route areas and no art support.
They combined wide power with no Silk Route areas and no art support.
They came from India but had no central Asian or Silk Route power.

why.They combined narrow power with no Silk: This wrongly denies their wide power, route control, and art support.
why.They combined wide power with no Silk Ro: This gets their wide power right but denies route control and art support.
why.They came from India but had no central: This reverses their origin and wrongly denies their Silk Route control.

activities.explanation: The facts show wide territory, Silk Route control, and royal support for art.

activities.prompt: The Heliodorus pillar praises Vāsudeva as god of gods. What does it show?
options: Some Indo-Greeks treated Vāsudeva with deep religious respect.
All Indo-Greeks rejected every Indian deity and custom.
Heliodorus was a king who ruled the whole region.
The pillar proves that daily life stayed purely Greek.

why.All Indo-Greeks rejected every Indian de: This turns one respectful act into a claim about every Indo-Greek.
why.Heliodorus was a king who ruled the whol: This mistakes an ambassador for a king.
why.The pillar proves that daily life stayed: This ignores the mixture of Greek and Indian elements in Indo-Greek life.

activities.explanation: The pillar praises Vāsudeva and comes from an Indo-Greek ambassador.

activities.prompt: The Śhakas ruled for many centuries. Their Śhaka Samvat became India's National Calendar in 1957. What does this suggest?
options: Their influence continued in India's calendar long after their rule.
Their rule itself continued steadily until the year 1957.
They came from central Asia, like the later Kuṣhāṇas.
They ruled only Silk Route areas and never northern India.

why.Their rule itself continued steadily unt: This confuses the calendar’s name with the actual end of Śhaka rule.
why.They came from central Asia, like the la: This confuses the Śhakas with the Kuṣhāṇas who came from central Asia.
why.They ruled only Silk Route areas and nev: This wrongly limits Śhaka rule and denies their wider position.

activities.explanation: The National Calendar kept the Śhaka name after their long rule had ended.

lessons.sceneCaption: The Heliodorus Pillar at Besnagar, erected by an Indo-Greek envoy to honour Vāsudeva.

lessons.title: Art, Culture and a Shared Heritage

activities.prompt: Did people long ago trade, share ideas, and make art together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Art and Shared Heritage
activities.body: Your lesson looks at art from long ago. Deities are gods and goddesses. The Mathurā style, from the Mathura region, used red sandstone. The Gāndhāra style grew in western Punjab. Its artists made fine Buddha images with flowing robes. Many cultures talked to each other and influenced each other. Trade grew a great deal, inside India and with other lands. Heritage means things passed down from the past, and this mixing is part of it.
keyPoints: The Mathurā style used red sandstone and showed deities.
The Gāndhāra style grew in western Punjab.
Cultures mixed their ideas, and trade grew a great deal.
activities.explanation: Ideas and goods moving between people is part of our shared heritage.

activities.prompt: Why can two different sculptures belong to one shared heritage?
steps: Red-sandstone images point to Mathurā because that style mainly used red sandstone.
Fine Buddha images point to Gāndhāra because its sculptors made realistic images.
The differences still show a shared past because cultures exchanged ideas.
Therefore, heritage is mixing, not one ruler's story.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which style grew in the western regions of Punjab?
options: The Mathurā style
The Gāndhāra style
The Kubera style
activities.explanation: The lesson says the Gāndhāra style grew in western Punjab. Mathurā grew in its own region.

activities.prompt: The Mathurā style mainly used ______ sandstone for its sculptures.
activities.hint: It is a colour.
activities.explanation: Mathurā sculptors mainly used red sandstone. Sandstone is a kind of stone.

activities.prompt: Match each style to what it shows or uses.
activities.explanation: Each style is linked with its own material or subjects in your lesson.

activities.prompt: Why do Kuṣhāṇa sculptures showing many deities matter?
options: They show different beliefs lived together peacefully.
They show that only one ruler controlled all the art.
They show that trade stopped for a long time.
activities.explanation: Many deities in one art style reflect peaceful co-existence of different beliefs. The other two ideas do not match your lesson.

activities.prompt: Gāndhāra sculptors made fine Buddha images with realistic anatomy and flowing robes.
activities.explanation: Realistic anatomy means bodies that look like real bodies. Your lesson says Gāndhāra artists did this well.

activities.prompt: Why should the past be seen as a process of mixing?
options: Many cultures talked to and influenced each other.
Only one ruler controlled all the art and ideas.
Each kingdom kept its ideas completely separate.
activities.explanation: Your lesson says cultures influenced each other, even during conflicts. The past was not limited to one kingdom or ruler.

activities.prompt: Trade grew inside India and with other lands. What does this explain?
options: It helps explain how different cultures exchanged ideas and mixed.
It proves every region used one identical style and belief.
It shows trade stopped contact between different cultures.
It means cultural exchange happened only between other lands.

why.It proves every region used one identica: This wrongly assumes trade removed all differences between cultures.
why.It shows trade stopped contact between d: This mistakes trade for a barrier to contact between cultures.
why.It means cultural exchange happened only: This wrongly limits exchange to other lands, despite inland trade.

activities.explanation: Growing trade fits a period of strong cultural exchange and mixing.

activities.prompt: A history card shows one king's reign. What should a student remember?
options: The past includes many cultures, not only that king's reign.
The card shows everything because one ruler controlled all cultures.
The card is useless because no other culture left any evidence.
The card proves that cultures never exchanged ideas.

why.The card shows everything because one ru: This wrongly treats one ruler's story as the whole shared past.
why.The card is useless because no other cul: This wrongly treats one source as if no other evidence exists.
why.The card proves that cultures never exch: This wrongly denies the period's strong cultural exchange.

activities.explanation: This follows the rule that the past includes many mixed cultures.

activities.prompt: A student says this age shaped only sculpture. What evidence best corrects the idea?
options: The Mahābhārata and Rāmāyana were composed then, showing more than sculpture.
The Mahābhārata and Rāmāyana were composed elsewhere, after this age.
Major texts replaced sculpture, so no styles developed in this age.
This age had no cultural exchange because texts kept cultures apart.

why.The Mahābhārata and Rāmāyana were compos: This misplaces both texts outside the age when they were composed.
why.Major texts replaced sculpture, so no st: This wrongly treats writing and sculpture as enemies.
why.This age had no cultural exchange becaus: This wrongly assumes that texts stopped cultural exchange.

activities.explanation: The two major texts show this age also produced important writing.

lessons.title: Test practice
lessons.sceneAlt: A map shows the Abhiras and other ancient Indian dynasties in the centuries following the Maurya Empire's decline.
lessons.sceneCaption: Map of the Abhiras and contemporary Indian dynasties around 200 BCE to 300 CE.
