activities.context: After the last Maurya emperor was killed around 185 BCE, the empire broke into many pieces. This happened barely fifty years after Aśhoka, and many new kingdoms appeared across the subcontinent. The north-west became weak, allowing outsiders to invade. Kings gained control through peaceful marriage alliances or by using force, competed for territory, and regarded border areas as important for safety.
activities.prompt: A ruler notices that outsiders may enter from the north-west. What should the ruler do first to help keep the kingdom safe?
options: Strengthen control over its border areas
Stop guarding all border areas
Focus only on growing literature
Give up all control of nearby territory

why.Focus only on growing literature: This does not protect the kingdom.

activities.explanation: This helps keep the kingdom safe.

activities.context: After the last Maurya emperor was killed around 185 BCE, the empire broke into many pieces. This happened barely fifty years after Aśhoka, and many new kingdoms appeared across the subcontinent. The north-west became weak, allowing outsiders to invade. Kings gained control through peaceful marriage alliances or by using force, competed for territory, and regarded border areas as important for safety.
activities.prompt: Two neighboring kings make a peaceful marriage alliance. What advantage could this give one king?
options: Control over another ruler's territory without using force
A reason to stop defending border areas
A way to ensure that no outsiders invade
A reason to stop competing for territory

why.A way to ensure that no outsiders invade: Outsiders could still invade the area.

activities.explanation: Marriage alliances could gain control peacefully.

activities.prompt: How does the breakup of the Maurya Empire differ from the age of reorganisation?
activities.answer: The breakup describes the empire dividing into many pieces after the last emperor's death. Reorganisation describes what followed: old regions became new kingdoms, competition and border control shaped politics, and the map of India changed greatly.
points: The empire divided into many pieces.
Old regions became new kingdoms.
New kingdoms competed for territory.
The map of India changed greatly.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A school is preparing an exhibition on the Śhunga period. One corner explains how Puṣhyamitra Śhunga used a Vedic ritual when he wanted to become the most powerful ruler. Another shows the territory controlled by the dynasty and compares its size with the Maurya empire. Students will also explain the change from early fighting with the Greeks to friendship. The final display will feature Vedic revival, Sanskrit literature, Patañjali’s Yoga Sūtras, and Śhunga support for art and architecture.
activities.prompt: Which caption should students place beside the ritual display?
options: It shows how Puṣhyamitra sought the greatest political power through a Vedic rite.
It shows how the ritual enlarged the Śhunga empire beyond the Maurya empire.
It shows how the rite replaced Puṣhyamitra’s early friendship with the Greeks.
It shows how Vedic practices ended when Puṣhyamitra became ruler.

why.It shows how the ritual enlarged the Śhu: The ritual was not intended to expand the empire, which remained smaller than the Maurya empire.
why.It shows how the rite replaced Puṣhyamit: Friendship with the Greeks came after some early fighting, not through the ritual.
why.It shows how Vedic practices ended when: Vedic rituals and practices were revived during this period rather than ending.

activities.explanation: This correctly explains the purpose of Puṣhyamitra’s Vedic ritual.

activities.context: A school is preparing an exhibition on the Śhunga period. One corner explains how Puṣhyamitra Śhunga used a Vedic ritual when he wanted to become the most powerful ruler. Another shows the territory controlled by the dynasty and compares its size with the Maurya empire. Students will also explain the change from early fighting with the Greeks to friendship. The final display will feature Vedic revival, Sanskrit literature, Patañjali’s Yoga Sūtras, and Śhunga support for art and architecture.
activities.prompt: Which final caption best matches the cultural features planned for the display?
options: Sanskrit was favoured in philosophy and literature, Patañjali compiled the Yoga Sūtras, and other schools of thought also grew stronger.
Sanskrit was avoided in philosophy and literature, Patañjali compiled a ritual manual, and other schools of thought weakened.
Sanskrit was used for philosophy, but Vedic practices ended and other schools disappeared.
The Śhungas supported only architecture, while Sanskrit and Patañjali belonged to a later period.

why.Sanskrit was avoided in philosophy and l: Sanskrit was a favourite for philosophy and literature, and other schools still grew strong.
why.Sanskrit was used for philosophy, but Ve: Vedic practices were revived, and other schools of thought continued to grow.
why.The Śhungas supported only architecture,: The Śhungas supported literature, art and architecture, while these developments occurred in this period.

activities.explanation: All three statements agree with the cultural developments of the Śhunga period.

activities.prompt: Explain how the Śhunga empire compared with the Maurya empire, and how the dynasty still encouraged cultural development despite its smaller size.
activities.answer: The Śhunga empire was smaller than the Maurya empire. Despite this, the Śhungas supported literature, art and architecture. Sanskrit became a favourite language for philosophy and literature, Patañjali compiled the Yoga Sūtras, and other schools of thought still grew strong during the period.
points: The Śhunga empire was smaller than the Maurya empire.
The dynasty supported literature, art and architecture.
Sanskrit became a favourite for philosophy and literature.
Patañjali compiled the Yoga Sūtras, while other schools grew strong.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a school exhibition, a guide shows coins with ships and explains that sea trade was important to the Sātavāhanas. A merchant from a coastal town asks whether sending goods toward the Roman Empire will bring the kingdom any income. Nearby, a display about Gautamī Balaśhrī says she gave land to Buddhist monks and performed the ashvamedha yajna. The guide adds that peace and wealth supported literature, art and culture.
activities.prompt: If fewer merchants began using the sea routes, what should the guide expect the kingdom’s income from trade to do?
options: The kingdom would probably receive less toll and tax because trade would be smaller.
The kingdom would probably receive more toll and tax because trade would be smaller.
The kingdom would probably receive the same toll and tax because its trade networks remained unchanged.
The kingdom would probably earn more from the merchant’s land than from the trade.

why.The kingdom would probably receive more: A decline in trade would not automatically increase trade income.
why.The kingdom would probably receive the s: The lesson links trade income with tolls and taxes, so less trade can mean less income.
why.The kingdom would probably earn more fro: The lesson does not identify merchants’ land as a source of kingdom income.

activities.explanation: Fewer traders would mean less trade for the kingdom to tax.

activities.context: At a school exhibition, a guide shows coins with ships and explains that sea trade was important to the Sātavāhanas. A merchant from a coastal town asks whether sending goods toward the Roman Empire will bring the kingdom any income. Nearby, a display about Gautamī Balaśhrī says she gave land to Buddhist monks and performed the ashvamedha yajna. The guide adds that peace and wealth supported literature, art and culture.
activities.prompt: If trade weakened so that the Sātavāhana kingdom became poorer and less peaceful, what would most likely happen to literature, art and culture?
options: Their growth would probably slow because peace and wealth would be reduced.
Their growth would probably speed up because poorer people would have more time for culture.
Their growth would probably remain unchanged because trade was not connected with cultural growth.
Their growth would probably stop completely because reduced trade would leave the kingdom without culture.

why.Their growth would probably speed up bec: Poverty does not automatically give artists more time to work.
why.Their growth would probably remain uncha: The lesson directly connects cultural growth with wealth and peace.
why.Their growth would probably stop complet: Reduced wealth and peace would weaken conditions for growth, though complete stopping is too certain.

activities.explanation: Peace and wealth helped literature, art and culture grow.

activities.prompt: How did sea trade matter to the Sātavāhana kingdom, and what evidence shows that its trade reached distant regions?
activities.answer: Sātavāhana trade networks reached the Roman Empire, so the kingdom was connected with distant markets. Many coins show ships, which suggests that sea trade was important. The kingdom also earned money from tolls and taxes on trade, making trade valuable to its income.
points: Trade networks reached the Roman Empire.
Many Sātavāhana coins show ships.
Sea trade was important to the kingdom.
Tolls and taxes on trade provided income.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After Mauryan power declined, Kalinga became a leading power under Chedi kings. Khāravela was devoted to Jain teachings, and the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves were probably made for Jain monks. The Hāthīgumphā inscription records his achievements year after year. Meanwhile, the Cheras, Cholas and Pānḍyas rose to prominence, remained independent of Mauryan power, and the Cheras traded widely with the Roman Empire and West Asia.
activities.prompt: If the Hāthīgumphā inscription were unavailable, what would be the main historical evidence lost?
options: Evidence showing what Khāravela accomplished in different years
Evidence of how Jain monks lived inside the caves
Evidence that the Cheras traded with the Roman Empire
Evidence of how the Grand Anicut supplied delta farmland

why.Evidence of how Jain monks lived inside: The caves do not directly record his achievements.
why.Evidence that the Cheras traded with the: Cheran trade with Rome is not recorded in the inscription.
why.Evidence of how the Grand Anicut supplie: The Grand Anicut belonged to the Cholas, not Khāravela's record.

activities.explanation: The inscription recorded Khāravela's achievements year after year.

activities.context: After Mauryan power declined, Kalinga became a leading power under Chedi kings. Khāravela was devoted to Jain teachings, and the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves were probably made for Jain monks. The Hāthīgumphā inscription records his achievements year after year. Meanwhile, the Cheras, Cholas and Pānḍyas rose to prominence, remained independent of Mauryan power, and the Cheras traded widely with the Roman Empire and West Asia.
activities.prompt: If trade with the Roman Empire and West Asia became more difficult, which kingdom would most likely be affected?
options: Cholas
Cheras
Pānḍyas
Kalinga

why.Cholas: The Cholas are associated here with the Grand Anicut.
why.Pānḍyas: The passage does not connect the Pānḍyas with this trade.
why.Kalinga: Kalinga's rise under Chedi kings is separate from Cheran trade.

activities.explanation: The Cheras traded widely with the Roman Empire and West Asia.

activities.prompt: Why do the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves and the Hāthīgumphā inscription together help us understand the Chedi period?
activities.answer: The caves probably served Jain monks, which connects them with Khāravela's devotion to Jain teachings. The inscription gives a year-by-year account of his achievements. Together, they provide evidence about the religious interests and achievements associated with the Chedi period.
points: Identifies the caves as probably made for Jain monks
Links the caves with Khāravela's Jain devotion
Explains that the inscription records achievements over successive years
Shows how different evidence helps students understand the period
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After Alexander retreated, he left behind satraps, or regional rulers. These rulers later set up independent domains of their own. As the Mauryas declined, the north-west became an easy target for the Indo-Greeks. Indo-Greek contact produced a mixture of Greek and Indian elements in daily life. Some Indo-Greek coins showed Indian deities such as Vāsudeva-Kṛiṣhṇa and Lakṣhmī. A school activity asks students to advise the regional rulers and explain the changes that followed.
activities.prompt: The regional rulers want their territories to remain self-governing after Alexander's retreat. What should they do next?
options: Create separate self-governing realms in the regions.
Wait for Alexander to return and restore his arrangements.
Combine all the regions under one ruler chosen from among themselves.
Leave each region without any organized government.

why.Wait for Alexander to return and restore: Option 1: Alexander had already retreated, so waiting for him is not suitable.
why.Combine all the regions under one ruler: Option 2: A single combined ruler would not follow the independent-domain pattern.
why.Leave each region without any organized: Option 3: Leaving the regions without government would not create stable self-rule.

activities.explanation: Option 0: This matches what the regional rulers later did.

activities.context: After Alexander retreated, he left behind satraps, or regional rulers. These rulers later set up independent domains of their own. As the Mauryas declined, the north-west became an easy target for the Indo-Greeks. Indo-Greek contact produced a mixture of Greek and Indian elements in daily life. Some Indo-Greek coins showed Indian deities such as Vāsudeva-Kṛiṣhṇa and Lakṣhmī. A school activity asks students to advise the regional rulers and explain the changes that followed.
activities.prompt: If Indo-Greek contact continued, what would students most expect to see in daily life?
options: Elements from both cultures combined in everyday life.
Only Greek elements in daily life.
Only Indian elements in daily life.
Neither Greek nor Indian elements in daily life.

Option 1: This overlooks the Indian elements in the mixture.
Option 2: This overlooks the Greek elements in the mixture.
why.Neither Greek nor Indian elements in dai: Option 3: This ignores both the mixture and the coins showing Indian deities.

activities.explanation: Option 0: Indo-Greek contact produced a mixture of both kinds of elements.

activities.prompt: Explain why the north-west became an easy target for the Indo-Greeks after the Mauryas declined.
activities.answer: Alexander's retreat had left satraps, or regional rulers, in the north-west, and some later established independent domains. When Mauryan power declined, the region was no longer protected by the Mauryas. This situation made the north-west an easy target for the Indo-Greeks.
points: Alexander left regional satraps when he retreated.
Some satraps later established independent domains.
Mauryan control weakened as their power declined.
The north-west became an easy target for the Indo-Greeks.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A school display compares Mathurā and Gāndhāra sculptures. The Mathurā section describes red sandstone and Kubera, while the Gāndhāra section presents Buddha images with realistic anatomy and flowing robes. A student asks why the styles differ and why the period can include many deities as well as Buddha images. The display also says that trade grew, cultures influenced one another, and different beliefs coexisted peacefully.
activities.prompt: If a Mathurā sculptor began using a different material instead of red sandstone, what would most likely happen?
options: The sculpture's usual style marker would weaken, although it could still show a deity.
The sculpture would automatically become a Gāndhāra-style work.
The sculptor would have to stop showing deities such as Kubera.
The change would prove that cultural exchange had not occurred.

why.The sculpture would automatically become: Using another material would weaken this feature.
why.The sculptor would have to stop showing: Gāndhāra style is not defined by using a different material.
why.The change would prove that cultural exc: Material does not necessarily decide which deity is shown.

activities.explanation: Red sandstone is a main feature of Mathurā sculpture.

activities.context: A school display compares Mathurā and Gāndhāra sculptures. The Mathurā section describes red sandstone and Kubera, while the Gāndhāra section presents Buddha images with realistic anatomy and flowing robes. A student asks why the styles differ and why the period can include many deities as well as Buddha images. The display also says that trade grew, cultures influenced one another, and different beliefs coexisted peacefully.
activities.prompt: A student says that one ruler created the entire shared heritage shown in the display. What is the best correction?
options: The evidence points to interaction among cultures, so no single ruler can explain the whole heritage.
One ruler probably designed both styles to keep religious beliefs separate.
Different styles arose because cultures refused to influence one another.
The heritage came only from trade and had no artistic or religious diversity.

why.One ruler probably designed both styles: Trade and cultural exchange grew within and beyond India.
why.Different styles arose because cultures: The shared heritage reflects mixing across cultures and beliefs.
why.The heritage came only from trade and ha: It cannot be limited to the work of one ruler.

activities.explanation: The period saw cultures talking to and influencing one another.

activities.prompt: Explain the main differences between the Mathurā and Gāndhāra styles.
activities.answer: The Mathurā style developed in the Mathura region of today's Uttar Pradesh, showed Indian deities including Kubera, and mainly used red sandstone. The Gāndhāra style grew in western Punjab and is known for fine Buddha images with realistic anatomy and flowing robes. Region, subjects, materials, and carving features distinguish them.
points: Mathurā developed in the Mathura region of today's Uttar Pradesh.
Mathurā showed deities such as Kubera and mainly used red sandstone.
Gāndhāra grew in western Punjab.
Gāndhāra is known for realistic Buddha images and flowing robes.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: The Age of Reorganisation

activities.prompt: What happened to the Maurya empire soon after Aśhoka's time?
options: It grew into a much bigger empire
It broke up into many pieces
It joined the Roman Empire
It stayed as one big empire
activities.explanation: The empire broke up barely fifty years after Aśhoka. Many new kingdoms then appeared across the land.

activities.prompt: Who founded the Śhunga dynasty?
options: Patañjali
Kaṇiṣhka
Puṣhyamitra Śhunga
Khāravela
activities.explanation: Puṣhyamitra Śhunga founded this dynasty. Patañjali was a scholar, not the founder.

activities.prompt: Match each Sātavāhana clue to the right idea.
activities.explanation: Coins, taxes and gifts all show how the Sātavāhanas used trade and faith.

activities.prompt: Put these events in time order, earliest first.
items: Sātavāhana empire breaks into smaller kingdoms
Śhaka Samvat becomes India's National Calendar
activities.explanation: Each event happened later than the one before it. Check the centuries to be sure.

activities.prompt: Which Chola king beat a joint force of the Cheras and Pānḍyas?
options: Khāravela
Puṣhyamitra
Gautamīputra Sātakarṇi
Karikāla
activities.explanation: Karikāla was a Chola king who won against the Cheras and Pānḍyas together.

activities.prompt: The Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves were probably made for Buddhist monks.
activities.explanation: The caves were probably made for Jain monks, not Buddhist ones.

activities.prompt: Patañjali compiled the ______ Sūtras in this period.
activities.hint: The name starts with the letter Y.
activities.explanation: Patañjali compiled the Yoga Sūtras. Sanskrit was a favourite language for such works.

activities.prompt: Match each art style or text to its clue.
pairs: Made fine Buddha images with flowing robes
Praises Vāsudeva as god of gods
Major texts composed in this age
activities.explanation: Each style or text has a special feature. Mathurā used red sandstone, and Gāndhāra showed flowing robes.

chapters.title: The Gupta Era
chapters.summary: In this chapter: a new power emerges; the warrior king and the gupta empire; a traveller’s account of gupta society; governance, administration and trade.

lessons.title: A New Power Emerges

activities.prompt: What made an iron pillar last so long?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Rise of the Guptas
activities.body: The Guptas first appeared as regional rulers near present-day Uttar Pradesh. New kingdoms then prepared the way for consolidation. Consolidation means a period when powers become stronger together. The Gupta Empire flourished from the 3rd to the 6th century CE. Pāṭaliputra, now Patna, was its capital. Art, architecture, literature and science flourished, especially during Chandragupta II’s time.
keyPoints: The Guptas first emerged as regional rulers.
The Gupta Empire flourished from the 3rd to the 6th century CE.
Art and science were especially strong during Chandragupta II’s time.
activities.explanation: You now know how the Gupta Empire began and flourished.

activities.prompt: A child sees the old iron pillar. The child asks why it has no rust after so long.
steps: The pillar is more than 1,600 years old.
A thin layer protects it from corrosion.
Because of that protection, it still stands without rusting.
Therefore, the thin layer explains its long-lasting condition.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Amazing Iron Pillar
activities.body: During Chandragupta II’s reign, a 6-tonne iron pillar was erected. The pillar is more than 1,600 years old. It still stands without rusting. A thin layer protects it from corrosion. Corrosion means rusting. This thin layer helps explain why the pillar has lasted so long.
keyPoints: The pillar was erected during Chandragupta II’s reign.
The pillar is more than 1,600 years old.
A thin layer protects it from corrosion.
activities.explanation: The pillar’s age and thin layer are linked in this card.

activities.title: The Gupta Capital
activities.prompt: Which place was the Gupta Empire’s capital?
options: Chandragupta II
Uttar Pradesh
Pāṭaliputra
The iron pillar
activities.explanation: Pāṭaliputra was the capital. It is now called Patna.

activities.prompt: Pāṭaliputra, now Patna, was the Gupta Empire’s capital.
activities.explanation: Yes. Pāṭaliputra was the Gupta capital, and it is now Patna.

activities.title: The Gupta Period
activities.prompt: The Gupta Empire flourished from the ______ to the 6th century CE.
activities.hint: This is the century when the empire began flourishing.
activities.explanation: The Gupta Empire flourished from the 3rd to the 6th century CE.

activities.title: The Pillar’s Ruler
activities.prompt: Who was the ruler when the 6-tonne pillar was erected?
options: Pāṭaliputra
Chandragupta II
Uttar Pradesh
The Gupta Empire
activities.explanation: Chandragupta II was the ruler during the pillar’s erection.

activities.title: Remember the Gupta Age
activities.prompt: Match each clue to its lesson answer.
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a Gupta clue with its matching answer.

activities.prompt: The Gupta Empire flourished only during Chandragupta II’s reign.
activities.explanation: It flourished from the 3rd to the 6th century CE. Developments were especially strong during his time.

activities.title: The Pillar’s Protection Story
activities.prompt: Put the pillar’s protection story in order.
items: A thin layer covers the pillar.
The layer protects it from corrosion.
activities.explanation: The pillar was erected first. Its thin layer then formed and protected it.

activities.prompt: An old iron pillar has a deep scratch. Its thin outer layer is damaged. What will likely happen?
options: The pillar will rust more quickly.
The pillar will rust much more slowly.
The pillar will become much stronger.
The pillar will turn into a thin layer.

This reverses the effect of losing protection from corrosion.
This confuses protection from corrosion with added strength.
This confuses the iron pillar with its thin protective layer.

activities.explanation: The scratch damages the layer that protects the pillar from corrosion.

activities.prompt: A timeline shows the Gupta period. This period ran from the 3rd to the 6th century CE. A source calls the empire the most powerful power of its time. What can a reader conclude?
options: The claim applies within the Gupta period.
The claim applies to all powers before it.
The claim applies to all powers after it.
The claim applies to all human history.

why.The claim applies to all powers before i: This treats a same-time claim as a claim about all earlier powers.
why.The claim applies to all powers after it: This treats a same-time claim as a claim about all later powers.
This turns a claim about one period into a claim about all history.

activities.explanation: The phrase 'of its time' limits the claim to the Gupta period.

lessons.sceneCaption: Built by Chandragupta II, Delhi’s iron pillar has resisted corrosion for more than 1,600 years.

lessons.title: The Warrior King and the Gupta Empire

activities.prompt: What might an ancient pillar reveal about the Gupta kings’ dreams and courage?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Rulers of the Gupta Empire
activities.body: Chandragupta I helped the Gupta Empire grow early. He is remembered for his coins and strategic alliances. Chandragupta II, also known as Vikramāditya, was a devotee of Viṣhṇu. His mount, Garuda, appears on many inscriptions. Harisena, the court poet, wrote the Prayāga pillar inscription praising Samudragupta’s achievements. Samudragupta wanted to unite the Earth. He restored many defeated kings, and they paid tribute. Many rulers submitted because they feared his strength.
keyPoints: Chandragupta I helped the Gupta Empire expand early.
Harisena praised Samudragupta in the Prayāga pillar inscription.
Samudragupta wanted to unite the Earth.
activities.explanation: These rulers helped shape the Gupta Empire in different ways.

activities.prompt: Why did many kings obey Samudragupta instead of fighting him?
steps: Samudragupta wanted to unite the Earth, because that was his clear goal.
Defeated kings were restored and paid tribute, because he kept royal power.
Other rulers submitted because they feared his strength, so fear also mattered.
Therefore, many rulers obeyed through tribute and fear while he pursued unification.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is Chandragupta I remembered for?
options: Coins and strategic alliances
Garuda and many inscriptions
Prayāga and court poetry
Earth and kings’ tribute
activities.explanation: Chandragupta I played an important part in the Gupta Empire’s early expansion.

activities.prompt: The name Chandra in the iron pillar’s inscription was linked to ______ II.
activities.hint: Type one ruler’s name.
activities.explanation: The name Chandra has been identified with Chandragupta II.

activities.prompt: Match each person or name with the correct detail.
pairs: Early expansion of the Gupta Empire
activities.explanation: Great matching! Each name links to an important detail.

activities.prompt: Why did other rulers submit to Samudragupta?
options: Because they loved his coins
Because they joined his alliances
Because they feared his strength
Because they praised Garuda
activities.explanation: Other rulers submitted because they feared Samudragupta’s strength.

activities.prompt: What did Samudragupta want to do?
options: Divide the Earth
Unite the Earth
End every tribute
Leave each throne empty
activities.explanation: Samudragupta wanted to unite the Earth.

activities.prompt: At its peak, the Gupta Empire covered most of ______ and western India.
activities.hint: Choose one direction from the lesson.
activities.explanation: The Gupta Empire covered most of northern and western India at its peak.

activities.prompt: Samudragupta wanted to unite the Earth. Many defeated kings returned to their thrones and paid tribute. What did this help him do?
options: It brought kings under his power while keeping them in place.
It removed kings from power and ended their rule.
It kept kings free because he did not want tribute.
It gave tribute to each king and gained no power.

why.It removed kings from power and ended th: He restored the defeated kings, so he did not remove their royal power.
why.It kept kings free because he did not wa: The defeated kings paid tribute, rather than being free of it.
why.It gave tribute to each king and gained: Samudragupta received the tribute, so it did not flow to the kings.

activities.explanation: Restoring kings while taking tribute brought them under Samudragupta's power.

activities.prompt: At its peak, the Gupta Empire covered most northern and western India and parts of central and eastern India. What does a shaded map show?
options: The empire spread widely, but did not cover all India.
The empire covered every part of India equally.
The empire stayed within one small northern region.
The empire had no land in central or eastern India.

why.The empire covered every part of India e: The facts mention parts of central and eastern India, not every part.
why.The empire stayed within one small north: The empire covered most northern and western India, not one region.
why.The empire had no land in central or eas: The facts say it included parts of central and eastern India.

activities.explanation: The shaded areas cover many regions, but some places are outside.

activities.prompt: Imagine a school group has many captains. The leader restores each defeated captain, but asks for supplies. Other captains join because they fear the leader. Which Gupta rule is similar?
options: Restore defeated rulers, accept tribute, and use fear to gain submission.
Remove defeated rulers, reject tribute, and force every captain to leave.
Restore defeated rulers, refuse tribute, and make every captain submit.
Keep defeated rulers away, accept tribute, and gain love from all.

why.Remove defeated rulers, reject tribute,: Samudragupta restored defeated kings and accepted their tribute.
why.Restore defeated rulers, refuse tribute,: He accepted tribute, so refusing it does not match his rule.
why.Keep defeated rulers away, accept tribut: Others submitted from fear, not love, and defeated kings were restored.

activities.explanation: Restoring rulers and taking their supplies matches tribute and restored thrones.

activities.prompt: The Prayāga pillar inscription praises Samudragupta's achievements. Harisena, his court poet, wrote it. What should a student understand about this source?
options: It shows the court's view, so we should check it carefully.
It proves that every person agreed with all the praise.
It shows that the court had no link to Samudragupta.
It proves that every achievement in the praise was unimportant.

why.It proves that every person agreed with: One court's praise cannot prove that everyone agreed.
why.It shows that the court had no link to S: Harisena was Samudragupta's court poet, so there was a court link.
why.It proves that every achievement in the: The inscription praises the achievements, so it does not call them unimportant.

activities.explanation: A court poet praising his king gives us the court's view, not all views.

activities.prompt: The iron pillar's Chandra has been linked to Chandragupta II. He was also called Vikramāditya and devoted to Viṣhṇu. How should we read these facts together?
options: They give different clues that identify the same ruler.
They show that Chandra and Vikramāditya were different rulers.
They prove that Viṣhṇu wrote the iron pillar inscription.
They show that devotion changed the pillar ruler's name.

why.They show that Chandra and Vikramāditya: Chandra and Vikramāditya both identify Chandragupta II, not two rulers.
why.They prove that Viṣhṇu wrote the iron pi: Viṣhṇu was the deity Chandragupta II devoted to, not the writer.
why.They show that devotion changed the pill: Nothing here says devotion changed his name; the pillar names Chandra.

activities.explanation: The name, title, and devotion all point to Chandragupta II.

lessons.sceneCaption: The Delhi Iron Pillar, built by Chandragupta II, has survived more than 1,600 years of exposure.

lessons.title: A Traveller’s Account of Gupta Society

activities.prompt: What stories did a traveller tell about life in Gupta India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Faxian’s journey and account
activities.body: Faxian was a traveller who visited India in the early 5th century CE. He travelled to Buddhist sites and learned from Indian scholars. He recorded Indian culture, government and society. Outcastes are people whom society excluded. Faxian described harsh treatment of these people. His account shows caring actions by some people. It gives only one writer's view of a limited part of society.
keyPoints: Faxian visited Buddhist sites and learned from Indian scholars.
People received care, food, medicines and charity.
Faxian also described harsh treatment of outcastes.
His account shows only one writer's limited view.
activities.explanation: This account is helpful, but it gives only a limited view.

activities.prompt: A family moves to a Gupta city and farms royal land. What must it do?
steps: The family need not register because people did not report to officials.
Royal land means giving part of the grain as tax.
So the family pays grain tax but does not register its household.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Why did Faxian travel to India?
options: To visit Buddhist sites and learn from Indian scholars.
To collect taxes from farmers working on royal land.
To register households and report them to government officials.
To care for poor people, orphans and sick people.
activities.explanation: He wanted to visit Buddhist sites and learn from Indian scholars.

activities.prompt: People had to register their households and report to officials.
activities.explanation: People did not need to register their households or report to officials.

activities.prompt: How did farmers who worked royal land pay tax?
options: Part of their grain.
Part of their houses.
Part of their clothes.
Part of their medicines.
activities.explanation: Farmers who worked royal land paid part of their grain as tax.

activities.prompt: Match each group or place with what Faxian recorded.
pairs: Part of their grain as tax
Poor people, orphans and sick people
activities.explanation: These pairs show farming duties, charitable work and care for people.

activities.prompt: Farmers who worked royal land paid ______ of their grain as tax.
activities.hint: Think of the portion farmers gave.
activities.explanation: Farmers who worked royal land paid part of their grain as tax.

activities.prompt: What did Faxian record during his journey?
options: Indian culture, government and society.
Royal land, grain and taxes.
Buddhist sites and Indian scholars.
Households, doctors and cities.
activities.explanation: Faxian recorded his observations of Indian culture, government and society.

activities.prompt: Put these parts of Faxian's journey in order.
items: He visited Buddhist sites and learned from scholars.
He recorded observations of Indian culture, government and society.
activities.explanation: Faxian first visited India, then travelled and learned, and later recorded observations.

activities.prompt: Why should we remember Faxian's account with care?
options: It shows one writer's limited view.
It shows every writer's complete view.
It covers every part of Indian society.
It lists all households and communities.
activities.explanation: His account shows only one writer's view of a limited part of society.

activities.prompt: A Vaishya family sees sick people. Why might it build a charity house?
options: To provide charity and medicines to people in need.
To collect household reports from every family.
To collect grain tax from every farmer.
To provide harsh treatment to people regarded as outcastes.

why.To collect household reports from every: This wrongly makes charity a tool for household reporting.
This wrongly makes charity a way to collect royal-land tax.
why.To provide harsh treatment to people reg: This wrongly makes charity a way to continue harsh treatment.

activities.explanation: Vaishya families built houses for charity and medicines.

activities.prompt: Poor people received care. People regarded as outcastes faced harsh treatment. What can this show?
options: Different groups in Gupta society did not receive the same care.
Every group in Gupta society received exactly the same care.
Only outcastes received food, care, and medicines.
The account proves care was equal for every group.

why.Every group in Gupta society received ex: It ignores the different treatment described for the two groups.
why.Only outcastes received food, care, and: It wrongly gives the care received by poor people to outcastes.
why.The account proves care was equal for ev: It wrongly treats a limited account as proof about every group.

activities.explanation: The two groups had different treatment in the account.

lessons.title: Governance, Administration and Trade

activities.prompt: How did Gupta rulers govern, grow their power, and trade with the world?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Governance and trade under the Guptas
activities.body: During the Gupta period, many kingdoms existed at the same time. Gupta rulers expanded their empire through warfare, diplomacy and alliances. Kauṭilya advised rulers to form alliances with other rulers. Prabhāvatī Gupta became regent ruler after the Vākāṭaka prince died. Government collected taxes from land, mines, irrigation, trade and crafts. Revenue paid for administration, the army, temples and infrastructure. India traded with the Mediterranean world, Southeast Asia and China.
keyPoints: Many kingdoms existed together.
Rulers used warfare, diplomacy and alliances.
Taxes supported administration and infrastructure.
India traded with regions across the sea.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect Gupta government, revenue and overseas trade.

activities.prompt: A trader has goods to sell, but needs to reach buyers in the Mediterranean world.
steps: India traded with the Mediterranean world, so Indian traders needed a way to reach it.
They exported textiles, spices, ivory and gemstones, so they had goods to sell.
Socotra Island was an important stop because it lay on the route to Mediterranean markets.
Pottery, Brahmi inscriptions and a Buddhist stūpa show that Indian traders lived there, supporting the stop's importance.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Finding the tax sources
activities.prompt: Which group lists only Gupta tax sources?
options: Armies, temples and roads
Kings, battles and grants
Land, mines and trade
Mines, temples and kings
activities.explanation: These are all sources listed for Gupta taxes.

activities.title: Kingdoms of the Gupta period
activities.prompt: Only one kingdom existed during the Gupta period.
activities.explanation: Many kingdoms existed at the same time during the Gupta period.

activities.title: The regent ruler
activities.prompt: After the Vākāṭaka prince died, who became regent ruler?
options: A Gupta merchant
Prabhāvatī Gupta
A Vākāṭaka priest
A Mediterranean trader
activities.explanation: Prabhāvatī Gupta became regent ruler after the prince's death.

activities.title: Temples linked with Prabhāvatī Gupta
activities.prompt: Prabhāvatī Gupta was linked with the building of ______ temples.
activities.hint: Use the number given in the lesson.
activities.explanation: She was linked with the building of seven temples.

activities.title: Matching the trade clues
activities.prompt: Match each trade clue with its correct detail.
pairs: Important stop on the trade route
activities.explanation: Socotra linked the route to Mediterranean markets and showed Indian traders' presence.

activities.title: Following the trade journey
activities.prompt: Put these stages of the trade journey in order.
activities.explanation: Socotra was an important stop on the route to Mediterranean markets.

activities.prompt: Kauṭilya advises alliances as part of the saptānga. A ruler faces a rival kingdom. What should the ruler do?
options: Form an alliance with another ruler.
Give all taxes to local leaders.
Stop trade with distant markets.
Wait for the rival kingdom to end.

This confuses land grants with the advice about alliances.
This mistakes trade policy for a rule about alliances.
This invents a waiting rule not given in the facts.

activities.explanation: This follows Kauṭilya's advice to form alliances.

activities.prompt: A child sees a copper plate recording a land grant. What can the child learn?
options: A local leader received land.
Local leaders paid no taxes.
Mines and crafts had disappeared.
The land grant was never made.

The record does not say that local leaders paid no taxes.
Nothing here says that mines or crafts disappeared.
The record itself shows that the grant was recorded.

activities.explanation: Copper plates record land grants given to local leaders.

lessons.sceneCaption: The Gupta Empire at its peak under Chandragupta II, including territories ruled by vassals.

lessons.title: New Ideas, Wonders and Art

activities.prompt: How did the Gupta period turn curiosity into new ideas, wonders, and art?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Achievements of the Gupta Period
activities.body: Peace and stability helped bring achievements during the Gupta period. This period is sometimes called the classical age of India. Knowledge from earlier periods was gathered and compiled into texts. Sanskrit literature flourished through Kālidāsa’s works. Āryabhaṭa and Varāhamihira recorded advances in mathematics and astronomy. Medical writers improved medical theories and practices. The rust-resistant Iron Pillar shows progress. Metallurgy means working with metals. Chandragupta II supported talented people, enriching his court.
keyPoints: Peace and stability helped achievements flourish.
Writers recorded advances in science and medicine.
Chandragupta II supported poets, artists and learned men.
activities.explanation: The Gupta period brought wonderful new ideas, art and learning.

activities.prompt: A student visits a Gupta exhibition showing books, sculptures, medical writings, and an Iron Pillar. Why does this support calling the period the classical age?
steps: Peace and stability helped bring major achievements, because calm conditions supported learning and art.
Chandragupta II surrounded himself with learned men, poets and artists, because their support enriched his court.
Sanskrit works, mathematical and astronomical texts, medical improvements, and the Iron Pillar show wide achievements, because they belong to different fields.
Therefore, calling it the classical age fits, because learning, art, and practical advances flourished together.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who surrounded himself with learned men, poets and artists?
options: Āryabhaṭa
Varāhamihira
Chandragupta II
Kālidāsa
activities.explanation: Chandragupta II surrounded himself with learned men, poets and artists.

activities.prompt: The Gupta period is sometimes called the classical age of India.
activities.explanation: Yes, this period is sometimes called the classical age of India.

activities.prompt: The book Āryabhaṭīya was written by ______.
activities.hint: He also explained that the Earth spins on its axis.
activities.explanation: Āryabhaṭa wrote Āryabhaṭīya about mathematics and astronomy.

activities.prompt: Match each person, book or place with its related achievement.
pairs: compiled and improved medical theories and practices
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an important person, book or place with Gupta learning.

activities.prompt: What did Āryabhaṭa explain about the Earth?
options: The Earth stays still all the time.
The Earth has no axis.
The Earth spins on its axis.
The Earth stops spinning at night.
activities.explanation: Āryabhaṭa explained that the Earth spins on its axis.

activities.prompt: Sārnāth was famous for the rust-resistant Iron Pillar.
activities.explanation: Sārnāth was famous for beautiful Buddha sculptures. The Iron Pillar shows advanced metallurgy.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the order they happened around Chandragupta II’s court.
items: He surrounded himself with learned men, poets and artists.
activities.explanation: His support for talented people greatly enriched his court.

activities.prompt: What did medical writers do during the Gupta period?
options: They compiled medical ideas but refused to improve them.
They stopped caring about medical theories and practices.
They worked only on poetry and never studied medicine.
They compiled and improved medical theories and practices.
activities.explanation: Medical writers compiled and improved medical theories and practices.

activities.prompt: A kingdom is peaceful and stable, and its ruler wants major achievements. What should happen next?
options: More people may create books, art, and new ideas.
People may stop learning because work feels easy.
Artists may leave because the court is quiet.
Old knowledge may disappear because no one needs it.

why.People may stop learning because work fe: This mistakes peace for a reason to stop learning.
why.Artists may leave because the court is q: This assumes quiet courts make artists leave.
why.Old knowledge may disappear because no o: This assumes stable periods erase old knowledge.

activities.explanation: This matches the Gupta example, where peace and stability helped bring achievements.

activities.prompt: A student finds Āryabhaṭīya and reads that the Earth spins on its axis. What can the source show?
options: Āryabhaṭa studied mathematics and astronomy.
Āryabhaṭa supported many poets and artists.
The Gupta court gathered only medical theories.
Sarnath was famous for medical texts.

why.Āryabhaṭa supported many poets and artis: Court support is a separate fact, not what this source shows.
why.The Gupta court gathered only medical th: The source does not say that medical theories were its only subject.
The source cannot show Sarnath’s medical history.

activities.explanation: The book is about mathematics and astronomy, as the source states.

lessons.title: Decline and Kingdoms in the South and Northeast

activities.prompt: What happened to the Gupta Empire, and which kingdoms rose in its place?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Gupta Decline and Regional Kingdoms
activities.body: The Gupta Empire began showing signs of decline by the 6th century CE. Hūṇa attacks and conflicts among regional rulers weakened it. In the south, the Pallavas supported art and architecture. They built magnificent temples and caves, and Kānchipuram became the city of a thousand temples. Samudragupta won battles but did not take direct control. The Gupta period influenced art, science, literature and governance for centuries.
keyPoints: Gupta decline involved Hūṇa attacks and regional conflicts.
Pallavas supported art, architecture, temples and caves.
The Gupta period influenced art, science, literature and governance.
activities.explanation: These ideas explain the decline, regional kingdoms and lasting Gupta influence.

activities.prompt: Why could a strong empire become weaker when danger comes from outside and inside?
steps: The empire began strong because the Guptas had built a stable and prosperous society.
Repeated Hūṇa attacks then put pressure on the empire from outside.
Powerful regional rulers caused internal conflicts, so order weakened inside too.
Outside attacks and inside conflicts together explain the decline visible by the sixth century CE.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Repeated Attacks
activities.prompt: What repeatedly attacked the Gupta Empire from Central Asia?
options: The Hūṇa tribe
The Pallava rulers
Samudragupta
The Kāmarūpa rulers
activities.explanation: The fierce Hūṇa tribe repeatedly attacked the Gupta Empire.

activities.title: The City of Temples
activities.prompt: Kānchipuram was known as the city of a ______ temples.
activities.hint: Think of the number used in the name.
activities.explanation: Kānchipuram was known as the city of a thousand temples.

activities.title: Places, Rulers and Their Details
activities.prompt: Match each place or ruler with its lesson detail.
pairs: defeated rulers without taking direct control
activities.explanation: Each detail connects a ruler or place with an important part of the lesson.

activities.title: After the Battle
activities.prompt: What did Samudragupta do after defeating the ruler of Kāmarūpa?
options: He did not take direct control.
He made it a Gupta province.
He ruled it directly himself.
He gave it to the Pallavas.
activities.explanation: Samudragupta defeated the Kāmarūpa ruler but did not take direct control.

activities.title: The Gupta Legacy
activities.prompt: Which statement best shows the Gupta period's lasting influence?
options: It shaped art, science, literature and governance.
It shaped only Pallava temple building plans.
It shaped only Kāmarūpa's northern borders.
It shaped no later art or governance.
activities.explanation: The Gupta period influenced these fields for centuries.

activities.title: Explaining the Decline
activities.prompt: Which causes best explain the Gupta Empire's decline?
options: Hūṇa attacks and internal regional conflicts.
Pallava art, temples and cave building.
Samudragupta's battles and direct control.
Gupta influence, science and literature.
activities.explanation: Hūṇa attacks and conflicts among regional rulers weakened the Gupta Empire.

activities.prompt: A Gupta child hears about attacks from Central Asia. Powerful regional rulers also fight each other. What is the best prediction?
options: The empire's unity and stability will probably weaken.
The empire will soon become strong and fully united.
The attacks and conflicts will probably have no effect.
The empire will probably gain more stable government.

why.The empire will soon become strong and f: This mistakes military action for lasting unity among regional rulers.
why.The attacks and conflicts will probably: This overlooks both outside attacks and internal conflict.
why.The empire will probably gain more stabl: This wrongly predicts that conflict will create more stability.

activities.explanation: Right: outside attacks and inside conflicts weakened the Gupta Empire.

activities.prompt: A book from centuries later contains Gupta ideas about art and government. The empire had weakened by the sixth century CE. What does this show?
options: Gupta influence lasted for centuries after political decline.
Gupta influence ended as soon as political decline began.
Later books preserved only Gupta military conflicts.
Gupta influence remained only in the Gupta homeland.

why.Gupta influence ended as soon as politic: This confuses political decline with the end of cultural influence.
why.Later books preserved only Gupta militar: This wrongly assumes only military conflicts influenced later life.
why.Gupta influence remained only in the Gup: This wrongly assumes Gupta influence stayed in one place.

activities.explanation: Right: Gupta influence affected many fields for centuries.

activities.prompt: A source says Samudragupta defeated two rulers but took over neither region. What can we safely conclude?
options: He showed military power without directly ruling those regions.
He never defeated any enemy in his campaigns.
He wanted to build temples in both conquered regions.
He ruled both regions through local temple rulers.

why.He never defeated any enemy in his campa: This ignores what the source clearly says about his victories.
why.He wanted to build temples in both conqu: This confuses military victory with a temple-building motive.
why.He ruled both regions through local temp: This invents a local rule system not given by the source.

activities.explanation: Right: Samudragupta defeated both rulers without taking direct control.

activities.context: A student prepares a school exhibition on “A New Power Emerges.” The display explains that the Guptas first appeared as regional rulers and that new kingdoms later prepared the way for consolidation. It highlights the iron pillar, Pāṭaliputra as the Gupta capital, and the flourishing of art, architecture, literature and science. The student asks whether the pillar’s survival and the empire’s achievements belong to the same historical period.
activities.prompt: If the thin protective layer on the iron pillar were damaged, what would be the most likely result?
options: The pillar would be more likely to rust.
The pillar would become even better protected.
The pillar would become completely immune to corrosion.
The pillar would immediately lose its ability to stand.

why.The pillar would become even better prot: A damaged layer would not improve the pillar’s condition.
why.The pillar would become completely immun: Complete immunity is not supported by the given information.
why.The pillar would immediately lose its ab: Losing the ability to stand is not given as an immediate result.

activities.explanation: Damage would reduce the protection against corrosion.

activities.context: A student prepares a school exhibition on “A New Power Emerges.” The display explains that the Guptas first appeared as regional rulers and that new kingdoms later prepared the way for consolidation. It highlights the iron pillar, Pāṭaliputra as the Gupta capital, and the flourishing of art, architecture, literature and science. The student asks whether the pillar’s survival and the empire’s achievements belong to the same historical period.
activities.prompt: If an exhibition places consolidation before the Guptas’ regional phase, which correction should the student make?
options: The Guptas began in a regional role; the appearance of other kingdoms set the stage for later consolidation.
Consolidation came first; the regional phase occurred after the Gupta Empire had ended.
Both stages occurred simultaneously at Pāṭaliputra.
The regional phase came first; consolidation happened before the appearance of other kingdoms.

why.Consolidation came first; the regional p: The regional phase began the Empire’s development.
why.Both stages occurred simultaneously at P: The two stages were not described as happening at the same time.
why.The regional phase came first; consolida: This option reverses the order of the kingdoms and consolidation.

activities.explanation: This correction gives the correct sequence of events.

activities.prompt: Explain how the iron pillar helps us understand Gupta-period achievements.
activities.answer: The pillar shows that construction achievements could last. It is more than 1,600 years old, yet it still stands without rusting because a thin protective layer guards it from corrosion. Its erection during Chandragupta II’s reign also connects it with a time when cultural and scientific progress was especially strong.
points: The pillar is more than 1,600 years old.
It still stands without rusting.
A thin layer protects it from corrosion.
It was erected during Chandragupta II’s reign.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: An exhibition connects Gupta rulers with records. The iron pillar identifies Chandra as Chandragupta II or Vikramāditya, a Viṣhṇu devotee. His mount, Garuda, appears on many inscriptions. Harisena wrote the Prayāga pillar inscription praising Samudragupta, who wanted to unite the Earth. Many defeated kings were restored and paid tribute; others submitted from fear of his strength. Chandragupta I aided early expansion. At peak, the empire covered most of northern and western India and parts of central and eastern India.
activities.prompt: If some rulers no longer feared Samudragupta’s strength, what would be a likely result of his effort to unite the Earth?
options: Some rulers might refuse to submit because fear had led them to obey.
Every ruler would still submit for exactly the same reason because fear would remain among them.
No ruler’s decision would change because fear had never influenced submission.
The campaign would gain greater obedience because removing fear would make rulers more respectful.

why.Every ruler would still submit for exact: Some rulers losing fear would remove one reason for submission.
why.No ruler’s decision would change because: The facts directly connect fear with the rulers’ submission.
why.The campaign would gain greater obedienc: The absence of fear would not necessarily make rulers more obedient.

activities.explanation: Other rulers submitted because they feared his strength.

activities.context: An exhibition connects Gupta rulers with records. The iron pillar identifies Chandra as Chandragupta II or Vikramāditya, a Viṣhṇu devotee. His mount, Garuda, appears on many inscriptions. Harisena wrote the Prayāga pillar inscription praising Samudragupta, who wanted to unite the Earth. Many defeated kings were restored and paid tribute; others submitted from fear of his strength. Chandragupta I aided early expansion. At peak, the empire covered most of northern and western India and parts of central and eastern India.
activities.prompt: Why could restored kings’ return to their thrones and payment of tribute fit Samudragupta’s goal of uniting the Earth?
options: They admired his coins and strategic alliances, so their return and payment showed respect for those achievements.
Harisena ordered the restorations and payments so that the inscription could praise the court poet.
They had lost to him, and the restored kings and payments showed the reach of his authority across the Earth.
They feared Garuda’s appearance on inscriptions, although Garuda was connected to Chandragupta II.

why.They admired his coins and strategic all: Coins and strategic alliances are associated with Chandragupta I.
why.Harisena ordered the restorations and pa: Harisena wrote the inscription but did not order the political actions it praises.
why.They feared Garuda’s appearance on inscr: The rulers’ fear was directed at Samudragupta’s strength, not Garuda.

activities.explanation: Many defeated kings were restored and paid tribute to Samudragupta.

activities.context: An exhibition connects Gupta rulers with records. The iron pillar identifies Chandra as Chandragupta II or Vikramāditya, a Viṣhṇu devotee. His mount, Garuda, appears on many inscriptions. Harisena wrote the Prayāga pillar inscription praising Samudragupta, who wanted to unite the Earth. Many defeated kings were restored and paid tribute; others submitted from fear of his strength. Chandragupta I aided early expansion. At peak, the empire covered most of northern and western India and parts of central and eastern India.
activities.prompt: If Chandragupta I had not aided the Gupta Empire’s early expansion, what would the museum be careful to say about its later size?
options: The later peak would certainly have been unchanged because Samudragupta’s achievements alone were enough.
The later peak might have been smaller because Chandragupta I played an important part in early expansion.
The later peak would have covered even more territory because losing early expansion would have strengthened later growth.
The later peak would have covered only northern India because the other areas depended entirely on Chandragupta I.

why.The later peak would certainly have been: The facts do not prove that the later peak would have remained exactly unchanged.
why.The later peak would have covered even m: Nothing shows that removing early expansion would have increased later territorial growth.
why.The later peak would have covered only n: The empire’s peak included western, central, and eastern areas as well as northern India.

activities.explanation: Chandragupta I’s important part in early expansion could have affected the later peak.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between Chandragupta I and Chandragupta II.
activities.answer: Chandragupta I helped the Gupta Empire expand early and is remembered for his coins and strategic alliances. Chandragupta II was also called Vikramāditya and was devoted to Viṣhṇu. Garuda was his mount, and the name Chandra in the iron pillar’s inscription has been identified with him.
points: Chandragupta I aided early expansion.
He is remembered for his coins and strategic alliances.
Chandragupta II was also known as Vikramāditya.
Chandragupta II was a Viṣhṇu devotee whose mount was Garuda.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Faxian passes through a rich and prosperous city in the Gangetic plains. He sees a family that does not register its household or report to officials. Nearby, a farmer works royal land and gives part of his grain as tax. A Vaishya family has built a house for charity and medicines, where poor people, orphans, and sick people receive care. However, Faxian also hears that people regarded as outcastes are treated harshly.
activities.prompt: Why did the farmer give part of his grain as tax?
options: Because the land he worked was royal land.
Because every farmer in the city had to pay tax.
Because his family provided charity and medicines.
Because sick people were cared for at a charitable house.

why.Because every farmer in the city had to: Registration is not mentioned as the reason for grain tax.
why.Because his family provided charity and: Charitable work is a separate part of the case.
why.Because sick people were cared for at a: Care for sick people does not explain a farmer's tax.

activities.explanation: Correct: grain tax applies to farmers working royal land.

activities.context: Faxian passes through a rich and prosperous city in the Gangetic plains. He sees a family that does not register its household or report to officials. Nearby, a farmer works royal land and gives part of his grain as tax. A Vaishya family has built a house for charity and medicines, where poor people, orphans, and sick people receive care. However, Faxian also hears that people regarded as outcastes are treated harshly.
activities.prompt: At the charitable house, a doctor is treating a sick person while a needy person receives food and medicine. Which action best matches the social care described in the case?
options: Treating illness with doctors and helping needy people with food and medicines.
Giving only medicine to the sick person and asking the needy person to find food.
Making both people pay part of their grain before receiving help.
Making both people register with officials before receiving help.

why.Giving only medicine to the sick person: This divides care instead of matching both forms of support.
why.Making both people pay part of their gra: The case describes charity and medicine, not a grain payment.
why.Making both people register with officia: Registration is not required for receiving this help.

activities.explanation: Correct: it combines treatment with support for needy people.

activities.prompt: Explain why Faxian's account shows both social support and unequal treatment.
activities.answer: Faxian's account showed two different experiences. Doctors treated people, while Vaishya families provided charity, food and medicines for poor people, orphans and sick people. Yet he also described harsh treatment for people regarded as outcastes. Thus, the account does not portray equal treatment for everyone.
points: Doctors treated people
Vaishya families gave charity, food and medicines
Poor people, orphans and sick people received care
People regarded as outcastes were treated harshly
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During the Gupta period, several kingdoms existed at the same time. A ruler planned to enlarge the empire through warfare, diplomacy and alliances. After the Vākāṭaka prince died, Prabhāvatī Gupta became regent ruler and was linked with the building of seven temples. The government recorded land grants to local leaders on copper plates. Traders carried textiles, spices, ivory and gemstones toward Mediterranean markets, sometimes stopping at Socotra Island. Indian traders lived there.
activities.prompt: The ruler wants to enlarge the empire while following Kauṭilya’s advice. What should the ruler do next?
options: Seek diplomatic and allied support as part of the saptānga.
Reject every alliance so that the ruler alone controls expansion.
Use alliances but leave them outside the saptānga.
Avoid warfare because expansion should depend only on diplomacy.

why.Reject every alliance so that the ruler: The advice supports alliances rather than rejecting them.
why.Use alliances but leave them outside the: Alliances should be included within the saptānga.
why.Avoid warfare because expansion should d: Warfare was also one of the methods used to expand the empire.

activities.explanation: This follows Kauṭilya’s advice to include alliances in the saptānga.

activities.context: During the Gupta period, several kingdoms existed at the same time. A ruler planned to enlarge the empire through warfare, diplomacy and alliances. After the Vākāṭaka prince died, Prabhāvatī Gupta became regent ruler and was linked with the building of seven temples. The government recorded land grants to local leaders on copper plates. Traders carried textiles, spices, ivory and gemstones toward Mediterranean markets, sometimes stopping at Socotra Island. Indian traders lived there.
activities.prompt: Which set of findings best shows that Indian traders lived on Socotra Island?
options: Pottery, Brahmi inscriptions and a Buddhist stūpa found there.
Textiles, spices, ivory and gemstones carried by traders.
Copper plates recording grants to local leaders.
The seven temples linked with Prabhāvatī Gupta.

why.Textiles, spices, ivory and gemstones ca: These were exports, not evidence of residence on the island.
why.Copper plates recording grants to local: Land grants were recorded for local leaders, not used as evidence of traders.
why.The seven temples linked with Prabhāvatī: The temple connection does not show where Indian traders lived.

activities.explanation: These findings show that Indian traders lived on Socotra.

activities.prompt: How did the Gupta government use different sources of income, and what did the revenue pay for?
activities.answer: The Gupta government collected taxes from land, mines, irrigation, trade and crafts. This revenue paid for administration, the army, temples and infrastructure. The government therefore used several sources of income to meet different needs and support the work of the state and religious institutions.
points: Taxes came from land, mines, irrigation, trade and crafts.
Revenue supported administration and the army.
Revenue also paid for temples and infrastructure.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain how Chandragupta II’s support for talented people enriched his court.
activities.answer: Chandragupta II surrounded himself with learned men, poets and artists. By supporting these talented people, he encouraged their contributions to court life. His support helped enrich the court, while peace and stability provided favourable conditions for major achievements during the Gupta period.
points: Chandragupta II gathered learned men, poets and artists.
He supported talented people.
Their contributions enriched his court.
Peace and stability supported major achievements.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A heritage club is preparing an exhibition on southern and northeastern kingdoms after Gupta decline. Members note that repeated Hūṇa attacks from Central Asia and conflicts among regional rulers weakened the empire. The Pallavas supported art and architecture; most rulers worshipped Śhiva and built magnificent temples and caves. Kānchipuram was known as the city of a thousand temples. Kāmarūpa covered the Brahmaputra valley and nearby northern areas. Samudragupta defeated rulers of both kingdoms but did not take direct control.
activities.prompt: Which explanation best accounts for why the Gupta Empire began showing signs of decline?
options: Both outside attacks and internal disputes added to the empire's weakness.
Only the outside attacks added to the weakness; internal disputes were unimportant.
Only internal disputes added to the weakness; outside attacks had no effect.
Both pressures remained outside Gupta territory and therefore could not affect the empire.

why.Only the outside attacks added to the we: This wrongly ignores conflicts among regional rulers.
why.Only internal disputes added to the weak: This wrongly ignores the repeated Hūṇa attacks.
why.Both pressures remained outside Gupta te: This mistakes the origin of the attacks for their effect on the empire.

activities.explanation: This answer identifies both causes of Gupta decline.

activities.context: A heritage club is preparing an exhibition on southern and northeastern kingdoms after Gupta decline. Members note that repeated Hūṇa attacks from Central Asia and conflicts among regional rulers weakened the empire. The Pallavas supported art and architecture; most rulers worshipped Śhiva and built magnificent temples and caves. Kānchipuram was known as the city of a thousand temples. Kāmarūpa covered the Brahmaputra valley and nearby northern areas. Samudragupta defeated rulers of both kingdoms but did not take direct control.
activities.prompt: What should the exhibition label say so that it does not confuse Samudragupta's victories with rule over the two kingdoms?
options: Military victory did not mean that Samudragupta ruled the Pallava or Kāmarūpa regions directly.
Both regions came under Samudragupta's direct rule after their rulers were defeated.
Samudragupta never defeated the ruler of either region.
Whenever a ruler was defeated in battle, the whole region automatically came under direct control.

why.Both regions came under Samudragupta's d: This wrongly treats defeat as direct rule.
why.Whenever a ruler was defeated in battle,: This wrongly assumes that every defeat leads to territorial control.

activities.explanation: This correctly separates military victory from political control.

activities.prompt: Explain why the Gupta Empire began showing signs of decline by the 6th century CE.
activities.answer: The empire faced pressure from two directions: repeated Hūṇa attacks from Central Asia and conflicts caused by powerful regional rulers. These outside attacks and internal disputes weakened the Gupta Empire, which had begun showing signs of decline by the 6th century CE.
points: Mentions repeated Hūṇa attacks from Central Asia.
Identifies conflict among powerful regional rulers.
Explains that outside attacks and internal disputes weakened the empire.
Places the beginning of decline in the 6th century CE.

chapters.title: How the Land Becomes Sacred
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what is sacredness?; pilgrimages and tīrthas; more sacred sites in nature; becoming aware of sacred geography.

lessons.title: What Is Sacredness?

activities.prompt: What makes a place feel sacred to people from different traditions?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Sacredness
activities.body: Sacredness means finding something of deep religious or spiritual importance. It can connect religion, spirituality and geography. A special place or shrine can bring deep respect and wonder. A pilgrimage is a special journey to a sacred place. Its route and the land it covers can also be sacred. Sacredness is connected with many different traditions.
keyPoints: Sacredness means deep religious or spiritual importance.
A pilgrimage is a special journey to a sacred place.
Sacredness connects religion, spirituality and geography.
activities.explanation: Sacredness can give places, journeys and land deep meaning.

activities.prompt: Why do people respect both a shrine and the path to it?
steps: A shrine can make people feel deep respect and wonder.
People call such a place sacred because it has deep religious or spiritual importance.
A pilgrimage is a special journey to a sacred place.
Its route and land can be sacred, so people can respect them.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Sacred Places of Different Traditions
activities.body: Buddhist sacred places include places visited by the Buddha and places where his relics are kept. Bodh Gaya receives more than four million visitors every year. In Sikhism, Takhts are seats or centres of spiritual authority. Their importance comes from their connection with Sikh Gurus.
keyPoints: Buddhist sacred places include places visited by the Buddha.
Some Buddhist sacred places keep the Buddha's relics.
Takhts are connected with Sikh Gurus.
activities.explanation: Different traditions have sacred places connected with important spiritual figures.

activities.prompt: What does sacredness mean?
options: A large number of visitors
A long journey by train
Religious or spiritual importance
A place for buying things
activities.explanation: Sacredness means finding something of deep religious or spiritual importance.

activities.prompt: Match each sacredness word with its correct meaning.
activities.explanation: Sacred places inspire respect, while Takhts hold spiritual authority in Sikhism.

activities.prompt: A special journey to a sacred place is called a ______.
activities.hint: This journey has a religious purpose.
activities.explanation: A pilgrimage is a special journey to a sacred place.

activities.prompt: Which statement about Bodh Gaya is correct?
options: More than four million visitors every month
Fewer than four million visitors every year
More than four million visitors every day
More than four million visitors every year
activities.explanation: Your book says Bodh Gaya receives more than four million visitors every year.

activities.prompt: What are Takhts in Sikhism?
options: Routes between sacred places
Shrines of other faiths
Seats of spiritual authority
Centres of Buddhist worship
activities.explanation: Takhts are seats or centres of spiritual authority in Sikhism.

activities.prompt: A pilgrim follows a special journey to a sacred place. What can also be sacred?
options: The traveller's new clothes
The route and the land it covers
The journey's bus tickets
Any nearby public park
activities.explanation: The route and the land covered by a pilgrimage can also be sacred.

activities.prompt: Children feel deep respect and wonder at a shrine. Why?
options: A special place can make people feel this way.
It is a busy market where people buy food.
It is close to many busy roads and shops.
It has more rooms than other nearby buildings.

why.It is a busy market where people buy foo: Wrong: this mistake treats shopping, not sacredness, as the cause.
why.It is close to many busy roads and shops: Wrong: this mistake focuses on nearby roads instead of sacred importance.
why.It has more rooms than other nearby buil: Wrong: this mistake focuses on room numbers instead of religious meaning.

activities.explanation: Right: a special place or shrine can create deep respect and wonder.

activities.prompt: After a pilgrimage, people respect the road and nearby land. Why?
options: A pilgrimage route and its land can also be sacred.
Only the final building can ever be sacred.
Every road becomes sacred after any journey.
Land cannot be sacred while a journey is happening.

why.Only the final building can ever be sacr: Wrong: this mistake limits sacredness to the destination.
why.Every road becomes sacred after any jour: Wrong: this mistake wrongly makes every journey route sacred.
why.Land cannot be sacred while a journey is: Wrong: this mistake wrongly separates sacred land from pilgrimages.

activities.explanation: Right: the route and the land it covers can also be sacred.

activities.prompt: The Buddha visited a marked place. Can it be sacred?
options: Yes, because places visited by the Buddha can be sacred.
No, because only places holding relics can be sacred.
No, because visited places are never religiously important.
Yes, because every visited building becomes a shrine.

why.No, because only places holding relics c: Wrong: this mistake wrongly leaves out places visited by the Buddha.
why.No, because visited places are never rel: Wrong: this mistake wrongly says visits cannot make places religious.
why.Yes, because every visited building beco: Wrong: this mistake confuses every visited building with a shrine.

activities.explanation: Right: Buddhist sacred places include places visited by the Buddha.

activities.prompt: Visitors from another faith enter an Indian shrine. What can this show?
options: It can show sacredness across many traditions.
It can show that only one faith visits shrines.
It can show that each faith rejects other shrines.
It can show that Indian shrines have no religious meaning.

why.It can show that only one faith visits s: Wrong: this mistake wrongly limits visits to one faith.
why.It can show that each faith rejects othe: Wrong: this mistake wrongly treats visits as rejection.
why.It can show that Indian shrines have no: Wrong: this mistake ignores the deep religious meaning of shrines.

activities.explanation: Right: sacredness connects with many traditions, and other-faith visitors visit shrines.
