lessons.title: Pilgrimages and Tīrthas

activities.prompt: What makes a journey to a sacred place special, inside and out?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is a Pilgrimage?
activities.body: Pilgrimages, also called tīrthayātrās, are journeys many Indians make to sacred sites. This ancient and continuous tradition has two parts: an outer journey and an inner journey. Pilgrims also follow a specified code of conduct. For thousands of years, people crossed the Subcontinent without modern transport. Their journeys made its geography sacred.
keyPoints: Pilgrimages are journeys to sacred sites.
A pilgrimage has an outer and inner journey.
Pilgrims follow a specified code of conduct.
activities.explanation: A pilgrimage joins an outer journey with an inner journey.

activities.prompt: A child reaches a sacred site but breaks its rules. Has the child completed a pilgrimage?
steps: The child's travel is the outer part of the pilgrimage.
The inner journey must also be part of the visit.
A specified code of conduct, or set of rules, is required.
Therefore, breaking the rules means the pilgrimage is not complete.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Sacred Places and Tīrthas
activities.body: In Jainism, tīrthas include places where Tīrthankaras attained liberation. Natural places visited by Tīrthankaras are also sacred. The Sabarimala temple is dedicated to Ayyappa and draws over ten million devotees every year. Natural landmarks along pilgrimage routes were also considered sacred.
keyPoints: Jain tīrthas include places of liberation.
Natural places can be sacred too.
Sabarimala is dedicated to Ayyappa.
activities.explanation: Natural places and pilgrimage landmarks can also hold sacred meaning.

activities.title: Pilgrims on a Journey
activities.prompt: What do many Indians undertake tīrthayātrās to visit?
options: Sacred sites
Large markets
New schools
Modern stations
activities.explanation: Many Indians undertake pilgrimages to sacred sites.

activities.title: An Old Tradition
activities.prompt: Pilgrimage is a new tradition in India.
activities.explanation: Pilgrimage is an ancient and continuous tradition in India.

activities.title: Two Kinds of Journey
activities.prompt: A pilgrimage is both an outer journey and an ______ journey.
activities.hint: Think about the journey within yourself.
activities.explanation: The lesson calls it both an outer journey and an inner journey.

activities.title: Match the Pilgrimage Links
activities.prompt: Match each place or idea with its lesson link.
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a place or group with its sacred role.

activities.title: Sabarimala Devotees
activities.prompt: How many devotees does the Sabarimala temple draw every year?
options: Over ten million
A small group
None every year
Only local visitors
activities.explanation: The Sabarimala temple draws over ten million devotees every year.

activities.title: Sacred Landmarks
activities.prompt: Natural landmarks along pilgrimage routes were also considered sacred.
activities.explanation: Natural landmarks along pilgrimage routes were considered sacred.

activities.prompt: A child reflects inwardly and follows site rules. What does this show?
options: It joins the outer and inner journeys while following conduct.
It makes only an outer journey because inward thoughts do not count.
It makes only an inner journey because walking there does not count.
It avoids pilgrimage because sacred sites require special rules.

why.It makes only an outer journey because i: This mistake treats the inner journey and conduct as unimportant.
why.It makes only an inner journey because w: This mistake thinks a pilgrimage has only an inner side.
why.It avoids pilgrimage because sacred site: This mistake thinks following rules means avoiding a pilgrimage.

activities.explanation: This choice connects the outer visit, inner journey, and required conduct.

activities.prompt: A map shows pilgrimage routes across the Subcontinent. What can we infer?
options: These journeys helped make the whole Subcontinent's geography sacred.
Every place on the map must be a Jain tīrtha.
Every route on the map must lead to one temple.
These routes show that pilgrims used modern transport across the region.

why.Every place on the map must be a Jain tī: This mistake treats every route endpoint as a Jain tīrtha.
why.Every route on the map must lead to one: This mistake assumes all pilgrimage routes led to one temple.
why.These routes show that pilgrims used mod: This mistake ignores that early pilgrims crossed without modern transport.

activities.explanation: Pilgrimage journeys made the Subcontinent's geography sacred.

activities.prompt: Sabarimala pilgrims follow rules and reflect inwardly. What journey are they making?
options: Both outer and inner, with the required code of conduct.
Only outer, because inward reflection is not part of pilgrimage.
Only inner, because the physical journey does not count.
Neither, because following rules means they are not pilgrims.

why.Only outer, because inward reflection is: This mistake believes pilgrimage has no inner journey.
why.Only inner, because the physical journey: This mistake treats only inward feelings as a pilgrimage.
why.Neither, because following rules means t: This mistake thinks code of conduct excludes people from pilgrimages.

activities.explanation: A pilgrimage includes both journeys and needs a code of conduct.

lessons.title: More Sacred Sites in Nature

activities.prompt: Why do people find divine meaning in mountains, rivers, trees, and stones?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sacred Elements of Nature
activities.body: Many Indian traditions regard elements of Nature as sacred. Some traditions also regard stones as sacred. Hindu traditions include many sacred mountains, rivers and forests. Many rivers are regarded as devīs. Some trees, animals and plants are regarded as especially holy. These traditions come from seeing a divine presence in all of Nature. Eventually, the whole of planet Earth is considered sacred.
keyPoints: Many Indian traditions regard elements of Nature as sacred.
Hindu traditions include sacred mountains, rivers and forests.
The whole of planet Earth is eventually considered sacred.
activities.explanation: This lesson explores how Nature is regarded as sacred in many Indian traditions.

activities.prompt: A family visits Niyam Dongar hill. They want to cut a tree for wood. What should they do?
steps: Because Niyam Dongar is sacred, its trees deserve respect.
Cutting trees there is prohibited because it shows disrespect to the deity.
Believing Niyam Raja provides their needs, they protect the hill.
So the family should leave the tree untouched and respect the hill.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which places are included in Hindu traditions?
options: Sacred mountains, rivers and forests
Busy markets, roads and shops
Plain houses and city gardens
Farm tools and clay pots
activities.explanation: Hindu traditions include many sacred mountains, rivers and forests.

activities.prompt: Some traditions regard stones as sacred.
activities.explanation: Yes, some traditions also regard stones as sacred.

activities.prompt: Match each part of Nature with what the lesson says.
pairs: Many Indian traditions regard them as sacred
Some traditions regard them as sacred
Hindu traditions include them as sacred
activities.explanation: The lesson connects many parts of Nature with ideas of sacredness.

activities.prompt: What does Niyam Raja provide for the Dongria Khond tribe?
options: What they need
Only a festival
A new sport
A type of food
activities.explanation: The Dongria Khond tribe believes Niyam Raja provides what they need.

activities.prompt: Which set of places did Sikkim identify as sacred?
options: Mountains, caves, lakes, rocks and hot springs
Shops, roads, buses and bridges
Toys, games, books and pens
Houses, farms, wells and fences
activities.explanation: Sikkim identified several sacred mountains, caves, lakes, rocks and hot springs.

activities.prompt: The hill sacred to the Dongria Khond tribe is ______ Dongar.
activities.hint: Think of the sacred hill mentioned in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Niyam Dongar hill is sacred to the Dongria Khond tribe.

activities.prompt: Niyam Dongar is sacred to the Dongria Khond tribe. What should visitors do?
options: Leave the trees there without cutting them.
Cut only young trees near the path.
Take wood after asking another visitor.
Remove branches but keep every trunk.

This mistakes visiting a sacred hill for permission to cut trees.
Taking wood still breaks the rule against cutting trees.
Removing branches also harms trees that should remain.

activities.explanation: Leaving the trees follows the rule against cutting them.

activities.prompt: Sikkim lists sacred mountains, caves, lakes, rocks and hot springs. The government rule says protect them from all damage. What must it do when a listed rock is damaged?
options: Stop the damage and protect the rock.
Move the rock to another sacred place.
Allow damage because the rock is old.
Ask visitors to ignore all listed places.

Moving the rock causes damage instead of preventing it.
This thinks age makes damage acceptable, but the rule forbids it.
why.Ask visitors to ignore all listed places: Visitors must not be told to ignore the protected places.

activities.explanation: The rule protects listed sacred places from every kind of damage.

activities.prompt: A map marks Niyam Dongar and peaks in the Nilgiris. What can the map and facts show together?
options: Both places have sacred meaning for communities.
Only the Nilgiri peaks belong to one tribe.
Niyam Dongar has no sacred meaning.
Only one place has special trees and rivers.

why.Only the Nilgiri peaks belong to one tri: This wrongly treats Niyam Dongar as having no sacred meaning.
This assumes sacred meaning belongs to only one community.
why.Only one place has special trees and riv: This confuses special places with places that have trees and rivers.

activities.explanation: Niyam Dongar and the Nilgiri peaks are both sacred to communities.

activities.prompt: A source says tree-cutting on Niyam Dongar disrespects the deity. What belief is behind this rule?
options: The trees are part of a sacred place.
The trees can provide food to everyone.
The trees cause the hill to become taller.
The trees are less important than metal.

This assumes the trees give food to everyone, which the source does not say.
why.The trees cause the hill to become talle: This reverses the meaning because the rule protects the sacred trees.
This ranks trees below metal, but no such rule is given.

activities.explanation: Niyam Dongar is sacred, so its trees must not be cut.

activities.prompt: Some rivers are regarded as devīs. Nature is seen as having a divine presence. What wider belief can follow?
options: The whole of planet Earth can be considered sacred.
Only rivers can be regarded as holy places.
Divine presence is found only in water.
People should stop seeing Nature as sacred.

why.Only rivers can be regarded as holy plac: This limits sacredness to rivers, but Nature is seen as divine throughout.
This wrongly restricts the divine presence to water.
why.People should stop seeing Nature as sacr: This mistakes belief in sacred Nature for a wish to reject it.

activities.explanation: A divine presence in all Nature leads to Earth being considered sacred.

activities.prompt: Sikkim protects listed sacred sites. The Dongria Khond tribe forbids cutting trees on Niyam Dongar. What do both actions show?
options: Sacred places should be protected from harm.
Sacred places should be used for cutting trees.
Sacred places matter only to local tourists.
Sacred places need no special care.

why.Sacred places should be used for cutting: This confuses protection with damaging sacred places.
why.Sacred places matter only to local touri: This wrongly limits sacred meaning to tourists.
This treats special care as unnecessary for sacred places.

activities.explanation: Both actions protect sacred places from harm or disrespect.

lessons.sceneCaption: Mawphlang Sacred Grove, a sacred forest in India.

lessons.title: Becoming Aware of Sacred Geography

activities.prompt: Have you ever wondered how sacred places connect people across India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sacred places and journeys across India
activities.body: Sacred places are spread across India, but they are closely connected. Some Hindus undertake the chār dhām yātrā, a journey to four sites. These sites lie near India's northern, southern, eastern and western corners. The 51 Shakti pīṭhas are sacred places linked with the divine mother. They cover the whole map of India. Pilgrims met different languages, customs, clothing and foods. They also saw what people had in common.
keyPoints: India's sacred places are spread out but interconnected.
Some Hindus undertake the chār dhām yātrā.
The Shakti pīṭhas belong to the divine mother's body story.
activities.explanation: Together, these ideas show a country connected by sacred places and journeys.

activities.prompt: A family travels between sacred places. Why might they meet different ways of life but still feel connected?
steps: They cross India, so they meet different languages, customs, clothing and foods.
These differences arise because people in different places live differently.
They also notice what people share, so common bonds appear among differences.
Thus, India's sacred places are spread across the country but interconnected.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does the lesson say about India's sacred places?
options: They all stand in the northern corner.
They are spread out but interconnected.
They cover only the eastern corner.
They are separate and never connected.
activities.explanation: These places are spread across India, but they remain interconnected.

activities.prompt: The 51 Shakti pīṭhas cover the whole map of ______.
activities.hint: This is the country where the sacred places stand.
activities.explanation: The lesson says the 51 Shakti pīṭhas cover the whole map of India.

activities.prompt: Put these stages of pilgrimage in the order described.
items: Meet different languages, customs, clothing and foods.
Notice what different people had in common.
activities.explanation: Pilgrims travelled, met varied ways of life, and also noticed shared things.

activities.prompt: Match each item to its connection in the lesson.
pairs: A journey undertaken by some Hindus
Places near India's northern, southern, eastern and western corners
Sacred places covering India's whole map
Ways to meet different languages, customs, clothing and foods
People with both differences and things in common
activities.explanation: These pairs connect different parts of the lesson about sites and journeys.

activities.prompt: The Shakti pīṭhas mark where parts of the divine mother's body ______.
activities.hint: The lesson gives this action in the story.
activities.explanation: The Shakti pīṭhas mark where parts of the divine mother's body fell.

activities.prompt: Which plan best matches the lesson's wider theme?
options: Connect sacred sites, India's land and pilgrims' observations.
Separate sacred sites, India's land and pilgrims.
Hide wider links and show only separate sites.
Show only foods and ignore India's sacred places.
activities.explanation: The lesson connects sacred places with India's land as the divine mother's body. It also connects them with pilgrims' observations.

activities.prompt: Some Hindus undertake the chār dhām yātrā. What does this journey show?
options: It connects sacred sites in different parts of India.
It keeps every sacred site in one small place.
It shows sacred places avoid the country's corners.
It means pilgrims never meet other cultures.

why.It keeps every sacred site in one small: This mistake assumes all sacred sites stay in one place.
why.It shows sacred places avoid the country: This mistake thinks the corner sites do not exist.
why.It means pilgrims never meet other cultu: This mistake assumes pilgrims avoid meeting other cultures.

activities.explanation: Right, because the four sites lie near different corners.

activities.prompt: A map shows four sites near corners and 51 Shakti pīṭhas. What do they show together?
options: Both spread sacred places across different parts of India.
Both gather every sacred site in one small area.
Both show that only one part of India matters.
Both show that sacred places avoid different regions.

why.Both gather every sacred site in one sma: This mistake puts all sacred places in one small area.
why.Both show that only one part of India ma: This mistake assumes one region is the only sacred region.
why.Both show that sacred places avoid diffe: This mistake thinks sacred places avoid different regions.

activities.explanation: Right, because corners and the whole map show wider spread.

activities.prompt: A source says Shakti pīṭhas mark where body parts fell. What idea is presented?
options: The whole Indian land is the divine mother's body.
Only one temple is the divine mother's body.
The mother's body lies beyond the Shakti pīṭhas.
Each pilgrim carries the mother's separate body.

why.Only one temple is the divine mother's b: This mistake limits her body to one temple.
why.The mother's body lies beyond the Shakti: This mistake places her body beyond the marked sites.
why.Each pilgrim carries the mother's separa: This mistake confuses a pilgrim with the whole land.

activities.explanation: Right, because the story presents all Indian land as her body.

activities.prompt: The 51 Shakti pīṭhas cover India's whole map. The story calls the land her body. What follows?
options: The whole country can be understood as the mother's body.
Only the northern corner can be the mother's body.
The mother's body must lie beyond India.
The 51 sites are separate from the country's land.

why.Only the northern corner can be the moth: This mistake limits the mother's body to one corner.
This mistake places the mother's body outside India.
why.The 51 sites are separate from the count: This mistake treats the sites as separate from the land.

activities.explanation: Right, because the sites cover the whole map of India.

activities.prompt: A class studies sacred-site maps and pilgrim stories. What should they conclude?
options: Journeys link spread-out sacred places and reveal shared ways.
Every place has identical customs and one sacred site.
Only local places are connected to sacred journeys.
Pilgrimage maps and stories show no connection.

why.Every place has identical customs and on: This mistake assumes all places have identical customs.
why.Only local places are connected to sacre: This mistake thinks only local places connect with journeys.
why.Pilgrimage maps and stories show no conn: This mistake assumes maps and stories reveal no links.

activities.explanation: Right, because maps and stories show spread, connections and shared ways.

lessons.title: Sacred Ecology: Rivers, Mountains and Forests

activities.prompt: Why do rivers, mountains, and forests feel special to people?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Nature as Sacred Space
activities.body: Many people see natural places as sacred. This sacred space is called puṇyakṣhetra. Tīrthas are often found beside rivers and lakes, or in forests and mountains. This sacred view has helped protect Nature. It joins geography, culture and spirituality. Sacred groves shelter great biodiversity.
keyPoints: Natural landscapes can be sacred puṇyakṣetras.
The sacred view helps protect Nature.
Geography, culture and spirituality meet in sacred places.
Sacred groves shelter plants and animals.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects sacred places with care for Nature.

activities.prompt: A town wants to protect a river and a forest. How can sacred ecology guide its choice?
steps: The river deserves care because rivers are lifelines for Indian civilisation.
The forest deserves care because sacred groves shelter great biodiversity.
Both fit puṇyakṣhetra because Nature can be seen as sacred space.
This sacred view has helped preserve Nature, so it can guide the town.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Name the Sacred Landscape
activities.prompt: Which term names the natural landscape as sacred space?
options: Kumbh Mela
puṇyakṣhetra
amṛta
Tīrtha
activities.explanation: Puṇyakṣhetra is the sacred name for the natural landscape.

activities.title: Match Sacred Places
activities.prompt: Match each place or idea with its lesson description.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a sacred view of nature. Sacred groves shelter plants and animals.

activities.title: The Kumbh Mela
activities.prompt: Where is the Kumbh Mela hosted every six years?
options: On a mountain
Inside a forest
In Prayagraj
In a sacred grove
activities.explanation: Prayagraj hosts the Kumbh Mela every six years.

activities.title: How Often?
activities.prompt: Prayagraj hosts the Kumbh Mela every ______ years.
activities.hint: Think about how often it returns.
activities.explanation: The Kumbh Mela returns to Prayagraj every six years.

activities.title: A Hymn about Rivers
activities.prompt: In the Ṛigveda hymn, how many major rivers are invoked?
options: Six
Three
Nineteen
Four
activities.explanation: The hymn invokes 19 major rivers of ancient northwest India.

activities.title: A Path through the Mountains
activities.prompt: Order the words along the mountain's sacred path.
activities.explanation: The lesson calls mountains gateways from earth to heaven.

activities.prompt: Rivers are lifelines for Indian civilisation, and Tīrthas often stand beside them. What may happen when people also see rivers as sacred?
options: They may protect nearby Nature more strongly.
They may stop caring about forests and groves.
They may hold a Kumbh Mela at every river.
They may treat mountains as the only sacred places.

why.They may stop caring about forests and g: This wrongly assumes sacred care would make people reject forests.
why.They may hold a Kumbh Mela at every rive: This confuses a special festival with what happens at every river.
why.They may treat mountains as the only sac: This wrongly makes mountains the only sacred landscapes.

activities.explanation: This is right because sacred views have helped people protect Nature.

activities.prompt: At Prayagraj, three rivers meet and the Kumbh Mela returns every six years. What makes its sacred journey different from a mountain journey?
options: Prayagraj centres on a river meeting; mountains centre on heaven.
Prayagraj centres on a sacred grove; mountains centre on rivers.
Prayagraj centres on amṛta drops; mountains centre on hymns.
Prayagraj centres on nineteen rivers; mountains centre on forests.

why.Prayagraj centres on a sacred grove; mou: This swaps the roles of river meeting places and forest groves.
why.Prayagraj centres on amṛta drops; mounta: This mistakes the amṛta legend for the main sacred feature.
why.Prayagraj centres on nineteen rivers; mo: This uses the hymn's nineteen rivers instead of Prayag's three.

activities.explanation: This is right because rivers meet at Prayag, while mountains lead toward heaven.

activities.prompt: A hymn in the Ṛigveda names 19 major rivers of ancient northwest India. What does this source tell us?
options: Rivers had an important place in ancient sacred thought.
Every ancient settlement stood beside a sacred grove.
Mountains were the only gateways from earth to heaven.
The Kumbh Mela began at nineteen separate river places.

why.Every ancient settlement stood beside a: This wrongly assumes every ancient settlement had a sacred grove.
why.Mountains were the only gateways from ea: This wrongly makes mountains the only sacred gateways.
why.The Kumbh Mela began at nineteen separat: This mixes the hymn's river count with the Kumbh legend's places.

activities.explanation: This is right because the hymn shows rivers mattered in sacred thought.

lessons.title: From Pilgrimage to Trade and Protecting Sacred Places

activities.prompt: What could pilgrims, traders, and communities learn from journeys to sacred places?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Journeys That Connected People
activities.body: Long journeys helped exchange goods and share beliefs. Pilgrims needed food and other items. Pilgrimage and trade routes often overlapped, and some traders travelled as pilgrims with goods. These journeys enriched people and integrated the Subcontinent’s culture. Sacred places and nature matter in many societies, so people often speak to protect them.
keyPoints: Travel connected goods, beliefs and different people.
Pilgrimage routes and trade routes often overlapped.
People protect environments, deities and values connected with sacred places.
activities.explanation: These links connected travel, beliefs, trade and care for sacred places.

activities.prompt: A pilgrim walks to a sacred place. A trader joins the same path and carries food.
steps: Pilgrims need food and other items, so traders can help them.
Pilgrimage and trade routes often overlap, so the two groups can meet.
Some traders travel as pilgrims while carrying goods, so one journey can serve both purposes.
Sharing goods, experiences and tales enriches the people who meet, so the journey can bring them together.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Sacred Places Across Societies
activities.body: Sacred geography means places that people treat as special. It is not unique to India. Ancient Greece had sacred mountains and groves. Native Americans traditionally had a special bond with Nature. The Maoris regard Taranaki Maunga as their sacred ancestor. People have spoken up to protect the environment, deities and values connected with sacred places.
keyPoints: Sacred geography is found beyond India.
Different societies connect special places with Nature and ancestors.
People speak up to protect sacred environments and values.
activities.explanation: Sacred places and Nature matter beyond India.

activities.prompt: Pilgrims needed ______ and other items that traders could provide.
activities.hint: This basic need is named in your book.
activities.explanation: Traders could provide food along with other needed items.

activities.prompt: How were pilgrimage routes and trade routes often connected?
options: They often shared the same routes.
They always stayed far apart.
They were used only by traders.
They carried no people or goods.
activities.explanation: The lesson says pilgrimage routes and trade routes often overlapped.

activities.prompt: Match each fact with its matching detail.
pairs: People travelled to discuss and debate
activities.explanation: Each pair shows how travel connected goods, beliefs and pilgrimage.

activities.prompt: What did Ancient Greece also have?
options: Trading ships and markets
Sacred mountains and groves
Pilgrims and sacred ancestors
Food and other items
activities.explanation: Ancient Greece had both sacred mountains and sacred groves.

activities.prompt: The Maoris regard ______ Maunga as their sacred ancestor.
activities.hint: Use the name given for the Maoris’ sacred ancestor.
activities.explanation: The Maoris regard Taranaki Maunga as their sacred ancestor.

activities.prompt: What have people spoken up to protect?
options: Trade routes, markets and merchants
Pilgrims, food and shared beliefs
Environment, deities and sacred values
Journeys, goods and distant places
activities.explanation: People have spoken up to protect sacred environments, deities and values.

activities.prompt: A merchant travels far to exchange goods. What may happen there?
options: He may share goods, experiences and tales with others.
He may keep every good hidden from other people.
He may meet only people from his own village.
He may finish every journey without speaking to anyone.

why.He may keep every good hidden from other: This assumes traders hide goods instead of exchanging them.
why.He may meet only people from his own vil: This wrongly assumes traders meet only people from one place.
why.He may finish every journey without spea: This assumes long journeys always end in isolation.

activities.explanation: Sharing goods, experiences and tales enriched the people who met.

activities.prompt: A pilgrim needs food. A trader shares that route. What may happen?
options: The pilgrim can get needed items from the trader.
The pilgrim should keep the trader away from the route.
The trader should wait until the pilgrim reaches home.
The pilgrim and trader must never meet each other.

why.The pilgrim should keep the trader away: This assumes sharing a route does not allow a useful meeting.
why.The trader should wait until the pilgrim: This assumes traders cannot help pilgrims along the way.
why.The pilgrim and trader must never meet e: This mistakes overlapping routes for a rule against meeting.

activities.explanation: Traders can provide pilgrims with food and other needed items.

activities.prompt: A map shows one path for pilgrims and traders. What can we infer?
options: The paths often overlap, so the groups may meet.
Traders never travel on any pilgrimage paths at all.
Pilgrims and traders always travel in separate groups.
Trade paths always run far away from pilgrimage paths.

why.Traders never travel on any pilgrimage p: This mistakes overlap for a rule that traders never join pilgrims.
why.Pilgrims and traders always travel in se: This assumes the two groups always stay completely separate.
why.Trade paths always run far away from pil: This overlooks that pilgrimage and trade routes often overlap.

activities.explanation: The map fits the fact that pilgrimage and trade routes often overlap.

activities.prompt: Native Americans valued Nature. Maoris honour Taranaki Maunga. What is the link?
options: Both show a special bond with Nature.
Both treat every mountain as their sacred ancestor.
Both think Nature has no spiritual importance.
Both follow exactly the same sacred traditions.

why.Both treat every mountain as their sacre: This turns one sacred mountain into a rule about every mountain.
why.Both think Nature has no spiritual impor: This mistakes a special bond with Nature for no spiritual bond.
why.Both follow exactly the same sacred trad: This assumes a shared bond means exactly the same traditions.

activities.explanation: Native Americans had a Nature bond, and Maoris see Taranaki as an ancestor.

activities.prompt: The government's rule protects sacred places. A local project may harm one. What should people do?
options: They should speak up to protect the place's environment.
They should ignore all harm to sacred places.
They should wait for the sacred place to disappear.
They should hide the harm from other people.

why.They should ignore all harm to sacred pl: This assumes a protective rule does not require care.
why.They should wait for the sacred place to: This mistakes delay for protection of the sacred place.
why.They should hide the harm from other peo: This treats harm as something to hide, not stop.

activities.explanation: Speaking up can protect the environment connected with sacred places.

activities.context: A family is planning a pilgrimage in India. They want to visit Bodh Gaya, where more than four million visitors arrive every year, and a Sikh Takht. One member believes that travelling along the route can make the journey sacred too. Another wonders why people of different faiths respect and visit these places. Together they consider how religion, spirituality and geography connect with the sites and the land they cover.
activities.prompt: If the family treats the route and covered land as sacred, what is most likely to happen?
options: They may feel respect and wonder throughout the journey.
They will regard every ordinary trip as a pilgrimage.
They will lose interest in the sacred places at the end.
They will avoid the route because its land cannot be holy.

why.They will regard every ordinary trip as: One sacred journey does not make every ordinary journey a pilgrimage.
why.They will lose interest in the sacred pl: Respecting the route does not remove interest in the destination.
why.They will avoid the route because its la: The situation treats the route and land as sacred, so avoiding them does not follow.

activities.explanation: Sacred places can create deep respect and wonder, so this may continue along the route.

activities.context: A family is planning a pilgrimage in India. They want to visit Bodh Gaya, where more than four million visitors arrive every year, and a Sikh Takht. One member believes that travelling along the route can make the journey sacred too. Another wonders why people of different faiths respect and visit these places. Together they consider how religion, spirituality and geography connect with the sites and the land they cover.
activities.prompt: Why might followers of other faiths also visit Indian shrines?
options: A shrine can have deep religious or spiritual importance for them too.
They believe a shrine matters only to people who share its faith.
They think visiting a shrine proves that all religions are exactly the same.
They believe every visit makes them followers of the shrine's faith.

why.They believe a shrine matters only to pe: The facts show that shrines can attract visitors from different faiths.
why.They think visiting a shrine proves that: Visiting a shrine does not prove that all religions are exactly the same.
why.They believe every visit makes them foll: Visiting a sacred place does not automatically change a person's faith.

activities.explanation: Followers of other faiths also visit many Indian shrines because these places can have spiritual importance.

activities.prompt: How are a pilgrimage and a sacred place different?
activities.answer: A pilgrimage is a special journey to a sacred place. Sacredness means deep religious or spiritual importance. The destination matters for this reason, but the route and land it covers can also be sacred. Thus, respect may include the whole journey and not only the final place.
points: A pilgrimage is a special journey.
Its destination is a sacred place.
Sacredness means deep religious or spiritual importance.
The route and land covered can also be sacred.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A family joins many Indians travelling to Sabarimala, where the temple is dedicated to Ayyappa. Their route crosses natural landmarks that people have regarded as sacred for thousands of years. For the student, the pilgrimage is not only the physical journey across the Subcontinent but also an inner journey. The family follows the required code of conduct while moving through this sacred geography.
activities.prompt: At a natural landmark on the route, what best shows that the student understands why it should be treated with respect?
options: Pause respectfully, because old journeys have made this part of the landscape sacred
Ignore it, since sacred geography concerns distant places rather than the route
Stop only to rest, because old journeys had no religious purpose
Treat it as an ordinary stop, because a place becomes sacred only after the pilgrimage ends

why.Ignore it, since sacred geography concer: This wrongly separates sacred places from the route travelled by pilgrims.
why.Stop only to rest, because old journeys: This mistakes the purpose of the old journeys.
why.Treat it as an ordinary stop, because a: This wrongly suggests that sacred meaning appears only at the destination.

activities.explanation: This connects the route with the Subcontinent's sacred geography.

activities.context: A family joins many Indians travelling to Sabarimala, where the temple is dedicated to Ayyappa. Their route crosses natural landmarks that people have regarded as sacred for thousands of years. For the student, the pilgrimage is not only the physical journey across the Subcontinent but also an inner journey. The family follows the required code of conduct while moving through this sacred geography.
activities.prompt: If the student feels tempted to ignore the pilgrimage's specified code of conduct, what should the student do?
options: Follow the code, because it is an essential part of undertaking a pilgrimage
Follow only the inner journey, because conduct rules do not matter
Choose personal behaviour freely, because crossing sacred geography has no religious meaning
Wait until the temple, because the code applies only to places of worship

why.Follow only the inner journey, because c: This wrongly treats the inner journey as separate from conduct.
why.Choose personal behaviour freely, becaus: This wrongly denies the religious meaning of the journey.
why.Wait until the temple, because the code: This wrongly limits the code to the destination.

activities.explanation: This correctly includes conduct within the idea of pilgrimage.

activities.prompt: How do the ideas of pilgrimage, sacred geography, and Tīrthas connect with one another?
activities.answer: A pilgrimage combines an outer journey, an inner journey, and a specified code of conduct. For thousands of years, people crossed the Subcontinent without modern transport, and this made the geography sacred. Tīrthas include places where Tīrthankaras attained liberation, while natural places visited by them are also sacred.
points: A pilgrimage has an outer and an inner journey.
A pilgrimage also requires a specified code of conduct.
Old journeys across the Subcontinent helped make its geography sacred.
Tīrthas and natural places visited by Tīrthankaras are connected with sacredness.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a school activity, Meera learns that the Dongria Khond tribe treats Niyam Dongar as a sacred hill. The community believes Niyam Raja provides what people need, so cutting trees there is not allowed. Meera also hears that Sikkim has protected sacred mountains, caves, lakes, rocks and hot springs from damage. She learns that the Toda community of the Nilgiris regards many mountain peaks as sacred. Her class begins asking how these traditions shape care for Nature.
activities.prompt: A visitor asks Meera whether a tree on Niyam Dongar may be cut. What should she advise?
options: Ask the visitor to leave the tree standing, because the community's sacred rule applies there.
Allow the tree to be removed, because sacred status applies to the hill rather than its trees.
Allow some branches to be cut, because a smaller cut may be treated differently.
Encourage the removal, because the visitor's wishes matter more than the community's belief.

why.Allow the tree to be removed, because sa: This wrongly separates the hill's sacredness from its trees.
why.Allow some branches to be cut, because a: The tradition gives no permission for partial cutting.
why.Encourage the removal, because the visit: This wrongly ignores the community's sacred belief.

activities.explanation: The community does not permit cutting trees on the hill.

activities.context: At a school activity, Meera learns that the Dongria Khond tribe treats Niyam Dongar as a sacred hill. The community believes Niyam Raja provides what people need, so cutting trees there is not allowed. Meera also hears that Sikkim has protected sacred mountains, caves, lakes, rocks and hot springs from damage. She learns that the Toda community of the Nilgiris regards many mountain peaks as sacred. Her class begins asking how these traditions shape care for Nature.
activities.prompt: Which conclusion best fits the Toda community's view of mountain peaks?
options: The peaks have spiritual importance and should not simply be treated as ordinary ground.
The peaks matter less than other features of Nature.
Sacred mountains do not need protection from damage.
Their sacred view applies only to peaks outside the Nilgiris.

why.The peaks matter less than other feature: This wrongly makes the peaks less important within Nature.
why.Sacred mountains do not need protection: Sacred traditions support protecting such places from harm.
why.Their sacred view applies only to peaks: The community's own tradition concerns peaks of the Nilgiris.

activities.explanation: The community regards many peaks as sacred.

activities.prompt: Explain how seeing a divine presence in all of Nature can lead to protecting sacred sites.
activities.answer: Seeing a divine presence in all of Nature leads people to treat natural features as sacred. Mountains, rivers, forests, stones, trees, animals and plants may therefore receive special care. Protected sites are kept from damage to show respect, and this wider idea eventually extends to the whole planet.
points: Nature is seen as containing a divine presence.
Natural features may be regarded as sacred.
Protecting sacred sites prevents damage and shows respect.
The idea eventually extends to the whole planet.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student joins a pilgrimage that connects sacred places in different parts of India. The route includes one of the four sites of the chār dhām yātrā and also passes near a Shakti pīṭha. While travelling, the student meets people who speak different languages and follow different customs. Their clothing and food also vary. Yet the student finds that they share common ways of understanding the sacred places. The journey shows how the whole land is connected through sacred geography.
activities.prompt: The student sees that people along the route have different languages, customs, clothing and foods. What conclusion best fits the idea of sacred geography?
options: The differences between regions do not remove what people share across the country.
People who speak different languages cannot recognise any common beliefs.
Common beliefs belong only to people living in one region.
Sacred journeys make regional languages, customs and foods unimportant.

why.People who speak different languages can: This wrongly assumes that language differences prevent shared beliefs.
why.Common beliefs belong only to people liv: This wrongly limits common beliefs to one region.
why.Sacred journeys make regional languages,: This wrongly treats regional differences as unimportant.

activities.explanation: This correctly recognises that differences and commonalities can exist together.

activities.context: A student joins a pilgrimage that connects sacred places in different parts of India. The route includes one of the four sites of the chār dhām yātrā and also passes near a Shakti pīṭha. While travelling, the student meets people who speak different languages and follow different customs. Their clothing and food also vary. Yet the student finds that they share common ways of understanding the sacred places. The journey shows how the whole land is connected through sacred geography.
activities.prompt: If the student travels onward to another part of India, what is most likely to happen next?
options: The student will meet more regional differences while also noticing shared understandings.
The student will find that all people have exactly the same language, customs, clothing and food.
The student will stop noticing differences because every sacred place has the same culture.
The student will meet only people from one region because sacred journeys stay in one place.

why.The student will find that all people ha: The facts state that differences exist, not that everything is exactly the same.
why.The student will stop noticing differenc: The facts do not suggest that every sacred place has the same culture.
why.The student will meet only people from o: Pilgrims travel across India rather than remaining in one place.

activities.explanation: Pilgrims encounter both regional differences and commonalities as they travel.

activities.prompt: Explain why sacred places can help people feel connected even when their journeys cross different regions.
activities.answer: The four sites of the chār dhām yātrā lie near India’s northern, southern, eastern and western corners. Pilgrims travelling among them cross India and encounter different languages, customs, clothing and foods. They also notice what people have in common, showing that people remain connected through sacred journeys.
points: The four sites lie near the four corners of India.
Pilgrims encounter different languages, customs, clothing and foods.
People can notice what they have in common despite these differences.
Sacred journeys help connect people across the country.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Prayagraj is preparing for the Kumbh Mela, which arrives every six years. Pilgrims come to worship at the meeting point of three rivers. Nearby forests and mountains are also treated as sacred space. As visitor numbers grow, town leaders want to clear trees and widen roads. Some residents argue that the community should protect Nature and respect the sacred character of the landscape instead.
activities.prompt: What should the town leaders do before clearing trees or widening roads?
options: Protect the trees and river areas while planning for visitors
Clear more forest to make room for roads and buildings
Remove the sacred meaning of the landscape to reduce pressure
Build over the river meeting point so pilgrims can gather more easily

why.Clear more forest to make room for roads: Extra clearing would damage forests that shelter wildlife.
why.Remove the sacred meaning of the landsca: Sacred meaning should not be removed for development.
why.Build over the river meeting point so pi: The river meeting point has religious importance.

activities.explanation: This protects Nature and respects sacred space.

activities.context: Prayagraj is preparing for the Kumbh Mela, which arrives every six years. Pilgrims come to worship at the meeting point of three rivers. Nearby forests and mountains are also treated as sacred space. As visitor numbers grow, town leaders want to clear trees and widen roads. Some residents argue that the community should protect Nature and respect the sacred character of the landscape instead.
activities.prompt: What could happen if the nearby sacred groves were cleared?
options: Wildlife could lose an important place of shelter
Wildlife could gain more shelter from sunlight
The river could lose its importance as a lifeline
The mountains could stop being viewed as sacred

why.Wildlife could gain more shelter from su: Less forest would not increase wildlife shelter.
why.The river could lose its importance as a: Clearing groves would not affect the river's role.
why.The mountains could stop being viewed as: Clearing forests does not change the meaning of mountains.

activities.explanation: Sacred groves shelter many plants and animals.

activities.prompt: Why are rivers, forests and mountains important in the lesson on sacred ecology?
activities.answer: Natural landscapes are understood as puṇyakṣhetra, or sacred space. Tīrthas may be beside rivers and lakes, in forests or on mountains. Rivers are lifelines for Indian civilisation, while sacred groves shelter great biodiversity. This sacred view joins geography, culture and spirituality and has helped people protect and preserve Nature.
points: Explains puṇyakṣhetra
Links sacred places with natural landscapes
Includes the importance of rivers and groves
Connects sacredness with protecting Nature
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Merchants travelled from town to town, carrying goods that pilgrims and local residents needed. On one route, a pilgrim and a trader travelled together. The trader also joined the pilgrimage, while the pilgrim shared stories from other places. Nearby, residents protected a sacred grove because it had religious importance. After meeting, everyone gained new experiences, and the cultures of the Indian Subcontinent became more integrated.
activities.prompt: If traders stopped providing food and other items along this route, what would most likely happen next?
options: Pilgrims would find it harder to complete their journeys.
Local residents would lose interest in meeting travellers.
The sacred grove would become more important to merchants.
Stories from other places would no longer be shared.

why.Local residents would lose interest in m: The loss of supplies would make travel more difficult.
why.The sacred grove would become more impor: Local residents would still meet travellers.
why.Stories from other places would no longe: People could still exchange stories and experiences.

activities.explanation: Pilgrims depended on traders for essential items.

activities.context: Merchants travelled from town to town, carrying goods that pilgrims and local residents needed. On one route, a pilgrim and a trader travelled together. The trader also joined the pilgrimage, while the pilgrim shared stories from other places. Nearby, residents protected a sacred grove because it had religious importance. After meeting, everyone gained new experiences, and the cultures of the Indian Subcontinent became more integrated.
activities.prompt: What should residents do if a trading activity threatens a sacred grove?
options: Speak up to protect the sacred place and its environment.
Remove the grove so traders can continue freely.
Ask the trader to ignore all local beliefs.
Replace the grove with goods for travellers.

why.Remove the grove so traders can continue: Protecting the environment can include defending a sacred grove.
why.Ask the trader to ignore all local belie: Removing a sacred place would not protect it.
why.Replace the grove with goods for travell: Ignoring local beliefs would not show respect.

activities.explanation: People have spoken up to protect sacred places.

activities.prompt: Explain how pilgrimage and trade helped integrate the culture of the Indian Subcontinent.
activities.answer: Merchants and pilgrims often used overlapping routes, and some traders also travelled as pilgrims. Pilgrims needed food and other supplies from traders. Their meetings allowed people to share goods, experiences and tales. These exchanges enriched the people involved and helped bring the different cultures of the Indian Subcontinent closer together.
points: Traders supplied food and other items to pilgrims.
Pilgrimage and trade routes often overlapped.
People exchanged goods, experiences and tales.
These exchanges promoted cultural integration.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: How the Land Becomes Sacred

activities.prompt: Which idea best matches sacredness?
options: Deep religious importance
A long journey to trade
A route without special meaning
A place used for daily work
activities.explanation: Sacredness means deep religious or spiritual importance. A sacred place can inspire respect and wonder.

activities.prompt: A pilgrimage can be both an outer journey and an inner journey.
activities.explanation: A pilgrimage includes the physical journey and the inner experience. This makes it both outer and inner.

activities.prompt: Bodh Gaya receives more than ______ million visitors every year.
activities.hint: Use the number from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Bodh Gaya receives more than four million visitors every year. It is connected with the Buddha.

activities.prompt: Match each tradition with its sacred places or features.
pairs: Places visited by the Buddha or holding his relics
activities.explanation: Each pair names a tradition and one of its sacred places or features.

activities.prompt: What does the lesson say about Sabarimala?
options: It is dedicated to Ayyappa
It is dedicated to Niyam Raja
It marks a place of Jain liberation
It holds the relics of the Buddha
activities.explanation: Sabarimala is dedicated to Ayyappa and draws over ten million devotees yearly. Natural landmarks on its route are also sacred.

activities.prompt: Put the four site corners in clockwise order, starting with north.
activities.explanation: The four sites lie near the northern, southern, eastern and western corners. Clockwise from north is east, south, then west.

activities.prompt: Cutting trees on Niyam Dongar shows respect to its deity.
activities.explanation: The Dongria Khond tribe prohibits cutting trees there. This act shows disrespect to the deity.

activities.prompt: Prayagraj hosts the Kumbh Mela every ______ years.
activities.hint: Think about how often the Kumbh Mela returns.
activities.explanation: Prayagraj hosts the Kumbh Mela every six years. Prayag lies where three rivers meet.

activities.prompt: What does the Shakti pīṭha story say about India's land?
options: As the body of the divine mother
As a record of every trade route
As a list of forest animals
As a map of modern cities
activities.explanation: The story presents the whole land as the divine mother's body. The Shakti pīṭhas mark where parts of her body fell.

activities.prompt: Match each group or place with its connection to sacred geography.
pairs: Sometimes travelled as pilgrims while carrying goods
Had sacred mountains and sacred groves
Regard Taranaki Maunga as a sacred ancestor
activities.explanation: These pairs show how journeys connect with sacred places. Sacred geography is also found beyond India.

chapters.title: Types of Governments
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what government does; democracy and the functions of government; how governments differ and democracy’s principles; different forms of democratic government.

lessons.title: What Government Does

activities.prompt: How does government help us every day?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What Government Does
activities.body: Government plays an important role in our lives. It maintains law and order, which means keeping society safe and peaceful. It helps ensure peace, stability and security. It manages relationships with other countries. It is responsible for national defence, or protecting the country. It delivers important goods and services, manages the economy, and works to improve people’s lives.
keyPoints: Government maintains law and order.
Government protects the country and manages relationships with other countries.
Government delivers important goods and services and works to improve people’s lives.
activities.explanation: Government helps society in many important ways.

activities.prompt: Children cannot play safely. Families also need clean water. What should the government do?
steps: Government must maintain law and order because children need safe spaces.
It must ensure peace and security because fear can stop daily life.
It should deliver important goods and services because families need clean water.
Together, these duties show that government works to improve people’s lives.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Democratic Governments
activities.body: India has a democratic form of government. Many countries have democratic governments too. Democratic governments are not all exactly the same. This means countries can have democratic governments that differ from one another. The lesson introduces these ideas about democratic government.
keyPoints: India has a democratic form of government.
Many countries have democratic governments.
Democratic governments are not all exactly the same.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you understand how countries can have different democratic governments.

activities.prompt: Which one is a responsibility of government?
options: Maintaining law and order in society
Managing relationships between shops
Choosing games for children
Deciding the weather each day
activities.explanation: Government maintains law and order in society. It also protects the country through national defence.

activities.prompt: Government manages ______ with other countries.
activities.hint: This word means the connections between countries.
activities.explanation: Government manages relationships with other countries.

activities.prompt: Government maintains law and order in society.
activities.explanation: Yes. Maintaining law and order helps keep society safe and peaceful.

activities.prompt: Which group contains only government responsibilities?
options: Law and order; the economy; national defence
Law and order; children’s games; the weather
Relationships with other countries; running games; family pets
National defence; delivering goods and services; family friendships
activities.explanation: Government maintains law and order, manages the economy, and is responsible for national defence.

activities.prompt: Match each government area to what it does.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an important government responsibility.

activities.prompt: Which statement about democratic governments is true?
options: Many countries have no democratic government.
India has a democratic form of government.
Democratic governments are all exactly the same.
Only one country can have a democratic government.
activities.explanation: India has a democratic form of government. Many countries have democratic governments too, and they are not all exactly the same.

activities.prompt: A market fight has started. Which action shows government maintaining law and order?
options: Arranging guards to stop the fighting and restore peace.
Buying goods that every market seller will sell.
Choosing a new song for the market opening.
Managing prices so the market economy keeps working.

why.Buying goods that every market seller wi: This confuses delivering goods with maintaining law and order.
why.Choosing a new song for the market openi: This mistake assumes a celebration can maintain law and order.
why.Managing prices so the market economy ke: This confuses managing the economy with maintaining law and order.

activities.explanation: Guards can maintain law and order by stopping the fight.

activities.prompt: A village has no safe water. Which action best shows government delivering important services?
options: Providing clean water as an important public service.
Stopping every fight in the nearby village.
Managing relations with the country next door.
Guarding the village from an outside attack.

why.Stopping every fight in the nearby villa: This repeats the law-and-order duty instead of showing service delivery.
why.Managing relations with the country next: This mistakes foreign relationships for delivery of a local service.
why.Guarding the village from an outside att: This confuses national defence with delivering important services.

activities.explanation: Clean water is an important service that government can deliver.

activities.prompt: India and another country have democratic governments. Which thought is correct?
options: Their governments can still differ from each other.
Their governments must work in exactly the same way.
Their governments cannot differ in any way.
Their governments must all choose the same leaders.

why.Their governments must work in exactly t: This mistake treats democratic governments as exactly identical.
why.Their governments cannot differ in any w: This mistake believes democratic governments cannot differ at all.
why.Their governments must all choose the sa: This mistake treats similar systems as having the same leaders.

activities.explanation: Democratic governments are not all exactly the same.

activities.prompt: A picture shows soldiers guarding the border. Which government duty is shown?
options: Protecting the country from outside threats.
Delivering water to families far away.
Managing relationships between nearby schools.
Keeping prices steady at the market.

This confuses national defence with delivering important services.
why.Managing relationships between nearby sc: This mistakes relationships between governments for relationships between schools.
This confuses managing the economy with national defence.

activities.explanation: Guarding the border shows the government protecting the country.

activities.prompt: After a market fight, guards restore peace. How can daily life improve?
options: They can shop and move around with greater safety.
They can trade directly with people in other countries.
They can stop needing any important public services.
They can use the same rules as every other country.

why.They can trade directly with people in o: This confuses foreign relationships with local law and order.
why.They can stop needing any important publ: This mistake assumes better security removes the need for services.
why.They can use the same rules as every oth: This mistake assumes democratic governments all follow exactly the same rules.

activities.explanation: Restored law, order and peace can make daily life feel safer.

activities.prompt: Two countries want to avoid trouble. Which government action helps most?
options: Managing their relationship so both countries stay peaceful.
Delivering water to every family in both countries.
Choosing the same songs for both national teams.
Running every shop in both countries directly.

why.Delivering water to every family in both: This confuses delivering services with managing foreign relationships.
why.Choosing the same songs for both nationa: This mistake assumes matching songs are part of foreign relationships.
why.Running every shop in both countries dir: This confuses managing the economy with managing foreign relationships.

activities.explanation: Managing relationships helps countries avoid trouble and keep peace.

lessons.title: Democracy and the Functions of Government

activities.prompt: How do people make choices, create rules, and shape their government?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Democracy Works
activities.body: Democracy means the rule of the people. In a democracy, people are the source of government power. They select representatives to govern them. Government creates, implements and enforces rules. These functions are called creating rules, implementing rules and ensuring obedience. Making rules is the legislative function.
keyPoints: People are the source of government power.
People select representatives to govern them.
Government creates, implements and enforces rules.
activities.explanation: Democracy gives power to the people through their representatives.

activities.prompt: Your class wants to choose a student representative. How can the class do this in a democratic way?
steps: Democracy means the rule of the people, so the people should choose.
Students can choose representatives through voting, so voting fits this choice.
The people select representatives to govern them, so the class should choose one.
Therefore, the class should vote, because people are the source of government power.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Meaning of Democracy
activities.prompt: What does democracy mean?
options: The rule of the people
The rule of one person
The rule of a small group
The rule of no one
activities.explanation: Democracy means that the people are the rulers.

activities.prompt: In democracy, the people are the source of government power.
activities.explanation: Government power comes from the people in a democracy.

activities.title: The Source of Power
activities.prompt: In a democracy, the people are the ______ of government power.
activities.hint: Power comes from the people.
activities.explanation: The people are the source of government power.

activities.title: People and Representatives
activities.prompt: Match each word to what the lesson says about it.
activities.explanation: People hold the power and select representatives. Students can choose them through voting.

activities.title: Who Governs the People?
activities.prompt: What do the people select to govern them?
options: Rules to implement daily
Representatives to govern them
Schools to manage classes
Duties to obey daily
activities.explanation: The people select representatives to govern them.

activities.title: A Famous Description
activities.prompt: Who described democracy as a government of, by and for the people?
options: A school leader
A local officer
Abraham Lincoln
A student voter
activities.explanation: Abraham Lincoln described democracy as a government of, by and for the people.

activities.prompt: Your class votes for two students to speak for everyone. Why is voting democratic?
options: The people choose representatives to govern them.
One student chooses all the representatives.
Representatives choose the people who voted.
The people give up their power to one leader.

why.One student chooses all the representati: This confuses choosing representatives with letting one person control the choice.
why.The people give up their power to one le: This wrongly treats chosen leaders as the only source of power.

activities.explanation: This is right because voting lets people select representatives.

activities.prompt: Place A lets people vote for representatives. Place B lets one leader choose every representative. Which place is more democratic?
options: Place A, because the people choose representatives.
Place B, because one leader chooses everyone.
Place A, because voting removes government power.
Place B, because representatives should select leaders.

why.Place B, because one leader chooses ever: This wrongly treats one leader's choice as the people's choice.
why.Place A, because voting removes governme: This confuses choosing representatives with removing government power.
why.Place B, because representatives should: This reverses the roles of representatives and people.

activities.explanation: This is right because the people select representatives in Place A.

activities.prompt: A class record shows students voting for a representative. What does this record tell us?
options: Students chose someone to govern them.
Students ruled without choosing any representative.
Representatives chose the students who voted.
Students had no power in choosing a leader.

why.Students ruled without choosing any repr: This confuses choosing representatives with ruling without representatives.
why.Students had no power in choosing a lead: This wrongly denies that people are the source of power.

activities.explanation: This is right because voting lets students select a representative.

activities.prompt: A government makes a rule. It puts the rule into action and checks obedience. Why are all three actions needed?
options: Creating, implementing, and enforcing rules are government functions.
Creating rules is useful, but the other two actions are not.
Implementing rules means making them for the first time.
Enforcing rules means replacing the rule with a new one.

why.Creating rules is useful, but the other: This wrongly leaves out implementation and enforcement.
why.Implementing rules means making them for: This confuses implementing a rule with creating it.
why.Enforcing rules means replacing the rule: This confuses enforcing a rule with replacing it.

activities.explanation: This is right because all three actions are government functions.

activities.prompt: People choose their leaders, and leaders make rules for everyone. Why is this government of, by, and for the people?
options: People are the source of government power.
Government power comes only from chosen leaders.
People choose leaders, but leaders hold all the power.
Rules are made by leaders without any people.

why.Government power comes only from chosen: This wrongly makes chosen leaders the only source of power.
why.People choose leaders, but leaders hold: This wrongly takes government power away from the people.
why.Rules are made by leaders without any pe: This wrongly removes the people from the government's authority.

activities.explanation: This is right because people are the source of government power.

lessons.title: How Governments Differ and Democracy’s Principles

activities.prompt: What helps us compare governments and understand what makes them fair?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Governments and Democracy
activities.body: In Indian democracy, people decide who holds authority. Democratic governments are usually formed through elections. A constitution contains the country’s fundamental rules. A theocracy gets authority from religious beliefs. In a kingdom, a ruling family member usually rules. Equality means equal treatment, and governments may seek shared prosperity. Universal adult franchise means eligible citizens can vote. Eligible means allowed to vote. All people may choose and elect representatives.
keyPoints: People choose who holds authority in Indian democracy.
Governments differ in where their authority comes from.
Equality, voting and representatives are important principles.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you compare governments and understand citizens’ rights.

activities.prompt: Two classes choose their monitors. Class A votes. Class B lets one family keep choosing. Which choice fits democracy?
steps: Class A gives people the choice because people decide who holds authority.
Voting fits democracy because democratic governments are usually formed through elections.
Class B resembles a kingdom because a ruling family usually continues to rule.
Therefore, Class A’s voting choice fits democracy better than Class B’s family choice.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Who Holds Authority?
activities.prompt: In Indian democracy, who decides who holds authority?
options: A ruling family decides
Religious leaders decide
The people decide
One body always decides
activities.explanation: In Indian democracy, the people decide who holds authority.

activities.title: Match Government Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each government idea with its correct description.
pairs: The people decide who holds authority
A ruling family member usually continues to rule
activities.explanation: Each description shows where authority or the country’s rules come from.

activities.title: The Country’s Rules
activities.prompt: A constitution contains the country’s ______ rules.
activities.hint: Choose the word before “rules”.
activities.explanation: A constitution contains the country’s fundamental rules.

activities.title: Government Functions
activities.prompt: Which answer correctly describes government functions?
options: Only one elected body
One or separate bodies
Only one royal body
Only one religious body
activities.explanation: Government functions may be performed by separate bodies or one body.

activities.title: Universal Adult Franchise
activities.prompt: What does universal adult franchise give eligible citizens?
options: Every citizen must vote
Only rulers may vote
Votes belong to leaders
The right to vote
activities.explanation: Universal adult franchise gives every eligible citizen the right to vote.

activities.title: Choosing Representatives
activities.prompt: Which right lets every person choose representatives?
options: Choosing and electing representatives
Choosing a family member
Choosing a religious leader
Keeping one ruler in power
activities.explanation: Every person has the right to choose and elect representatives.

activities.prompt: People in a country vote to choose their representatives. Who will hold authority?
options: The people will decide who holds authority.
Religious beliefs will decide who holds authority.
The ruling family will usually continue to rule.
One separate body will perform every government function.

why.Religious beliefs will decide who holds: This mistake assumes authority must come from religious beliefs.
why.The ruling family will usually continue: This mistake assumes a ruling family keeps power without a vote.
why.One separate body will perform every gov: This mistake confuses government functions with who holds authority.

activities.explanation: This is right because voting lets the people choose who holds authority.

activities.prompt: Place A holds elections. Place B lets a king decide how it works. What difference does this show?
options: In Place A, people choose who holds authority.
In Place A, religious beliefs choose who holds authority.
In Place A, the ruling family usually continues to rule.
In Place A, one body performs all government functions.

why.In Place A, religious beliefs choose who: This mistake treats religious beliefs as the source of government authority.
why.In Place A, the ruling family usually co: This mistake assumes a kingdom’s family rule belongs in Place A.
why.In Place A, one body performs all govern: This mistake confuses authority with how government functions are done.

activities.explanation: Place A uses elections, so the people choose who holds authority.

activities.prompt: A country’s constitution sets its fundamental rules. A new voting rule changes those basic rules. What should happen?
options: The new voting rule should follow the constitution.
The voting rule should ignore the constitution completely.
The voting rule should come only from religious beliefs.
The voting rule should choose a ruling family instead.

why.The voting rule should ignore the consti: This mistake treats fundamental rules as if they do not matter.
why.The voting rule should come only from re: This mistake thinks religious beliefs should replace constitutional rules.
why.The voting rule should choose a ruling f: This mistake uses family rule instead of the country’s fundamental rules.

activities.explanation: The constitution sets fundamental rules, so the new rule must follow them.

activities.prompt: Some governments work towards equality and prosperity for everyone. Two students have the same need. One gets better treatment only because the teacher likes them. Which rule should guide the teacher?
options: Give the same needed help to both students.
Give extra help only to the student the teacher likes.
Give no help to either student because their needs are equal.
Give help first to the family that holds more power.

why.Give extra help only to the student the: This mistake lets personal liking decide treatment instead of equality.
why.Give no help to either student because t: This mistake thinks equal treatment means giving no needed help.
why.Give help first to the family that holds: This mistake lets family power decide who receives equal treatment.

activities.explanation: Equality means every person should be treated equally.
