lessons.title: Different Forms of Democratic Government

activities.prompt: How do people make decisions together, and who gets to choose their leaders?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Different Democracies Work
activities.body: Direct democracy lets citizens join decisions directly. Representative democracy uses elected representatives. People elect them through universal adult franchise. Universal adult franchise means all adult citizens vote. Representatives stay accountable to people. Most democracies today use this form. A legislature is an elected group of legislators. In parliamentary democracy, executive members also belong to this group. In presidential democracy, people elect the president. The executive works independently of the legislature.
keyPoints: Direct democracy lets citizens join decisions directly.
Representative government stays accountable to the people.
Most democracies today are representative democracies.
Parliamentary executive members belong to the legislature.
Presidential executives work independently of the legislature.
activities.explanation: These features help you compare how citizens, representatives and executives take part.

activities.prompt: A large country finds direct democracy hard. Can citizens still have a say through elected representatives?
steps: Direct democracy lets citizens take part in decisions directly.
It is difficult in a large country because decisions need direct participation.
Representative democracy lets people elect representatives through universal adult franchise.
Thus, a large country can use representative democracy and stay accountable to people.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Citizens Taking Part
activities.prompt: In direct democracy, citizens take part in decisions:
options: Through the president
Through representatives
Through elections only
Directly
activities.explanation: That is the key idea of direct democracy. Citizens take part in decisions directly.

activities.title: India's Election Interval
activities.prompt: In India, general elections take place every ______ years.
activities.hint: Use the fixed interval given for India.
activities.explanation: India holds general elections every five years. These elections take place at regular and fixed intervals.

activities.title: Forms and Features
activities.prompt: Match each democracy form with a feature from the lesson.
pairs: Executive members belong to the legislature
The executive works independently of the legislature
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a feature of that democracy form. You matched citizens and government members correctly.

activities.title: Parliamentary Democracy
activities.prompt: What happens in parliamentary democracy?
options: People elect the executive directly.
Executive members also belong to the legislature.
The president works independently of the legislature.
Adult voters belong to the legislature.
activities.explanation: People elect the legislature, but not the executive. Executive members also belong to the legislature.

activities.title: Presidential Democracy
activities.prompt: Who is elected by the people in presidential democracy?
options: The legislature
The executive
Adult voters
The president
activities.explanation: In presidential democracy, people elect the president. The executive works independently of the legislature.

activities.title: Comparing Democracy Forms
activities.prompt: Which statement about democracy is correct?
options: Most democracies are direct; governments avoid elections.
Parliamentary executives are directly elected by people.
Most democracies are representative; governments stay accountable.
Presidential executives work with the legislature.
activities.explanation: Most democracies today are representative democracies. Their governments stay accountable to the people.

activities.prompt: In a large country, direct democracy is difficult. What may happen if every citizen must decide each matter?
options: Many citizens may find participation hard every time.
Every citizen will decide each matter very easily.
The country will soon stop holding any elections.
The executive will work outside the elected legislature.

why.Every citizen will decide each matter ve: This wrongly assumes that many citizens make participation easy.
why.The country will soon stop holding any e: This wrongly assumes that direct democracy removes elections.
why.The executive will work outside the elec: This wrongly mixes direct democracy with presidential democracy.

activities.explanation: Direct democracy is difficult because many citizens must take part.

activities.prompt: Place A has citizens deciding directly. Place B has people electing representatives. In which place must elected officials remain accountable to the people?
options: Place B, because its government is representative.
Place A, because its government is representative.
Neither place, because only presidents are accountable.
Place B, because its citizens make every decision.

why.Place A, because its government is repre: This confuses direct democracy with representative democracy.
why.Neither place, because only presidents a: This wrongly limits accountability to presidential governments.
why.Place B, because its citizens make every: This confuses choosing representatives with deciding directly.

activities.explanation: A representative government must always be accountable to the people.

activities.prompt: A map shows a large country. A source says people elect representatives. Why may this match representative democracy?
options: Direct democracy is difficult in such a large country.
Direct democracy needs no citizens to take part.
Representatives are chosen only by the executive.
Large countries can hold elections at changing times.

why.Direct democracy needs no citizens to ta: This wrongly assumes that citizens do not participate directly.
why.Representatives are chosen only by the e: This wrongly says that the executive chooses representatives.
why.Large countries can hold elections at ch: This wrongly denies that elections have fixed intervals.

activities.explanation: Direct democracy is difficult to practise in large countries.

activities.prompt: Representatives are chosen through universal adult franchise. Elections come at regular, fixed intervals. What must be true of this government?
options: It remains accountable to the people.
It need not remain accountable to the people.
Citizens make every government decision directly.
Representatives are elected once, with no later elections.

why.It need not remain accountable to the pe: This wrongly denies the accountability of representative government.
why.Citizens make every government decision: This confuses representative democracy with direct democracy.
why.Representatives are elected once, with n: This wrongly ignores regular, fixed elections.

activities.explanation: A representative government is always accountable to the people.

lessons.title: Early Republics and Monarchy

activities.prompt: How could ancient communities choose leaders without passing power to their children?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How republics and monarchies work
activities.body: A republic has an elected head of state, not a monarch who inherits the position. The Uttaramerur inscriptions describe village sabhā elections. In the Vajji mahajanapada, leaders were chosen for merit, not birth. In some ancient Greece, women, workers and slaves could not vote. A monarchy is ruled by a monarch. Absolute monarchs control law-making. Constitutional monarchs have little real power. In Britain, the elected parliament makes laws.
keyPoints: A republic has an elected head of state.
A monarchy is ruled by a monarch.
Britain's elected parliament makes laws.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you compare republics and monarchies.

activities.prompt: Two toy countries have different rules. One has an elected parliament making laws and a monarch with nominal power. The other lets its monarch control laws. Which is a constitutional monarchy?
steps: The first country is constitutional because its monarch has only nominal power.
Its elected parliament makes laws, so elected representatives have law-making power.
The second country is absolute because its monarch controls law-making.
Therefore, a monarchy alone does not show who really makes the laws.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which statement describes a republic?
options: An elected head of state leads it.
A hereditary monarch leads it.
A ruler makes all laws alone.
A monarch has only nominal power.
activities.explanation: A republic has an elected head of state who is not a hereditary monarch.

activities.prompt: In the Vajji mahajanapada, leaders were chosen for ______ rather than birth.
activities.hint: This word means worth or ability.
activities.explanation: The Vajji mahajanapada chose leaders for merit rather than birth.

activities.prompt: Which statement about voting in ancient Greece is correct?
options: In some parts, women, workers and slaves could not vote.
In some parts, women, workers and slaves could all vote.
In some parts, women could vote, but workers could not.
In some parts, slaves could vote, but women could not.
activities.explanation: Women, workers and slaves could not vote in some parts of ancient Greece.

activities.prompt: The Uttaramerur inscriptions describe elections to the village ______.
activities.hint: Use the name given in your book.
activities.explanation: The inscriptions describe elections to the village sabhā.

activities.prompt: Match each government system to its feature.
activities.explanation: Each system has a different way of choosing leaders and making laws.

activities.prompt: Which statement about absolute monarchy is correct?
options: The monarch controls the making of laws.
The elected parliament makes the laws.
The monarch has only nominal power.
The people elect the head of state.
activities.explanation: In an absolute monarchy, the monarch controls the making of laws.

activities.prompt: In Britain, the elected parliament makes laws. In Saudi Arabia, the monarch controls law-making. How do the two systems differ?
options: Britain's elected parliament makes laws; Saudi Arabia's monarch controls them.
Saudi Arabia's elected parliament makes laws; Britain's monarch controls them.
Both countries let elected parliaments make all the laws.
Both countries give monarchs full control over every law.

why.Saudi Arabia's elected parliament makes: This swaps the law-making power of Britain and Saudi Arabia.
why.Both countries let elected parliaments m: This wrongly gives both countries elected parliaments with law-making power.
why.Both countries give monarchs full contro: This wrongly gives both countries monarch control over law-making.

activities.explanation: This matches the stated law-making power in each country.

activities.prompt: A historian studies the Uttaramerur inscriptions. What can the source show about village sabhā membership?
options: Members of the village sabhā were chosen through elections.
Members of the village sabhā were chosen only by royal birth.
The village sabhā held no elections for any of its members.
The village sabhā received members from a hereditary king alone.

why.Members of the village sabhā were chosen: This mistakes elected membership for choosing leaders by birth.
why.The village sabhā held no elections for: This denies the elections that the inscriptions actually describe.
why.The village sabhā received members from: This turns recorded elections into hereditary royal selection.

activities.explanation: The inscriptions directly describe elections to the village sabhā.

activities.prompt: A guide says that all people in ancient Greece could vote. Which detail would correct this broad claim?
options: In some parts, women, workers and slaves could not vote.
In some parts, women, workers and slaves could vote.
In some parts, women and workers could vote but slaves could not.
In some parts, slaves could vote but women and workers could not.

why.In some parts, women, workers and slaves: This reverses the fact by making all three groups able to vote.
why.In some parts, women and workers could v: This wrongly allows women to vote, although they could not.
why.In some parts, slaves could vote but wom: This wrongly allows slaves to vote, although they could not.

activities.explanation: This gives the exact groups excluded and keeps the “some parts” limit.

activities.prompt: A raja is guided by an assembly. People say that the raja can be questioned. Why can they say this?
options: The raja's power was not absolute, and people's welfare came first.
The raja's power was absolute, so nobody could question decisions.
The raja cared mainly for personal power, not people's welfare.
Assemblies existed only to make every royal command unquestionable.

why.The raja's power was absolute, so nobody: This confuses limited raja power with absolute monarchy.
why.The raja cared mainly for personal power: This reverses the raja's priority of the people's welfare.
why.Assemblies existed only to make every ro: This misreads assemblies that guided kings as unquestioning supporters.

activities.explanation: This fits the facts on limited power and welfare first.

lessons.title: Theocracy, Dictatorship, Oligarchy and Democracy

activities.prompt: Have you ever wondered who should have the power to make decisions?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Four Forms of Government
activities.body: Governance can take several forms. A theocracy follows religious rules and leaders. A dictatorship gives absolute power to one person or a small group. An oligarchy lets a small powerful group make important decisions. Democracy is considered better than other forms. Its government protects rights, and people can change representatives through elections.
keyPoints: A theocracy follows religious rules and leaders.
A dictatorship gives absolute power to one person or a small group.
An oligarchy gives important decisions to a small powerful group.
A democracy protects rights and allows people to change representatives.
activities.explanation: These forms differ in who holds power and how decisions are made.

activities.prompt: How can citizens stop one leader from gaining absolute power?
steps: This resembles a dictatorship because one person holds absolute power.
A democratic government is accountable because it must protect people's rights.
Elections help because citizens can change their representatives.
Therefore, democracy is better because it makes government accountable and gives people a way to change it.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: How is a theocracy ruled?
options: Through elected representatives
According to religious rules
By a small powerful group
With one absolute leader
activities.explanation: A theocracy is ruled according to religious rules and leaders.

activities.prompt: Match each form of government with its main feature.
activities.explanation: You matched each form with its main feature. Nice work!

activities.prompt: In a dictatorship, one person or a small group has absolute power.
activities.explanation: Yes! A dictatorship gives absolute power to one person or a small group.

activities.prompt: Which statement about Iran is correct?
options: It combines religious rules and absolute power.
It combines theocratic and democratic elements.
It combines small-group rule and absolute power.
It contains only theocratic government elements.
activities.explanation: Iran combines theocratic and democratic governance, as your lesson explains.

activities.prompt: People can change their representatives through ______.
activities.hint: This is how people choose new representatives.
activities.explanation: The lesson says that elections can change representatives.

activities.prompt: How can corruption, unequal wealth and excessive control affect democracy?
options: Democracy may be protected.
Democracy may be hindered.
Democracy may be improved.
Democracy may be unchanged.
activities.explanation: Corruption, unequal wealth and excessive control can all hinder democracy.

activities.prompt: One person makes every important decision in a country. What problem is most likely?
options: One person may use absolute power without limits.
One person must follow rules made by citizens.
One person will need to protect citizens' rights.
One person will soon lose power through elections.

why.One person must follow rules made by cit: This wrongly assumes dictatorship makes leaders answerable to citizens.
why.One person will need to protect citizens: This confuses dictatorship with democracy, where government protects rights.
why.One person will soon lose power through: This confuses dictatorship with democracy, where elections can change representatives.

activities.explanation: One person with absolute power can act without limits.

activities.prompt: A map marks Iran, Afghanistan and Vatican City with religious rule. What can we learn?
options: All three are theocracies, but Iran also has democratic elements.
All three are democracies, but Iran also has religious elements.
Only Iran is theocratic, while the other two are democracies.
Only Vatican City is theocratic, while the other two are democratic.

why.All three are democracies, but Iran also: This mistakes religious rule for democracy and misses Iran's democratic elements.
why.Only Iran is theocratic, while the other: This misses that Afghanistan and Vatican City are also theocracies.
why.Only Vatican City is theocratic, while t: This misses that Iran and Afghanistan also have religious rule.

activities.explanation: Iran combines religious and democratic rule; the other two are theocracies.

activities.prompt: Hitler passed laws giving himself full power and removing opposition. Why did this weaken opposition?
options: The laws left him with full power and took away rivals.
The laws gave opponents more power and protected their rights.
The laws made every leader answerable through elections.
The laws gave opposition groups more control over leaders.

why.The laws gave opponents more power and p: This reverses the laws, which took power from Hitler's rivals.
why.The laws made every leader answerable th: This confuses dictatorship with democracy, where representatives can be changed.
why.The laws gave opposition groups more con: This assumes opposition gained control, which the laws prevented.

activities.explanation: The laws gave Hitler full power and eliminated opposition.

activities.prompt: Idi Amin was responsible for mercilessly killing thousands. Why is democratic accountability important?
options: It helps them protect rights and stop unchecked power.
It helps them keep all power in one pair of hands.
It lets them remove elections and concentrate government power.
It makes cruel killing an accepted part of government.

why.It helps them keep all power in one pair: This mistakes accountability for concentrating absolute power.
why.It lets them remove elections and concen: This confuses accountability with removing democratic elections.
why.It makes cruel killing an accepted part: This mistakes protection of rights for accepting cruel killing.

activities.explanation: Accountability helps protect rights and prevents power from becoming unchecked.

activities.prompt: A small powerful group makes important decisions. No single person has absolute power. Which comparison is right?
options: An oligarchy has group power; dictatorship can give one person absolute power.
An oligarchy has one-person power; dictatorship gives power to every citizen.
An oligarchy gives citizens elections; dictatorship gives leaders religious rules.
An oligarchy protects every right; dictatorship gives all citizens power.

why.An oligarchy has one-person power; dicta: This swaps oligarchy's group power for one-person power.
why.An oligarchy gives citizens elections; d: This confuses oligarchy with elections and dictatorship with religious rule.
why.An oligarchy protects every right; dicta: This confuses oligarchy's limited group power with power for everyone.

activities.explanation: Oligarchy uses group power; dictatorship can give one person absolute power.

activities.context: A community in India faced concerns about safety and the uneven availability of important goods and services. The government maintained law and order, delivered support, and worked to improve people’s lives. It also managed relations with another country and upheld national defence. Residents knew that India had a democratic form of government, but they had learned that democratic governments in different countries were not exactly the same.
activities.prompt: If the government stopped maintaining law and order in the community, what would be the most likely result?
options: People could feel less safe and secure.
More important goods and services would reach the community.
The country’s relationship with another country would improve.
The government would find it easier to improve people’s lives.

why.More important goods and services would: Delivering goods and services does not directly maintain security.
why.The country’s relationship with another: Foreign relationships do not by themselves maintain law and order.
why.The government would find it easier to i: Improving lives often depends on people feeling safe and secure.

activities.explanation: Maintaining law and order helps ensure peace, stability, and security.

activities.context: A community in India faced concerns about safety and the uneven availability of important goods and services. The government maintained law and order, delivered support, and worked to improve people’s lives. It also managed relations with another country and upheld national defence. Residents knew that India had a democratic form of government, but they had learned that democratic governments in different countries were not exactly the same.
activities.prompt: If the government did not manage its relationship with another country, which result would be most likely?
options: Its ability to support national defence and security could be affected.
The delivery of important goods and services would stop completely.
The government would no longer work to improve people’s lives.
India’s democratic form of government would change.

why.The delivery of important goods and serv: Government services can continue while foreign relationships are managed.
why.The government would no longer work to i: Improving daily life can remain a goal even if foreign relations change.
why.India’s democratic form of government wo: The democratic form of government is separate from foreign relationships.

activities.explanation: Managing foreign relationships can support national defence and security.

activities.context: A community in India faced concerns about safety and the uneven availability of important goods and services. The government maintained law and order, delivered support, and worked to improve people’s lives. It also managed relations with another country and upheld national defence. Residents knew that India had a democratic form of government, but they had learned that democratic governments in different countries were not exactly the same.
activities.prompt: How should the residents compare India’s democratic government with the democratic government of another country?
options: Study how each improves daily life without assuming they are identical.
Treat them as identical because both have democratic governments.
Compare only their economic management and ignore other responsibilities.
Assume that one government has no responsibility for maintaining security.

why.Treat them as identical because both hav: A shared democratic label does not make every government exactly the same.
why.Compare only their economic management a: Comparing only the economy ignores other important government duties.
why.Assume that one government has no respon: Democratic governments still have responsibilities such as maintaining security and serving people.

activities.explanation: Democratic governments can differ while still working to improve people’s lives.

activities.prompt: Why does the government play an important role in our lives?
activities.answer: Government is important because it keeps society orderly and helps people feel safe. It provides important goods and services, manages the economy and relationships with other countries, and is responsible for national defence. These duties help create peace, stability, security, and better everyday lives.
points: Maintains law and order
Helps ensure peace, stability, and security
Provides goods and services and manages the economy
Handles foreign relationships and national defence
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A community held an election so that the people could select representatives to govern them. After voting, the elected representatives agreed that the community needed rules for its meetings. One representative said that making rules was the government’s legislative function. The representatives then had to implement the rules and make sure people obeyed them.
activities.prompt: The community wants a new rule for its meetings. What should the representatives do first?
options: Use the government’s law-making power to create the meeting rule.
Implement an existing rule instead of creating the new one.
Ensure obedience to a rule that has not yet been made.
Select new representatives before creating the meeting rule.

why.Implement an existing rule instead of cr: Implementation comes after the rule has been created.
why.Ensure obedience to a rule that has not: Obedience cannot be ensured before a rule exists.
why.Select new representatives before creati: Voting selects representatives; it is not a rule-making function.

activities.explanation: Creating a rule is the government’s legislative function.

activities.context: A community held an election so that the people could select representatives to govern them. After voting, the elected representatives agreed that the community needed rules for its meetings. One representative said that making rules was the government’s legislative function. The representatives then had to implement the rules and make sure people obeyed them.
activities.prompt: Why did the election give the selected representatives authority to govern the community?
options: Because the people chose them to govern, showing that government power comes from the people.
Because voting allowed the representatives to become the source of government power.
Because the representatives created their own power after the election.
Because government power belongs to the rules rather than to the people.

why.Because voting allowed the representativ: Representatives receive authority to govern from the people.
why.Because the representatives created thei: Representatives govern because the people select them.
why.Because government power belongs to the: Government power comes from the people, not from rules.

activities.explanation: The people are the source of government power in democracy.

activities.context: A community held an election so that the people could select representatives to govern them. After voting, the elected representatives agreed that the community needed rules for its meetings. One representative said that making rules was the government’s legislative function. The representatives then had to implement the rules and make sure people obeyed them.
activities.prompt: The representatives have made a meeting rule, but it is not being followed. What should they do?
options: Implement the rule and ensure that it is obeyed.
Make another rule instead of putting the first one into practice.
Select new representatives instead of dealing with the rule.
Use voting to create government power before enforcing the rule.

why.Make another rule instead of putting the: Making another rule does not deal with obedience to the first rule.
why.Select new representatives instead of de: The problem concerns implementing and enforcing a rule, not choosing representatives.
why.Use voting to create government power be: Voting identifies representatives but does not replace the need to enforce rules.

activities.explanation: Implementing and enforcing rules are government functions.

activities.prompt: Explain why making rules is different from implementing and enforcing rules.
activities.answer: Making rules is the legislative function because it involves creating the rule that guides the community. Implementing and enforcing rules are separate functions: implementation puts the rule into practice, while enforcement ensures obedience. A government must perform all three functions.
points: Creating rules is the legislative function.
Implementing rules puts them into practice.
Enforcing rules ensures obedience.
A government performs all three functions.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In India, an election has been held, and eligible adult citizens have chosen representatives to govern. The constitution states the country’s fundamental rules, and separate bodies perform different government functions. The government says it will work towards equality and prosperity for everyone. However, some eligible adults are still being left out of voting, and citizens argue that every person should have the right to choose representatives.
activities.prompt: If elections were cancelled and a member of the ruling family took over, what would happen to the country’s form of government?
options: It would take a monarchy-like form because authority would rest with the ruling family.
It would remain democratic because the people chose the earlier representatives.
It would become a theocracy because religious beliefs would now decide authority.
Authority would still belong to the people because voting had already taken place.

why.It would remain democratic because the p: An earlier election alone would not preserve democratic government after the change.
why.It would become a theocracy because reli: Religious authority is a feature of a theocracy, but it is not mentioned in the change.
why.Authority would still belong to the peop: People hold authority in democracy, but a ruling family taking over changes that arrangement.

activities.explanation: A ruling family continuing to hold authority is characteristic of a monarchy.

activities.context: In India, an election has been held, and eligible adult citizens have chosen representatives to govern. The constitution states the country’s fundamental rules, and separate bodies perform different government functions. The government says it will work towards equality and prosperity for everyone. However, some eligible adults are still being left out of voting, and citizens argue that every person should have the right to choose representatives.
activities.prompt: If voting is changed so that every eligible citizen can vote, which principle has been adopted?
options: Universal adult franchise.
A system in which only some eligible adults may vote.
A system in which representatives choose who may vote.
A system in which voting depends on membership in one family.

why.A system in which only some eligible adu: Leaving some eligible adults without voting rights does not provide universal adult franchise.
why.A system in which representatives choose: Allowing representatives to choose voters would remove citizens’ direct voting rights.
why.A system in which voting depends on memb: Family membership should not determine the right to vote.

activities.explanation: Universal adult franchise gives every eligible citizen the right to vote.

activities.prompt: How do democracy, theocracy and kingdom differ in the source of authority?
activities.answer: In a democracy, the people decide who holds authority, and democratic governments are usually formed through elections. In a theocracy, authority comes from religious beliefs. In a kingdom, a member of the ruling family usually continues to rule. Therefore, the source and usual method of authority are different.
points: In democracy, the people decide who holds authority.
Democratic governments are usually formed through elections.
In a theocracy, authority comes from religious beliefs.
In a kingdom, the ruling family usually continues to rule.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: India is a large country, so holding a direct vote on every public decision is difficult. Instead, people use representative democracy: adults elect representatives through universal adult franchise, and the representatives remain accountable to the people. Elections are held at regular, fixed intervals, with general elections every five years. Most democracies today work in this representative way.
activities.prompt: If India tried to replace representative government with direct democracy for all decisions, what problem would be most likely?
options: It would be hard to manage because the country is large.
It would give the executive sole control over decisions.
It would make every decision quicker and easier.
It would make representatives answerable to the executive instead of voters.

why.It would give the executive sole control: Direct participation means citizens, not the executive, make decisions directly.
why.It would make every decision quicker and: A large country makes direct decision-making difficult, not easy.
why.It would make representatives answerable: A representative government must always remain accountable to the people.

activities.explanation: Direct democracy is difficult to practise in large countries.

activities.context: India is a large country, so holding a direct vote on every public decision is difficult. Instead, people use representative democracy: adults elect representatives through universal adult franchise, and the representatives remain accountable to the people. Elections are held at regular, fixed intervals, with general elections every five years. Most democracies today work in this representative way.
activities.prompt: If the next general election in India were brought forward before the usual time, what would change?
options: India would break its usual five-year election cycle.
India would become a direct democracy.
Representatives would no longer be accountable to the people.
The executive and legislature would automatically become one.

Changing election timing does not change the form of democracy.
why.Representatives would no longer be accou: A change in timing does not remove representatives' accountability.
why.The executive and legislature would auto: Changing when elections occur does not merge the executive and legislature.

activities.explanation: India holds general elections every five years.

activities.prompt: Explain how parliamentary democracy differs from presidential democracy.
activities.answer: In parliamentary democracy, people elect the legislature, and executive members also belong to the legislature. In presidential democracy, people elect the president, and the executive works independently of the legislature. Therefore, the key differences are the method of choosing the executive and its relationship with the legislature.
points: People elect the legislature in parliamentary democracy.
Executive members also belong to the legislature.
People elect the president in presidential democracy.
The presidential executive works independently of the legislature.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A village held an election for its sabhā, as described in the Uttaramerur inscriptions. In the Vajji mahajanapada, leaders were chosen for merit rather than birth. Elsewhere, a raja consulted an assembly and regarded his people’s welfare as his highest priority. His power was not always absolute. In Britain, the elected parliament makes the laws.
activities.prompt: If the village elected a head of state who was not a hereditary monarch, what form of government would it have?
options: A republic
A monarchy
An absolute monarchy
A constitutional monarchy

why.A monarchy: A monarchy is ruled by a monarch.
why.An absolute monarchy: An absolute monarchy gives the monarch control over laws.
why.A constitutional monarchy: A constitutional monarchy gives the monarch only nominal power.

activities.explanation: An elected, non-hereditary head indicates a republic.

activities.context: A village held an election for its sabhā, as described in the Uttaramerur inscriptions. In the Vajji mahajanapada, leaders were chosen for merit rather than birth. Elsewhere, a raja consulted an assembly and regarded his people’s welfare as his highest priority. His power was not always absolute. In Britain, the elected parliament makes the laws.
activities.prompt: Suppose the raja in the case ignored the assembly and controlled the making of laws. Which system would the government most closely resemble?
options: An absolute monarchy
A republic
A constitutional monarchy
A monarchy led by an elected head of state

why.A republic: A republic has an elected, non-hereditary head of state.
why.A constitutional monarchy: A constitutional monarch has only nominal power.
why.A monarchy led by an elected head of sta: A monarchy is ruled by a monarch, not an elected head.

activities.explanation: Controlling lawmaking is a feature of absolute monarchy.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a republic and a monarchy.
activities.answer: A republic has an elected head of state who is not a hereditary monarch. A monarchy is government ruled by a monarch. An absolute monarchy is one in which the monarch controls the making of laws. A constitutional monarchy gives the monarch only nominal power.
points: Republic: elected head of state
Head of state is not a hereditary monarch
Monarchy: ruled by a monarch
Absolute and constitutional monarchies differ in royal power
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In Iran, governance combines elements of theocratic and democratic rule. In the democratic part, citizens can change representatives through elections, and government is accountable for protecting people’s rights. However, corruption, unequal wealth, and excessive control can hinder democracy. A group of citizens is considering how to respond when representatives fail to protect rights.
activities.prompt: The citizens think representatives are not protecting people’s rights. What is the most democratic response?
options: Use an election to replace the representatives.
Give one person absolute power to correct the problem quickly.
Keep the same representatives even if rights remain unprotected.
Stop elections and leave representatives in place permanently.

why.Give one person absolute power to correc: Giving one person absolute power would move government toward dictatorship.
why.Keep the same representatives even if ri: Keeping representatives despite unprotected rights would not use the democratic means of change.
why.Stop elections and leave representatives: Ending elections would prevent citizens from changing representatives and weaken democratic accountability.

activities.explanation: Elections allow people to change representatives and demand better protection of rights.

options: Maintaining social order

activities.explanation: Democratic governments are not all exactly the same.

activities.prompt: Democracy means the rule of the ______.
activities.hint: This group is the source of government power.
activities.explanation: In democracy, the people are the source of government power.

activities.prompt: Match each government idea with its correct feature.
activities.explanation: Making rules is legislative, and direct participation defines direct democracy. Adult franchise gives eligible citizens voting rights; absolute monarchs control laws.

activities.prompt: Put these government functions in the correct order.
activities.explanation: A government creates rules, implements them and ensures obedience.

activities.prompt: In parliamentary democracy, who also belongs to the legislature?
options: The executive members
Only religious leaders
All market traders
Every foreign visitor
activities.explanation: In parliamentary democracy, executive members also belong to the legislature.

activities.prompt: In presidential democracy, the president is elected by the people.
activities.explanation: The executive works independently of the legislature in presidential democracy.

activities.prompt: What does a country's constitution contain?
options: Its fundamental rules
Its family tree
Its weather records

activities.prompt: Match each form of government with its correct feature.
pairs: Power held by one or a few
activities.explanation: Monarchies are ruled by monarchs. Republics have elected non-hereditary heads, theocracies use religious rules, and dictators hold absolute power.

chapters.title: The Constitution of India — An Introduction
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what is a constitution?; writing the constitution of india; what shaped and influenced the indian constitution?; key features of the constitution of india.

lessons.title: What Is a Constitution?

activities.prompt: How does a constitution help a country stay fair and organized?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Constitution as a Rulebook
activities.body: The Constitution of India is the supreme document that important national officials pledge to uphold. It gives a nation's basic principles and laws in writing. It sets the framework of the legislature, executive and judiciary. They are the three parts of government. It explains their roles and responsibilities. It uses checks and balances to keep government fair and accountable. It lists citizens' rights, duties, long-term goals and aspirations.
keyPoints: The Constitution gives basic principles and laws in writing.
It explains the framework and roles of government organs.
It protects fairness and lists citizens' rights and duties.
activities.explanation: A Constitution works like a rulebook for the whole country.

activities.prompt: A country needs rules for government, laws, citizens, and future goals. What should guide it, and why?
steps: It writes basic principles and laws, so the nation's rules are clear.
It explains lawmaking, implementation, and government formation, so government work is clear.
It balances government branches and lists citizens' rights and duties for fairness.
It records long-term goals, so the supreme rulebook covers the nation's future.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which statement about the Constitution of India is correct?
options: It records citizens' favourite festivals and foods.
It sets basic principles, laws and government roles.
It chooses the daily work of every government officer.
It removes checks between the three government organs.
activities.explanation: The Constitution writes down basic principles, laws and the structure of government.

activities.prompt: The Constitution sets out the framework of the legislature, ______ and judiciary.
activities.hint: This is one of the three parts of government.
activities.explanation: The legislature, executive and judiciary are the three parts of government.

activities.prompt: The Constitution gives a nation's basic principles and laws in writing.
activities.explanation: Yes. The written Constitution sets down these principles and laws.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the Constitution with what it includes.
activities.explanation: The Constitution covers laws, citizens, national goals and the structure of government.

activities.prompt: Why does a Constitution use checks and balances?
options: To choose the country's long-term holidays.
To remove the roles of government organs.
To keep government fair and accountable.
To keep laws outside the written Constitution.
activities.explanation: Checks and balances help make government fair and accountable.

activities.prompt: A constitution explains how laws are made and implemented. What else does it explain?
options: How families choose their meals for every evening of the week.
Which cities open their biggest local markets during each year.
What schools serve in their canteens during every school week.
Who elects the executive and how the judiciary is formed.
activities.explanation: The Constitution also explains the election of the executive and the formation of the judiciary.

activities.prompt: A rule stops one government branch from controlling another. What effect does this have?
options: It makes government fairer and more accountable.
It gives citizens a list of duties.
It chooses the nation's long-term goals.
It decides who forms the judiciary.

This confuses checks with citizens' rights.
This confuses government fairness with citizens' duties.
This confuses government fairness with national goals.

activities.explanation: This is the direct effect of checks and balances.

activities.prompt: A source shows three government branches and citizens' rights and duties. It also shows national goals. What does it show?
options: It is only a citizens' list, because rights come first.
It is a voting list, because it includes government branches.
It is a Constitution, bringing key national rules together.
It is a yearly plan, because it includes future goals.

why.It is only a citizens' list, because rig: This overlooks government rules and national goals.
why.It is a voting list, because it includes: This confuses government branches with an election list.
why.It is a yearly plan, because it includes: This confuses long-term goals with a yearly plan.

activities.explanation: A Constitution covers government branches, citizens, and national goals.

activities.prompt: Citizen A has rights, but also duties. A plan protects A's rights but ignores every duty. Is the plan complete?
options: Yes. Rights alone are enough for citizens.
No. A Constitution lists both citizens' rights and duties.
No. Only national goals belong in a Constitution.
Yes. Duties belong to branches, not citizens.

why.Yes. Rights alone are enough for citizen: This wrongly assumes rights are more important than duties.
why.No. Only national goals belong in a Cons: This confuses citizens' duties with national goals.
why.Yes. Duties belong to branches, not citi: This wrongly places citizens' duties with government branches.

activities.explanation: The Constitution lists citizens' rights and duties together.

activities.prompt: Document A explains how laws are made. It also explains how the judiciary is formed. Document B only lists long-term goals. Which better fits a Constitution?
options: Document B, because goals matter more than basic rules.
Document A, because it explains key parts of government.
Document A, because a Constitution cannot list goals.
Document B, because basic principles need not be written.

why.Document B, because goals matter more th: This wrongly treats goals as more important than basic rules.
why.Document A, because a Constitution canno: This wrongly assumes a Constitution cannot include goals.
why.Document B, because basic principles nee: This confuses goals with a Constitution's written basic rules.

activities.explanation: A Constitution explains lawmaking and how the judiciary is formed.

lessons.title: Writing the Constitution of India

activities.prompt: How did people come together to create India’s Constitution?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How the Constitution was written
activities.body: The Constituent Assembly formed in 1946. It had 389 members, including fifteen women. Members came from different regions, professions and social groups. They were chosen by provincial assembly members, elected by people. The Assembly wrote the Constitution over almost three years. Dr Rajendra Prasad chaired it. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into effect on 26 January 1950.
keyPoints: The Assembly had 389 members, including fifteen women.
Members represented different regions, professions and social groups.
The Constitution was written over almost three years.
activities.explanation: The people of India helped choose the members who wrote the Constitution.

activities.prompt: A child sees 26 November 1949 and 26 January 1950 on a calendar. Which date should Republic Day use, and why?
steps: The draft was completed on 26 November 1949, so writing had ended.
The Constitution came into effect on 26 January 1950, marking its start.
Republic Day is 26 January, which matches the Constitution’s effect.
So Republic Day marks the start, not the adoption, of the Constitution.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Who chose the Assembly members?
activities.body: Members represented India’s different regions, professions and social groups. People had elected members of the provincial legislative assemblies. Those elected members then chose the Constituent Assembly members. This process brought different parts of society into the work of writing the Constitution.
keyPoints: Members represented different regions, professions and social groups.
People elected members of the provincial legislative assemblies.
Elected members then chose the Constituent Assembly members.
activities.explanation: The Assembly represented many parts of India through its chosen members.

activities.prompt: Fifteen members of the Constituent Assembly were women.
activities.explanation: Yes, fifteen of the Assembly's 389 members were women.

activities.title: When it came into effect
activities.prompt: The Constitution came into effect on ______ 1950.
activities.hint: This date is celebrated as Republic Day every year.
activities.explanation: The Constitution came into effect on 26 January 1950.

activities.title: Important dates and leader
activities.prompt: Match each event with its date or leader.
activities.explanation: The Assembly formed first. Its Constitution was later adopted and implemented.

activities.title: Put the dates in order
activities.prompt: Put these dates in order from earliest to latest.
activities.explanation: The Assembly formed in 1946 before the Constitution was adopted in 1949.

activities.title: The choosing process
activities.prompt: Which sentence correctly explains how the Constituent Assembly members were chosen?
options: The Assembly chose members of provincial legislative assemblies.
Elected provincial members chose members of the Constituent Assembly.
People directly chose every member of the Constituent Assembly.
The Assembly elected members of all provincial legislative assemblies.
activities.explanation: People elected the provincial assembly members. Those members chose the Constituent Assembly members.

activities.prompt: The Assembly adopted the Constitution in the same year it came into effect.
activities.explanation: The Constitution was adopted in 1949 and came into effect in 1950.

activities.prompt: Fifteen of 389 Assembly members were women. What does this show?
options: It included women while representing different regions and groups.
It had only women from one profession in the Assembly.
It gave every region exactly the same number of members.
It included women but ignored every other social group.

why.It had only women from one profession in: This wrongly assumes that women came from only one profession.
why.It gave every region exactly the same nu: This assumes equal numbers, but equal group sizes are not stated.
why.It included women but ignored every othe: This mistakes women’s inclusion for the exclusion of other groups.

activities.explanation: This is right because the Assembly included women and many other groups.

activities.prompt: People voted for provincial assemblies. Those assemblies then chose Assembly members. What follows?
options: The Assembly members came through an elected choice.
The Assembly members were chosen without any popular vote.
The provincial assemblies chose only the people who elected them.
The people directly voted for every Assembly seat.

why.The Assembly members were chosen without: This wrongly treats the choosing process as having no popular vote.
why.The provincial assemblies chose only the: This confuses who voted with who chose the Assembly members.
why.The people directly voted for every Asse: This wrongly says people voted directly for Assembly seats.

activities.explanation: The people elected the assemblies, and the assemblies chose the members.

activities.prompt: The Assembly began on 9 December 1946. It adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949. What can we learn?
options: Writing the Constitution took almost three years.
The Constitution was adopted before the Assembly began.
The Assembly began its work after the Constitution was adopted.
The Constitution came into effect on 9 December 1946.

why.The Constitution was adopted before the: This reverses the order of the Assembly and the adoption.
why.The Assembly began its work after the Co: This wrongly places the Assembly’s work after the adoption.
why.The Constitution came into effect on 9 D: This confuses the Assembly’s formation with the Constitution’s effect.

activities.explanation: The dates fit the fact that writing took almost three years.

activities.prompt: Imagine your class uses the same choosing rule. Which process fits?
options: The elected class group chooses the final members.
One leader chooses members without any group election.
Each member chooses only themselves without voting.
The class skips voting and asks outside adults to choose.

why.One leader chooses members without any g: This skips the first election and puts choice with one leader.
why.Each member chooses only themselves with: This removes the elected group’s role in making the choice.
why.The class skips voting and asks outside: This skips both elections and adds a choice outside the class.

activities.explanation: This matches the rule: an elected group makes the final choice.

activities.prompt: A list shows Assembly members from several regions, professions, and social groups. What can this source show us?
options: The Assembly represented many parts of Indian society.
The Assembly represented only people from one profession.
The list proves every group had the same size.
The Assembly ignored regions when choosing its members.

why.The Assembly represented only people fro: This wrongly limits the Assembly to members of one profession.
why.The list proves every group had the same: This assumes equal group sizes, but the list does not prove that.
why.The Assembly ignored regions when choosi: This contradicts the members from different regions.

activities.explanation: This is right because the members came from many regions and groups.

activities.prompt: A poster says, ‘We celebrate Republic Day because the Constitution was adopted.’ Why is this weak?
options: Republic Day marks when the Constitution came into effect.
Republic Day marks when the Constituent Assembly was formed.
Republic Day marks the day the drafting work was completed.
Republic Day marks when the provincial assemblies chose members.

why.Republic Day marks when the Constituent: The Assembly formed on 9 December, not on Republic Day.
why.Republic Day marks the day the drafting: Drafting ended on 26 November, not on 26 January.
why.Republic Day marks when the provincial a: The assemblies chose members before the Constitution was written.

activities.explanation: This is right because 26 January marks the Constitution’s effect.

lessons.title: What Shaped and Influenced the Indian Constitution?

activities.prompt: What inspired the people who created our Constitution?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Many Influences Shaped the Constitution
activities.body: The freedom movement and India’s culture shaped the Constitution. Useful lessons from constitutions in other countries were also considered. The freedom struggle supported equality and justice and helped protect cultural heritage. The Constitution presents India as one country. Indian culture accepts different views and respects nature, learning, knowledge and women. Indian tradition also welcomes good thoughts from every side.
keyPoints: The freedom movement and Indian culture shaped the Constitution.
Equality, justice and heritage protection were important.
The Constitution presents India as one country.
activities.explanation: The freedom movement, Indian culture and other constitutions all influenced the Constitution.

activities.prompt: A school group is making shared rules for children with different views and cultures. What should guide these rules?
steps: The freedom struggle shaped equality and justice, so the rules should treat every child fairly.
Indian culture accepts different views, so the rules should allow respectful disagreement.
Useful lessons from other constitutions were considered, so they can guide better rules.
Therefore, the rules should be fair, protect culture, and keep everyone together as one school.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Freedom Struggle
activities.prompt: Which influence helped shape values such as equality and justice?
options: The freedom movement
Lessons from other countries
The idea of one country
Different points of view
activities.explanation: The freedom struggle helped shape values such as equality and justice.

activities.title: The World as One Family
activities.prompt: The phrase vasudhaiva kutumbakam means the world is ______ family.
activities.hint: It describes people across the world as one family.
activities.explanation: Vasudhaiva kutumbakam means that the world is one family.

activities.title: Match Influences and Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each influence to what it contributed.
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an influence with the idea it helped provide.

activities.title: The French Ideals
activities.prompt: From which country were liberty, equality and fraternity adopted?
options: France
Ireland
The UK
Australia
activities.explanation: The ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity were adopted from France.

activities.title: Countries in Alphabetical Order
activities.prompt: Put these countries in alphabetical order.
activities.explanation: This order follows the alphabet, from Australia to USA.

activities.title: Match the Sources
activities.prompt: Which pair matches liberty and the Directive Principles to their sources?
options: France and Ireland
Ireland and France
Australia and the UK
The USA and Ireland
activities.explanation: The French ideals included liberty. Ireland inspired the Directive Principles of State Policy.

activities.prompt: The freedom movement helped shape equality and justice. How did it shape India's Constitution?
options: It inspired values such as equality and justice.
It made people reject all old culture.
It stopped makers learning from foreign constitutions.
It proved every country should have one culture.

This mistakes influence for a demand to reject culture.
why.It stopped makers learning from foreign: This wrongly says useful foreign lessons were ignored.
why.It proved every country should have one: This wrongly assumes one culture should replace different views.

activities.explanation: This is right because the freedom struggle shaped equality and justice.

activities.prompt: The freedom movement shaped India's Constitution. Foreign constitutions also gave useful lessons. What explains the result?
options: Freedom, Indian culture, and foreign constitutions shaped it.
Foreign constitutions alone shaped India's Constitution.
Indian culture alone shaped India's Constitution.
Only ancient traditions shaped India's Constitution.

why.Foreign constitutions alone shaped India: Foreign constitutions mattered, but they were not the only influence.
why.Indian culture alone shaped India's Cons: Indian culture mattered, but it was not the only influence.
why.Only ancient traditions shaped India's C: The freedom movement and foreign constitutions also shaped the Constitution.

activities.explanation: The Constitution was shaped by freedom, culture, and useful foreign lessons.

activities.prompt: A government wants policies inspired by the Irish Constitution. Which part of India's Constitution should guide its work?
options: Directive Principles of State Policy should guide it.
French ideals of liberty, equality, and fraternity should guide it.
Vasudhaiva kutumbakam should guide its state policies.
Freedom-struggle values of equality and justice should guide it.

why.French ideals of liberty, equality, and: Liberty, equality, and fraternity were adopted from France.
why.Vasudhaiva kutumbakam should guide its s: Vasudhaiva kutumbakam means the world is one family.
why.Freedom-struggle values of equality and: Equality and justice were shaped by the freedom struggle.

activities.explanation: The Irish Constitution inspired the Directive Principles of State Policy.

activities.prompt: Students in one group give different views about a school rule. What Indian cultural idea should guide their discussion?
options: Listen to good thoughts from every side before deciding.
Choose only the view held by the largest group.
Reject old ideas because they come from the past.
Decide first and then refuse every different opinion.

why.Choose only the view held by the largest: Choosing only the largest group ignores useful views from others.
why.Reject old ideas because they come from: Indian culture values heritage, so old ideas are not simply rejected.
why.Decide first and then refuse every diffe: Welcoming different views does not mean refusing to listen.

activities.explanation: Indian culture welcomes good thoughts from every side.

lessons.title: Key Features of the Constitution of India

activities.prompt: How does our Constitution keep different parts of government balanced?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How the Constitution organises government
activities.body: The Constitution of India recognises three main organs of government. The legislature makes laws, the executive implements them, and the judiciary checks laws and decides cases. Separate powers help these organs work effectively. The Constitution sets out their roles, duties and ways of being answerable. India has central, state and local levels of government. Important parts include Fundamental Duties, Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.
keyPoints: The legislature makes laws.
The executive implements laws.
The judiciary checks laws and decides cases.
India has central, state and local levels of government.
activities.explanation: The Constitution organises government and gives each organ a clear role.

activities.prompt: How can a country make laws, put them into action, and judge violations well?
steps: The legislature makes laws because law-making needs one clearly responsible organ.
The executive implements laws because rules must become actions.
The judiciary checks and judges laws because violations need decisions and punishment.
Separating these powers helps each organ work effectively and answer for its duties.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which organ implements the laws?
options: The legislature
The judiciary
The executive
Eligible citizens
activities.explanation: The executive implements the laws.

activities.prompt: Match each organ with its job.
pairs: Checks that laws follow the Constitution
activities.explanation: Each organ has a different job under the Constitution.

activities.prompt: The legislature makes the country's laws.
activities.explanation: The legislature makes the country's laws.

activities.prompt: The judiciary checks that laws follow the ______.
activities.hint: Think about what the judiciary checks.
activities.explanation: The judiciary checks that laws follow the Constitution.

activities.prompt: What are Directive Principles?
options: Strict rules that must always be obeyed
Goals that the government should try to achieve
Promises made only to voters
Jobs of local government
activities.explanation: Directive Principles are government goals and guidelines, not strict rules.

activities.prompt: Which statement about the electoral system is correct?
options: Every eligible citizen can vote
Only the central government can vote
Only members of the legislature can vote
Only local officials can vote
activities.explanation: The electoral system allows every eligible citizen to vote.

activities.prompt: A law is ignored. Which organ must put it into action?
options: The executive, because it implements laws
The legislature, because it makes laws
The judiciary, because it checks laws
The judiciary, because it gives punishment

why.The legislature, because it makes laws: This confuses making laws with implementing them.
why.The judiciary, because it checks laws: This confuses checking laws with implementing them.
why.The judiciary, because it gives punishme: This confuses giving punishment with implementing laws.

activities.explanation: This is right because the executive implements laws.

activities.prompt: A diagram shows law-maker, law-implementer, and law-checker. What does it show?
options: The three organs of government
The three levels of government
The main parts of the Constitution
The promises in Fundamental Rights

why.The three levels of government: This confuses organs of government with levels of government.
why.The main parts of the Constitution: This confuses the three organs with parts of the Constitution.
why.The promises in Fundamental Rights: This confuses government organs with constitutional promises.

activities.explanation: These are the legislature, executive, and judiciary.

activities.prompt: A map shows India, state, and town decisions. Which government idea fits?
options: Central, state, and local levels
Legislature, executive, and judiciary
Fundamental Rights and Fundamental Duties
Directive Principles and electoral rules

why.Legislature, executive, and judiciary: These are organs of government, not levels of government.
why.Fundamental Rights and Fundamental Dutie: These are important parts of the Constitution, not government levels.
why.Directive Principles and electoral rules: These are constitutional features, not the levels shown.

activities.explanation: India, a state, and a town show these three government levels.

activities.prompt: Why should each organ’s roles, duties, and accountability measures be clearly defined?
options: So every organ knows its job and limits
So all three organs can do every job
So the legislature can implement its own laws
So the judiciary can write new laws

why.So all three organs can do every job: This mixes the separated roles instead of dividing them.
why.So the legislature can implement its own: This confuses making laws with implementing laws.
why.So the judiciary can write new laws: This confuses judging laws with making laws.

activities.explanation: Clear definitions help each organ work effectively within its role.

lessons.title: The Constitution Is a Living Document

activities.prompt: How can a Constitution change while keeping its promises to everyone?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How the Constitution Changes
activities.body: The Constitution is a living document because it can change as time passes. The makers knew that new laws and rules would be needed. An amendment is a change to the Constitution. Amendments are carefully debated in Parliament. Some must also be debated in state legislative assemblies. The government sometimes asks the public for its opinion. Popular movements can also begin changes.
keyPoints: The Constitution can change as time passes.
An amendment is a change to the Constitution.
Parliament carefully debates amendments.
The public and popular movements can begin changes.
activities.explanation: You can now describe how the Constitution can change.

activities.prompt: A child hears that the home flag rule changed in 2004. Why can that rule change?
steps: The makers knew new laws and rules would be needed later, because passing time brings new needs.
Changes are called amendments, and Parliament debates them carefully before accepting them.
The flag rule changed in 2004, so even an old rule can change.
Therefore, the Constitution is living because its rules can change through careful amendments.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Name a Constitutional Change
activities.prompt: What is a change to the Constitution called?
options: A debate in Parliament
An amendment
A public opinion
A state assembly
activities.explanation: Yes! An amendment is a change to the Constitution. Parliament debates amendments before they are accepted.

activities.prompt: Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution in 1976.
activities.explanation: Correct! The lesson says Fundamental Duties were added in 1976.

activities.prompt: A change to the Constitution is called an ______.
activities.hint: It means a change to the Constitution.
activities.explanation: Great! This word means a change to the Constitution.

activities.title: Match the Work
activities.prompt: Match each person or group with their part.
pairs: Wrote the Constitution's text by hand
Illustrated its pages with Indian history scenes
Sometimes asks the public for its opinion
Can give feedback on proposed laws and changes
activities.explanation: Correct! Raizada wrote the text, while Bose's team illustrated it. Parliament debates amendments, and people can give feedback.

activities.title: A Change in 2004
activities.prompt: What changed in 2004?
options: The rule about flying the national flag at home
The rule about adding Fundamental Duties
The rule about adding Panchayati Raj
activities.explanation: Correct! The home flag rule changed in 2004. Before that, flying it at home was not allowed.

activities.prompt: Some amendments must also be debated in state legislative assemblies.
activities.explanation: Correct! Some amendments need debate in state legislative assemblies too.

activities.title: Changes in Date Order
activities.prompt: Put these constitutional changes in date order, earliest first.
activities.explanation: Correct order! These changes happened in 1976, 1992, and 2004.

activities.title: Public Views and Flag Flying
activities.prompt: Which statement matches public views and flag flying?
options: People cannot comment; flying the flag is a right.
People can comment; flying the flag is only a duty.
People can comment; flying the flag is a right.
People cannot comment; flying the flag is only a duty.
activities.explanation: Correct! People can comment on proposed changes. Flying the flag is part of the Fundamental Right to Freedom.

activities.prompt: The makers expected new needs to appear over time. Why is the Constitution a living document?
options: It can change through amendments as new needs appear.
It must stay unchanged because the makers finished its text.
Its pictures make every amendment happen without any debate.
Only state governments can change its written rules.

why.It must stay unchanged because the maker: Finishing the text does not mean its rules must remain unchanged.
why.Its pictures make every amendment happen: The pictures show history, but they do not make amendments happen.
why.Only state governments can change its wr: State debates do not mean only state governments can change the Constitution.

activities.explanation: Changes called amendments let the Constitution respond to new needs.

lessons.title: The Preamble and the Constitution’s Guiding Values

activities.prompt: What secrets do the Constitution’s guiding values hold about how India should be governed?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Constitution’s Guiding Values
activities.body: The Constitution’s core values are guiding ideas for government policies and decisions. Their essence is written in the Preamble, which introduces these values in plain words. These values support equal treatment, help for groups with less, and sharing wealth. They also support citizens’ right to decide and India’s freedom from outside orders. Citizens may follow any religion, but the country has no official religion.
keyPoints: The Preamble contains the essence of the core values.
The values support equality, sharing wealth and citizens’ decisions.
No outside power can give orders to the Indian government.
activities.explanation: Together, these ideas guide fair policies and protect citizens’ rights.

activities.prompt: Only some groups can receive government support. Who should receive it first?
steps: Start with the Constitution, because its values guide government choices.
Include everyone, because government should work for everyone.
Give priority to groups with less, because they deserve special attention.
Thus, help should go to those groups first, following the Constitution's values.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where is the essence of the Constitution’s core values written?
options: In the Preamble
In outside orders
In private decisions
In one religion
activities.explanation: The Preamble contains the essence of the Constitution’s core values.

activities.prompt: The people of India made the Constitution through their elected representatives.
activities.explanation: The people made it through their elected representatives, not an outside power.

activities.prompt: Citizens cannot be treated differently because of caste, religion or ______.
activities.hint: This word names one kind of unfair treatment.
activities.explanation: Gender is one reason citizens cannot be treated differently.

activities.prompt: Which action best follows the values for everyone?
options: Sharing wealth so inequalities become smaller
Keeping wealth differences larger
Helping only groups that already have more
Leaving decisions to any outside power
activities.explanation: Sharing wealth helps make social and economic inequalities smaller. This follows the values for everyone.

activities.prompt: Match each part to its meaning.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins an idea with its meaning in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Who made India’s Constitution?
options: The people through elected representatives
A king by handing it down
An outside power by giving orders
One group by making private choices
activities.explanation: The people of India made the Constitution through elected representatives.

activities.prompt: Although people have the supreme right to decide, an outside power can still order the government.
activities.explanation: People have the supreme right to decide for the country. No outside power can give government orders.

activities.prompt: Which plan best follows the values about equality, help, wealth and religion?
options: Equal citizens, helping the less, shared wealth and any religion
Equal citizens, help for the few, larger wealth gaps and one religion
One official religion, outside orders, private choices and unequal treatment
Outside orders, narrow help, larger wealth gaps and one chosen religion
activities.explanation: This plan includes equal treatment and help for the less. It also shares wealth and allows any religion.

activities.prompt: A government has limited help for many people. Which plan best follows the Constitution's values?
options: Give the least help first to people who have less.
Give the most help first to people who have more.
Give equal help to everyone in the same way always.
Give no help to anyone who asks the government.

why.Give the most help first to people who h: This mistakes having more for needing more help.
why.Give equal help to everyone in the same: This treats equal amounts as fairer than attention to those with less.
why.Give no help to anyone who asks the gove: This mistakes self-help for government responsibility to work for everyone.

activities.explanation: This puts support first where the Constitution says attention is needed.

activities.prompt: The Preamble gives the essence of the Constitution's values. What problem would one official religion create?
options: It would weaken citizens' freedom to follow any religion.
It would strengthen citizens' freedom to follow any religion.
It would remove religion from the country completely.
It would make every citizen follow the same religion.

why.It would strengthen citizens' freedom to: This thinks naming one religion protects religious freedom.
why.It would remove religion from the countr: This confuses an official religion with having no religion.
why.It would make every citizen follow the s: This assumes every citizen must follow the same religion.

activities.explanation: This weakens the rule that citizens may follow any religion.
