chapters.title: Understanding Markets
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what is a market?; prices and markets; physical and online markets; domestic, international and supply markets.

lessons.title: What Is a Market?

activities.prompt: What brings buyers and sellers together in a market?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet a Market
activities.body: A market is a place where people buy and sell goods. Goods are things sold in markets. It is also called a bazaar. A market can be a physical place or online. An online marketplace is an online place for buying and selling. Markets make goods and services available. People have long used markets to fulfil their needs and wants. Markets also connect people, traditions and ideas.
keyPoints: Markets are places for buying and selling goods.
A market can be physical or online.
Markets connect people and make goods and services available.
activities.explanation: Markets help people buy and sell, and they bring people together.

activities.prompt: A child cannot visit a physical market. Can the child still use a market?
steps: The child can use an online marketplace because markets can be online.
The child can get goods because markets make them available to people.
The child and seller must agree on price because every market has both.
So yes, the child can still use a market online.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where do people buy and sell goods?
options: At a market
At a school
At a library
At a park
activities.explanation: A market is a place where people buy and sell goods.

activities.prompt: Match each word or phrase with its correct description.
pairs: A place where people buy and sell goods
A successful market in the Vijayanagara Empire
Many kinds traded at Hampi Bazaar
activities.explanation: Hampi Bazaar was a successful market in the Vijayanagara Empire. Many kinds of products were traded there.

activities.prompt: Who can receive goods and services made available by markets?
options: People and households only
People, households and businesses
Businesses and sellers only
Goods and services only
activities.explanation: Markets make goods and services available to people, households and businesses.

activities.prompt: People have long used markets to fulfil their needs and ______.
activities.hint: People use markets to get things they wish for.
activities.explanation: Markets have long helped people fulfil both their needs and wants.

activities.prompt: Match each market word with its correct description.
pairs: The person who buys a product
The person who sells a product
What the buyer and seller must agree on
activities.explanation: Every market has a buyer and a seller. They must agree on a price.

activities.prompt: At a market like Hampi Bazaar, what must a buyer and seller do?
options: Choose separate prices
Avoid naming any price
Pay two market prices
Agree on one price
activities.explanation: Every market has a buyer and seller. They must agree on a price.

activities.prompt: A local market brings buyers and sellers from different traditions together. What can the market do?
options: It can connect people, traditions, and ideas.
It can only connect goods with their prices.
It can replace the need for buyers and sellers.
It can stop people from sharing their ideas.

why.It can only connect goods with their pri: This thinks markets only connect goods and prices, missing their social role.
why.It can replace the need for buyers and s: This thinks buyers and sellers are not needed, but every market has both.
why.It can stop people from sharing their id: This thinks markets stop idea sharing, but they help connect ideas.

activities.explanation: This is right because markets connect people, traditions, and ideas.

activities.prompt: One market is in a square, while another is on a website. How are they different?
options: One is a physical place, while the other is online.
One uses a buyer, while the other uses no seller.
One sells goods, while the other makes no goods available.
One needs price agreement, while the other does not.

why.One uses a buyer, while the other uses n: This thinks an online market has no seller, but both have buyers and sellers.
why.One sells goods, while the other makes n: This thinks online markets do not make goods available, but they do.
why.One needs price agreement, while the oth: This thinks price agreement is optional, but buyers and sellers must agree.

activities.explanation: This is right because a market can be physical or online.

activities.prompt: A buyer likes an item, but the seller wants a different price. What must happen next?
options: The buyer and seller must agree on one price.
The buyer must take the item at any price.
The seller must end the market that day.
The buyer and seller need no price agreement.

why.The buyer must take the item at any pric: This thinks liking an item removes the need for price agreement.
This thinks a price disagreement ends the whole market.
why.The buyer and seller need no price agree: This thinks agreement is unnecessary, but the rule requires it.

activities.explanation: This is right because the buyer and seller must agree on a price.

activities.prompt: If a town has no market, what is likely to happen?
options: People, households, and businesses may lack available goods and services.
People, households, and businesses may only lack different market names.
Only businesses may lack available goods and services.
No one may lack goods, because markets do not provide them.

why.People, households, and businesses may o: This focuses on market names instead of goods and services.
why.Only businesses may lack available goods: This leaves out people and households, who also use markets.
why.No one may lack goods, because markets d: This denies that markets make goods and services available.

activities.explanation: This is right because markets make goods and services available to all three groups.

lessons.sceneCaption: The Virupaksha Temple’s main gopuram stands at the end of a street in Hampi Bazaar.

lessons.title: Prices and Markets

activities.prompt: How do people decide what price feels fair to both sides?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Prices Are Agreed
activities.body: Buyers and sellers bargain to reach an acceptable price. Bargaining means discussing prices until both accept one. A seller may ask ₹80 per kilogram for guavas. A buyer may ask for a lower price when this price is too high. The seller may reject an offer if it would not be profitable. The transaction may not happen if they cannot agree. A suitable price suits both sides.
keyPoints: Buyers and sellers bargain
A suitable price suits both sides
No agreement may mean no transaction
activities.explanation: Bargaining helps buyers and sellers find a suitable price.

activities.prompt: Can a guava seller and buyer agree when ₹80 is too high?
steps: Buyer asks for less because the seller asks ₹80 per kilogram.
Seller may reject because the lower offer would not be profitable.
Both bargain because they want an acceptable price.
Transaction may fail because they cannot agree on one price.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Buying and Selling
activities.prompt: What do buyers and sellers often do to reach an acceptable price?
options: Wait without speaking
Bargain together
Leave the market at once
Choose different shops
activities.explanation: They bargain until they agree on a price that suits both sides.

activities.title: A Lower Price
activities.prompt: When the asking price is too high, a buyer may ask for a ______ price.
activities.hint: Choose the word that means not as high.
activities.explanation: A lower price may help the buyer and seller agree.

activities.title: Rejecting an Offer
activities.prompt: Why might a seller reject a buyer's offer?
options: It would use a different colour
It would need a larger basket
It would not be profitable
It would arrive before sunrise
activities.explanation: A seller may reject an offer when it would not be profitable.

activities.title: Market Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each market idea to its closest meaning.
pairs: What buyers and sellers try to reach
The price a seller may ask for guavas
A request when the asking price is too high
A possible reason for a seller to reject an offer
activities.explanation: Bargaining connects the asking price, lower offers, and final agreement.

activities.title: Bargaining Steps
activities.prompt: Put these bargaining steps in order.
items: A seller asks ₹80 per kilogram for guavas.
A buyer finds this price too high.
A buyer asks for a lower price.
The buyer and seller bargain until they agree.
activities.explanation: The buyer asks for less, and bargaining continues until both agree.

activities.title: What Helps Set the Price?
activities.prompt: A seller estimates how many guavas buyers need. What can also help determine the price?
options: The colours and sizes of the market signs
The number of empty crates beside the stall
The amounts sellers offer and buyers require
The time when the market gate opens
activities.explanation: Sellers' offers and buyers' requirements help set a price that suits both sides.

activities.prompt: A seller asks ₹80 per kilogram for guavas. The buyer asks for less. What will bargaining help them do?
options: Find a price both sides can accept.
Make the seller's asking price higher.
Give guavas to buyers without payment.
Stop the buyer and seller from bargaining.

This mistake thinks bargaining only helps the seller.
This mistake thinks bargaining means giving goods away.
why.Stop the buyer and seller from bargainin: This mistake thinks bargaining stops when prices are discussed.

activities.explanation: Correct: bargaining helps both sides reach an acceptable price.

activities.prompt: A buyer's offer would not be profitable for the seller. What should happen next?
options: Continue bargaining until both sides agree.
Accept the offer even if it is unprofitable.
End bargaining and leave without a sale.
Change the price without asking either side.

why.Accept the offer even if it is unprofita: This mistake accepts an offer the seller may reject.
This mistake thinks one refusal ends all bargaining.
why.Change the price without asking either s: This mistake changes price without the two sides.

activities.explanation: Correct: bargaining can continue until both sides agree.

activities.prompt: At one market, buyer and seller cannot agree. At another, they bargain and agree. What changed between the markets?
options: The final price suited both buyer and seller.
The guavas were free in both markets.
Sellers stopped asking for any price.
Buyers made only higher offers.

This mistake thinks agreement always means free goods.
This mistake thinks agreement removes every asking price.
This mistake thinks buyers cannot ask for lower prices.

activities.explanation: Correct: agreement means the price suits both sides.

activities.prompt: A seller estimates how many guavas buyers will need. How can this help set a price?
options: Consider what buyers require and sellers offer.
Remove all bargaining from the market.
Make every buyer's offer identical.
Ensure every market transaction succeeds.

This mistake thinks bargaining has no part in pricing.
This mistake thinks buyers always offer the same amount.
why.Ensure every market transaction succeeds: This mistake thinks estimation guarantees every sale.

activities.explanation: Correct: sellers' offers and buyers' needs help set price.

lessons.sceneCaption: An Indian guava seller in Chanditala illustrates the role of sellers in fruit markets.

lessons.title: Physical and Online Markets

activities.prompt: How can we shop without meeting the seller?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Ways to Shop
activities.body: Physical markets let buyers meet sellers in person. They are the most common kind of market. Weekly markets, haats, local shops and malls are examples. Online markets let people buy and sell without meeting. You can shop through apps or websites. Purchases may reach your home. Some services can also be got from home.
keyPoints: Physical markets include weekly markets, haats, local shops and malls.
Online markets use apps or websites, and purchases can reach your home.
Some services need the customer present, but others can be got from home.
activities.explanation: This lesson helps you compare markets and choose where to shop.

activities.prompt: Can Meena shop and receive her goods without meeting a seller?
steps: Online shopping works through apps or websites.
Buyers and sellers do not have to meet in person there.
An online purchase can be delivered to her home.
So Meena can shop from home and still receive her goods.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where do buyers meet sellers in a physical market?
options: At the same place
Only through an app
Only on a website
Without meeting
activities.explanation: In a physical market, buyers and sellers come to the same place.

activities.prompt: You can shop through apps and ______.
activities.hint: It is a place you open on a computer.
activities.explanation: Shopping can happen through apps or websites.

activities.prompt: Match each market with its description.
activities.explanation: Each example matches the goods or feature described in the lesson.

activities.prompt: What does an aggregator do?
options: Packs and delivers products
Meets every buyer and seller
Provides online classes
Supplies production components
activities.explanation: An aggregator packs products and delivers them to online buyers.

activities.prompt: You need tailoring. Can you get it only through an online market?
options: No, the customer must be present.
Yes, every service stays online.
Yes, nobody needs to attend.
Yes, all services reach homes.
activities.explanation: Tailoring needs the customer to be present.

activities.prompt: Which statement about production components is true?
options: Manufacturers can buy components online.
Manufacturers sell components online.
Online buyers make all components.
Components only come from aggregators.
activities.explanation: Manufacturers can buy production components through online markets.

activities.prompt: A local shop sells street food and small goods. Shopping can also be done through an app. How do these markets differ?
options: The local shop needs a meeting; the app does not.
The local shop has no seller; the app has many sellers.
Both places always need buyers and sellers to meet.
The app is the same kind of market as a mall.

why.The local shop has no seller; the app ha: This wrongly assumes that a physical market has no seller.
why.Both places always need buyers and selle: This wrongly believes that online shopping also needs a meeting.
why.The app is the same kind of market as a: This wrongly treats an app as a physical market.

activities.explanation: A local shop needs face-to-face buying; an app does not.

activities.prompt: A mall has many stores inside. What does this allow a shopper to do?
options: Visit many sellers without leaving the mall.
Meet one seller and then leave the market.
Buy goods only through an app or website.
Receive every purchase at home from the mall.

why.Meet one seller and then leave the marke: This wrongly assumes that many stores mean only one seller.
why.Buy goods only through an app or website: This wrongly treats a mall as an online market.
why.Receive every purchase at home from the: This wrongly assumes that mall shopping always uses home delivery.

activities.explanation: Many stores inside one mall let a shopper visit many sellers.

activities.prompt: A maker needs production components for making goods. Why might an online market help?
options: The maker can buy parts without meeting the seller.
The maker must visit every component seller in person.
The maker can make all components without buying them.
The maker can buy parts only inside large malls.

why.The maker must visit every component sel: This wrongly assumes that online buying always needs a meeting.
why.The maker can make all components withou: This wrongly thinks buying components means making them instead.
why.The maker can buy parts only inside larg: This wrongly limits component buying to physical malls.

activities.explanation: Online markets let manufacturers buy components without meeting sellers.

activities.prompt: Neha wants online classes and a tailored shirt. Which plan matches how these services work?
options: She takes classes at home, but visits the tailor.
She gets both services at home without any visit.
She visits the tailor, then takes classes at the market.
She takes classes only by meeting the tailor in person.

why.She gets both services at home without a: This wrongly assumes that every service can be obtained from home.
why.She visits the tailor, then takes classe: This wrongly puts online classes at a market and makes tailoring come first.
why.She takes classes only by meeting the ta: This wrongly treats online classes like tailoring, which needs presence.

activities.explanation: Online classes work from home, but tailoring needs the customer present.

activities.prompt: Most markets are physical, while online markets also exist. What does this show about meeting sellers?
options: People usually meet sellers, but do not always need to.
People always meet sellers, even when shopping online.
People never meet sellers because online buying is common.
People meet sellers only inside large malls.

why.People always meet sellers, even when sh: This ignores that online shopping can happen without a meeting.
why.People never meet sellers because online: This wrongly says that meeting sellers is never needed.
why.People meet sellers only inside large ma: This wrongly treats large malls as the most common markets.

activities.explanation: Since physical markets are most common, in-person meetings are the usual pattern.

lessons.sceneAlt: Families sell vegetables and buy goods at the weekly village market of Doraguda, Odisha.
lessons.sceneCaption: Families sell produce and buy goods at Doraguda’s weekly village market in Odisha.

lessons.title: Domestic, International and Supply Markets

activities.prompt: How do goods travel from a farm to your family’s kitchen?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Markets and Trade
activities.body: Markets can be domestic or international. A domestic market trades within a country's geographical boundaries. International markets work beyond the boundaries of one nation. Exporting is selling goods or services to a buyer in another country. Importing is buying goods or services from another country. International trade happens across national borders.
keyPoints: Domestic markets trade within a country's boundaries.
Exporting sells to buyers in another country.
Importing buys from another country.
activities.explanation: This card introduces domestic markets, international markets, exporting and importing.

activities.prompt: A shop sells vegetables to a family inside our country. Is this domestic or international trade?
steps: The shop and the family are inside our country.
No border is crossed because the shop and family stay in one country.
Therefore, this is domestic trade, not international trade.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Selling Within the Country
activities.prompt: A seller buys fruit from a grower in the same country and sells it there. Which market is this?
options: Domestic market
International market
Cross-border market
Cold-storage market
activities.explanation: The trade happens within the country's geographical boundaries, so it is a domestic market.

activities.title: Keeping Goods Cool
activities.prompt: Cold storage facilities keep perishable goods at low ______.
activities.hint: Think about how cold storage keeps perishable goods fresh.
activities.explanation: Low temperatures help cold storage facilities keep perishable goods fresh.

activities.title: Match Markets and Traders
activities.prompt: Match each market role with its meaning.
pairs: Trades within the country's geographical boundaries
Operates beyond the boundaries of one nation
Buy large quantities from producers or manufacturers
activities.explanation: Domestic markets stay within a country, while international markets operate beyond national boundaries.

activities.title: The Mandi
activities.prompt: Where is stored produce brought for sale?
options: Mandis
Godowns
Cold storage facilities
Nearby shops and stores
activities.explanation: Stored produce is brought to markets called mandis.

activities.title: The Supply Route
activities.prompt: Put these market roles in the correct order.
activities.explanation: Wholesalers buy from producers or manufacturers, then supply shops where retailers sell to consumers.

activities.title: Selling Across Borders
activities.prompt: A clothing maker sells clothes to a shop in another country. What is this selling called?
options: Exporting
Importing
Domestic trading
Wholesaling
activities.explanation: The maker is exporting because the buyer is in another country. Importing means buying from another country.

activities.prompt: A map shows a trade arrow crossing our country's border. What kind of market is shown?
options: A market within the country's boundaries
A market beyond one nation's boundaries
A market using warehouses inside the country
A market selling only to final consumers

why.A market within the country's boundaries: This describes a domestic market because the trade stays inside the country.
why.A market using warehouses inside the cou: This confuses a market with godowns used to store produce.
why.A market selling only to final consumers: This confuses a market with retailers who sell to final consumers.

activities.explanation: This is correct because the trade crosses a national border.

activities.prompt: Wholesalers buy large quantities from manufacturers and supply nearby shops. What may happen if they buy less?
options: Nearby shops may receive fewer goods.
Nearby shops may receive more goods.
More produce may stay inside cold storage.
More families may buy directly from manufacturers.

This reverses the effect of wholesalers buying less produce.
why.More produce may stay inside cold storag: This confuses buying less with the purpose of cold storage.
why.More families may buy directly from manu: This skips the wholesaler-to-shop step in the supply chain.

activities.explanation: This is correct because wholesalers supply goods to nearby shops.

activities.prompt: Produce is kept in a godown before being taken to a mandi. How does its journey change?
options: The produce stays in a large warehouse for the whole journey.
The produce reaches a market after leaving the warehouse.
The produce reaches cold storage after visiting a mandi.
The produce moves from a retailer directly into a godown.

why.The produce stays in a large warehouse f: This confuses the storage stop with the produce's final destination.
why.The produce reaches cold storage after v: This puts cold storage after the mandi without a stated reason.
why.The produce moves from a retailer direct: This reverses the movement between retailers, godowns, and mandis.

activities.explanation: This is correct because stored produce is brought to markets called mandis.

activities.prompt: A godown stores produce. Cold storage keeps perishable goods at low temperatures. Why are their roles different?
options: Cold storage controls temperature; a godown mainly stores produce.
Cold storage buys produce; a godown supplies nearby shops.
Cold storage sells to families; a godown stores large quantities.
Cold storage crosses borders; a godown only works within them.

why.Cold storage buys produce; a godown supp: This confuses cold storage with wholesalers who buy large quantities.
why.Cold storage sells to families; a godown: This confuses cold storage with retailers who sell to final consumers.
why.Cold storage crosses borders; a godown o: This confuses storage facilities with markets that can cross borders.

activities.explanation: This is correct because cold storage controls temperature while godowns store produce.

activities.prompt: A seller sends goods to a buyer in another country. How is the seller acting?
options: As an exporter, because the buyer is elsewhere.
As an importer, because the buyer is elsewhere.
As a wholesaler, because the buyer buys large quantities.
As a retailer, because the buyer is a final consumer.

why.As an importer, because the buyer is els: This uses the buyer's role instead of the seller's role.
why.As a wholesaler, because the buyer buys: This assumes a cross-border seller must also be a wholesaler.
why.As a retailer, because the buyer is a fi: This confuses the seller's role with the final buyer's role.

activities.explanation: This is correct because selling to a buyer in another country is exporting.

activities.prompt: A shop buys many boxes from a wholesaler. It sells one small box to a family. Why does it act as a retailer?
options: It sells smaller quantities meant for consumption, not resale.
It buys large quantities from producers or manufacturers.
It stores produce in large warehouses called godowns.
It supplies goods to nearby shops and stores.

why.It buys large quantities from producers: This describes the shop's purchase, but does not explain its retail role.
why.It stores produce in large warehouses ca: This describes a godown's role rather than a retailer's role.
why.It supplies goods to nearby shops and st: This describes a wholesaler's role rather than a retailer's role.

activities.explanation: This is correct because retailers sell smaller quantities for consumption rather than resale.

lessons.sceneCaption: Mumbai’s container terminal shows the port infrastructure used to trade goods across borders.

lessons.title: Markets in People's Lives and Government's Role

activities.prompt: How do markets shape our daily lives, and when should the government step in?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Markets and Government
activities.body: Markets help buyers and sellers complete exchanges called transactions. Producers learn what buyers are willing to buy. Markets can build lasting relationships. They matter beyond money matters. Governments can set the highest price sellers may charge. They can set the lowest price for essential farm products. They set the lowest pay for employees and require quality and safety standards. They also provide public goods, such as roads and parks.
keyPoints: Producers and consumers complete transactions.
Markets build lasting relationships and matter beyond money matters.
Governments set maximum prices, minimum farm prices, and minimum wages.
Governments require standards and provide public goods.
activities.explanation: This card connects market exchanges with everyday life and government rules.

activities.prompt: A seller charges above the government's maximum price. What should happen?
steps: The government sets the maximum charge, so the seller has a limit.
The seller charged above the limit, so the price must be lowered.
This follows the government rule, so the transaction uses an allowed price.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which best explains how markets help producers and consumers?
options: They complete transactions with each other.
They set prices for every good.
They provide roads and parks.
They set wages for all employers.
activities.explanation: Correct! Producers and consumers use markets to complete transactions.

activities.prompt: Producers can learn what consumers are willing to buy.
activities.explanation: Yes! Producers learn what consumers are willing to buy.

activities.prompt: Mother's Market in Imphal is run by about ______ women.
activities.hint: The lesson gives an approximate number.
activities.explanation: Great! Mother's Market is run by about 3000 women in Imphal.

activities.prompt: Match each government rule to what it does.
pairs: The highest price sellers may charge
The lowest price set for essential farm products
The fair pay rule for employers
activities.explanation: Well done! These pairs show the government's price, pay, and safety rules.

activities.prompt: A seller charges too much for a certain good. What can the government do?
options: Set a minimum wage for consumers.
Set the maximum price sellers may charge.
Set a quality rule for every transaction.
Set the lowest farm price for every shop.
activities.explanation: Correct! The government can set the maximum price sellers may charge.

activities.prompt: A market activity causes harm. What can strict government rules do?
options: They can finish every market transaction.
They can remove all public services.
They can reduce the harmful effects.
They can make every seller earn more.
activities.explanation: Correct! Strict rules can reduce harmful effects of market activities.

activities.prompt: A seller plans to charge above the government's highest allowed price. What should apply?
options: The seller must pay the minimum wage.
The seller must set a minimum farm price.
The seller must provide roads and parks.
The seller cannot charge above that limit.
activities.explanation: Well done! The maximum price is the most sellers may charge.

activities.prompt: Producers learn what consumers will buy. How can this guide them?
options: They can focus on products that consumers are willing to buy.
They can focus on products that consumers refuse to buy.
They must stop learning about what consumers want.
They must sell the same product as every seller.

why.They can focus on products that consumer: This mistake reverses willingness to buy into unwillingness to buy.
why.They must stop learning about what consu: This mistake thinks producers should not learn from consumers.
why.They must sell the same product as every: This mistake thinks all producers must sell the same product.

activities.explanation: This is right because producers can use buyers' wishes to guide their choices.

activities.prompt: An employer pays less than the government's minimum wage. The town also needs roads and parks. What should government do?
options: Enforce the minimum wage and provide public goods and services.
Set wages below the minimum and provide public goods.
Allow lower wages but leave public services to sellers.
Allow lower wages and remove all public services.

why.Set wages below the minimum and provide: This mistake wrongly treats pay below the minimum as acceptable.
why.Allow lower wages but leave public servi: This mistake wrongly gives public services to sellers.
why.Allow lower wages and remove all public: This mistake wrongly treats low pay and fewer services as good.

activities.explanation: This is right because government protects fair pay and provides public services.

lessons.sceneAlt: A woman sells glutinous rice at Eema Bazaar, a bazaar in Imphal run exclusively by women.
lessons.sceneCaption: An Eema sells glutinous rice at Eema Bazaar, an Imphal bazaar run exclusively by women.

lessons.title: Assessing the Quality of Goods and Services

activities.prompt: How can you tell whether a product is really good before buying it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Checking Quality
activities.body: Every consumer needs to judge the quality of products before buying them. Useful checks include price, size, strength and attractive colours. Government certification marks can also help. The ISI mark covers products such as electrical appliances and paper. AGMARK certifies agricultural products. More BEE stars mean less energy use. Reviews, feedback and word of mouth also guide your choice.
keyPoints: More stars mean the appliance uses less energy.
AGMARK certifies grains, pulses and honey.
Reviews and word of mouth guide buying choices.
activities.explanation: Each clue gives useful information for checking a product.

activities.prompt: A family is buying an electrical appliance and wants to judge its quality.
steps: Comparing price, size, strength and colours gives useful quality checks.
Looking for ISI adds a check because certification marks help assess quality.
Comparing BEE stars shows energy use because more stars mean less energy.
Reviews and word of mouth add clues, so buyers can judge quality well.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which check helps you judge how strong a product is?
options: Price
Size
Strength
Colour
activities.explanation: Strength is one of the useful quality checks listed in the lesson.

activities.prompt: The ISI mark is used on products such as electrical appliances and ______.
activities.hint: The lesson gives one example beside electrical appliances.
activities.explanation: The ISI mark is used on electrical appliances and paper.

activities.prompt: Attractive colours are among the useful quality checks.
activities.explanation: The lesson includes attractive colours among useful quality checks.

activities.prompt: Which mark certifies agricultural products such as grains, pulses and honey?
options: AGMARK
ISI mark
FSSAI
BEE rating
activities.explanation: AGMARK certifies agricultural products, including grains, pulses and honey.

activities.prompt: Match each mark or clue with its correct use.
activities.explanation: The lesson gives a special use for each mark and clue.

activities.prompt: An appliance has more BEE stars. What does this show?
options: It uses more energy
It uses less energy
It costs more
It is heavier
activities.explanation: More stars on a BEE rating show that an appliance uses less energy.

activities.prompt: A grain bag tears easily. Which quality check would find this weakness?
options: Check the strength.
Check the price.
Check the size.
Check the colour.

Price shows cost, but it does not show strength.
Size shows how big something is, but not how strong it is.
Colour shows appearance, but it does not show strength.

activities.explanation: Strength is right because the bag tears easily.

activities.prompt: A seller praises goods. Other buyers agree. What should a buyer do?
options: Use buyer feedback to judge the goods.
Trust only the seller and ignore buyers.
Use bright colour and ignore the buyers.
Use large size and ignore the buyers.

The seller's words may agree with other buyers, so ignoring them is wrong.

Size is useful, but it should not replace buyer feedback.

activities.explanation: Buyer feedback helps because it includes reviews and word of mouth.

activities.prompt: Few praise a product at first. Later, good reviews appear. What grew?

Product price
Product size
Product colour

why.Product price: Praise and reviews do not show that the price grew.
why.Product size: Praise and reviews do not show that the product grew larger.
why.Product colour: Praise and reviews do not show that the product's colour changed.

activities.explanation: Reputation grows because praise and reviews spread good word of mouth.

activities.context: An online marketplace connected a household with a seller. The household wanted a product, and the seller offered it for a price. They discussed the price and finally agreed, so the product could become available to the household. This kind of market can be physical or online. Long ago, the Hampi Bazaar was a prosperous market in the Vijayanagara Empire, where many kinds of products were traded.
activities.prompt: If the buyer and seller cannot agree on a price, what should happen to the sale?
options: The sale cannot be completed unless both accept the same price.
The seller must give the product without receiving any payment.
The buyer can take the product and choose a price later.
The seller can decide the final price after the buyer leaves.

why.The seller must give the product without: The facts do not allow a sale without payment.
why.The buyer can take the product and choos: The buyer and seller must agree before the sale.
why.The seller can decide the final price af: The seller cannot set the final price alone after agreement is required.

activities.explanation: A sale needs agreement on the price.

activities.context: An online marketplace connected a household with a seller. The household wanted a product, and the seller offered it for a price. They discussed the price and finally agreed, so the product could become available to the household. This kind of market can be physical or online. Long ago, the Hampi Bazaar was a prosperous market in the Vijayanagara Empire, where many kinds of products were traded.
activities.prompt: If the household visits a physical market instead of using an online one, what must still happen for a sale to take place?
options: A buyer and seller must agree on a price.
Only the buyer needs to be present.
The seller may set a different price for each buyer without agreement.
The household must buy every product displayed.

A seller is also required in every market.
why.The seller may set a different price for: A different price cannot replace agreement between buyer and seller.
why.The household must buy every product dis: There is no rule that a buyer must purchase everything displayed.

activities.explanation: Every market needs a buyer, a seller and agreement on the price.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between a physical market and an online marketplace?
activities.answer: A physical market is an actual place where people buy and sell goods. An online marketplace is a market that operates online. Either kind can connect buyers with sellers. In both, the buyer and seller must agree on a price.
points: A physical market is a physical place.
An online marketplace operates online.
Both kinds can involve buyers and sellers.
Both require agreement on the price.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A guava seller asks ₹80 per kilogram. A buyer thinks this is too high and asks for a lower price. The seller does not want to sell at a price that would not be profitable, so the two continue bargaining. The seller estimates how many guavas buyers will need. Their offers and requirements help determine a possible final price, which should be acceptable to both. If they cannot agree, no sale occurs.
activities.prompt: The buyer says ₹80 per kilogram is too high and asks for less. What is the most likely next step?
options: They negotiate a price that both sides can accept.
The buyer pays ₹80 per kilogram without further discussion.
The seller accepts any lower offer to complete the sale quickly.
Both leave immediately and never discuss another price.

why.The buyer pays ₹80 per kilogram without: The buyer had already said the asking price was too high.
why.The seller accepts any lower offer to co: A seller need not accept an unprofitable price.
why.Both leave immediately and never discuss: The parties should continue bargaining before ending the transaction.

activities.explanation: Bargaining may lead to a price acceptable to both.

activities.context: A guava seller asks ₹80 per kilogram. A buyer thinks this is too high and asks for a lower price. The seller does not want to sell at a price that would not be profitable, so the two continue bargaining. The seller estimates how many guavas buyers will need. Their offers and requirements help determine a possible final price, which should be acceptable to both. If they cannot agree, no sale occurs.
activities.prompt: Suppose the seller rejects the buyer’s offer because it would not be profitable. What could happen if bargaining continues?
options: The transaction could still occur at a different, acceptable price.
The seller must accept the rejected amount to ensure a sale.
The buyer must immediately pay the original asking price.
The transaction must finish at the rejected offer.

why.The seller must accept the rejected amou: An unprofitable offer does not have to be accepted.
why.The buyer must immediately pay the origi: The buyer had already requested a lower price.
why.The transaction must finish at the rejec: A rejected offer is not automatically the agreed price.

activities.explanation: Further bargaining may find a price acceptable to both.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between an asking price and an agreed price for guavas.
activities.answer: The asking price is the seller’s initial proposal, such as ₹80 per kilogram for guavas. The agreed price is reached after the buyer and seller bargain and accept an amount suitable for both. If they cannot agree on such a price, the transaction may not happen.
points: The seller first proposes an asking price.
The parties bargain to reach an agreed price.
The agreed price must be acceptable to both.
Without agreement, the sale may not occur.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Every Saturday, a family visits the weekly market, where sellers offer vegetables and other essential goods. The family meets the sellers in person. Nearby, a local market has shops selling street food and small goods. Later, the family orders an item through a website and expects it to be delivered to their home.
activities.prompt: If the family cannot visit the weekly market, what should it do to get the vegetables it needs?
options: Place an online order for the vegetables and arrange for their delivery home.
Visit the local market instead, because its shops are the only places that sell essential goods.
Go to a mall and ask a store there to bring vegetables to the weekly market.
Wait for the weekly-market sellers to visit the house, because physical markets also deliver to buyers.

why.Visit the local market instead, because: The facts do not say that local-market shops are the only sellers of essential goods.
why.Go to a mall and ask a store there to br: Malls have many stores, but the facts do not say that they deliver vegetables.
why.Wait for the weekly-market sellers to vi: Physical markets involve meeting sellers in person, not sellers visiting buyers at home.

activities.explanation: Online shopping can be done through apps or websites, and purchases can be delivered home.

activities.context: Every Saturday, a family visits the weekly market, where sellers offer vegetables and other essential goods. The family meets the sellers in person. Nearby, a local market has shops selling street food and small goods. Later, the family orders an item through a website and expects it to be delivered to their home.
activities.prompt: Why was the weekly market suitable for the family's purchase of vegetables?
options: It is a physical market that sells essentials, so the family could meet the sellers there.
It is an online market, so the family could receive vegetables without meeting sellers.
It is a mall where buyers can visit many stores instead of meeting individual sellers.
It sells only small goods, making the vegetables available from another seller.

why.It is an online market, so the family co: Online markets do not require buyers and sellers to meet in person.
why.It is a mall where buyers can visit many: A mall is a large physical market with many stores, unlike the weekly market described.
why.It sells only small goods, making the ve: Weekly markets sell vegetables and essential goods, not only small goods.

activities.explanation: Weekly markets are physical markets and sell vegetables and other essential goods.

activities.prompt: How are physical and online markets different, and what can be done in each?
activities.answer: In a physical market, buyers meet sellers in person. Physical markets are the most common kind. Online markets allow buyers and sellers to trade without meeting. Shopping can happen through apps or websites, and purchases can be delivered to the buyer's home.
points: Physical markets bring buyers and sellers together in person.
Physical markets are the most common kind of market.
Online markets do not require an in-person meeting.
Online shopping can use apps or websites and can include home delivery.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A producer sends goods to a buyer in another country. This is exporting because the buyer is outside the producer's country. The receiving buyer is importing because the purchase comes from another country. In the home market, wholesalers buy large quantities from manufacturers. They store produce in godowns, while cold storage facilities keep perishable goods at low temperatures. Stored produce is brought to mandis. Wholesalers then supply nearby shops and stores, and retailers sell smaller quantities to families.
activities.prompt: The producer has perishable goods that need to be stored. Which type of place should be chosen?
options: A low-temperature storage place suitable for the perishable produce
A large warehouse used to keep produce until it is traded
A market where stored produce is brought for wholesale supply
A local selling place where small quantities reach consumers

why.A large warehouse used to keep produce u: Godowns store produce but are not described as maintaining low temperatures.
why.A market where stored produce is brought: Mandis are markets where stored produce is brought, not cold-storage places.
why.A local selling place where small quanti: Shops and stores sell to consumers; they are not storage facilities for perishable produce.

activities.explanation: Cold storage facilities are meant to keep perishable goods at low temperatures.

activities.context: A producer sends goods to a buyer in another country. This is exporting because the buyer is outside the producer's country. The receiving buyer is importing because the purchase comes from another country. In the home market, wholesalers buy large quantities from manufacturers. They store produce in godowns, while cold storage facilities keep perishable goods at low temperatures. Stored produce is brought to mandis. Wholesalers then supply nearby shops and stores, and retailers sell smaller quantities to families.
activities.prompt: What makes the producer's first sale international rather than domestic?
options: The sale crosses a national border and goes to a buyer in another country.
The producer is buying goods from a business located in another country.
The goods remain within the producer's country's geographical boundaries.
The transaction supplies a nearby shop with goods for resale.

why.The producer is buying goods from a busi: This describes importing from the buying side, not the producer's exporting sale.
why.The goods remain within the producer's c: Trade within one country's geographical boundaries is domestic.
why.The transaction supplies a nearby shop w: Supplying nearby shops is part of domestic distribution, not the cross-border sale.

activities.explanation: The buyer is in another country, so the transaction crosses national borders.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between domestic and international markets, and explain how exporting and importing are connected to international trade.
activities.answer: A domestic market trades within a country's geographical boundaries. International markets operate beyond the boundaries of one nation. Exporting means selling goods or services to a buyer in another country, while importing means buying goods or services from another country. International trade therefore occurs across national borders.
points: Domestic trade stays within a country's geographical boundaries.
International markets operate beyond one nation's boundaries.
Exporting is selling to a buyer in another country.
Importing is buying from another country.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At Mother's Market in Imphal, about 3000 women sell goods to shoppers. A vegetable seller notices which products customers choose to buy, so she can plan what to bring next time. She may develop long-lasting relationships with buyers who come again. The government controls the prices of certain goods, can set maximum prices, and requires manufacturers to follow quality and safety standards. It also provides public goods such as roads and parks.
activities.prompt: If the government sets a maximum price for one of the goods sold at Mother's Market, what should the seller do?
options: The seller cannot charge more than the government's stated limit.
The seller must calculate the minimum wage for the workers.
The seller can ignore the limit because quality standards already exist.
The seller should provide roads and parks instead of following the price control.

why.The seller must calculate the minimum wa: Option 1 confuses price controls with minimum wages.
why.The seller can ignore the limit because: Option 2 wrongly treats the maximum price as optional.
why.The seller should provide roads and park: Option 3 confuses price controls with providing public goods.

activities.explanation: Option 0 is correct because a maximum price limits what sellers may charge.

activities.context: At Mother's Market in Imphal, about 3000 women sell goods to shoppers. A vegetable seller notices which products customers choose to buy, so she can plan what to bring next time. She may develop long-lasting relationships with buyers who come again. The government controls the prices of certain goods, can set maximum prices, and requires manufacturers to follow quality and safety standards. It also provides public goods such as roads and parks.
activities.prompt: If fewer shoppers choose one of the vegetable seller's products, what should she do next time she comes to the market?
options: She should bring less of that product because she has learned what consumers are willing to buy.
She should bring more of that product because fewer buyers mean more stock is needed.
She should bring the same amount because shoppers' choices do not affect producers.
She should change the quality standards herself because sellers can decide those rules.

why.She should bring more of that product be: Option 1 confuses lower demand with a need for more stock.
why.She should bring the same amount because: Option 2 ignores what the seller can learn from shoppers' choices.
why.She should change the quality standards: Option 3 wrongly gives sellers control over government quality standards.

activities.explanation: Option 0 is correct because producers learn what consumers are willing to buy.

activities.prompt: Explain why the government has an important role in markets in people's lives.
activities.answer: Government plays a role because markets have importance beyond economic activity. It controls certain prices, sets maximum prices and minimum prices for essential farm products, and sets minimum wages. It also requires quality and safety standards, reduces harmful effects through strict rules, and provides roads and parks.
points: Markets have importance beyond economic activity.
The government controls certain prices.
It sets minimum wages and quality and safety standards.
Strict rules can reduce harmful effects, and the government provides public goods.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A household is choosing an electrical appliance. One model has an ISI mark, more stars on its BEE rating, and attractive colours. Neighbours have recommended it, and online reviews say that people are satisfied. The seller says it is strong and well priced. The buyer wants to judge the quality instead of relying only on the seller’s claim.
activities.prompt: Before buying the appliance, what should the buyer do?
options: Verify the ISI mark, compare the BEE stars, and read feedback from other buyers.
Choose it because attractive colours and the seller’s statement are enough.
Buy whichever model has fewer BEE stars, since more stars indicate greater energy use.
Trust only the neighbours’ recommendation and ignore certification marks and reviews.

why.Choose it because attractive colours and: Colours and the seller’s claim do not provide enough evidence.
why.Buy whichever model has fewer BEE stars,: More stars show lower energy use, not greater energy use.
why.Trust only the neighbours’ recommendatio: Word of mouth should be considered along with other quality checks.

activities.explanation: This checks quality, energy efficiency and consumer feedback.

activities.context: A household is choosing an electrical appliance. One model has an ISI mark, more stars on its BEE rating, and attractive colours. Neighbours have recommended it, and online reviews say that people are satisfied. The seller says it is strong and well priced. The buyer wants to judge the quality instead of relying only on the seller’s claim.
activities.prompt: Why should the buyer read the online reviews before deciding?
options: They provide other consumers’ feedback that can help guide the purchase.
They guarantee that the appliance is strong and correctly priced.
They remove the need to check government certification marks.
They prove that attractive colours are the only sign of good quality.

why.They guarantee that the appliance is str: Reviews can guide a decision but cannot guarantee every quality aspect.
why.They remove the need to check government: Feedback should be used together with certification marks.
why.They prove that attractive colours are t: Attractive colours are only one of several useful quality checks.

activities.explanation: Reviews are consumer feedback that helps people decide what to buy.

chapters.title: The Story of Indian Farming
chapters.summary: In this chapter: agriculture and farming in india; climate, monsoons and cropping seasons; soil and crops; caring for soil, water and seeds.

lessons.title: Agriculture and farming in India

activities.prompt: Have you ever wondered what farming in India looked like long ago?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is agriculture?
activities.body: Agriculture is among humanity’s oldest occupations. It means preparing soil, growing plants and rearing livestock. In its broad sense, it includes farming, animal husbandry, forestry and horticulture. Some farmers rear fish too. “Agri” means field, and “culture” means to cultivate.
keyPoints: One of humanity’s oldest occupations.
Soil preparation, plant growing and livestock rearing.
About 18 per cent of India’s goods and services come from agriculture and allied activities.
About 46 per cent of India’s working population earns its livelihood from agriculture and allied activities.
At least 75 per cent of people working in agriculture are women.
activities.explanation: These words and areas help you understand what agriculture includes.

activities.prompt: A family grows wheat, keeps goats, and also rears fish. One student says only wheat growing is agriculture. How should the student think?
steps: Agriculture includes preparing soil, growing plants, and rearing livestock.
So wheat and goats both count, because agriculture includes livestock and plants.
Rearing fish also counts, because some farmers include it in their farming.
The student should include all three, because agriculture is broader than farming.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which word means to cultivate?
options: Agri
Culture
Barley
Rice
activities.explanation: “Culture” means to cultivate in the lesson.

activities.prompt: The word ______ means field.
activities.hint: Think of the first part of the word agriculture.
activities.explanation: The lesson says that “agri” means field.

activities.prompt: Match each term or crop with its meaning or place.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins a term or crop with its stated meaning or place.

activities.prompt: Which crops were staple crops during the Harappan period?
options: Rice and millets
Barley and wheat
Barley and millets
Wheat and millets
activities.explanation: Barley and wheat were staple crops during the Harappan period.

activities.prompt: The cultivation of barley and millets at Mehrgarh dates to the 8th millennium BCE.
activities.explanation: It dates to the 7th millennium BCE, not the 8th.

activities.prompt: Ancient Indian texts contain valuable information about which two things?
options: Farming and plant diversity
Animal husbandry and forestry
Forestry and horticulture
Livestock and fish rearing
activities.explanation: The lesson says ancient Indian texts contain valuable information about farming and plant diversity.

activities.prompt: About 18 per cent of India’s goods and services come from agriculture. About 46 per cent of workers earn their living from it. What does this show?
options: Many workers depend on agriculture for income, more than its goods share.
Few workers depend on agriculture, because agriculture makes so few goods.
Farm workers earn more, because agriculture makes most goods and services.
Goods from agriculture matter less to workers than to the whole economy.

why.Few workers depend on agriculture, becau: This mistake reads 18 per cent of goods as few working farmers.
why.Farm workers earn more, because agricult: It reads 18 per cent as most goods.
why.Goods from agriculture matter less to wo: It confuses the goods share with workers’ livelihoods.

activities.explanation: This is right because 46 per cent of workers depend on agriculture.

activities.prompt: Archaeologists found rice grains in the Ganga Plain. Mehrgarh had barley and millets from the 7th millennium BCE. The Ganga Plain rice dates to the 7th or 8th millennium BCE. What do both finds show?
options: People grew the same crops in both places, so farming began together.
Mehrgarh had no farming, because its crops cannot be found elsewhere.
People farmed in both places, but the finds show different crops.
Only the Ganga Plain had farming, because its rice grains were older.

why.People grew the same crops in both place: It mistakes different finds for proof of the same crop everywhere.
why.Mehrgarh had no farming, because its cro: It mistakes one Mehrgarh find for proof that farming did not exist.
why.Only the Ganga Plain had farming, becaus: It mistakes overlapping dates for proof that the Ganga Plain was older.

activities.explanation: This is right because both finds show farming, with different crops.

activities.prompt: Barley and wheat were Harappan staple crops. Mehrgarh grew barley and millets in the 7th millennium BCE. What can both sources tell us?
options: All Harappan staple crops were first grown at Mehrgarh.
Both sources show barley, but they do not connect the farmers.
It proves the Harappan period began in the 7th millennium BCE.
The Harappan evidence shows barley was never grown at Mehrgarh.

why.All Harappan staple crops were first gro: It mistakes Mehrgarh crops for the start of all Harappan crops.
why.It proves the Harappan period began in t: It treats one dated find as the Harappan period’s beginning date.
why.The Harappan evidence shows barley was n: It mistakes evidence from Mehrgarh for proof against Mehrgarh farming.

activities.explanation: Both sources name barley, but they do not link the farmer groups.

activities.prompt: A farmer wants to sow seeds, but the soil needs work. The farmer prepares it first. Why does this already count as agriculture?
options: Preparing soil is not farming, because farming starts after sowing.
Preparing soil is only forestry, because fields can grow only trees.
Preparing soil is part of agriculture, even before plants start growing.
Preparing soil is not agriculture, unless livestock are also reared.

why.Preparing soil is not farming, because f: It misses that preparing soil is one of agriculture’s main jobs.
why.Preparing soil is only forestry, because: It wrongly limits agriculture to forestry and trees.
why.Preparing soil is not agriculture, unles: It wrongly makes livestock a condition for all agricultural work.

activities.explanation: This is right because preparing soil is part of agriculture.

activities.prompt: At least 75 per cent of agriculture workers are women. A child says they all grow plants. What is wrong?
options: Agriculture work includes livestock, so women workers may rear livestock too.
They must all grow plants, because most agriculture workers are women.
They cannot rear livestock, because plant growing is their main job.
They do no farm work, because most agriculture workers are women.

why.They must all grow plants, because most: It wrongly turns many women workers into one kind of work.
why.They cannot rear livestock, because plan: It wrongly assumes that women workers cannot do livestock work.
why.They do no farm work, because most agric: It wrongly reads many workers as a lack of farm work.

activities.explanation: This is right because agriculture includes rearing livestock, not only plants.

lessons.title: Climate, monsoons and cropping seasons

activities.prompt: How do India’s monsoons and seasons shape what farmers grow?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How climate and monsoons help farmers
activities.body: India’s varied geography and climate influence crops. The chapter introduces seven climate types. India has 15 agroclimatic zones. The southwest monsoon brings rain from June to September. It helps kharif crops in northern and central India. The northeast monsoon brings rain from October to December to eastern and southern India. India has three cropping seasons: kharif for monsoon crops, rabi for winter crops, and zaid for summer crops.
keyPoints: Different regions grow different crops because of geography and climate.
The southwest and northeast monsoons bring rain during different months.
Kharif, rabi, and zaid are India’s three cropping seasons.
activities.explanation: This card connects climate, monsoons, and the three cropping seasons.

activities.prompt: A farmer in northern India needs a crop that depends on southwest monsoon rain. Which cropping season should the farmer choose?
steps: The southwest monsoon brings rain from June to September, so timing matters.
The farmer needs that rain because it is crucial for kharif crops.
Kharif is the season for monsoon crops, so it fits the farmer.
Therefore, the farmer should choose kharif and plan around the monsoon rain.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: How many agroclimatic zones does India have?
activities.explanation: Good choice! India is divided into 15 agroclimatic zones.

activities.prompt: The southwest monsoon brings rain from ______ to September.
activities.hint: This is the first month of the southwest monsoon.
activities.explanation: Well done! The southwest monsoon brings rain from June to September.

activities.prompt: Match each cropping season with its crop season.
activities.explanation: Great matching! These are India’s three main cropping seasons.

activities.prompt: Which monsoons give rain to the Malabar and Coromandel plains?
options: Only southwest monsoon
Only northeast monsoon
Both southwest and northeast
Neither monsoon
activities.explanation: Exactly right! These plains receive rain from both monsoons.

activities.prompt: Put these monsoon events in time order.
items: Southwest monsoon rain begins in June
Southwest monsoon rain ends in September
activities.explanation: Well done! The southwest monsoon comes before the northeast monsoon.

activities.prompt: A farmer in northern India grows kharif crops. Which rain is crucial for them?
options: Southwest monsoon
Northeast monsoon
Either monsoon
No monsoon rain
activities.explanation: Great thinking! Southwest monsoon rain is crucial for kharif crops in northern India.

activities.prompt: A northern farm's crop needs southwest monsoon rain from June to September. Which plan should the farmer follow?
options: Use kharif for the southwest monsoon crop.
Use rabi for the southwest monsoon crop.
Use zaid for the southwest monsoon crop.
Use kharif for the northeast monsoon crop.

This wrongly treats a monsoon crop as a winter crop.
This wrongly treats a monsoon crop as a summer crop.
why.Use kharif for the northeast monsoon cro: This pairs the right season with the wrong monsoon.

activities.explanation: Kharif is for monsoon crops, and southwest rain matters in northern India.

activities.prompt: A rain calendar shows June to September over northern India. Another shows October to December over eastern India. Which pair names both monsoons correctly?
options: North: southwest; East: northeast
North: northeast; East: southwest
North: southwest; East: southwest
North: northeast; East: northeast

why.North: northeast; East: southwest: This swaps the two monsoons between the calendars.
why.North: southwest; East: southwest: Both calendars show southwest, but eastern rain is northeast.
why.North: northeast; East: northeast: Both calendars show northeast, but northern rain is southwest.

activities.explanation: The north's June-to-September rain is southwest; the east's October-to-December rain is northeast.

activities.prompt: Southwest monsoon rain is crucial for kharif crops in northern India. Malabar and Coromandel plains receive both monsoons. Which comparison is correct?
options: North gets southwest rain; both plains also get northeast rain.
North gets northeast rain; both plains also get southwest rain.
North gets both monsoons; both plains get only southwest.
North gets no monsoon rain; both plains get both.

why.North gets northeast rain; both plains a: This swaps the monsoons and misses that both plains get two.
why.North gets both monsoons; both plains ge: This wrongly says north gets two and the plains get only one.
why.North gets no monsoon rain; both plains: This wrongly says north gets no monsoon rain at all.

activities.explanation: North's key rain is southwest; both plains also receive northeast rain.

activities.prompt: A map shows seven climate types in India. It also shows 15 agroclimatic zones. What should we expect about crops?
options: Different regions can grow different crops.
Every region grows the same crops.
Only monsoon rain decides every crop.
One climate and one crop cover all India.

This wrongly ignores India's different climates and agroclimatic zones.
This wrongly says monsoon rain is the only influence on crops.
why.One climate and one crop cover all India: This wrongly ignores seven climates and 15 agroclimatic zones.

activities.explanation: India's varied geography and climate influence crops in different regions.

lessons.title: Soil and crops

activities.prompt: What helps a tiny seed grow into a healthy plant?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is soil?
activities.body: Soil is the thin upper layer of Earth's crust that supports plant life. It forms over millions of years. Rocks break down, and organic matter decays. This dark, nutrient-rich organic matter is called humus. India has six major soil types. The type of soil strongly influences the crops that grow in it.
keyPoints: Soil supports plant life.
Soil forms over millions of years.
Humus is dark and rich in nutrients.
activities.explanation: Soil takes a very long time to form, but it helps plants grow.

activities.prompt: A farmer wants to grow a crop. One field has river silt. Another has weathered volcanic rock. The farmer needs moist soil. Which field should they choose?
steps: The river-silt field has alluvial soil because rivers carried the silt there.
The volcanic-rock field has black soil because weathering formed it from volcanic rocks.
Black soil holds plenty of moisture, so it meets the farmer's need.
The farmer should choose the volcanic-rock field for moist soil.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose the description
activities.prompt: Which sentence describes soil?
options: The upper layer that supports plants
The lower layer of solid rock
The layer of air above Earth
The water stored below ground
activities.explanation: Soil is Earth's thin upper layer, and it supports plant life.

activities.title: True or false
activities.prompt: Black soil becomes hard in hot weather as minerals are washed away.
activities.explanation: Laterite soil becomes hard this way. Black soil forms from weathered volcanic rocks.

activities.title: Complete the sentence
activities.prompt: Soil forms over millions of years as rocks ______ down and organic matter decays.
activities.hint: Think about how rocks change into smaller pieces.
activities.explanation: Rocks break down slowly while organic matter decays, helping soil form.

activities.title: Match the soil
activities.prompt: Match each soil with its feature.
activities.explanation: Each soil has a special feature linked to how it forms.

activities.title: Which soil is this?
activities.prompt: Which soil is made from rich silt deposits brought down by rivers?
options: Alluvial soil
Black soil
Red soil
Laterite soil
activities.explanation: Rivers carry silt down and deposit it, forming rich alluvial soil.

activities.title: True or false
activities.prompt: Sandy soil consists mostly of small grains of sand.
activities.explanation: You are right. Small grains of sand make up most sandy soil.

activities.title: Find the soil
activities.prompt: A soil gets its reddish colour from iron. Which soil is it?
options: Red soil
Black soil
Alluvial soil
Sandy soil
activities.explanation: Good choice! Iron gives red soil its reddish colour.

activities.title: Order the soil-forming steps
activities.prompt: Put the soil-forming steps in order.
items: Soil develops over millions of years
activities.explanation: Weathering breaks rocks and minerals into soil particles as soil develops over millions of years.

activities.prompt: A river carries silt down to low land. What soil forms there?
options: The soil is alluvial, made from rich river silt.
The soil is black, made from weathered volcanic rock.
The soil is red, coloured by iron in it.
The soil is sandy, made mostly from small grains.

why.The soil is black, made from weathered v: This wrongly connects river silt with volcanic rocks.
This wrongly says river soil gets its colour from iron.
why.The soil is sandy, made mostly from smal: This wrongly treats sand grains as river silt.

activities.explanation: River silt forms alluvial soil, so this answer is right.

activities.prompt: A soil sample is reddish. The farmer wants to know why. What in the soil gives this colour?
options: The iron in it gives the soil its reddish colour.
The humus in it gives the soil its reddish colour.
The sand in it gives the soil its reddish colour.
The moisture in it gives the soil its reddish colour.

why.The humus in it gives the soil its reddi: This wrongly believes dark humus gives soil a red colour.
why.The sand in it gives the soil its reddis: This wrongly believes sand gives soil its red colour.
why.The moisture in it gives the soil its re: This wrongly believes moisture gives soil its red colour.

activities.explanation: Iron gives red soil its colour, so this answer is right.

lessons.title: Caring for soil, water and seeds

activities.prompt: How can we care for soil, water, and seeds?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Looking after soil, water and seeds
activities.body: Soil organisms break down organic material and improve soil health. Farmers rotate crops or grow several crops in a field. Contour ploughing follows hill curves to reduce soil erosion. Terracing makes flat steps that slow water runoff. Cow dung puts nutrients back into soil. Rain-fed farming depends entirely on rainfall. Irrigation supplies crop water through drip and sprinkler systems. Seeds pass down through families for generations.
keyPoints: Different practices protect soil and supply crop water.
Organic material, organic fertilisers and soil organisms improve soil.
Families have passed seeds down for generations.
activities.explanation: These practices help care for soil, water and seeds.

activities.prompt: A farmer wants to protect soil while growing crops on a hill.
steps: Contour ploughing follows the hill’s curves, so less soil washes away.
Terracing makes flat steps, so water runs off more slowly.
Using both methods can protect the soil on the hill.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does afforestation mean?
options: Planting trees to prevent soil erosion
Making flat steps on hills
Putting nutrients into soil
Carrying spring water to fields
activities.explanation: Afforestation means planting trees to help prevent soil erosion.

activities.prompt: Farmers have passed ______ down through their families for generations.
activities.hint: Farmers keep and pass these on to their families.
activities.explanation: Seeds have passed down through farmers’ families for generations.

activities.prompt: Match each farming method with its meaning.
pairs: Plant trees to prevent soil erosion
activities.explanation: Each method has a clear meaning linked to soil, crops, water or trees.

activities.prompt: Which method creates flat farming steps on hills and slows water runoff?
options: Terracing
Crop rotation
Multiple cropping
Afforestation
activities.explanation: Terracing creates flat farming steps that slow water runoff.

activities.prompt: Put the water’s path in order.
activities.explanation: Bamboo pipes carry spring water to fields in north-eastern India.

activities.prompt: Which farming method depends entirely on rainfall?
options: Rain-fed agriculture
Irrigated agriculture
Modern irrigation
Terracing
activities.explanation: Rain-fed agriculture depends entirely on rainfall. Irrigated agriculture uses artificial methods.

activities.prompt: A farmer ploughs along a hill slope’s curves. What will likely happen to the soil?
options: Soil will wash away more quickly than before.
Less soil will wash away down the hill.
Cow dung will add nutrients to the soil.
Flat farming terraces will form across the hillside.

why.Soil will wash away more quickly than be: Right: ploughing along curves reduces soil erosion.
This confuses contour ploughing with adding organic fertiliser.
why.Flat farming terraces will form across t: This confuses contour ploughing with making flat farming steps.

activities.explanation: This reverses the effect of following the slope’s curves.

activities.prompt: A hillside farm has flat steps for growing crops. How will rain affect the water?
options: Water will run off the steps more quickly.
Water will run off the steps more slowly.
Rain will add nutrients to every crop.
Rain will carry spring water into fields.

This confuses added nutrients with the effect of terracing.
why.Rain will carry spring water into fields: This confuses bamboo pipes with water moving on terraces.

activities.explanation: This reverses what terracing does to water runoff.

activities.prompt: Farmers add cow dung, and soil organisms break down organic material. What should happen to the soil?
options: The soil’s health should improve because of this.
More soil should wash down from the hill.
The field should depend only on rainfall now.
The crops should need no more water now.

why.More soil should wash down from the hill: This confuses added nutrients with soil washing away.
why.The field should depend only on rainfall: This confuses fertiliser with rain-fed farming.
This confuses soil health with the water crops need.

activities.explanation: Right: soil organisms improve soil health as organic material breaks down.
