chapters.title: Turning Tides: 11th and 12th Centuries
chapters.summary: In this chapter: the ghaznavid invasions; al-bīrūnī and bhāskarāchārya; eastern india and new southern powers; the cholas, masters of the seas.

lessons.title: The Ghaznavid Invasions

activities.prompt: Why did the Ghaznavid invasions travel so far into India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Ghaznavid Advance
activities.body: The Ghaznavids defeated a rival Muslim kingdom and overran the Hindu Shāhis. The Hindu Shāhis controlled the Khyber Pass, an important mountain route. Ghazna was the Ghaznavids' capital. Mahmūd conducted seventeen campaigns in India and returned with huge booty. He destroyed the Somanātha Śhiva temple.
keyPoints: The Ghaznavids defeated a rival Muslim kingdom.
The Hindu Shāhis controlled the Khyber Pass.
Mahmūd returned to Ghazna with huge booty.
activities.explanation: This card introduces the main people, places and events.

activities.prompt: Why did controlling the Khyber Pass matter to the Hindu Shāhis?
steps: The Khyber Pass was an important mountain route into the Subcontinent.
The Hindu Shāhis controlled it, so they controlled an important way inward.
This control helped them resist enemies before the Ghaznavids’ attack.
After the Ghaznavids overran them, the Shāhis lost this control.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Campaigns, Wealth and Resistance
activities.body: During Mahmūd's campaigns, he found Mathura, a city of enormous wealth. He destroyed the Somanātha Śhiva temple and looted its enormous treasures. At Bahraich, Suheldev resisted Sālār Masūd, who fell in battle. Mahmūd returned to Ghazna with huge amounts of booty.
keyPoints: Mathura was a city of enormous wealth.
Mahmūd destroyed the Somanātha Śhiva temple.
Suheldev resisted Sālār Masūd at Bahraich.
activities.explanation: These details show the scale of Mahmūd's campaigns and the fighting at Bahraich.

activities.prompt: Who controlled the Khyber Pass before the Ghaznavids overran the Hindu Shāhis?
options: Jayapāla
Suheldev
Hindu Shāhis
Ānandapāla
activities.explanation: The Hindu Shāhis controlled this important mountain route before the Ghaznavid advance.

activities.prompt: Mahmūd defeated Jayapāla and then overcame his son ______ in 1008.
activities.hint: He was Jayapāla's son.
activities.explanation: Mahmūd overcame Jayapāla's son, Ānandapāla, in 1008.

activities.prompt: Suheldev successfully resisted Sālār Masūd at which place?
options: Ghazna
Bahraich
Mathura
Khyber Pass
activities.explanation: Suheldev resisted Sālār Masūd there, and Sālār Masūd fell.

activities.prompt: Match each name with the correct detail.
activities.explanation: Ghazna was the capital, and Mathura was wealthy. Mahmūd destroyed the temple, while Sālār Masūd fell at Bahraich.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order described in the lesson.
items: The Hindu Shāhis controlled the Khyber Pass
The Ghaznavids defeated a rival Muslim kingdom
The Ghaznavids overran the Hindu Shāhis
activities.explanation: The route was controlled before the invasion. The rival kingdom was defeated before the Shāhis were overrun.

activities.prompt: What did Mahmūd do to the Somanātha Śhiva temple?
options: He protected it and guarded its wealth
He repaired it and shared its wealth
He ignored it and left its wealth
He destroyed it and looted its treasures
activities.explanation: Mahmūd destroyed the Somanātha Śhiva temple and looted its enormous treasures.

activities.prompt: The Ghaznavids defeated a rival Muslim kingdom and overran the Hindu Shāhis. What does this order show?
options: Defeating one enemy helped them attack the Hindu Shāhis.
The rival kingdom was defeated after the Hindu Shāhis.
The Hindu Shāhis helped defeat the rival Muslim kingdom.
The Ghaznavids stopped fighting after beating their rivals.

why.The rival kingdom was defeated after the: This reverses the order of the two victories.
why.The Hindu Shāhis helped defeat the rival: This mistakes the Ghaznavids’ enemies for their helpers.
why.The Ghaznavids stopped fighting after be: This mistakes one victory for the end of all fighting.

activities.explanation: It shows the rival’s defeat came before the attack on the Shāhis.

activities.prompt: A map marks Ghazna as the Ghaznavid capital. The Khyber Pass was an important mountain route. Which journey fits?
options: Start in Ghazna, then use the Khyber Pass into India.
Start in Mathura, then travel to Ghazna through Somanātha.
Start in Somanātha, then enter India by going to Ghazna.
Start in Ghazna, then enter India through Mathura.

why.Start in Mathura, then travel to Ghazna: This confuses the capital, route, and direction of travel.
why.Start in Somanātha, then enter India by: This mistakes Somanātha for the capital and the route.
why.Start in Ghazna, then enter India throug: This mistakes Mathura for the mountain route.

activities.explanation: Ghazna was the capital, and the Khyber Pass led into India.

activities.prompt: Mahmūd defeated Jayapāla and then overcame Ānandapāla. He found Mathura wealthy. He destroyed and looted the Somanātha Śhiva temple. He returned to Ghazna with huge booty. What do these events show?
options: His campaigns combined fighting, plundering, and gaining wealth.
His campaigns involved fighting, but never gaining wealth.
His campaigns gained wealth, but involved no fighting.
His campaigns protected temples and returned no booty.

why.His campaigns involved fighting, but nev: This ignores the huge booty that Mahmūd brought back.
why.His campaigns gained wealth, but involve: This ignores the rulers that Mahmūd defeated.
why.His campaigns protected temples and retu: This mistakes temple destruction and looting for protection.

activities.explanation: Fighting, plundering, and returning with booty appear together.

lessons.title: Al-Bīrūnī and Bhāskarāchārya

activities.prompt: How did these scholars exchange ideas across languages and faraway lands?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two brilliant scholars
activities.body: Al-Bīrūnī was a Persian scholar from Khwārizm in present-day Uzbekistan. He was a mathematician, astronomer, geographer, historian and linguist. In India, he learned Sanskrit, read texts and spoke with scholars. He created an encyclopaedic survey of Indian knowledge. Bhāskarāchārya was born in 1114, probably in present-day Maharashtra. He was a great mathematician and astronomer. His work, Līlāvatī, taught basic mathematics through lively riddles and problems.
keyPoints: Al-Bīrūnī studied Sanskrit and Indian texts.
His survey covered many fields of Indian knowledge.
Bhāskarāchārya used riddles to teach basic mathematics.
activities.explanation: Great start! These scholars shared and developed knowledge in different ways.

activities.prompt: How did Al-Bīrūnī’s journey turn India’s knowledge into new learning?
steps: He joined Mahmūd’s campaign around 1017, so he entered India.
He learned Sanskrit, read texts and spoke with scholars, widening his knowledge.
He gathered mathematical and astronomical knowledge from Indian works.
His survey and Arabic translation spread Indian learning, so his journey mattered.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which place was Al-Bīrūnī from?
options: Khwārizm
Maharashtra
India
Europe
activities.explanation: Great! Al-Bīrūnī was from Khwārizm in present-day Uzbekistan.

activities.prompt: Al-Bīrūnī joined Mahmūd of Ghazni on a campaign into India around 1017.
activities.explanation: Correct! He joined Mahmūd of Ghazni on that campaign around 1017.

activities.prompt: Match each name or work with its matching fact.
pairs: Learning Sanskrit and reading Indian texts
Using lively riddles to teach basic mathematics
activities.explanation: You matched Al-Bīrūnī’s learning, translation and gathering of knowledge. You also matched Bhāskarāchārya’s lively teaching method.

activities.prompt: What kind of work did Al-Bīrūnī produce?
options: An encyclopaedic survey of Indian knowledge
A book about European travel plans
A guide to learning one trade
A record of one scholarly debate
activities.explanation: Nice work! His survey covered religion, philosophy, literature, geography and sciences.

activities.prompt: Al-Bīrūnī translated Patanjali’s Yogasūtras into ______.
activities.hint: Name the language used for the translation.
activities.explanation: Well done! Al-Bīrūnī translated Patanjali’s Yogasūtras into Arabic.

activities.prompt: What happened to some of Bhāskarāchārya’s pioneering techniques?
options: Europe rediscovered them after centuries
They stayed unknown outside India forever
They were used for astronomy alone
activities.explanation: Excellent! Europe took several centuries to rediscover some of these techniques.

activities.prompt: Al-Bīrūnī came from Khwārizm. Bhāskarāchārya was probably born in Maharashtra. What is different?
options: They came from different present-day regions.
They most likely came from the same present-day region.
Both scholars worked for Mahmūd of Ghazni.
Both scholars were born in present-day Uzbekistan.

why.They most likely came from the same pres: This mistake assumes two different places were actually the same.
why.Both scholars worked for Mahmūd of Ghazn: This mistake treats a campaign companion as a shared employer.
why.Both scholars were born in present-day U: This mistake makes one scholar’s birthplace the other’s birthplace too.

activities.explanation: Khwārizm and Maharashtra are two different present-day regions.

activities.prompt: Al-Bīrūnī joined Mahmūd’s campaign. Why does this not prove he praised it?
options: He believed India had no science before the campaigns.
He wanted every Indian text translated into Persian.
He disliked learning Sanskrit from Indian scholars.
He believed the campaigns damaged India’s scientific traditions.

why.He believed India had no science before: This mistake replaces his concern for damaged science with a stronger claim.
why.He wanted every Indian text translated i: This mistake guesses a translation aim that the facts do not give.
why.He disliked learning Sanskrit from India: This mistake makes personal dislike the reason instead of damaged science.

activities.explanation: He joined the campaign but believed its campaigns harmed scientific traditions.

activities.prompt: Bhāskarāchārya’s Līlāvatī uses lively riddles for basic mathematics. Al-Bīrūnī’s survey covers many subjects. Why are their books different?
options: Līlāvatī teaches mathematics, while the survey presents Indian knowledge.
Līlāvatī covers religion, while the survey teaches only riddles.
Both books focus only on astronomy and geography.
The survey was for children, while Līlāvatī was for scholars.

why.Līlāvatī covers religion, while the surv: This mistake swaps the broad survey with the mathematics teaching book.
why.Both books focus only on astronomy and g: This mistake narrows both books to two scientific fields.
why.The survey was for children, while Līlāv: This mistake guesses audiences that the facts do not support.

activities.explanation: Līlāvatī teaches basic mathematics, but the survey covers many Indian fields.

activities.prompt: Al-Bīrūnī joined Mahmūd’s campaign around 1017. Bhāskarāchārya was born in 1114. Which came first?
options: Bhāskarāchārya wrote Līlāvatī for mathematics.
Europe later rediscovered some pioneering techniques.
Al-Bīrūnī joined Mahmūd’s campaign into India.
Bhāskarāchārya was born in present-day Maharashtra.

why.Bhāskarāchārya wrote Līlāvatī for mathem: Bhāskarāchārya’s work came after his birth, not before the campaign.
why.Europe later rediscovered some pioneerin: This mistake puts a later rediscovery before the 1017 campaign.
why.Bhāskarāchārya was born in present-day M: This mistake ignores that Bhāskarāchārya’s birth was in 1114.

activities.explanation: The campaign happened around 1017, before Bhāskarāchārya’s birth in 1114.

lessons.title: Eastern India and New Southern Powers

activities.prompt: Which rulers shaped the temples and kingdoms of eastern and southern India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Powers, Capitals and Buildings
activities.body: The Eastern Gangas became a stable power in eastern India. Their kingdom stretched from the Gangā to the Godāvarī. They began temples at Puri and Konark. The Senas ruled Bengal from Nādīya and supported Hindu literature. The Western Chālukyas faded. The Kākatīyas and Hoysalas grew stronger. The Kākatīyas ruled from Orugallu. Their fort had stone gateways called toraṇas. Hoysala temples had carved pillars, sculptures and panels.
keyPoints: Eastern Gangas: stable power; kingdom from the Gangā to the Godāvarī
Senas: dominant over much of Bengal; capital at Nādīya
Kākatīyas and Hoysalas: grew stronger and replaced the Western Chālukyas
Hoysalas: famous for temple architecture with carved details
activities.explanation: These details connect the powers, their capitals and their building skills.

activities.prompt: A child asks who began the temples at Puri and Konark.
steps: The Eastern Gangas were stable, so they could begin grand building work.
Their kingdom stretched from Gangā to Godāvarī, showing their wide reach.
They began the Jagannātha temple at Puri and Konark’s Sun temple.
Thus, the Eastern Gangas led the temple building shown at both places.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which description fits the Eastern Gangas?
options: A stable power in eastern India
A fading power in eastern India
A weak power in eastern India
A narrow power in eastern India
activities.explanation: The Eastern Gangas became one of eastern India's most stable powers.

activities.prompt: Match each group with its capital or building.
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a group with a capital or building linked to it.

activities.prompt: The Senas had their capital at ______.
activities.hint: Name the capital of the Senas.
activities.explanation: Nādīya was the capital of the Senas, who dominated much of Bengal.

activities.prompt: What were the Kākatīyas' impressive stone gateways called?
options: pillars
sculptures
toraṇas
panels
activities.explanation: The Kākatīyas' fort at Orugallu had impressive stone gateways called toraṇas.

activities.prompt: The Senas promoted Hindu thought and literature.
activities.explanation: The Senas supported Hindu thought, literature and poets such as Jayadeva.

activities.prompt: Which pair contains the capitals of the Hoysalas?
options: Velāpura and Dvārasamudra
Nādīya and Orugallu
Puri and Konark
Gangā and Godāvarī
activities.explanation: Velāpura and Dvārasamudra became the Hoysalas' capitals.

activities.prompt: The Eastern Gangas were stable, with a kingdom reaching from Gangā to Godāvarī. Why did they begin two great temples?
options: Their stable rule and wide kingdom helped them build temples.
Their kingdom was too small to support temple building.
Their rule ended before they could begin temple work.
They built temples only after the Senas became strong.

why.Their kingdom was too small to support t: This mistake treats their wide kingdom as too small.
why.Their rule ended before they could begin: This mistake claims their rule ended before the projects began.
why.They built temples only after the Senas: This mistake puts the temple work after Sena power.

activities.explanation: Stability and a wide kingdom made temple building possible.

activities.prompt: A map shows the Eastern Ganga kingdom, from Gangā to Godāvarī. It also shows Kākatīyas ruling much of present-day Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. What do both maps show together?
options: Both powers ruled areas across a wide region.
Both powers ruled from the same capital city.
Only one power ruled across a wide area.
Both powers ruled exactly the same full area.

why.Both powers ruled from the same capital: This mistake confuses where powers ruled with their capitals.
This mistake overlooks that both powers ruled wide areas.
why.Both powers ruled exactly the same full: This mistake assumes both maps show exactly equal borders.

activities.explanation: Each map shows a power ruling a wide area.

activities.prompt: A map shows rule over much of present-day Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. The ruler’s fort has impressive stone gateways. Which capital fits the map?
options: Orugallu, the Kākatīya capital.
Velāpura, a Hoysala capital.
Dvārasamudra, a Hoysala capital.
Nādīya, the Sena capital.

Velāpura was a Hoysala capital, not the Kākatīya capital.
Dvārasamudra was a Hoysala capital, not the Kākatīya capital.
Nādīya was the Sena capital, not the Kākatīya capital.

activities.explanation: Orugallu was the Kākatīya capital for the area on the map.

lessons.title: The Cholas, Masters of the Seas

activities.prompt: How did rulers build an empire across distant lands and oceans?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Chola Power Across Land and Sea
activities.body: The Cholas rose to prominence in present-day Tamil Nadu. Rājarāja Chola conquered parts of Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and northern Sri Lanka. He built the Bṛhadīśhvara temple at Thanjavur. He helped the Śhrīvijaya ruler build a Buddhist monastery. Rājendra Chola I led naval expeditions, defeated the Śhrīvijaya forces and expanded the empire. The Cholas also built useful public works.
keyPoints: Rājarāja built a temple at Thanjavur.
Rājendra won a naval victory over the Śhrīvijaya Empire.
Public works included roads, tanks, wells, canals and artificial lakes.
activities.explanation: The Cholas won land, strengthened trade and built great public works.

activities.prompt: A Chola king wants a strong empire and better roads. Which plans should he follow?
steps: Rājendra defeated Śhrīvijaya at sea, because naval power could challenge a rival.
Trade with China thrived, because sea links helped Chola merchants trade overseas.
Cholas built roads, wells, and canals, because public works helped daily life.
He should build roads and protect trade, because both strengthened Chola rule.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Sea Trade and Chola Expansion
activities.body: Trade with China thrived under the Cholas, as archaeological evidence and inscriptions show. Chola power reached across the sea. Rājarāja conquered parts of present-day Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and northern Sri Lanka. Rājendra Chola I expanded the empire into parts of Odisha and Bengal. His navy defeated the Śhrīvijaya forces and captured their capital. A sea route through the Strait of Malacca brought both trade and competition.
keyPoints: Archaeological evidence and inscriptions show thriving trade with China.
Rājendra expanded the empire into parts of Odisha and Bengal.
The Strait of Malacca route increased rivalry with the Śhrīvijaya king.
activities.explanation: Chola power grew through conquest, naval strength and busy sea trade.

activities.prompt: Where did Rājarāja build the great Bṛhadīśhvara temple?
options: Thanjavur
Nāgapaṭṭinam
Anurādhapura
Sri Lanka
activities.explanation: Rājarāja built the great Bṛhadīśhvara temple at Thanjavur.

activities.prompt: The Cholas built roads, tanks, wells, canals and artificial lakes.
activities.explanation: These public works helped people in the Chola empire.

activities.prompt: Rājendra’s navy captured the capital of the ______ Empire.
activities.hint: This empire faced the Cholas over a sea route.
activities.explanation: Rājendra’s navy defeated the Śhrīvijaya forces and captured their capital.

activities.prompt: Match each place with what it is linked to in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Each place has a special connection with the Chola story.

activities.prompt: What did the sea route through the Strait of Malacca create?
options: Rivalry with the Śhrīvijaya king
Trade with northern Sri Lanka
Expansion into present-day Bengal
Public works in present-day Tamil Nadu
activities.explanation: The route created competition between the Cholas and the Śhrīvijaya king.

activities.prompt: The Malacca sea route removed all competition between the Cholas and the Śhrīvijaya king.
activities.explanation: The route actually created competition between the Cholas and the Śhrīvijaya king.

activities.prompt: A sea route passes through the Strait of Malacca. Why did the two kings compete?
options: They wanted the trade that the sea route could bring.
They wanted to build a Buddhist monastery near that route.
They wanted to conquer Odisha and Bengal by land.
They wanted to capture northern Sri Lanka from each other.

why.They wanted to build a Buddhist monaster: This mistakes trade rivalry for the earlier religious help at Nāgapaṭṭinam.
why.They wanted to conquer Odisha and Bengal: This confuses the route with Rājendra’s later conquests in eastern India.
why.They wanted to capture northern Sri Lank: This confuses sea rivalry with Rājarāja’s conquest of northern Sri Lanka.

activities.explanation: This fits because the route linked trade and rivalry between the kings.

activities.prompt: The map shows Chola lands in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. It also shows northern Sri Lanka. Which ruler fits it?
options: Rājarāja Chola’s conquests
Rājendra Chola I’s conquests
The Śhrīvijaya Empire’s conquests
The Cholas’ public works

why.Rājendra Chola I’s conquests: Rājendra expanded eastward, not into these three areas.
why.The Śhrīvijaya Empire’s conquests: The map shows conquered territories, not Śhrīvijaya gains.
why.The Cholas’ public works: Public works are built places, not the conquests shown on this map.

activities.explanation: These three areas match Rājarāja’s conquests.

activities.prompt: The king builds a road and a canal. What does this show about Chola rule?
options: The Cholas valued public works for everyday life.
The Cholas valued only wars on distant seas.
The Cholas valued only trade with China.
The Cholas avoided spending money on public needs.

why.The Cholas valued only wars on distant s: This wrongly treats naval power as the Cholas’ only goal.
This confuses trade with the Cholas’ public works.
why.The Cholas avoided spending money on pub: Building a road shows the opposite of avoiding public needs.

activities.explanation: Roads and canals were public works, so this choice fits Chola practice.

activities.prompt: Rājarāja helped the Śhrīvijaya ruler build a monastery. What can we say about Chola ties?
options: The rulers sometimes cooperated, even though conflict came later.
The rulers always stayed close and never fought.
The rulers never met or shared any projects.
The rulers shared one navy for trade with China.

why.The rulers always stayed close and never: Earlier help does not mean the rulers never fought later.
why.The rulers never met or shared any proje: The shared monastery proves that rulers did meet and work together.
why.The rulers shared one navy for trade wit: Trade with China does not mean the rulers shared a navy.

activities.explanation: Rājarāja’s help came before Rājendra’s later attack, so ties changed.

lessons.title: The Paramāras and the Ghūrids

activities.prompt: How did the Paramāras and Ghūrids rise to power?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Rises to Power
activities.body: Paramāras began as vassals of the Pratihāras and Rāṣhṭrakūṭas. They became independent in Malwa. Bhoja helped the Hindu Shāhi rulers against Mahmūd of Ghazni. He built the Bhojeshwar Temple. Ghūrid chiefs took control of Ghazni. Muhammad Ghūrī brought parts of Punjab and Sindh under his rule. He defeated Pṛithvīrāja and captured Delhi. Qutb-ud-din Aibak later founded the Delhi Sultanate. Bakhtiyār Khiljī destroyed Nālandā and Vikramaśhilā.
keyPoints: Paramāras began as vassals and became independent in Malwa.
Bhoja aided Hindu Shāhi rulers and built the Bhojeshwar Temple.
Ghūrid expansion led to Delhi and the Delhi Sultanate.
activities.explanation: These events trace the rise of the Paramāras and Ghūrids.

activities.prompt: A ruler fails in one direction, but still grows power. How can both happen?
steps: Muhammad Ghūrī’s Gujarat expansion failed in 1178.
That failure shows one expansion did not work.
But Muhammad Ghūrī later captured Delhi.
So defeat in one place did not stop his later expansion.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Ghūrid Victories and Setbacks
activities.body: Muhammad Ghūrī expanded Ghūrid power in several directions. He brought parts of Punjab and Sindh under his rule. His attempt to expand into Gujarat ended in defeat in 1178. He defeated and executed Pṛithvīrāja at the Second Battle of Tarain. He then captured Delhi. Qutb-ud-din Aibak later founded the Delhi Sultanate. Bakhtiyār Khiljī destroyed major Buddhist learning centres.
keyPoints: Gujarat expansion ended in defeat in 1178.
Tarain was followed by the capture of Delhi.
Bakhtiyār Khiljī destroyed major Buddhist learning centres.
activities.explanation: The Gujarat defeat sat beside later victories in Punjab, Sindh, and Delhi.

activities.prompt: Who were the Paramāras at first?
options: The Mughals and the Ghūrids
The Pratihāras and Rāṣhṭrakūṭas
The Delhi Sultanate rulers
The chiefs of Nālandā
activities.explanation: The Paramāras began as vassals of these two ruling families.

activities.prompt: Muhammad Ghūrī brought parts of Punjab and ______ under his rule.
activities.hint: This region is paired with Punjab in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Muhammad Ghūrī brought parts of both Punjab and Sindh under his rule.

activities.prompt: Match each person or group with their action.
activities.explanation: Each action is linked directly to the ruler or group named in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Why did Bhoja help the Hindu Shāhi rulers?
options: To rule Punjab and Sindh
To control the city of Ghazni
To fight Mahmūd of Ghazni
To defend Nālandā and Vikramaśhilā
activities.explanation: Bhoja helped the Hindu Shāhi rulers fight Mahmūd of Ghazni.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order given in your lesson.
items: The chiefs of Ghūr took control of Ghazni
Muhammad Ghūrī brought parts of Punjab and Sindh under his rule
Qutb-ud-din Aibak later founded the Delhi Sultanate
activities.explanation: The lesson moves from Ghazni to Punjab and Sindh, then Delhi and the Sultanate.

activities.prompt: Which statement correctly compares their beginnings?
options: The Paramāras began as vassals; Ghūrid chiefs took Ghazni.
The Ghūrids began as vassals; Paramāra chiefs took Ghazni.
Both groups began as vassals of the Pratihāras.
Both groups first took control of Ghazni.
activities.explanation: Paramāras began as vassals, while the chiefs of Ghūr took control of Ghazni.

activities.prompt: A family serves two rulers, then rules Malwa. What does this show?
options: The family stayed a vassal of both rulers.
The family became an independent power in Malwa.
The family moved its power to Ghazni.
The family ruled only parts of Punjab and Sindh.

why.The family stayed a vassal of both ruler: This ignores that the family later ruled Malwa itself.
This confuses Malwa with the Ghūr power in Ghazni.
why.The family ruled only parts of Punjab an: Punjab and Sindh came under Muhammad Ghūrī, not this family.

activities.explanation: Becoming an independent power in Malwa matches this change.

activities.prompt: Bhoja helps Hindu Shāhi rulers fight Mahmūd. Why would this help them?
options: It gives them an ally against their enemy.
It gives them a new temple to use.
It brings the Ghūr chiefs into Malwa.
It lets them capture Delhi immediately.

Bhoja's temple building did not provide help against Mahmūd.
The Ghūr chiefs' rise belongs to a different power and place.
Delhi was captured later by Muhammad Ghūrī, not immediately.

activities.explanation: An extra ally could help them fight Mahmūd of Ghazni.

activities.prompt: A timeline shows Gujarat defeat, then Delhi capture. What does this show?
options: One defeat ended all later expansion.
Expansion continued, because Delhi was captured later.
The Gujarat attack captured Delhi.
The Delhi capture happened before the Gujarat attack.

This confuses one defeat with the end of all expansion.
why.The Delhi capture happened before the Gu: This also reverses the order of the events.

activities.explanation: The later capture of Delhi proves expansion continued.

activities.prompt: A timeline shows Muhammad Ghūrī capturing Delhi. What later change fits it?
options: Qutb-ud-din Aibak founded the Delhi Sultanate.
Bhoja built the Bhojeshwar Temple in Delhi.
The Paramāras became Delhi’s vassals.
Bakhtiyār Khiljī captured Delhi first.

why.Bhoja built the Bhojeshwar Temple in Del: Bhoja's temple building is a separate event from Delhi's rule.
The Paramāras' power in Malwa does not fit Delhi's rule.
The fact gives Delhi's capture to Muhammad Ghūrī, not Bakhtiyār.

activities.explanation: Aibak founded the Delhi Sultanate after Delhi was captured.

lessons.title: Governance, Trade and Cultural Life

activities.prompt: How did trade, kingship, and beliefs shape life across Asia?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Governance, Trade and Cultural Life
activities.body: Governance helped rulers organise armies, land and irrigation. Muhammad Ghūrī gave officers temporary land for revenue collection and military service. Rulers maintained irrigation works. Trade with China and Southeast Asia grew. Cultural life included an encyclopaedia about many subjects and royal life. Temples and religious ideas also developed. This transitional period brought both change and continuity.
keyPoints: Government supported armies and irrigation.
Trade with China and Southeast Asia grew.
Culture included books, temples and religious ideas.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect governance, trade and cultural life during a changing period.

activities.prompt: A farmer’s field often dries after seasonal rains. What should the ruler do to reduce this problem?
steps: Seasonal rains can leave fields short of water, so this is a serious farming problem.
Irrigation works are useful because rulers maintained them to reduce problems from seasonal rains.
An army or trade route is wrong because neither directly provides the missing field water.
Therefore, the ruler should maintain irrigation works to reduce the water problem.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did every powerful king need?
options: A sizable army
A sizable fleet
A royal library
A trading post
activities.explanation: Every powerful king needed a sizable army. This made efficient government essential.

activities.prompt: Muhammad Ghūrī gave officers ______ land assignments for revenue collection and military service.
activities.hint: These assignments did not last forever.
activities.explanation: Officers received temporary land assignments. They collected revenue and provided military service.

activities.prompt: India's trade with China and which region kept growing?
options: Central Asia
Southeast Asia
Western Asia
Northern Asia
activities.explanation: India's trade with China and Southeast Asia kept growing during this period.

activities.prompt: Match each person or thing with its lesson connection.
pairs: Encyclopaedia about many subjects and royal life
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a direct link in the lesson. This helps you remember people, works and beliefs.

activities.prompt: Put these governance ideas in the order given by the lesson.
items: Every powerful king needed a sizable army
Officers collected revenue and gave military service
activities.explanation: The lesson links the need for an army with efficient government. It then explains temporary land assignments and their duties.

activities.prompt: Which statement matches both irrigation and trade?
options: Rulers ended irrigation works; trade with China and Central Asia grew.
Rulers maintained irrigation works; trade with China and Southeast Asia grew.
Rulers maintained irrigation works; trade with China and Southeast Asia fell.
Rulers ended irrigation works; trade with China and Southeast Asia grew.
activities.explanation: Rulers maintained irrigation works. Trade with China and Southeast Asia kept growing during this period.

activities.prompt: A king faces many rivals. His army is large, but orders are often delayed. What should he improve first, and why?
options: He should improve government, because an efficient army needs it.
He should collect more revenue, because government and revenue collection are the same.
He should build more temples, because building temples is part of government.
He should stop collecting revenue, because efficient government means fewer collections.

why.He should collect more revenue, because: This wrongly treats revenue collection as the whole of government.
why.He should build more temples, because bu: This confuses one cultural activity with efficient government.
why.He should stop collecting revenue, becau: This wrongly believes efficient government means collecting less revenue.

activities.explanation: This is right because a powerful king needs an efficient government.

activities.prompt: A new officer collects land revenue and provides military service. What should the ruler give him, and why?
options: Temporary land, because his service and revenue work are linked.
Permanent land, because temporary duties should earn permanent rewards.
A trading ship, because revenue collection and soldiers sail together.
A temple grant, because military service has no connection with land.

why.Permanent land, because temporary duties: This confuses temporary land assignments with permanent grants.
why.A trading ship, because revenue collecti: This wrongly links a land-and-service reward to maritime trade.
why.A temple grant, because military service: This confuses religious grants with the land reward for service.

activities.explanation: This is right because temporary land assignments rewarded revenue collection and military service.

activities.prompt: A map shows more ships travelling between India, China, and Southeast Asia. What does this suggest?
options: India’s trade with China and Southeast Asia kept growing.
India’s trade with China and Southeast Asia stayed unchanged.
India’s trade moved only toward China, not Southeast Asia.
India stopped trading with China and Southeast Asia altogether.

why.India’s trade with China and Southeast A: This ignores the growing number of ships shown on the map.
why.India’s trade moved only toward China, n: This wrongly treats growth with two regions as growth with only one.
why.India stopped trading with China and Sou: This turns more shipping into no shipping, the opposite of the map.

activities.explanation: This matches the map’s evidence that the trade kept growing.

activities.prompt: Seasonal rains leave a village’s fields without water at times. What should the ruler do, and why?
options: Maintain irrigation works, because they reduce problems from seasonal rains.
Build a larger army, because a stronger army solves the water problem.
Change the trade route, because growing trade always supplies field water.
Give officers land, because land assignments are the same as irrigation.

why.Build a larger army, because a stronger: This confuses the need for an army with the need for irrigation.
why.Change the trade route, because growing: This confuses growing trade with managing field water.
why.Give officers land, because land assignm: This confuses temporary land assignments with irrigation works.

activities.explanation: This is right because maintained irrigation works reduce problems caused by seasonal rains.

activities.prompt: A poster shows Khajuraho temples. Another shows Angkor Wat. A book names Mānasollāsa. A class names viṣhiṣṭādvaita vedānta and the lingāyat movement. What do these sources show about cultural life?
options: Cultural life included learning, building, and religious thought.
Cultural life focused only on armies and land grants, not beliefs.
Cultural life focused only on trade routes, not learning or building.
Cultural life included temples, but books and beliefs did not matter.

why.Cultural life focused only on armies and: The book shows learning, so culture was not only about armies and grants.
why.Cultural life focused only on trade rout: The temples and book show that culture also included building and learning.
why.Cultural life included temples, but book: The book and teachings show that learning and beliefs also mattered.

activities.explanation: All the sources point to learning, architecture, and religious thought.

activities.prompt: Old customs remain, while trade grows and new religious ideas appear. What best describes this period?
options: It brought both change and continuity, not just one.
It brought only change, because old customs had no power.
It brought only continuity, because new ideas did not spread.
It brought no change, because trade and customs stayed the same.

why.It brought only change, because old cust: Old customs show continuity, so this answer leaves part of the evidence out.
why.It brought only continuity, because new: New ideas show change, so this answer leaves part of the evidence out.
why.It brought no change, because trade and: Growing trade and new ideas show that change did happen.

activities.explanation: Growing trade and new ideas show change, while old customs show continuity.

activities.context: After the Ghaznavids defeated a rival Muslim kingdom, Mahmūd overran the Hindu Shāhis. His campaigns reached much deeper into north India than earlier Arab attempts, while the Shāhis controlled the Khyber Pass, an important mountain route into the Subcontinent. Mahmūd found Mathura extremely wealthy and destroyed the Somanātha Śhiva temple, taking its treasures. At Bahraich, Suheldev successfully resisted Sālār Masūd, who fell in battle.
activities.prompt: If the Hindu Shāhis had not controlled the Khyber Pass, what was likely to happen?
options: Turkic armies would probably have been able to travel farther into north India.
The Hindu Shāhis would probably have become stronger everywhere.
The rival Muslim kingdom would probably have defeated Mahmūd.
Ghazna would probably have become the capital of the Hindu Shāhis.

why.The Hindu Shāhis would probably have bec: Control of one route does not show that the Shāhis would become stronger everywhere.
why.The rival Muslim kingdom would probably: The rival kingdom had already been defeated by the Ghaznavids.
why.Ghazna would probably have become the ca: Nothing in the case suggests that Ghazna would become a Shāhi capital.

activities.explanation: This follows from the deeper reach of the Turkic invasions.

activities.context: After the Ghaznavids defeated a rival Muslim kingdom, Mahmūd overran the Hindu Shāhis. His campaigns reached much deeper into north India than earlier Arab attempts, while the Shāhis controlled the Khyber Pass, an important mountain route into the Subcontinent. Mahmūd found Mathura extremely wealthy and destroyed the Somanātha Śhiva temple, taking its treasures. At Bahraich, Suheldev successfully resisted Sālār Masūd, who fell in battle.
activities.prompt: If Suheldev had not successfully resisted Sālār Masūd at Bahraich, which outcome was possible?
options: Sālār Masūd could have survived the battle and continued his advance.
Sālār Masūd would have fallen before reaching Bahraich.
Suheldev could have survived the battle while Sālār Masūd fell.
Both Sālār Masūd and Suheldev could have survived and continued fighting.

why.Sālār Masūd would have fallen before rea: The case says Masūd reached Bahraich and fell there.
why.Suheldev could have survived the battle: This outcome still includes Masūd falling in battle.
why.Both Sālār Masūd and Suheldev could have: There is no evidence that both men survived or continued fighting.

activities.explanation: Without successful resistance, Masūd might have survived.

activities.prompt: How did Mahmūd’s campaigns show that gaining booty was important to him?
activities.answer: Mahmūd’s campaigns were closely connected with gaining booty. He found Mathura to be a city of enormous wealth. He also destroyed the Somanātha Śhiva temple and looted its enormous treasures. After seventeen campaigns in India, he returned to Ghazna with huge amounts of booty.
points: Mahmūd found enormous wealth in Mathura.
He destroyed the Somanātha Śhiva temple.
He looted the temple’s enormous treasures.
He returned to Ghazna with huge amounts of booty.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A school exhibition asks two groups to present the work of Al-Bīrūnī and Bhāskarāchārya. The first group studies how a scholar from Khwārizm joined Mahmūd of Ghazni on a campaign into India, learned Sanskrit, read Indian texts and spoke with Indian scholars before creating an encyclopaedic survey. The second group examines how one of India’s greatest mathematicians and astronomers made basic mathematics enjoyable through riddles and problems. Visitors also consider Al-Bīrūnī’s belief that Mahmūd’s campaigns damaged India’s scientific traditions.
activities.prompt: The first group wants to show that Al-Bīrūnī studied Indian knowledge directly rather than relying only on information available before his journey. Which action best supports this?
options: He consulted Indian scholars and studied mathematical and astronomical works by Āryabhaṭa, Varāhamihira and Brahmagupta.
He relied only on the knowledge he possessed before entering India, so no direct study of Indian knowledge is shown.
He translated Patanjali’s Yogasūtras, which means he did not need to read Indian texts directly.
He learned from the military campaign alone and never required the knowledge of Indian scholars.

why.He relied only on the knowledge he posse: Option 2: His Persian background does not show that he directly studied Indian sources.
why.He translated Patanjali’s Yogasūtras, wh: Option 3: The translation alone does not demonstrate his wide study of Indian knowledge.
why.He learned from the military campaign al: Option 4: The campaign does not replace his documented reading and conversations.

activities.explanation: Correct: Reading Sanskrit works and consulting scholars provided direct access to Indian knowledge.

activities.context: A school exhibition asks two groups to present the work of Al-Bīrūnī and Bhāskarāchārya. The first group studies how a scholar from Khwārizm joined Mahmūd of Ghazni on a campaign into India, learned Sanskrit, read Indian texts and spoke with Indian scholars before creating an encyclopaedic survey. The second group examines how one of India’s greatest mathematicians and astronomers made basic mathematics enjoyable through riddles and problems. Visitors also consider Al-Bīrūnī’s belief that Mahmūd’s campaigns damaged India’s scientific traditions.
activities.prompt: The second group wants its display to help beginners learn basic mathematics while also showing the work’s long-lasting importance. Which choice best fits the available facts?
options: Present Līlāvatī’s riddles and problems, and explain that Europe took several centuries to rediscover some pioneering techniques.
Present Līlāvatī’s riddles and problems, and claim that Europe quickly adopted all the same methods.
Present an encyclopaedic survey of Indian knowledge and describe it as Bhāskarāchārya’s problem-based mathematics book.
Present Patanjali’s Yogasūtras in Arabic and describe their lively riddles as innovations in basic mathematics.

why.Present Līlāvatī’s riddles and problems,: Option 2: This contradicts the statement that rediscovery took several centuries.
why.Present an encyclopaedic survey of India: Option 3: The encyclopaedic survey was Al-Bīrūnī’s work, not Bhāskarāchārya’s mathematics book.
why.Present Patanjali’s Yogasūtras in Arabic: Option 4: The Yogasūtras translation was Al-Bīrūnī’s, not a basic-mathematics problem book.

activities.explanation: Correct: Līlāvatī used riddles and problems, while the European rediscovery supports its lasting importance.

activities.prompt: Explain how Al-Bīrūnī’s activities in India helped him produce an encyclopaedic survey of Indian knowledge.
activities.answer: Al-Bīrūnī learned Sanskrit, read Indian texts and spoke with Indian scholars. He also studied mathematical and astronomical works by Āryabhaṭa, Varāhamihira and Brahmagupta. These activities gave him direct access to Indian religion, philosophy, literature, geography and sciences, which he brought together in his encyclopaedic survey.
points: He learned Sanskrit.
He read Indian texts and spoke with Indian scholars.
He studied works by three named Indian scholars.
He combined knowledge from many subjects in a survey.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A guide prepares an exhibition on eastern and southern powers. The stable Eastern Gangas had a kingdom from the Gangā to the Godāvarī and began the Jagannātha temple at Puri and the Sun temple at Konark. The Senas dominated much of Bengal, with Nādīya as capital, and supported Hindu thought, literature and Jayadeva. The Western Chālukyas faded as the Kākatīyas and Hoysalas grew stronger. The Kākatīyas ruled from Orugallu, whose fort had toraṇas. The Hoysalas became famous for temple architecture.
activities.prompt: A panel links the Eastern Gangas with religious construction at Puri and Konark. Which explanation best supports this panel?
options: Their stable rule was accompanied by the beginning of major temple projects.
The Senas’ literary support identifies them as the patrons of both sites.
The Kākatīyas’ rule from Orugallu explains their building work at both sites.
The Hoysalas’ fame for temple architecture identifies them as the patrons of both sites.

why.The Senas’ literary support identifies t: This confuses Sena support for literature with the Eastern Gangas’ temple work.
why.The Kākatīyas’ rule from Orugallu explai: Orugallu was the Kākatīyas’ capital, not the base of the Eastern Gangas.
why.The Hoysalas’ fame for temple architectu: Hoysala temple fame belongs to a different power from the one that began these projects.

activities.explanation: The Eastern Gangas were stable and began the temple projects at Puri and Konark.

activities.context: A guide prepares an exhibition on eastern and southern powers. The stable Eastern Gangas had a kingdom from the Gangā to the Godāvarī and began the Jagannātha temple at Puri and the Sun temple at Konark. The Senas dominated much of Bengal, with Nādīya as capital, and supported Hindu thought, literature and Jayadeva. The Western Chālukyas faded as the Kākatīyas and Hoysalas grew stronger. The Kākatīyas ruled from Orugallu, whose fort had toraṇas. The Hoysalas became famous for temple architecture.
activities.prompt: A visitor points to the toraṇas at Orugallu and calls them the best-known work of the Hoysalas. How should the guide correct the visitor?
options: Those gateways were a Kākatīya feature, while the Hoysalas were famous for temple architecture.
Those gateways were a Sena feature, and the Hoysalas were based at Orugallu.
Those gateways were built by the Eastern Gangas, who also ruled from Orugallu.
Those gateways show Hoysala temple work, especially carved pillars and panels.

why.Those gateways were a Sena feature, and: Both the Sena connection and Hoysala connection to Orugallu are incorrect.
why.Those gateways were built by the Eastern: The Eastern Gangas did not rule from Orugallu, and the gateways belonged to the Kākatīyas.
why.Those gateways show Hoysala temple work,: Carved pillars, sculptures and panels describe Hoysala temple architecture, not the Kākatīya gateways.

activities.explanation: The Kākatīyas’ fort at Orugallu had toraṇas, while Hoysala fame was in temple architecture.

activities.prompt: Explain why the Eastern Gangas and the Senas should be shown as different powers in the exhibition.
activities.answer: The Eastern Gangas were a stable power in eastern India and began the Jagannātha temple at Puri and the Sun temple at Konark. The Senas became dominant over much of Bengal, had their capital at Nādīya, and promoted Hindu thought, literature and poets such as Jayadeva.
points: The Eastern Gangas were a stable power in eastern India.
They began the Jagannātha temple at Puri.
They began the Sun temple at Konark.
The Senas dominated much of Bengal, had Nādīya as capital, and supported Jayadeva.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a school exhibition, a student explains how Rājarāja Chola’s conquests connected the Chola kingdom with northern Sri Lanka and mentions the great Bṛihadīśhvara temple at Thanjavur. The display also describes trade with China and a Buddhist monastery at Nāgapaṭṭinam. Another map shows Rājendra Chola I’s naval expedition against the Śhrīvijaya Empire and his conquests in present-day Odisha and Bengal.
activities.prompt: If Rājarāja had not conquered northern Sri Lanka, including Anurādhapura, what would most directly have been different?
options: The Chola sphere of control in northern Sri Lanka would have been smaller.
Chola control in present-day Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh would have expanded instead.
All Chola trade with China would have stopped immediately.
Rājendra’s later conquests in Bengal would have been impossible.

why.Chola control in present-day Karnataka a: The other conquests were in present-day Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Bengal.
why.All Chola trade with China would have st: Trade with China thrived under the Cholas.
why.Rājendra’s later conquests in Bengal wou: Rājendra’s conquest of Bengal was separate from Rājarāja’s Sri Lankan campaign.

activities.explanation: Correct: Northern Sri Lanka was part of Rājarāja’s conquests.

activities.context: At a school exhibition, a student explains how Rājarāja Chola’s conquests connected the Chola kingdom with northern Sri Lanka and mentions the great Bṛihadīśhvara temple at Thanjavur. The display also describes trade with China and a Buddhist monastery at Nāgapaṭṭinam. Another map shows Rājendra Chola I’s naval expedition against the Śhrīvijaya Empire and his conquests in present-day Odisha and Bengal.
activities.prompt: Why was Rājendra Chola I’s naval expedition against the Śhrīvijaya Empire an important response to changing sea-route conditions?
options: Rivalry over the Strait of Malacca encouraged a direct challenge to Śhrīvijaya.
The expedition was mainly intended to build wells, tanks and canals at home.
Rājendra needed a naval force to restore Anurādhapura after Rājarāja’s conquest.
The expedition was undertaken to enlarge the Bṛihadīśhvara temple at Thanjavur.

why.The expedition was mainly intended to bu: Public works included roads, tanks, wells, canals and artificial lakes.
why.Rājendra needed a naval force to restore: Anurādhapura had already been conquered by Rājarāja in northern Sri Lanka.
why.The expedition was undertaken to enlarge: The great temple at Thanjavur was built by Rājarāja.

activities.explanation: Correct: Competition over the Malacca sea route shaped Chola–Śhrīvijaya relations.

activities.context: At a school exhibition, a student explains how Rājarāja Chola’s conquests connected the Chola kingdom with northern Sri Lanka and mentions the great Bṛihadīśhvara temple at Thanjavur. The display also describes trade with China and a Buddhist monastery at Nāgapaṭṭinam. Another map shows Rājendra Chola I’s naval expedition against the Śhrīvijaya Empire and his conquests in present-day Odisha and Bengal.
activities.prompt: After Rājendra’s navy defeated the Śhrīvijaya forces and captured their capital, what conclusion should the student draw from the expedition?
options: It produced a major Chola victory over Śhrīvijaya.
It was mainly a public-works project for local communities.
It proved that Chola military power had reached China through trade.
It left Śhrīvijaya’s forces and capital completely unchanged.

why.It was mainly a public-works project for: The expedition was military, not a public-works project.
why.It proved that Chola military power had: Trade with China thrived, but the expedition was directed against Śhrīvijaya.
why.It left Śhrīvijaya’s forces and capital: The defeat and capture clearly changed the situation in Śhrīvijaya.

activities.explanation: Correct: The navy won a victory, defeated the enemy forces and captured the capital.

activities.prompt: Explain how the achievements of Rājarāja Chola differed from those of Rājendra Chola I.
activities.answer: Rājarāja Chola expanded the realm into present-day Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and northern Sri Lanka, including Anurādhapura. He built the Bṛihadīśhvara temple at Thanjavur and helped build a Buddhist monastery at Nāgapaṭṭinam. Rājendra Chola I led a naval expedition, defeated Śhrīvijaya forces, captured their capital and expanded into parts of Odisha and Bengal.
points: Rājarāja conquered parts of present-day Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh.
Rājarāja conquered northern Sri Lanka, including Anurādhapura.
Rājarāja built the Bṛihadīśhvara temple and helped establish the monastery at Nāgapaṭṭinam.
Rājendra led a naval expedition and expanded into parts of Odisha and Bengal.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Malwa, in present-day Madhya Pradesh, shows how political power can change. The Paramāras began as vassals of the Pratihāras and Rāṣhṭrakūṭas before becoming an independent power there. Muhammad Ghūrī brought parts of Punjab and Sindh under his rule. After his Gujarat campaign ended in defeat in 1178, he defeated and executed Pṛithvīrāja at the Second Battle of Tarain and captured Delhi. Bakhtiyār Khiljī later destroyed major Buddhist learning centres, including Nālandā and Vikramaśhilā.
activities.prompt: If the Paramāras had continued serving the Pratihāras and Rāṣhṭrakūṭas, what would most likely be different?
options: Malwa would not have come under their independent rule.
They would have become vassals of the Ghūrids instead.
They would have remained independent while serving those rulers.
They would have become the rulers of Ghazni instead.

why.They would have become vassals of the Gh: The Paramāras’ overlords were the Pratihāras and Rāṣhṭrakūṭas, not the Ghūrids.
why.They would have remained independent whi: Vassal status and independent rule were different positions.
why.They would have become the rulers of Gha: Ghazni was associated with the chiefs of Ghūr, not the Paramāras.

activities.explanation: Remaining vassals would prevent the stated move to independent rule in Malwa.

activities.context: Malwa, in present-day Madhya Pradesh, shows how political power can change. The Paramāras began as vassals of the Pratihāras and Rāṣhṭrakūṭas before becoming an independent power there. Muhammad Ghūrī brought parts of Punjab and Sindh under his rule. After his Gujarat campaign ended in defeat in 1178, he defeated and executed Pṛithvīrāja at the Second Battle of Tarain and captured Delhi. Bakhtiyār Khiljī later destroyed major Buddhist learning centres, including Nālandā and Vikramaśhilā.
activities.prompt: A student claims that Bakhtiyār Khiljī’s campaign helped Buddhist learning centres grow. Which correction does the case support?
options: Places such as Nālandā and Vikramaśhilā suffered destruction.
Places such as Nālandā and Vikramaśhilā became stronger learning centres.
The Paramāras’ independent rule in Malwa was destroyed instead.
The chiefs of Ghūr lost control of Ghazni.

why.Places such as Nālandā and Vikramaśhilā: This wrongly reverses the destruction described in the case.
why.The Paramāras’ independent rule in Malwa: His campaign is connected with Buddhist learning centres, not Paramāra rule.
why.The chiefs of Ghūr lost control of Ghazn: The case does not connect his campaign with the chiefs of Ghūr losing Ghazni.

activities.explanation: Bakhtiyār Khiljī destroyed major Buddhist learning centres.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between the rise of the Paramāras and the rise of the Ghūrid power?
activities.answer: The Paramāras served as vassals of the Pratihāras and Rāṣhṭrakūṭas, then became independent in Malwa. The chiefs of Ghūr took control of Ghazni and built power, while Muhammad Ghūrī brought parts of Punjab and Sindh under his rule. Both groups grew power, but through different stages and in different regions.
points: The Paramāras began as vassals.
They later became independent in Malwa.
The chiefs of Ghūr controlled Ghazni and built power.
Muhammad Ghūrī brought parts of Punjab and Sindh under his rule.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a period when India’s trade with China and Southeast Asia kept growing, a powerful king needed a sizeable army. Muhammad Ghūrī assigned officers temporary land so that they collected revenue and also provided military service. Seasonal rains caused problems, and rulers maintained irrigation works to reduce those problems. The king wanted an efficient government so that the army, revenue arrangements, trade, and waterworks could be managed together.
activities.prompt: If the king stopped maintaining irrigation works during seasonal rains, what would the case predict?
options: Problems caused by seasonal rains would become harder to reduce.
Seasonal-rain problems would disappear without maintenance.
The need for irrigation works would fall to zero.
Trade with China and Southeast Asia would certainly stop growing.

why.Seasonal-rain problems would disappear w: Ignoring maintenance would not make seasonal-rain problems disappear.
why.The need for irrigation works would fall: Seasonal rains would continue causing problems, so irrigation works would remain necessary.
why.Trade with China and Southeast Asia woul: Stopping irrigation maintenance would not necessarily stop trade from growing.

activities.explanation: Maintaining irrigation works helped reduce seasonal-rain problems.

activities.context: During a period when India’s trade with China and Southeast Asia kept growing, a powerful king needed a sizeable army. Muhammad Ghūrī assigned officers temporary land so that they collected revenue and also provided military service. Seasonal rains caused problems, and rulers maintained irrigation works to reduce those problems. The king wanted an efficient government so that the army, revenue arrangements, trade, and waterworks could be managed together.
activities.prompt: If the king wants revenue collection and military service to support efficient government, what should he do?
options: Tie temporary land assignments to both revenue collection and military service.
Tie temporary land assignments to revenue collection only.
Tie temporary land assignments to military service only.
Make land assignments permanent and drop both required duties.

why.Tie temporary land assignments to revenu: Leaving out military service would fail to support the army.
why.Tie temporary land assignments to milita: Leaving out revenue collection would fail to support government revenue.
why.Make land assignments permanent and drop: Permanent assignments without the required duties would not follow the case.

activities.explanation: This arrangement supported government revenue and the king’s army.

chapters.summary: In this chapter: jews in india; syriac christians and the arrival of the parsis; parsis, arab merchants and siddis; armenians and baha’is in india.

lessons.title: Jews in India

activities.prompt: How did Jewish communities build new lives in India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Safe Haven
activities.body: Jews fled their homes because of persecution in several countries. India became a safe haven where they could practise their faith without fear. The Bene Israel community lived on the Konkan coast just south of Mumbai. They came around 175 BCE from the ancient Kingdom of Israel. Their ship was caught in a storm and shipwrecked near the coast. Survivors settled in India and started a new life.
keyPoints: Jews fled homes because of persecution.
India became a safe haven.
The Bene Israel settled on the Konkan coast.
activities.explanation: You will learn why Jews came to India and where they settled.

activities.prompt: The Bene Israel ship has been wrecked. Why did the survivors settle in India and build a new life?
steps: Persecution had made Jews leave their homes in several countries.
India was a safe haven, so Jews could practise their faith without fear.
After the shipwreck, the survivors settled in India and started again.
Their community grew over time and became India's largest Jewish community.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Why did Jews leave?
activities.prompt: Why did Jews leave their homes?
options: They wanted a new trade
They feared persecution
They needed warmer weather
They wanted to build ships
activities.explanation: They fled their homes because of persecution in several countries.

activities.title: A Date from History
activities.prompt: The Bene Israel came around ______ BCE from the ancient Kingdom of Israel.
activities.hint: Use the year given in the lesson.
activities.explanation: They came around 175 BCE from the ancient Kingdom of Israel.

activities.title: People and Places
activities.prompt: Match each group or person with what the lesson tells us.
pairs: Konkan coast just south of Mumbai
granted the Jews land free of cost
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a community or ruler with an event from the lesson.

activities.title: The Purpose of a Synagogue
activities.prompt: What did the synagogue enable the Jews to do?
options: Practise their faith
Trade with merchants
Build new houses
Teach children songs
activities.explanation: The synagogue enabled the Jews to practise their faith.

activities.title: The Bene Israel Journey
activities.prompt: Put the events of the Bene Israel journey in order.
items: The Bene Israel came around 175 BCE
Their ship was caught in a storm
Their ship was shipwrecked near the coast
The survivors settled in India and started a new life
activities.explanation: They came from Israel, met a storm, shipwrecked, and then settled in India.

activities.title: New Jewish Communities
activities.prompt: What happened between the 12th and 19th centuries?
options: The Bene Israel left India
All Jews went to Cochin
Several Jewish groups arrived
The communities stopped practising their faith
activities.explanation: Several Jewish groups arrived between the 12th and 19th centuries.

activities.prompt: A map marks the Konkan coast just south of Mumbai and Cochin separately. Which conclusion fits the facts?
options: Bene Israel lived south of Mumbai; others lived near Kochi.
Bene Israel lived near Kochi; others lived north of Mumbai.
Both groups lived together on the Konkan coast.
Bene Israel lived north of Mumbai; others lived near Kochi.

why.Bene Israel lived near Kochi; others liv: It swaps the locations of the two Jewish communities.
why.Both groups lived together on the Konkan: It wrongly places both groups together on the Konkan coast.
why.Bene Israel lived north of Mumbai; other: It puts the Bene Israel on the wrong side of Mumbai.

activities.explanation: This matches the Bene Israel’s Konkan home and Jewish settlement near Kochi.

activities.prompt: The Bene Israel remembered a prayer about one God. Why might this help during a crisis?
options: It kept their shared belief alive after the shipwreck.
It taught them how to repair the wrecked ship.
It gave them money to buy land in India.
It showed them the route to ancient Israel.

why.It taught them how to repair the wrecked: A prayer about belief did not teach ship repair.
The prayer promised no money for buying land.
why.It showed them the route to ancient Isra: The prayer expressed belief, not directions to Israel.

activities.explanation: The prayer expressed one God and could preserve their belief.

activities.prompt: The Raja of Kochi granted Jewish settlers land free of cost. Why could they build a synagogue?
options: The free land gave them space to practise their faith.
The storm carried ready-made walls to Kochi.
The prayer ordered the Raja to build for them.
The Bene Israel had already lived in Kochi.

why.The storm carried ready-made walls to Ko: The shipwreck concerned the Bene Israel, not Kochi building materials.
why.The prayer ordered the Raja to build for: The prayer spoke about one God, not about construction.
why.The Bene Israel had already lived in Koc: Bene Israel lived on the Konkan coast; some Jews lived near Kochi.

activities.explanation: Free land helped them build a place for Jewish worship.

activities.prompt: The Bene Israel settled after a shipwreck. Over time, they became India's largest Jewish community. What does this show?
options: Settling in India helped their community grow over time.
The storm made every other Jewish community disappear.
They grew because they stayed on their wrecked ship.
They grew only after returning to ancient Israel.

why.The storm made every other Jewish commun: The facts do not say that other Jewish communities disappeared.
why.They grew because they stayed on their w: They left the wrecked ship and settled in India.
why.They grew only after returning to ancien: They settled in India; the facts do not say they returned.

activities.explanation: They settled in India, and over time became India's largest Jewish community.

lessons.title: Syriac Christians and the Arrival of the Parsis

activities.prompt: How did faith and journeys bring new communities to India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Communities Come to India
activities.body: Some Christian groups used the ancient Syriac language in worship. The Roman Empire sometimes treated them as heretics. Persians suspected them of helping the Romans. Some travelled east along trade routes to India’s Malabar coast. They lived and worshipped freely there. In India, they are also called Syrian Christians. Parsis came to escape religious persecution in Persia and reach India. Their community is divided into several separate groups called sects.
keyPoints: Some Christians used ancient Syriac in worship.
Some Syriac Christians travelled to the Malabar coast.
Parsis fled persecution in Persia.
Syriac Christians are also called Syrian Christians in India.
activities.explanation: Read about the Christians who travelled east and the Parsis who came from Persia.

activities.prompt: Why did some Syriac Christians travel east to Kerala?
steps: Some used ancient Syriac in worship, so Romans sometimes treated them as heretics.
Persians suspected them of helping Romans, so some feared staying in Persia.
Some travelled east along trade routes, because those routes led toward India.
They reached Kerala, where they could live and worship freely.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which language did some Christian groups use in worship?
options: Roman
Ancient Syriac
Persian
Malabar
activities.explanation: Some Christian groups used the ancient Syriac language during worship.

activities.prompt: Where in present-day Kerala did the travellers reach?
options: The Malabar coast
The Roman Empire
Present-day Persia
The ancient Syriac language
activities.explanation: Travelling Syriac Christians reached the Malabar coast in present-day Kerala.

activities.prompt: Match each group or people with what happened.
pairs: Suspected them of helping the Romans
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a name, another name, or an event from the lesson.

activities.prompt: In India, Syriac Christians are also called ______ Christians.
activities.hint: This name is used in India.
activities.explanation: The lesson says that Syriac Christians are also called Syrian Christians in India.

activities.prompt: Put the Parsis’ journey in order.
items: They could not freely practise their faith
They came to India to escape persecution
activities.explanation: Their faith was restricted, so they fled Persia and came to India.

activities.prompt: Why did the Parsis come to India?
options: To use ancient Syriac in worship
To reach the Malabar coast
To join the Roman Empire
To escape religious persecution
activities.explanation: They came mainly to escape persecution, forced conversion, and religious taxes in Persia.

activities.prompt: A church uses ancient Syriac in worship. Romans call the group heretics. What will Persians most likely suspect?
options: the group is secretly helping the Romans
the group wants to rule Persia
the group has stopped trading eastwards
the group plans to convert to Islam

why.the group wants to rule Persia: This confuses Roman suspicion with a wish for power.
why.the group has stopped trading eastwards: This confuses Roman suspicion with a change in trade.
why.the group plans to convert to Islam: This confuses Persian persecution of Parsis with this group's story.

activities.explanation: Persians suspected them of secretly helping the Romans.

activities.prompt: A map shows an eastbound trade route ending on India's Malabar coast. What does this support?
options: some Syriac Christians reached present-day Kerala
all Persians moved to the Malabar coast
Romans built churches along this route
the route began near the Roman Empire

why.all Persians moved to the Malabar coast: The fact says some Syriac Christians, not all Persians.
why.Romans built churches along this route: The facts mention worship, not Roman church building.
why.the route began near the Roman Empire: Nothing says the route began near the Roman Empire.

activities.explanation: The facts connect eastward travel with reaching Kerala.

activities.prompt: A Syriac Christian family worships freely on the Malabar coast. Persia restricts its faith. What main difference is shown?
options: Persia restricted faith; the Malabar coast allowed free worship
Malabar forced conversion; Persia allowed free worship
Both places required religious taxes from every family
Both places treated Syriac groups as Roman heretics

why.Malabar forced conversion; Persia allowe: This swaps the places; forced conversion happened in Persia.
why.Both places required religious taxes fro: The taxes affected Parsis in Persia, not every Kerala family.
why.Both places treated Syriac groups as Rom: Romans treated some groups as heretics, not every place alike.

activities.explanation: Persia restricted faith, while Kerala allowed free worship.

activities.prompt: A Parsi family in Persia faces forced conversion and religious taxes. Why might they leave for India?
options: they cannot freely practise their faith
they want to join Roman church groups
they hope to find the Syriac language
they plan to travel west along trade routes

why.they want to join Roman church groups: Roman Christians were a different group from the Parsis.
why.they hope to find the Syriac language: The Parsis left because of persecution, not to find Syriac.
why.they plan to travel west along trade rou: The facts describe fleeing Persia, not a journey west.

activities.explanation: Persian persecution stopped them from practising their faith freely.

activities.prompt: A Syriac Christian group travels east along trade routes. A Parsi family also reaches India. What best explains their different reasons?
options: The first followed trade routes; the second fled faith persecution.
The first fled Persia; the second followed Romans to Kerala.
The first sought Roman help; the second wanted Persian taxes.
The first wanted trade; the second wanted forced conversion.

why.The first fled Persia; the second follow: This wrongly makes the first group come from Persia.
why.The first sought Roman help; the second: The second family was escaping persecution, not seeking taxes.
why.The first wanted trade; the second wante: The second family fled forced conversion, not seeking it.

activities.explanation: One journey followed trade routes; the other mainly escaped persecution.

activities.prompt: In India, people call them Syrian Christians. The community has several sects. What does this show?
options: one shared name does not mean one single sect
several sects must all use Persian
the name proves every member came from Persia
different sects mean they rejected Christianity

why.several sects must all use Persian: The facts do not say that every sect uses Persian.
why.the name proves every member came from P: A shared name does not prove where every member came from.
why.different sects mean they rejected Chris: Several sects still belong to the Christian community.

activities.explanation: The community has several sects, even with one shared name.

lessons.title: Parsis, Arab Merchants and Siddis

activities.prompt: How did three very different communities find their place in India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Different Communities, Shared Connections
activities.body: Parsis combined their ancient traditions with local culture. India now has the world's largest population of followers of Zoroastrianism. Arab merchants came from the seventh century onwards. They traded goods and married local women. In Kerala, their settlers became part of the Mappila Muslim community. The Siddis came from Africa and were brought to India as slaves. Their identity combines African and Indian traditions.
keyPoints: Parsis joined ancient traditions with local culture
Arab merchants traded and married local women
Siddis combine African and Indian traditions
activities.explanation: This lesson introduces the histories of three communities connected with India.

activities.prompt: The Parsis need a place to settle, but the kingdom is full. How can they show there is room?
steps: Jadi Rāṇā showed the Parsis a jug full of milk.
The full milk showed that the kingdom could take no more people.
A wise Parsi dissolved sugar without spilling, showing that more could fit.
Therefore, Jadi Rāṇā gave the Parsis a secure place to settle.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did the Parsis do with their traditions?
options: They kept ancient traditions separate from local culture.
They became part of the Mappila Muslim community.
They were enslaved and brought to India.
They combined ancient traditions with local culture.
activities.explanation: Well done! The Parsis brought together their ancient traditions and the local culture.

activities.prompt: The wise Parsi dissolved ______ into the milk without spilling it.
activities.hint: It was added to the full jug of milk.
activities.explanation: Great work! The wise Parsi dissolved sugar into the milk without spilling any.

activities.prompt: Match each group or person with what the lesson says.
pairs: Gave the Parsis a secure place
Part of the Mappila Muslim community
activities.explanation: Nice matching! Each community or person has a special connection in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Which statement about Arab merchants is correct?
options: They began coming from the seventh century onwards.
They were enslaved and brought to India.
They combined ancient traditions with local culture.
They showed Parsis a jug full of milk.
activities.explanation: Correct! Arab merchants began coming to India from the seventh century onwards.

activities.prompt: Put the events from the milk story in order.
items: Raja Jadi Rāṇā showed the Parsis the milk
The milk showed that the kingdom was full
A wise Parsi dissolved sugar into the milk
Jadi Rāṇā gave the Parsis a secure place
activities.explanation: You found the clear sequence! The milk was shown, understood, and sweetened before a settlement was given.

activities.prompt: Which statement describes the Siddis?
options: Their identity combines African and Indian traditions.
They began coming from the seventh century onwards.
They combined ancient traditions with local culture.
They became part of the Mappila Muslim community.
activities.explanation: Excellent! The Siddis are of African origin, and their identity combines African and Indian traditions.

activities.prompt: The Parsis dissolved sugar into full milk without spilling it. What did their cleverness show?
options: The kingdom could accept more people.
The kingdom could never accept anyone.
The Parsi wanted to spoil the milk.
The Parsi planned to leave India.

A full jug means no room, but the sugar showed some room.
The story shows a peaceful solution, not an attempt to spoil milk.
Their settlement shows they wanted a home, not to leave.

activities.explanation: The dissolved sugar showed there was still room.

activities.prompt: India has the largest Zoroastrian population. Parsis joined ancient and local ways. What does this show?
options: A community can keep old roots while living locally.
A large community must keep old ways unchanged.
Local living always removes a community's old roots.
Population size shows a community cannot change.

why.A large community must keep old ways unc: They did change by adding local culture to old traditions.
why.Local living always removes a community': Their identity kept ancient traditions while taking local culture.
why.Population size shows a community cannot: A large population does not stop traditions from changing.

activities.explanation: The Parsis combined ancient traditions with local culture.

activities.prompt: The Siddis were enslaved and brought to India as slaves. What does their mixed identity tell us?
options: Indian life joined with their African roots.
Indian life erased all their African roots.
African roots had no place in their identity.
Slavery was the only thing shaping their identity.

why.Indian life erased all their African roo: Combining traditions means both sides remained part of their identity.
why.African roots had no place in their iden: The fact says their identity includes African traditions.
why.Slavery was the only thing shaping their: Their identity also includes Indian traditions, not only slavery.

activities.explanation: Their identity combines African and Indian traditions.

activities.prompt: The wise Parsi added sugar to full milk without spilling. What response fits Jadi Rāṇā's decision?
options: Give the group a secure place to settle.
Keep the group outside the kingdom forever.
Fill the jug with more milk first.
Ask the group to leave their traditions.

why.Keep the group outside the kingdom forev: He accepted their clever proof and let them settle.
The sugar showed there was room, so more milk was not needed.
The decision solved their need for a home, not their traditions.

activities.explanation: Jadi Rāṇā gave the Parsis a secure place to settle.
