lessons.title: Armenians and Baha’is in India

activities.prompt: How did Armenians and Baha’is find their place in India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Armenians and Baha’is in India
activities.body: Armenians settled in Surat, Kolkata and Chennai, building schools, churches and cemeteries. Kolkata became an Armenian centre. Akbar allowed Armenians to build a church and follow their practices. They held important roles in his royal household. The Baha’i faith began in Persia in the mid-1800s. Baha’u’llah taught unity among people and harmony between religions. India was one of the first safe places for Baha’is, and many Indians later joined.
keyPoints: Akbar allowed Armenians to build a church and follow their practices.
Abdul Hai was the Chief Justice, while Lady Juliana was a royal doctor.
India was an early safe place for Baha’is, and many Indians joined.
activities.explanation: These people made important contributions to life in India.

activities.prompt: An Armenian family moves to India. Why can it build a church and join community life?
steps: Akbar allowed Armenians to build a church and follow their religious practices.
This permission meant they could practise their faith in India.
They settled in Surat, Kolkata and Chennai, where they built community places.
So the family could build a church and join Armenian community life.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who allowed the Armenians to build a church?
options: Akbar
Abdul Hai
Lady Juliana
Baha’u’llah
activities.explanation: Akbar allowed Armenians to build a church and follow their practices.

activities.prompt: Match each person or place with its description.
activities.explanation: Each description matches the person or place connected with it in the lesson.

activities.prompt: What did Akbar allow the Armenians to do?
options: Build a church and follow practices
Run the Mughal court and judge cases
Settle only in Kolkata
Start the Baha’i religion
activities.explanation: Akbar gave Armenians permission to build a church and follow their practices.

activities.prompt: Put these events in their historical order.
items: The Baha’i religion began in Persia in the mid-1800s.
Baha’u’llah taught unity among people and harmony between religions.
Iran’s religious leaders branded the Baha’is as heretics.
India was one of the first safe places where Baha’is went to live.
Many Indians later joined the Baha’i faith.
activities.explanation: The order moves from the faith’s beginning to Indian people joining it.

activities.prompt: Which statement about the Baha’is in India is correct?
options: India was an early safe place for Baha’is.
Baha’is first lived only in Persia.
Many Indians joined before the faith began.
Iran’s leaders gave Baha’is safe homes.
activities.explanation: India was one of the first safe places where Baha’is went to live.

activities.prompt: Baha’u’llah taught ______ among people and harmony between religions.
activities.hint: This word means bringing people together.
activities.explanation: Baha’u’llah taught unity among people and harmony between religions.

activities.prompt: Armenians settled in Surat, Kolkata and Chennai. Kolkata became a major Armenian centre. Which city best fits a family seeking a large Armenian community?
options: Kolkata, because it became a major Armenian centre.
Surat, because it was the first Armenian centre.
Chennai, because it was the only Armenian centre.
Surat, because Kolkata had no Armenian settlers.

why.Surat, because it was the first Armenian: This wrongly treats the first settled city as the major centre.
why.Chennai, because it was the only Armenia: This wrongly treats the only settled city as the major centre.
why.Surat, because Kolkata had no Armenian s: This denies the known Armenian settlement in Kolkata.

activities.explanation: Kolkata is right because it became a major Armenian centre.

activities.prompt: A map shows Armenian schools, churches and cemeteries in three cities. What does this map suggest about life in these cities?
options: Armenians settled there and built community places.
Armenians stayed away and built places in Persia.
Armenians lived there, but built no shared places.
Armenians used only private royal homes.

why.Armenians stayed away and built places i: This wrongly suggests Armenians stayed away from these cities.
why.Armenians lived there, but built no shar: This wrongly says Armenians built no shared places.
This wrongly says Armenians used only private royal homes.

activities.explanation: This is right because Armenians settled and built these community places.

activities.prompt: Baha’u’llah taught unity among people and harmony between religions. Iran’s religious leaders branded the Baha’is as heretics. What might happen when Baha’is look for a safe home?
options: They may settle in India, which was an early safe place.
They must stay in Persia, because harmony means no moving.
They must avoid India, because Persia became safer.
They may settle in Persia, because India had no Baha’is.

why.They must stay in Persia, because harmon: This wrongly treats Baha’i teaching as a rule against moving.
why.They must avoid India, because Persia be: This wrongly assumes Persia became safe for Baha’is.
why.They may settle in Persia, because India: This wrongly claims India had no Baha’is to welcome them.

activities.explanation: India fits because it was one of the first safe places.

activities.prompt: The Baha’i religion began in Persia in the mid-1800s. Later, many Indians joined the Baha’i faith. What change does this show?
options: The Baha’i faith spread from Persia to India.
It began in India and later moved to Persia.
It stayed in Persia, because Indians joined another faith.
It started in India before reaching Persia.

why.It began in India and later moved to Per: This wrongly reverses the direction of the spread.
why.It stayed in Persia, because Indians joi: This wrongly says Indians joined a different faith.
why.It started in India before reaching Pers: This wrongly places the faith’s beginning in India.

activities.explanation: This is right because the Baha’i faith spread from Persia to India.

lessons.title: Polish Children and Tibetan Refugees

activities.prompt: How did kindness help Polish children and Tibetan refugees?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Rescue and Refuge
activities.body: During the Second World War, Poland was invaded. Families were separated, and children became orphans. The Red Cross and Maharaja rescued Polish children. He gave them food and care, saving around a thousand orphans. After the uprising in Lhasa, the 14th Dalai Lama fled across the Himalaya. He is an honoured guest in India. India supported Tibetan refugees and education for their children. He promotes compassion, forgiveness and tolerance.
keyPoints: Polish children were rescued and cared for.
The Dalai Lama fled to India after the Lhasa uprising.
India supported Tibetan refugees and their children's education.
activities.explanation: This introduces rescue, refuge, care and tolerance.

activities.prompt: A student plans to give only food to Polish orphans and Tibetan refugees. Why is this plan incomplete?
steps: Polish orphans needed a safe place, food and care because war separated families.
Tibetan refugees needed rehabilitation and education because they needed a new life in India.
Therefore, compassionate help must meet several needs, not only food.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Support in India
activities.body: The Central Tibetan Administration works as a government-in-exile. A government-in-exile continues working away from its country. The Indian government rehabilitated Tibetan refugees and provided education for their children. Sowa Rigpa combines Ayurveda with knowledge from other parts of Asia. India has included Sowa Rigpa in its AYUSH programme.
keyPoints: The Central Tibetan Administration works as a government-in-exile.
India rehabilitated refugees and provided education.
Sowa Rigpa joins Ayurveda with knowledge from other parts of Asia.
activities.explanation: This card explains government-in-exile and Sowa Rigpa.

activities.title: Who Led the Rescue?
activities.prompt: Who used the Red Cross and other groups to rescue Polish children?
options: The Maharaja
The Dalai Lama
The Red Cross
The Tibetan administration
activities.explanation: The Maharaja used the Red Cross and other groups for the rescue.

activities.title: Food and Care
activities.prompt: The Maharaja gave rescued Polish children food and care.
activities.explanation: He gave the children a safe place, food and care.

activities.title: Match Actions and Needs
activities.prompt: Match each clue with the correct answer.
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an action or need with its stated result.

activities.title: A Government in Exile
activities.prompt: The Central Tibetan Administration works as a government-in-______.
activities.hint: This describes government work away from its country.
activities.explanation: The Central Tibetan Administration works as a government-in-exile.

activities.title: From War to Rescue
activities.prompt: Put these events in order from the war to the rescue and care.
items: Poland was invaded during the Second World War
Families were separated and children became orphans
The Maharaja used the Red Cross and other groups
Polish children received a safe place, food and care
activities.explanation: The events move from invasion and separation to organised rescue and care.

activities.title: Actions of the Indian Government
activities.prompt: Which sentence correctly describes two Indian government actions?
options: Supported refugees and included Sowa Rigpa in AYUSH
Rescued Polish children and invaded Poland during war
Created refugees and ended children's education in India
Rejected Ayurveda and abandoned support for Tibetan people
activities.explanation: The government supported refugees and included Sowa Rigpa in its AYUSH programme.

activities.prompt: The Maharaja used the Red Cross and other groups after Poland’s invasion. He gave them a safe place, food and care. Why did this rescue matter?
options: It helped about a thousand orphans survive.
It sent every child back to Poland.
It ended all support for war families.
It gave children food but no care.

This mistake assumes rescue meant sending children back to Poland.
This mistake thinks rescue stopped help for needy families.
This mistake believes food alone was enough for every child.

activities.explanation: This is right because his care saved around a thousand Polish orphans.

activities.prompt: Polish children faced danger after Poland was invaded. The Dalai Lama was advised to flee after the Lhasa uprising. What do both situations show about danger?
options: It can break families and make people leave.
It always makes people feel safer at home.
It can bring schools and health care closer.
It can stop communities from helping one another.

why.It always makes people feel safer at hom: This mistake thinks danger makes homes safer instead of less safe.
why.It can bring schools and health care clo: This mistake assumes danger improves schools and health care.
why.It can stop communities from helping one: This mistake confuses harm to communities with their ability to help.

activities.explanation: This is right because war broke families, while the uprising caused flight.

activities.prompt: A map shows Lhasa beside the Himalaya. The Dalai Lama later became an honoured guest in India. Which route fits the facts?
options: Across the Himalaya into India.
Within Lhasa and stay there.
Toward Poland to find children.
Around India without crossing mountains.

This mistake treats Lhasa as a safe place after the uprising.
This mistake mixes the Polish rescue with the Dalai Lama’s journey.
This mistake misreads crossing the Himalaya as staying within India.

activities.explanation: This is right because he fled across the Himalaya and later stayed in India.

activities.prompt: The Dalai Lama commits to compassion, forgiveness and tolerance. A student sees two classmates disagree. What is the best response?
options: Keep the anger and always refuse forgiveness.
Invite only students who fully agree with them.
Listen closely and try to understand both.
Call one student wrong and laugh often.

why.Keep the anger and always refuse forgive: This mistake confuses forgiveness with keeping anger.
why.Invite only students who fully agree wit: This mistake thinks tolerance means accepting only identical views.
This mistake treats disagreement as a reason for mockery.

activities.explanation: This is right because compassion and tolerance guide understanding.

lessons.title: The Whole World as Family

activities.prompt: How can our shared family spirit help us care for one another?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: One world, one family
activities.body: The whole world as a family has been practised for thousands of years. India welcomes people who seek refuge or better opportunities. Atithi devo bhava means a guest is like God. Sarve bhavantu sukhinah means happiness for all creatures. Indian communities have kept traditions and found secure places in India. The unity of humankind can help the world face shared challenges.
keyPoints: People may seek refuge or better opportunities in India.
Indian values welcome guests and wish happiness for all creatures.
Communities have found secure places and maintained traditions.
Unity can help the world face wars and other challenges.
activities.explanation: The lesson connects welcome, shared values and unity.

activities.prompt: A visitor asks why people from different faiths find a safe home in India. How does this show the world as a family?
steps: Some people came to India for refuge or better opportunities.
India welcomed people with different faiths and ideas.
This welcome gave small communities a secure place.
Security helped traditions last, showing that the world can be a family.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Why people choose India
activities.prompt: Why have some people made India their home?
options: Refuge or better opportunities
Sports or tourism
Rainfall or farming
Cities or villages
activities.explanation: These are the two reasons stated in the lesson.

activities.title: Join each idea with its meaning
activities.prompt: Match each idea with what your book says about it.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins an idea with its meaning in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Atithi devo bhava teaches that a guest is like God.
activities.explanation: This value says that every guest should be treated like God.

activities.title: Communities abroad
activities.prompt: Which description fits Indian communities abroad?
options: Calm, lawful and wealthy
Noisy, unlawful and poor
Calm, unlawful and poor
Busy, lawful and poor
activities.explanation: The lesson describes these communities as peaceful, law-abiding and prosperous.

activities.title: Challenges we can face
activities.prompt: The unity of humankind can help face only wars and climate change.
activities.explanation: Unity can also help face inequality and discrimination.

activities.title: The power of unity
activities.prompt: Which statement about the unity of humankind is correct?
options: Unity can stop the world facing challenges.
Unity can help the world face challenges.
Unity can make the world face no challenges.
Unity can divide the world during challenges.
activities.explanation: Unity can help the world face wars, climate change, inequality and discrimination.

activities.prompt: India has accepted people of different faiths for a long time. What has this acceptance helped India become?
options: A safe home for people who face persecution
A place where everyone must think in one way
A place where every person shares one faith
A place where old communities must leave home

why.A place where everyone must think in one: Acceptance does not mean everyone must think alike.
why.A place where every person shares one fa: India accepts different faiths, not one shared faith.
why.A place where old communities must leave: Acceptance helps communities stay, not leave their homes.

activities.explanation: This is exactly what acceptance helped India become.

activities.prompt: Small communities have found a secure place in India. Indian communities abroad are often peaceful. What do these facts show together?
options: Indian values can help communities build security and peace
Indian values can make communities leave their own traditions
Only communities outside India can possibly live in peace
Communities gain security by refusing every new person

why.Indian values can make communities leave: Leaving traditions is opposite to communities maintaining them.
why.Only communities outside India can possi: Indian communities abroad are peaceful too.
why.Communities gain security by refusing ev: Refusing newcomers is opposite to India's accepting welcome.

activities.explanation: Indian values helped communities in India, while communities abroad are peaceful.

activities.prompt: A map shows communities with different faiths across India. It also shows old traditions. What can we conclude together?
options: Welcoming different beliefs helped communities keep traditions
Keeping old traditions made India reject new beliefs
One shared faith made every old community secure
Communities kept traditions only after leaving India

why.Keeping old traditions made India reject: India accepted different beliefs, so traditions did not cause rejection.
why.One shared faith made every old communit: One shared faith is opposite to India's acceptance of different faiths.
why.Communities kept traditions only after l: Leaving India is opposite to communities staying secure in India.

activities.explanation: Acceptance gave security, and security helped traditions continue.

activities.prompt: A guest comes to your home for the first time. How should Indian values guide your welcome?
options: Treat the guest with respect, as you would a god
Ask the guest to leave before offering a seat
Ignore the guest until your own work is finished
Make the guest prove that they deserve your help

why.Ask the guest to leave before offering a: Indian values do not tell you to ask guests to leave.
why.Ignore the guest until your own work is: Ignoring a guest contradicts respect for guests.
why.Make the guest prove that they deserve y: Atithi devo bhava does not ask the guest to prove worth.

activities.explanation: Atithi devo bhava means a guest should be treated like God.

activities.prompt: A bird and your classmates need happiness. How should sarve bhavantu sukhinah guide your choices?
options: Wish happiness for every creature, not only yourself
Choose your own happiness before anyone else's needs
Wish happiness only for people who live nearby
Care for creatures only when they can pay you

why.Choose your own happiness before anyone: This choice puts your happiness before the happiness of others.
why.Wish happiness only for people who live: This choice limits happiness to nearby people, not all creatures.
why.Care for creatures only when they can pa: This choice helps only creatures that can give something back.

activities.explanation: Sarve bhavantu sukhinah wishes happiness for all creatures.

lessons.title: Test practice
lessons.sceneAlt: Members of the Jewish community pray inside Magen Abraham Synagogue during Tisha Be’Av.
lessons.sceneCaption: The Ahmedabad Jewish community prays inside Magen Abraham Synagogue during Tisha Be’Av.

activities.context: Jews who fled persecution in several countries found that India offered safety and allowed them to practise their faith without fear. The Bene Israel came around 175 BCE from the ancient Kingdom of Israel, but a storm wrecked their ship near the coast, where the survivors settled and began a new life. Other Jewish groups settled near Cochin, now called Kochi. The Raja of Kochi granted them land, and they built a synagogue.
activities.prompt: Suppose the Jews who reached India still faced persecution there. What would they most sensibly do next?
options: Look for another safe place where they could settle and practise their faith.
Remain where they were and expect the persecution to stop on its own.
Abandon their faith so that they would no longer be threatened.
Choose a new home but continue to fear practising their faith.

why.Remain where they were and expect the pe: Remaining would leave the original danger unresolved.
why.Abandon their faith so that they would n: Persecution does not require giving up one's faith.
why.Choose a new home but continue to fear p: A new home would not remove fear of religious practice.

activities.explanation: Another place might offer the safety they need.

activities.context: Jews who fled persecution in several countries found that India offered safety and allowed them to practise their faith without fear. The Bene Israel came around 175 BCE from the ancient Kingdom of Israel, but a storm wrecked their ship near the coast, where the survivors settled and began a new life. Other Jewish groups settled near Cochin, now called Kochi. The Raja of Kochi granted them land, and they built a synagogue.
activities.prompt: After the Raja of Kochi granted the Jewish settlers land free of cost, what should they do next to support their faith?
options: Construct a synagogue so the group can practise its faith together.
Use the land only for housing and provide no shared place for worship.
Build a synagogue but keep it closed to members of their own community.
Leave the land unused until a larger Jewish group arrived.

why.Use the land only for housing and provid: Housing alone would not meet their religious needs.
why.Build a synagogue but keep it closed to: The synagogue should enable the community's religious practice.
why.Leave the land unused until a larger Jew: They already had a reason to build a synagogue without waiting.

activities.explanation: A synagogue would let them practise their faith together.

activities.prompt: Explain why India became an important place for Jews who had fled persecution.
activities.answer: India became a safe haven for Jews fleeing persecution. They could practise their faith without fear and begin life again. The Bene Israel settled on the Konkan coast after their ship was wrecked, while Jewish groups near Cochin received land from the Raja of Kochi and built a synagogue.
points: Jews fled persecution in several countries.
India was a safe haven.
They could practise their faith without fear.
They were able to settle and begin a new life.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A Parsi family in Persia faces forced conversion and religious taxes, while some Persian authorities also suspect Syriac Christians of secretly helping the Romans. The family cannot freely practise its faith and considers leaving Persia. Meanwhile, some Syriac Christians travel eastward along trade routes and reach the Malabar coast of India, in present-day Kerala, where they can live and worship freely. India’s Syriac Christians are also called Syrian Christians, and their community includes several sects.
activities.prompt: What should the Parsi family most likely do next?
options: Leave Persia for India to escape the persecution.
Remain in Persia and accept the religious tax.
Stay in Persia and accept forced conversion to Islam.
Move to the Roman Empire, where they are treated as heretics.

why.Remain in Persia and accept the religiou: Paying a tax would not restore their freedom to practise their faith.
why.Stay in Persia and accept forced convers: Forced conversion would prevent free practice of their religion.
why.Move to the Roman Empire, where they are: Heretic treatment applied to some Syriac Christians under the Roman Empire, not the Parsis in Persia.

activities.explanation: Moving to India was the Parsis’ main way of escaping such persecution.

activities.context: A Parsi family in Persia faces forced conversion and religious taxes, while some Persian authorities also suspect Syriac Christians of secretly helping the Romans. The family cannot freely practise its faith and considers leaving Persia. Meanwhile, some Syriac Christians travel eastward along trade routes and reach the Malabar coast of India, in present-day Kerala, where they can live and worship freely. India’s Syriac Christians are also called Syrian Christians, and their community includes several sects.
activities.prompt: Suppose the Malabar coast no longer allowed the Syriac Christians to worship freely. What would be the most direct effect on the community?
options: They would lose the freedom to follow their religion there.
They would be forced to change the name Syrian Christians.
The community would become a single sect.
They would no longer be able to live on the coast.

why.They would be forced to change the name: The community’s name does not depend on rules about worship.
why.The community would become a single sect: Having several sects is separate from the freedom to worship.
why.They would no longer be able to live on: Losing freedom to worship would not necessarily prevent them from living there.

activities.explanation: Free worship is the specific ability that would be restricted.

activities.prompt: Explain how the reasons for coming to India differed between Syriac Christians and Parsis.
activities.answer: Some Syriac Christians travelled east along trade routes and reached Kerala, where they could live and worship freely; their movement is not described mainly as an escape from persecution. Parsis, by contrast, came to India chiefly to escape Persian persecution and gain freedom to practise their faith.
points: Some Syriac Christians travelled east along trade routes.
They reached the Malabar coast in present-day Kerala.
They could live and worship freely there.
Parsis came mainly to escape Persian persecution.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: An exhibition compares communities in India. One display shows how Parsis combined ancient traditions with local culture and notes that India has the largest population of followers of Zoroastrianism in the world. Another recalls Raja Jadi Rāṇā’s jug of milk and the wise Parsi who dissolved sugar without spilling, followed by a secure place granted to the Parsis. Displays present Arab merchants trading goods and marrying local women, and Siddis of African origin whose identity combines African and Indian traditions.
activities.prompt: A visitor notices that the guide says the Parsis kept their inherited customs completely separate from local culture. What should the visitor do?
options: Agree with the guide because the two cultures were always separate.
Explain that inherited customs and local ways were brought together.
Tell the guide that the Parsis abandoned their inherited customs.
Say that only local culture influenced the Parsis.

why.Agree with the guide because the two cul: This contradicts the exhibition’s account of the Parsis.
why.Tell the guide that the Parsis abandoned: The Parsis did not abandon their inherited customs.
why.Say that only local culture influenced t: The account does not say that local culture was their only influence.

activities.explanation: The correct account describes a meeting of two cultural traditions.

activities.context: An exhibition compares communities in India. One display shows how Parsis combined ancient traditions with local culture and notes that India has the largest population of followers of Zoroastrianism in the world. Another recalls Raja Jadi Rāṇā’s jug of milk and the wise Parsi who dissolved sugar without spilling, followed by a secure place granted to the Parsis. Displays present Arab merchants trading goods and marrying local women, and Siddis of African origin whose identity combines African and Indian traditions.
activities.prompt: A student is writing a caption that mentions only the Siddis’ African origin. How should the caption be revised?
options: Leave it as it is because African origin is the only part of their identity.
Include both their African background and Indian influences in the explanation.
Replace African origin with a claim that their identity was only Indian.
Remove both origins because their identity was unrelated to either place.

why.Leave it as it is because African origin: The Siddis’ identity includes more than one background.
why.Replace African origin with a claim that: Their identity is not based on India alone.
why.Remove both origins because their identi: The exhibition links their identity to both places.

activities.explanation: Their identity draws on both African and Indian traditions.

activities.prompt: Explain how the experiences of the Parsis and Siddis were different.
activities.answer: The Parsis combined ancient traditions with local culture. The Siddis were enslaved and brought to India as slaves, and their identity combines African and Indian traditions. Both communities have identities shaped by different backgrounds, but the Parsis’ story includes settling in India, while the Siddis’ includes enslavement and African origins.
points: The Parsis combined inherited traditions with local culture.
The Siddis were enslaved and brought from Africa to India.
Siddi identity includes both African and Indian traditions.
Both communities show cultural mixing, but their histories differ.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a class presentation, a student says Akbar allowed Armenians to build a church and follow their religion. Armenians held important roles in the Mughal royal household: Abdul Hai was Chief Justice, and Lady Juliana was a palace doctor. Communities in Surat, Kolkata and Chennai built schools, churches and cemeteries; Kolkata became a major Armenian centre. The lesson introduces Baha’u’llah’s teaching of unity and harmony between religions and India as an early safe place for Baha’is.
activities.prompt: If Akbar had not allowed Armenians to build a church and follow their religious practices, what would most likely have happened?
options: Their ability to practise their religion openly would have been reduced.
They would probably have gained greater freedom to practise their religion.
Abdul Hai would probably have been allowed to ignore all his duties in the Mughal court.
Lady Juliana would probably have been unable to work as a doctor in the royal palace.

why.They would probably have gained greater: This is the opposite of what would happen.
why.Abdul Hai would probably have been allow: The court role was separate from religious permission.
why.Lady Juliana would probably have been un: Her medical work was also separate from religious permission.

activities.explanation: This follows directly from the loss of permission.

activities.context: At a class presentation, a student says Akbar allowed Armenians to build a church and follow their religion. Armenians held important roles in the Mughal royal household: Abdul Hai was Chief Justice, and Lady Juliana was a palace doctor. Communities in Surat, Kolkata and Chennai built schools, churches and cemeteries; Kolkata became a major Armenian centre. The lesson introduces Baha’u’llah’s teaching of unity and harmony between religions and India as an early safe place for Baha’is.
activities.prompt: Why can the presentation describe Kolkata as a major Armenian centre?
options: Armenian settlement and community buildings helped the city become an important centre.
The start of the Baha’i religion there in the mid-1800s made it an Armenian centre.
Lady Juliana’s work in the royal palace was the reason Armenians settled there.
Akbar’s permission to practise religion was first granted in that city.

why.The start of the Baha’i religion there i: The Baha’i religion began in Persia, not Kolkata.
why.Lady Juliana’s work in the royal palace: The facts do not connect her work to settlement there.
why.Akbar’s permission to practise religion: Permission came from Akbar, not from a particular city.

activities.explanation: Settlement and community buildings support this conclusion.

activities.context: At a class presentation, a student says Akbar allowed Armenians to build a church and follow their religion. Armenians held important roles in the Mughal royal household: Abdul Hai was Chief Justice, and Lady Juliana was a palace doctor. Communities in Surat, Kolkata and Chennai built schools, churches and cemeteries; Kolkata became a major Armenian centre. The lesson introduces Baha’u’llah’s teaching of unity and harmony between religions and India as an early safe place for Baha’is.
activities.prompt: Based on Baha’u’llah’s teaching, how should the students treat classmates who follow different religions?
options: They should encourage unity and respect for different religious traditions.
They should ask Iranian religious leaders to decide which religion everyone should follow.
They should keep religious groups separate so that they never learn from one another.
They should assume that harmony requires everyone to give up their own religion.

why.They should ask Iranian religious leader: Baha’u’llah taught harmony, not one authorised religion.
why.They should keep religious groups separa: Separating groups contradicts the teaching of unity.
why.They should assume that harmony requires: Harmony does not require giving up one’s religion.

activities.explanation: This reflects unity and religious harmony.

activities.prompt: Explain how the experiences of Armenians and Baha’is in India were alike and different.
activities.answer: Armenians received Akbar’s permission to build a church and practise their religion, and they settled in Indian cities and built institutions. Baha’is began in Persia and were branded heretics by Iranian leaders, but India was among their first safe places. Both found a place in India through different circumstances.
points: Akbar permitted Armenian religious buildings and practices
Armenians settled in Indian cities and built institutions
Iranian leaders branded the Baha’is as heretics
India was an early safe place for the Baha’is
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A class prepares an exhibition on children affected by war. It explains that Poland was invaded during the Second World War, separating thousands of families and leaving many children as orphans. The Maharaja used the Red Cross and other groups to rescue Polish children and gave them a safe place, food and care. Another display examines India’s response after the uprising in Lhasa, when the 14th Dalai Lama was advised to flee across the Himalaya.
activities.prompt: If the Red Cross and other rescue groups had not worked with the Maharaja, what would most likely have happened to the Polish children?
options: Many children would have remained without the safety, food and care he arranged.
Most children would have found permanent homes immediately.
The Maharaja would have needed to provide less food and care.
The Red Cross alone would have provided exactly the same support.

why.Most children would have found permanent: Being orphaned did not guarantee that children would find homes.
why.The Maharaja would have needed to provid: Without the groups, his ability to reach and support children would have been reduced.
why.The Red Cross alone would have provided: The facts show that the rescue effort involved several groups, not only the Red Cross.

activities.explanation: The groups helped him reach and rescue displaced children.

activities.context: A class prepares an exhibition on children affected by war. It explains that Poland was invaded during the Second World War, separating thousands of families and leaving many children as orphans. The Maharaja used the Red Cross and other groups to rescue Polish children and gave them a safe place, food and care. Another display examines India’s response after the uprising in Lhasa, when the 14th Dalai Lama was advised to flee across the Himalaya.
activities.prompt: The exhibition needs to explain why Sowa Rigpa is part of India’s AYUSH programme. Which reason should the students give?
options: It combines Ayurveda with knowledge from other parts of Asia.
It is the only programme connected with the Dalai Lama’s work.
It was created to provide education for Tibetan refugees.
It replaced the Central Tibetan Administration’s government work.

why.It is the only programme connected with: Sowa Rigpa is not described as the Dalai Lama’s only programme.
why.It was created to provide education for: Traditional healing knowledge and refugee education are separate matters.
why.It replaced the Central Tibetan Administ: Sowa Rigpa is a healing system, not a replacement government.

activities.explanation: This is the stated nature of Sowa Rigpa and explains its inclusion in AYUSH.

activities.prompt: Explain why the Maharaja’s use of rescue organisations was important for Polish children.
activities.answer: The rescue organisations helped reach children who had been separated from their families and left as orphans. With their help, the Maharaja could give the children a safe place, food and care. His actions saved the lives of around a thousand Polish orphans during the Second World War.
points: Families were separated and many children became orphans.
Rescue organisations helped reach displaced children.
The Maharaja provided safety, food and care.
Around a thousand Polish orphans were saved.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A family facing persecution seeks refuge in India. India's long acceptance of people with different faiths and ways of thinking gives the family a haven. A small Indian community welcomes them and helps them feel secure. The family maintains its traditions, while the community remains peaceful and follows Indian values of respect and happiness for all.
activities.prompt: Based on the case, what can happen if India's acceptance of the family continues?
options: The newcomers may continue their traditions while enjoying a peaceful and secure life in India.
They must give up their traditions to become accepted.
They will face persecution because India rejects people who are different.
They cannot live with a community that has different ways of thinking.

why.They must give up their traditions to be: Indian values have helped small communities find a secure place in India.
why.They will face persecution because India: Indian communities have maintained their traditions for centuries.
why.They cannot live with a community that h: Acceptance does not mean that the newcomers must abandon their traditions.

activities.explanation: India has long accepted people with different faiths and ways of thinking.

activities.context: A family facing persecution seeks refuge in India. India's long acceptance of people with different faiths and ways of thinking gives the family a haven. A small Indian community welcomes them and helps them feel secure. The family maintains its traditions, while the community remains peaceful and follows Indian values of respect and happiness for all.
activities.prompt: If the Indian community stopped treating guests like God, what is a likely result for the newcomer?
options: The newcomer may feel less welcome and less secure.
The newcomer would be guaranteed to feel safer than before.
The community would have to abandon its traditions immediately.
The unity of humankind would immediately be achieved.

why.The newcomer would be guaranteed to feel: Respect for guests helps the family feel secure.
why.The community would have to abandon its: Changing this value would weaken the sense of welcome.
why.The unity of humankind would immediately: One community's treatment of guests cannot immediately unite the whole world.

activities.explanation: Atithi devo bhava teaches that a guest should be respected like God.

activities.title: A New Home
activities.prompt: Where did the Bene Israel settle after reaching India?
options: On a mountain plateau
Along the Konkan coast
In a forest settlement
On an inland island
activities.explanation: They lived on the Konkan coast, just south of Mumbai.

activities.hint: Think about what the groups did.
activities.explanation: Persia used forced conversion and religious taxes against them.

activities.title: The Bene Israel’s Journey
activities.prompt: Put the Bene Israel’s journey in the correct order.

Ship was wrecked near the coast

activities.title: The Jug of Milk

options: Drank the full milk
Broke the full jug
Made the milk vanish

activities.explanation: The Siddis combine African and Indian traditions, so this statement is too narrow.

India accepted different faiths.
India changed every faith.

chapters.title: The State, the Government, and You
chapters.summary: In this chapter: state: people, land, government and sovereignty; government and police; democracy and republic; legislature and executive.

lessons.title: State: People, Land, Government and Sovereignty

activities.prompt: What makes a group of people and their land become a state?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What makes a state?
activities.body: A state is a political organisation. It governs a defined territory and the people living there. A state has four important parts: people, land, government and sovereignty. People are citizens who live in the country. Land is a fixed area with clear boundaries. Government runs the country. Sovereignty gives the state power to make laws. Outside powers cannot interfere in its internal matters.
keyPoints: People: citizens who live in the country.
Land: a fixed area with clear boundaries.
Government and sovereignty: running the country and making laws.
activities.explanation: This gives you the main parts of a state and what each one does.

activities.prompt: A group has permanent people and clear land, but no government. Can it be a state?
steps: A state must govern its land and people, because authority is needed.
The group has no government, so it cannot run the country.
Permanent people and clear boundaries help, but do not replace government.
So it is not a state because a needed part is missing.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How a state governs itself
activities.body: A state needs a permanent population. Its land is a fixed territory with clear boundaries. The government runs the country. Sovereignty gives the state power to make laws. It also means no outside power can interfere in the state's internal matters. Internal matters are things happening inside the state. Together, these features help the state govern its own country.
keyPoints: People: a permanent population is necessary.
Land: a fixed territory with clear boundaries.
Government and sovereignty: the state runs itself and makes laws.
activities.explanation: These features show how a state governs its territory and people.

activities.prompt: A state governs a defined territory and its people.
activities.explanation: A state governs a defined territory and the people living there.

activities.prompt: Who are the people of a state?
options: Travellers passing through the country
Citizens who live in the country
Officials from another country
Visitors staying for a short time
activities.explanation: The people of a state are the citizens who live in the country.

activities.prompt: Which power belongs to sovereignty?
options: The power to make laws
The power to choose citizens
The power to change its land
The power to follow outside rules
activities.explanation: Sovereignty gives a state the power to make laws.

activities.prompt: Match each part of a state with its meaning.
pairs: A fixed area with clear boundaries
activities.explanation: Each state part has a clear job, from citizens to law-making power.

activities.prompt: Sovereignty gives a state the power to make ______.
activities.hint: These are rules made by the state.
activities.explanation: Sovereignty gives a state law-making power.

activities.prompt: A state can exist without a permanent population.
activities.explanation: A permanent population is necessary for a state to exist.

activities.prompt: A country has a permanent population, fixed land, clear boundaries, a government and law-making power. Which choice identifies it correctly?
options: A political organisation with only two important parts.
A political organisation without a government and sovereignty.
A political organisation without fixed land and clear boundaries.
A political organisation with all four important parts.
activities.explanation: It has a permanent population, fixed land, government and law-making power.

activities.prompt: People and land exist, but no government exists. Is this a state?
options: Yes, because people and land are enough.
No, because a government is needed.
Yes, because its land has clear boundaries.
No, because it has no permanent population.

This thinks people and land alone make a state.
why.Yes, because its land has clear boundari: This thinks land and people remove the need for government.
why.No, because it has no permanent populati: This blames the population, but the missing part is government.

activities.explanation: A state needs a government to run the country.

activities.prompt: A map shows fixed land with clear boundaries. What does it show?
options: It shows the state's fixed land area.
It shows who leads the state government.
It shows if the state can make laws.
It shows the state's permanent citizen population.

The map does not show who leads the government.
The map does not show the power to make laws.
why.It shows the state's permanent citizen p: The map does not show the state's permanent population.

activities.explanation: This is the state's fixed land area.

lessons.title: Government and Police

activities.prompt: What does the government do, and how do police help keep us safe?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Government and Police
activities.body: The government is a group or system that runs the country. It is only one part of the state. Its leaders, ministers and officials make laws, enforce laws and resolve disputes. The government can change after elections, but the state continues. The police maintain law and order in each state and protect constitutional rights.
keyPoints: The government runs the country and acts for the state.
Government leaders, ministers and officials make and enforce laws.
The police maintain law and order and protect constitutional rights.
activities.explanation: The government runs the country, while the police help people live safely within each state.

activities.prompt: A child sees a new government after an election and asks: Does the whole state change too?
steps: The government may change after elections, because new leaders can take over.
The state continues, because it exists beyond one government.
The government still acts for the state, even after it changes.
So police work continues, because police serve the state government.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is the government?
options: A group that runs the country
Police working with local communities
A state lasting after elections
Courts and prisons working together
activities.explanation: The government runs the country. The police, state and courts have different roles.

activities.prompt: The government is only one part of the state.
activities.explanation: The government is one part of the larger state.

activities.prompt: The government acts on behalf of the ______.
activities.hint: This continues even when the government changes.
activities.explanation: The government acts for the state. The state continues even when the government changes.

activities.prompt: Match each group with its duty.
pairs: Parts of the criminal justice system
activities.explanation: Government officials make and enforce laws. Police maintain law and order within each state.

activities.prompt: What can happen after elections?
options: The government can change
The state always stops
The police leave their states
The Constitution loses its rights
activities.explanation: The government may change after elections, but the state continues.

activities.prompt: Children need clear information about road safety. What should the police do?
options: Share road safety awareness
Make laws for the country
Resolve disputes between leaders
Change the state after elections
activities.explanation: Police share awareness about road safety, drug abuse and women’s safety.

activities.prompt: Police awareness work covers only road safety.
activities.explanation: Police awareness includes road safety, drug abuse and women’s safety.

activities.prompt: A dangerous situation needs action, but rights must stay protected. What should police do?
options: Use lawful force for safety
Use force without legal limits
Ignore rights to keep order
End all local safety work
activities.explanation: Police may use force legally for safety. They must respect and protect constitutional rights.

activities.prompt: A new government begins after an election. What happens to the state?
options: The state continues, because it lasts beyond governments.
The state ends, because its government has changed.
The state changes size, because its government changed.
The state waits, because its government has changed.

why.The state ends, because its government h: This confuses a change of government with the end of the state.
why.The state changes size, because its gove: This wrongly treats the state and government as the same thing.
why.The state waits, because its government: This wrongly suggests that the state stops between elections.

activities.explanation: This is right because the state continues beyond any one government.

activities.prompt: Two states have different governments. What stays the same in both states?
options: Each state continues, even when its government changes.
Both states end whenever their governments change.
Both states become parts of their new governments.
Police leave whenever their state governments change.

why.Both states end whenever their governmen: This wrongly thinks a new government ends the state.
why.Both states become parts of their new go: This confuses the state with the group that runs it.
why.Police leave whenever their state govern: This wrongly assumes that police leave when governments change.

activities.explanation: This is right because each state continues beyond government changes.

lessons.title: Democracy and Republic

activities.prompt: How can a country let people choose leaders while keeping everyone’s rights safe?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Democracy and Republic
activities.body: Democracy means government chosen by the people. The words demos and kratos mean people and rule. A republic has an elected highest office. Its rulers have limited powers. A constitution is a set of rules. India is a democratic republic. Its constitution guarantees fundamental rights to all Indian citizens.
keyPoints: People choose the government through free and fair elections.
A republic's highest office is elected, not inherited.
India's constitution guarantees fundamental rights to all citizens.
activities.explanation: You now know the main ideas of democracy and republic.

activities.prompt: A country has free and fair elections. Its highest office is elected, not inherited. Can the president’s child inherit that office?
steps: Free and fair elections show that people choose the government, so this country is a democracy.
Not every democracy is a republic, so we must check how the highest office is chosen.
The highest office is elected, not inherited, so this country is a republic.
The child cannot inherit the office, because the highest office holder must be elected.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Rights and Limits
activities.body: A democratic republic protects rights and limits government power. India's constitution guarantees fundamental rights to all its citizens. The rule of a representative majority cannot violate any citizen's fundamental rights. No part of the government is allowed to become too powerful. Elected leaders cannot make laws against people's basic rights.
keyPoints: India's constitution guarantees fundamental rights to all its citizens.
A representative majority cannot violate any citizen's fundamental rights.
Elected leaders cannot make laws against people's basic rights.
activities.explanation: You can see how rights and limits protect citizens.

activities.title: Choosing a Government
activities.prompt: Which statement describes democracy?
options: People choose their government through free and fair elections.
The highest office always passes to the ruler's family.
Only one chosen person makes every government decision.
One chosen person rules without any legal limits.
activities.explanation: Great choice! People choose their government through free and fair elections.

activities.title: An Inherited Office
activities.prompt: In a republic, the highest office is inherited.
activities.explanation: Good try! In a republic, the highest office is elected rather than inherited.

activities.title: The Meaning of Words
activities.prompt: The words ______ and kratos mean people and rule.
activities.hint: This word means people.
activities.explanation: Yes! Demos means people, while kratos means rule.

activities.title: Match the Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each idea with its correct description.
pairs: People choose their government through free and fair elections
The highest office is elected rather than inherited
Elected by a group of elected representatives
activities.explanation: Well matched! Each pair shows a key idea from your lesson.

activities.title: Limits on Rulers
activities.prompt: Why are rulers' powers limited in a republic?
options: A constitution or laws set limits.
Every election gives rulers more power.
Only the president can make laws.
Majority rule removes all legal limits.
activities.explanation: Correct! A constitution or laws limit the powers of rulers.

activities.title: Making Laws Against Rights
activities.prompt: Imagine elected leaders want to make a law against citizens' basic rights. What must happen?
options: They must not make that law.
They may make it if a majority supports it.
They may make it if one leader supports it.
They may make it if the president supports it.
activities.explanation: Exactly! Elected leaders cannot make laws against people's basic rights. A majority cannot violate citizens' fundamental rights.

activities.prompt: Place A has free and fair elections. Its highest office is elected, not inherited. Place B’s highest office is inherited. Which place fits a republic?
options: Place A, because its highest office is elected.
Place B, because its highest office is inherited.
Place A, because every democracy is a republic.
Place B, because inherited offices always limit rulers.

why.Place B, because its highest office is i: Place B’s inherited highest office does not fit a republic.
why.Place A, because every democracy is a re: It wrongly assumes every democracy must be a republic.
why.Place B, because inherited offices alway: It wrongly treats limited power as enough for a republic.

activities.explanation: Place A fits because its highest office is elected rather than inherited.

activities.prompt: Most voters want a law that removes one citizen’s basic rights. What should the elected leaders do?
options: They should not make that law at all.
They should make that law because most want it.
They should make that law for a small group.
They should let the rulers decide about the law.

why.They should make that law because most w: It wrongly thinks a majority can cancel basic rights.
why.They should make that law for a small gr: It wrongly thinks the size of the group changes the rule.
why.They should let the rulers decide about: It wrongly leaves the decision only with the rulers.

activities.explanation: This protects the citizen’s fundamental rights.

activities.prompt: A map marks the highest office with an election marker. It also shows a constitution beside the government. What can you conclude?
options: The highest office is elected, and rulers are limited.
The highest office is inherited, and rulers are unlimited.
The highest office is elected, but rulers are unlimited.
The highest office is inherited, but rulers are limited.

why.The highest office is inherited, and rul: It wrongly treats an inherited office as an elected one.
why.The highest office is elected, but ruler: It wrongly assumes a constitution gives rulers unlimited power.
why.The highest office is inherited, but rul: It wrongly treats an inherited office as compatible with a republic.

activities.explanation: An elected highest office and constitutional limits fit a republic.

activities.prompt: Voters choose representatives. The representatives then elect the president. What effect can this two-step choosing have?
options: It shares choosing power between people and representatives.
It gives all choosing power to one single person.
It makes the highest office inherited by the family.
It removes the people from choosing representatives.

why.It gives all choosing power to one singl: It wrongly concentrates all choosing power in one person.
why.It makes the highest office inherited by: It wrongly changes an elected office into an inherited one.
why.It removes the people from choosing repr: It wrongly removes the people’s first choosing step.

activities.explanation: Two steps share choosing power and help prevent too much power.

lessons.title: Legislature and Executive

activities.prompt: How do laws and leaders turn people’s choices into everyday actions?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Branches of Government
activities.body: The legislature makes laws for the country. In a democracy, it represents the people and creates rules for everyone. Governance means managing the country through clear laws, not personal wishes. The executive implements laws and takes policy decisions. Elected leaders normally stay in power for five years. Permanent officers are selected through examinations. They advise leaders, implement policies and manage public services.
keyPoints: The legislature makes laws and represents the people.
The executive implements laws and takes policy decisions.
Permanent executive officers support elected leaders.
activities.explanation: The legislature creates rules, while the executive puts them into action.

activities.prompt: A state needs a clear rule for everyone. Who should make it, and who should carry it out?
steps: The legislature should make the rule because it represents the people.
The rule should be clear so governance does not depend on personal wishes.
The executive should carry it out because the executive implements laws.
Together, the legislature and executive make and carry out laws for everyone.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Elected Leaders and Permanent Officers
activities.body: The political executive has leaders chosen by the people. Elected leaders normally stay in power for a fixed time of five years. Permanent executive officers are selected through examinations. They are not replaced after every election. They advise leaders, implement policies and manage public services.
keyPoints: The people choose political leaders.
Elected leaders normally stay in power for five years.
Permanent officers advise leaders and manage services.
activities.explanation: Elected leaders guide the executive, while permanent officers support its work.

activities.title: Who Makes Laws?
activities.prompt: Who makes laws for the country?
options: The executive
The legislature
Permanent officers
State legislatures
activities.explanation: The legislature makes laws for the country. State legislatures make laws for their own states.

activities.title: How Are Officers Selected?
activities.prompt: Permanent executive officers are selected through ______.
activities.hint: Look for the method used for selection.
activities.explanation: Permanent executive officers are selected through examinations.

activities.title: State Laws
activities.prompt: State legislatures make laws for their own state.
activities.explanation: Each state has its own legislature. It makes laws only for that state.

activities.title: Match the Roles
activities.prompt: Match each part of government with its role.
pairs: Implements laws and takes policy decisions
Consists of leaders chosen by the people
activities.explanation: Each branch and group has a different role in government.

activities.title: Officers After Elections
activities.prompt: Permanent executive officers are replaced after every election.
activities.explanation: Permanent executive officers are not replaced after every election.

activities.title: Who Supports the Leaders?
activities.prompt: A government needs advice and public service management. Who should do this?
options: The political executive
Permanent executive officers
The legislature
State legislatures
activities.explanation: Permanent executive officers advise leaders, implement policies and manage public services.

activities.prompt: A state legislature makes a rule about public services. What should the executive do with it?
options: The executive should implement it and make policy decisions.
The legislature should implement it and make policy decisions.
The permanent officers should replace it with a personal wish.
The elected leaders should rewrite it after every election.

why.The legislature should implement it and: This mistake confuses making laws with implementing them.
why.The permanent officers should replace it: This mistake treats a personal wish as more important than a clear law.
why.The elected leaders should rewrite it af: This mistake wrongly assumes that every election rewrites laws.

activities.explanation: This is right because the executive implements laws and takes policy decisions.

activities.prompt: Permanent executive officers were selected through examinations. What usually happens after an election?
options: They stay in post because elections do not replace them.
They leave because every election starts their work again.
They become elected leaders because people choose all officers.
They become legislators because each state needs new laws.

why.They leave because every election starts: This mistake assumes that every election replaces permanent officers.
why.They become elected leaders because peop: This mistake confuses permanent officers with people-chosen political leaders.
why.They become legislators because each sta: This mistake confuses executive service work with the legislature's lawmaking work.

activities.explanation: This is right because permanent officers are not replaced after every election.

activities.prompt: A map shows State A and State B as separate areas. What can we correctly conclude?
options: Each state has its own legislature and makes laws for itself.
One legislature makes all laws for the two states together.
The executive makes laws for each state shown on the map.
The two states share rules because their leaders are elected.

why.One legislature makes all laws for the t: This mistake wrongly treats the states as having one shared legislature.
why.The executive makes laws for each state: This mistake confuses implementing laws with making laws.
why.The two states share rules because their: This mistake wrongly assumes that elected leaders make state laws.

activities.explanation: This is right because each state has its own legislature for its own state.

activities.prompt: A leader wants a different rule from the clear law. How should governance decide?
options: It should follow the clear law, not the leader's personal wish.
It should follow the leader's wish because leaders are elected.
It should wait for permanent officers to make a new law.
It should let each person choose the rule they prefer.

why.It should follow the leader's wish becau: This mistake wrongly gives an elected leader's wish priority over law.
why.It should wait for permanent officers to: This mistake gives permanent officers the legislature's lawmaking power.
why.It should let each person choose the rul: This mistake replaces clear common rules with separate personal choices.

activities.explanation: This is right because governance should depend on clear laws, not personal wishes.

activities.prompt: Elected leaders usually stay in power for five years. What helps services continue after that?
options: Permanent officers remain and keep managing public services.
Permanent officers are replaced and must start services again.
State legislatures make all service decisions after five years.
People choose new permanent officers at every election.

why.Permanent officers are replaced and must: This mistake contradicts the fact that officers are not replaced after every election.
why.State legislatures make all service deci: This mistake gives the legislature responsibility for managing public services.
why.People choose new permanent officers at: This mistake wrongly assumes that elections select permanent executive officers.

activities.explanation: This is right because permanent officers remain and manage public services.

lessons.title: The Government, Citizens and Judiciary

activities.prompt: How can citizens question power and seek justice in their community?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Government and Citizens Work Together
activities.body: The government acts as a protector, provider and regulator. Government departments have offices where people can register grievances. Vigilance commissions investigate corruption. Citizens can ask for information, raise concerns and write to representatives. They should vote in local, state and national elections. Judiciary means the system that settles disputes, protects rights and checks laws. It stays independent and acts as a referee when the law is broken.
keyPoints: Government offices help people register grievances.
Citizens can question officials and vote in elections.
The judiciary settles disputes and protects rights.
activities.explanation: This card shows how citizens hold power to account.

activities.prompt: A citizen sees a public decision and suspects the law was broken. What can the citizen do, and who can fairly settle the issue?
steps: The citizen should ask for information about the public action, because citizens must be able to question those in power.
They can register a grievance at a government department office, because that is a place for complaints.
They can write to representatives, because representatives can be asked to act on an issue.
If the law was broken, the judiciary should settle it fairly, because it is independent and acts as a referee.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which one is a role of the government?
options: Protector
Painter
Coach
Singer
activities.explanation: The government acts as a protector, provider and regulator.

activities.prompt: Government departments have offices where people can register grievances.
activities.explanation: Yes, these offices give people a place to register their grievances.

activities.prompt: Vigilance commissions investigate cases of ______.
activities.hint: This is the wrongdoing investigated by vigilance commissions.
activities.explanation: Vigilance commissions investigate cases of corruption.

activities.prompt: Match each action or group with its role.
pairs: Ask them to act on an issue
Work on education, health and environment
activities.explanation: Each group or action has a clear role in helping citizens and checking power.

activities.prompt: Put election levels from local to national.
activities.explanation: Citizens should vote in local, state and national elections.

activities.prompt: How do citizens and the judiciary help make government responsible?
options: They hide actions and ignore laws
They avoid voting and choose laws
They question actions and check laws
They support every official decision
activities.explanation: Those in power must answer the public. The judiciary checks whether government laws are fair.

activities.prompt: After a public action, citizens want details. They use the Right to Information Act. Why is this useful?
options: They can learn what the government did in public.
They can order the government to stop its work.
They can become judges in the next court case.
They can choose officials for the next election.

why.They can order the government to stop it: This confuses asking for information with ordering the government to stop.
why.They can become judges in the next court: This confuses seeking information with becoming part of the judiciary.
why.They can choose officials for the next e: This confuses seeking information with choosing election candidates.

activities.explanation: This is right because the Act lets citizens ask about public actions.

activities.prompt: One town has a government office for registering grievances. Another has none. What difference does this make?
options: People in the first town have a clear place for complaints.
People in the first town can settle all legal disputes.
People in the first town get fewer choices at elections.
People in the first town no longer need public information.

why.People in the first town can settle all: This confuses a grievance office with the independent judiciary.
why.People in the first town get fewer choic: This mistake assumes that complaint offices change election choices.
why.People in the first town no longer need: This mistake assumes that complaint offices remove the need for information.

activities.explanation: This is right because government offices let people register grievances.

activities.prompt: People read a newspaper story about a public decision. They want those in power to explain. Why can the press help?
options: It can bring the concern to wider public attention.
It can order every official to come to court.
It can make the government decision automatically fair.
It can replace citizens' votes at elections.

why.It can order every official to come to c: This confuses media reports with powers given to the judiciary.
why.It can make the government decision auto: This mistake assumes that public attention makes every decision fair.
why.It can replace citizens' votes at electi: This confuses raising concerns with the citizens' power to vote.

activities.explanation: This is right because print and electronic media can raise concerns.

activities.prompt: Parents want better education, so they join a civil society organisation. Why is joining useful?
options: The group can work together on the education issue.
The group can settle all court disputes fairly.
The group can register official complaints at courts.
The group can investigate every corruption case.

why.The group can settle all court disputes: This confuses a civil society organisation with the independent judiciary.
why.The group can register official complain: This mistake mixes civil society work with government grievance offices.
why.The group can investigate every corrupti: This mistake mixes civil society work with vigilance commissions.

activities.explanation: This is right because civil society organisations work on issues such as education.

activities.prompt: Election day arrives, and citizens can vote at three levels. Why should they use this chance?
options: They help choose people for local, state and national offices.
They settle court disputes and protect citizens' rights.
They make information about public actions available.
They investigate cases of corruption for government.

why.They settle court disputes and protect c: This confuses voting with the work of the judiciary.
why.They make information about public actio: This confuses voting with the Right to Information Act.
why.They investigate cases of corruption for: This confuses voting with the work of vigilance commissions.

activities.explanation: This is right because citizens should vote in local, state and national elections.

activities.prompt: Government and other people break a rule. Citizens want a fair referee. Which institution should act?
options: The judiciary, because it is independent and acts as a referee.
A government department, because it protects and provides services.
A civil society group, because it works on public issues.
An elected representative, because citizens can ask them to act.

why.A government department, because it prot: This mistakes government departments for the independent judiciary.
why.A civil society group, because it works: This mistakes a civil society organisation for the independent judiciary.
why.An elected representative, because citiz: This mistakes an elected representative for the independent judiciary.

activities.explanation: This is right because the judiciary is independent and acts as a referee.
