lessons.title: Three Tiers of Government

activities.prompt: How can your community have a say in decisions?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How India's government works
activities.body: India has central, state and local levels of government. Panchayats and municipalities form the third tier. The central government handles matters affecting the whole country. State governments meet the needs of people in each state. Local governments solve problems in villages, towns and cities. Decentralisation spreads power and decision-making instead of concentrating them in one place.
keyPoints: Central, state and local levels.
Panchayats and municipalities form the third tier.
Each level has its own responsibilities.
activities.explanation: Power is shared between levels, so each serves people in a different area.

activities.prompt: Our village has a problem. Who should solve it, and why?
steps: Our village has a problem in daily life.
Decentralisation puts decisions near people, so local government should solve it.
Local leaders should guide it because they understand local needs and traditions better.
So residents should join them, because participation makes panchayats and municipalities stronger.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Government levels
activities.prompt: Which statement about India's government levels is correct?
options: India has central, state and local levels.
India has central and local levels.
India has central and state levels.
India has one level for all places.
activities.explanation: India has central, state and local levels of government.

activities.title: The central government
activities.prompt: The central government handles matters affecting the whole ______.
activities.hint: This place includes every state.
activities.explanation: The central government handles matters affecting the whole country.

activities.title: Match each government level
activities.prompt: Match each government level with the area it serves.
activities.explanation: Each level serves a different area, from the country to local places.

activities.title: Understanding local needs
activities.prompt: What do local leaders understand especially well?
options: They know distant areas better.
They know every state's needs.
They know local needs and traditions.
They know whole-country needs.
activities.explanation: Local leaders understand their area's needs and traditions better than distant officials.

activities.title: Who solves local problems?
activities.prompt: Which level should solve a local problem whenever possible?
options: Central government alone
State government alone
Distant officials alone
Local governments
activities.explanation: Local governments solve problems in villages, towns and cities.

activities.title: More say in daily life
activities.prompt: A group wants more say in decisions about their daily lives. Which idea should they support?
options: Concentrating all power
Decentralisation
Keeping decisions in one place
Reducing local involvement
activities.explanation: Decentralisation spreads power and gives people more involvement in daily-life decisions.

activities.prompt: Decentralisation spreads power and decisions. A distant office makes one village choice. Why may residents have less say?
options: Concentrating the choice in one place leaves residents with less involvement.
Spreading the choice locally leaves residents with less involvement.
Giving local leaders the choice makes residents' needs less understood.
Keeping the choice distant makes local leaders understand traditions better.

why.Spreading the choice locally leaves resi: This reverses decentralisation, which spreads power and involvement.
why.Giving local leaders the choice makes re: This mistakes local knowledge, since local leaders understand needs better.
why.Keeping the choice distant makes local l: This reverses local knowledge, since distant officials know less about local traditions.

activities.explanation: Right: one place concentrates power and reduces residents' involvement.

activities.prompt: The central government handles whole-country matters. Local governments solve village, town, and city problems. Which plan fits?
options: Let local government solve it, because village problems belong to it.
Let central government solve it, because it handles every problem.
Let state government solve it, because states handle local problems.
Let a panchayat solve it, because panchayats handle whole-country matters.

why.Let central government solve it, because: This confuses whole-country matters with local village problems.
why.Let state government solve it, because s: This confuses state-level needs with problems limited to one village.
why.Let a panchayat solve it, because pancha: This confuses panchayats' local role with whole-country work.

activities.explanation: Right: village problems belong with local government.

activities.prompt: A map places panchayats and municipalities within states. Compared with the central government, what are they closer to?
options: Local decisions about people's daily lives.
All decisions affecting the whole country.
Every decision made by state governments.
Only decisions made far from the central government.

why.All decisions affecting the whole countr: This confuses local work with matters affecting the whole country.
why.Every decision made by state governments: This gives local bodies work that belongs to state governments.
why.Only decisions made far from the central: This treats distant work as local, but local bodies work near people.

activities.explanation: Right: local governments handle village, town, and city problems.

activities.prompt: In one area, one distant office controls daily-life decisions. In another, residents help decide local matters. Which area shows decentralisation?
options: The second area, because power and decisions are spread locally.
The first area, because one distant office holds all power.
The second area, because all decisions are kept in one place.
The first area, because local people have more involvement.

why.The first area, because one distant offi: This mistakes one place holding power for spreading it.
why.The second area, because all decisions a: This says power is spread but describes it staying concentrated.
why.The first area, because local people hav: This reverses the link between local involvement and local decisions.

activities.explanation: Right: spreading power locally is decentralisation.

activities.context: In a country, permanent residents live within clearly marked borders. The government is responsible for running the country and has announced a new law affecting everyone in that territory. A government from outside the country asks the government to change the law. The residents ask whether the outside government has this authority, and the government explains the country's position on the matter.
activities.prompt: In the case, what should happen when the outside government tries to interfere in the country's internal affairs?
options: It must stop, because no outside power can interfere in the country's internal affairs.
It may continue, because the government's duty to run the country gives it no power to make laws.
It may continue, because a fixed territory can be governed by an outside power.
It may continue, because having citizens gives another government the right to interfere.

why.It may continue, because the government': Running the country does not give other governments such a right.
why.It may continue, because a fixed territo: Boundaries define the territory but do not give outsiders authority.
why.It may continue, because having citizens: Having citizens does not give another government power to interfere.

activities.explanation: This follows the rule that outside powers cannot interfere in internal affairs.

activities.context: In a country, permanent residents live within clearly marked borders. The government is responsible for running the country and has announced a new law affecting everyone in that territory. A government from outside the country asks the government to change the law. The residents ask whether the outside government has this authority, and the government explains the country's position on the matter.
activities.prompt: In the case, why can the government make the new law for people within the country's borders?
options: Sovereignty gives the state the power to make laws.
The fixed boundaries make every law by themselves.
The permanent population gives the government law-making power.
The outside government's request gives the country law-making power.

why.The fixed boundaries make every law by t: Fixed land identifies the territory but is not itself law-making authority.
why.The permanent population gives the gover: A population is necessary for statehood but does not itself create law-making power.
why.The outside government's request gives t: An outside request cannot replace the state's own sovereignty.

activities.explanation: Sovereignty is the source of the state's law-making power.

activities.prompt: How does sovereignty help the government respond to the outside government's request?
activities.answer: Sovereignty gives the state the power to make laws. It therefore allows the government to make the law in the case for people living in the defined territory. It also means that no outside power can interfere in the country's internal affairs, so the outside government's request has no authority.
points: Sovereignty gives the state law-making power.
The government uses this power to govern the territory and people.
No outside power may interfere in internal affairs.
The outside government cannot order the law to be changed.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After an election, the government changed, but the state continued. A resident asked a local official for help, while another reported unsafe road conditions. The police discussed road safety with the community. When a crowd became unsafe, officers considered whether force was legally needed to help people live safely. They were reminded to respect and protect rights guaranteed by the Constitution. The resident wanted to know which organisation acts for the state and how police work with courts and prisons.
activities.prompt: What does the change after the election show about the government and the state?
options: The government is the changing part of the state, while the state continues.
The state is the changing part, while the government remains the same.
The government and the state are two names for exactly the same thing.
Both the government and the state end whenever an election is held.

why.The state is the changing part, while th: Option 2 wrongly reverses the parts of the state.
why.The government and the state are two nam: Option 3 wrongly treats the government and the state as identical.
why.Both the government and the state end wh: Option 4 wrongly suggests that both end after an election.

activities.explanation: Option 1 matches the case: the government may change while the state continues.

activities.context: After an election, the government changed, but the state continued. A resident asked a local official for help, while another reported unsafe road conditions. The police discussed road safety with the community. When a crowd became unsafe, officers considered whether force was legally needed to help people live safely. They were reminded to respect and protect rights guaranteed by the Constitution. The resident wanted to know which organisation acts for the state and how police work with courts and prisons.
activities.prompt: What should the resident understand about the organisation that handles requests from the public?
options: It performs government work on behalf of the state.
It is outside the state and acts only for itself.
It deals only with courts and prisons, not requests from the public.
It changes in the same way as the state after every election.

why.It is outside the state and acts only fo: Option 2 wrongly separates the government from the state.
why.It deals only with courts and prisons, n: Option 3 wrongly limits the government’s work to courts and prisons.
why.It changes in the same way as the state: Option 4 confuses the changing government with the continuing state.

activities.explanation: Option 1 is correct because the government acts on behalf of the state.

activities.context: After an election, the government changed, but the state continued. A resident asked a local official for help, while another reported unsafe road conditions. The police discussed road safety with the community. When a crowd became unsafe, officers considered whether force was legally needed to help people live safely. They were reminded to respect and protect rights guaranteed by the Constitution. The resident wanted to know which organisation acts for the state and how police work with courts and prisons.
activities.prompt: If the police decide that force is needed in the unsafe crowd, what should guide their action?
options: They may use legally permitted force for safety while protecting constitutional rights.
They may use any amount of force because their aim is to keep people safe.
They must use force even when it is not legally allowed.
They should ignore constitutional rights once the situation becomes unsafe.

why.They may use any amount of force because: Option 2 wrongly removes the legal limit on police force.
why.They must use force even when it is not: Option 3 wrongly treats unlawful force as acceptable.
why.They should ignore constitutional rights: Option 4 wrongly suggests that constitutional rights no longer matter.

activities.explanation: Option 1 correctly combines legal force for safety with the duty to protect rights.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between the government and the state.
activities.answer: The government is the group or system that runs the country. Its leaders, ministers and officials make laws, enforce laws and resolve disputes. The government is only one part of the state. After elections, the government may change, but the state continues.
points: The government runs the country.
Its leaders, ministers and officials make, enforce and resolve through laws.
The government is only one part of the state.
The government may change after elections, but the state continues.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After an election, a student learned that India’s president had been selected by a group of elected representatives. The student’s family discussed how India is a democratic republic. They said that people choose their government through free and fair elections. They also explained that the highest office is elected rather than inherited, and rulers’ powers are limited by the constitution or laws. The student asked whether elected leaders could ignore citizens’ rights, and was told that they cannot.
activities.prompt: India’s president is selected by a group of elected representatives. What does this show about the presidency?
options: Its holder gains the office through voting.
Its holder inherits the office from the previous ruler.
Its holder is chosen by citizens in a direct vote.
No voting is needed to choose its holder.

why.Its holder inherits the office from the: In a republic, the highest office is elected rather than inherited.
why.Its holder is chosen by citizens in a di: The representatives selected the president, not citizens directly.
why.No voting is needed to choose its holder: Choosing the office holder requires an election.

activities.explanation: The president was selected by elected representatives.

activities.context: After an election, a student learned that India’s president had been selected by a group of elected representatives. The student’s family discussed how India is a democratic republic. They said that people choose their government through free and fair elections. They also explained that the highest office is elected rather than inherited, and rulers’ powers are limited by the constitution or laws. The student asked whether elected leaders could ignore citizens’ rights, and was told that they cannot.
activities.prompt: Why does the situation require the government’s powers to be limited?
options: So that no part of the government can become too powerful.
So that elected leaders can make laws without limits.
So that the highest office can be inherited instead of elected.
So that free and fair elections can be replaced by an unelected ruler.

why.So that elected leaders can make laws wi: A republic requires rulers’ powers to be limited by the constitution or laws.
why.So that the highest office can be inheri: The highest office in a republic is elected rather than inherited.
why.So that free and fair elections can be r: Democracy requires people to choose their government through free and fair elections.

activities.explanation: Limited powers help prevent any part of the government from becoming too powerful.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between democracy and republic.
activities.answer: A democracy is a system in which people choose their government through free and fair elections. A republic is a system in which the highest office is elected rather than inherited and rulers’ powers are limited by a constitution or laws. India follows both ideas, but not every democracy is a republic.
points: Democracy involves choosing the government through free and fair elections.
In a republic, the highest office is elected rather than inherited.
Rulers’ powers in a republic are limited by a constitution or laws.
Not every democracy is a republic, while India is a democratic republic.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between the legislature and the executive.
activities.answer: The country has a legislature that makes laws for the country, while each state has its own legislature for laws concerning that state. The executive implements laws and takes policy decisions. Its leaders are elected, while permanent officers are selected through examinations, advise leaders, implement policies, and manage public services.
points: Makes laws and creates rules
Each state legislature serves only its own state
Implements laws and takes policy decisions
Distinguishes elected leaders from permanent officers
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A citizen learns that a government department has an office for registering complaints. She reports a public-service problem there, asks for information about the government’s actions under the Right to Information Act, and also writes to her representative. A civil society organisation is working on the same issue. People disagree about whether the department’s actions are fair, and one side says the law was broken. Local, state and national elections are approaching, and she plans to vote.
activities.prompt: If the citizen wants official information about the department’s actions, what should she do?
options: Make a formal request using the Right to Information Act
Ask only the civil society organisation and expect it to answer as the government
Wait for an election and ask a political candidate to explain the actions
Ask the judiciary to obtain the information, treating it as the government’s information office

why.Ask only the civil society organisation: Civil society organisations work on issues but do not act as government information offices.
why.Wait for an election and ask a political: An election does not replace the right to request information.
why.Ask the judiciary to obtain the informat: The judiciary settles disputes and checks laws rather than serving as an information office.

activities.explanation: This is the stated method for obtaining information about public actions.

activities.context: A citizen learns that a government department has an office for registering complaints. She reports a public-service problem there, asks for information about the government’s actions under the Right to Information Act, and also writes to her representative. A civil society organisation is working on the same issue. People disagree about whether the department’s actions are fair, and one side says the law was broken. Local, state and national elections are approaching, and she plans to vote.
activities.prompt: Why should the citizen vote in local, state and national elections as well as raise complaints?
options: It helps citizens make those in power answer for their actions and decisions
It gives the judiciary power to make government laws
It turns a civil society organisation into the government
It makes complaints and information requests unnecessary

why.It gives the judiciary power to make gov: Voting does not give the judiciary lawmaking power.
why.It turns a civil society organisation in: Voting does not turn a civil society organisation into the government.
why.It makes complaints and information requ: Voting is important, but it does not remove other ways of raising concerns.

activities.explanation: Voting helps citizens influence those in power, who must answer the public.

activities.prompt: How can citizens use government offices, representatives and the media to raise a concern?
activities.answer: A citizen can register a grievance at a government department’s office, request information about public actions under the Right to Information Act, and write to a representative asking for action. The citizen can also raise the concern through print or electronic media. Civil society organisations can also work on the issue.
points: Grievances can be registered at a government department’s office.
The Right to Information Act allows requests about public actions.
Representatives can be asked to act on an issue.
Concerns can be raised through print or electronic media.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A problem begins affecting daily life in a town. The municipal government discusses it with local leaders and residents, and residents actively offer ideas. The central government handles matters affecting the whole country, while the state government meets the needs of people in the state. The town resident wonders which level should solve the local problem and what may happen if participation continues.
activities.prompt: Which level of government should solve the problem described in the case?
options: The local government, because the problem is within the town
The central government, because it is the highest level
The state government, because it governs a larger area
All three levels separately, because each has the same responsibility for every problem

why.The central government, because it is th: The central government handles matters affecting the whole country.
why.The state government, because it governs: State governments meet the needs of people in each state.
why.All three levels separately, because eac: Different levels have different responsibilities, so they do not handle every problem equally.

activities.explanation: Local governments solve problems in towns.

activities.context: A problem begins affecting daily life in a town. The municipal government discusses it with local leaders and residents, and residents actively offer ideas. The central government handles matters affecting the whole country, while the state government meets the needs of people in the state. The town resident wonders which level should solve the local problem and what may happen if participation continues.
activities.prompt: Why is the local government best placed to solve this town's problem?
options: Local leaders know the area's needs and traditions better than distant officials
Central officials always know local problems better than local leaders
State leaders are responsible for every problem in all towns
Residents are unable to understand problems in their own area

why.Central officials always know local prob: The central government handles matters affecting the whole country.
why.State leaders are responsible for every: State governments meet state-level needs, not every town problem separately.
why.Residents are unable to understand probl: People's participation gives useful knowledge about local needs and daily life.

activities.explanation: Local leaders have a closer understanding of their area.

activities.prompt: Explain how decentralisation can improve decision-making in local areas.
activities.answer: Decentralisation spreads power and decision-making instead of concentrating them in one place. Local problems should be solved locally whenever possible. It also allows people to take part in decisions about their daily lives and helps local leaders respond to the needs and traditions of their area.
points: Spreads power and decision-making
Solves local problems locally
Encourages people's participation
Uses local knowledge of needs and traditions
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: The State, the Government, and You

activities.title: What is a state?
activities.prompt: A state governs a defined area and its people. What is a state?
options: a political organisation
a fixed territory
a group of citizens
a government department
activities.explanation: A state is a political organisation that governs a defined territory and its people.

activities.prompt: A state can end when an election changes the government.
activities.explanation: The government can change after elections, while the state continues.

activities.prompt: Sovereignty gives a state the power to make ______.
activities.hint: Sovereignty means the state has power to make these rules.
activities.explanation: Sovereignty gives a state the power to make laws.

activities.title: Parts of a state
activities.prompt: Match each part of a state with its meaning.
pairs: a fixed area with clear boundaries
the body that runs the country
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an important part of a state with its meaning.

activities.title: Police and safety
activities.prompt: Which action can the police legally take to help people live safely?
options: legally use force
make laws for the country
settle disputes in courts
elect the president
activities.explanation: The police can legally use force to help people live safely.

activities.prompt: Not every democracy is a republic.
activities.explanation: A democracy and a republic are different, so not every democracy is a republic.

activities.title: How government branches work together
activities.prompt: Put these government jobs in their correct order.
items: The judiciary checks whether laws are fair.
activities.explanation: Laws are made first, then implemented, then checked for fairness.

activities.title: Solving local problems
activities.prompt: Which level of government solves problems in villages, towns and cities?
options: Central government
State government
Local government
National judiciary
activities.explanation: Local governments solve problems in villages, towns and cities.

activities.title: Public bodies and their jobs
activities.prompt: Match each public body with its main job.
pairs: implements laws and takes policy decisions
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a public body with its main job.

chapters.title: Infrastructure: Engine of India’s Development
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what physical infrastructure does; roads, highways and living root bridges; railways and metro trains; air transport, shipping and ports.

lessons.title: What Physical Infrastructure Does

activities.prompt: What connects your home to school, shops, and the wider world?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Physical Infrastructure
activities.body: Physical infrastructure is the backbone of the nation. This means it supports the country and makes life easier. It is a vast network of real structures. Roads, bridges and railways are transport systems. Electricity and water pipelines are utilities. Internet, telephone lines and telecom towers form communication networks. Windmills, solar parks, oil and gas pipelines provide energy.
keyPoints: Physical infrastructure supports the nation and makes life easier.
Transport, utilities, communication and energy are important parts.
Roads, railways, pipelines and towers form connected networks.
activities.explanation: These connected systems help cities and villages work.

activities.prompt: A village maker cannot reach a distant market. How can better transport help?
steps: Goods are made in one place and sold in markets elsewhere.
Roads, railways, airways and shipping connect these two kinds of places.
Better links make moving goods easier and help trade grow.
So better transport can help a village maker reach distant markets.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How Infrastructure Helps People
activities.body: Trade means buying and selling goods. Roads, railways, airways and shipping help goods reach markets. Modern infrastructure helps trade grow within India and with other countries. Better infrastructure supports tourism, or holiday visits. It also connects remote areas, which are places far from towns. Better access to terrain helps India’s defence forces. Terrain means different kinds of land. Canals and electric pumps help farmers irrigate, or water, their fields.
keyPoints: Transport connects places where goods are made with markets.
Better infrastructure supports trade, tourism and remote areas.
Terrain access helps defence forces, while pumps and canals help farmers.
activities.explanation: These links support farming, trade, tourism, defence and remote areas.

activities.prompt: Which phrase describes physical infrastructure?
options: A vast network of real structures
A single type of transport system
A group of farming tools
A form of communication
activities.explanation: Correct! Physical infrastructure is a vast network of real structures.

activities.prompt: Roads, bridges and ______ are transport systems.
activities.hint: This is another transport system.
activities.explanation: Good work! Railways belong to the transport network.

activities.prompt: Match each infrastructure system with a correct example.
activities.explanation: Correct! These examples fit transport, utility, communication and energy systems.

activities.prompt: Which pair helps connect goods makers with markets?
options: Roads and shipping
Canals and pumps
Solar parks and telecom towers
Electricity and water pipelines
activities.explanation: Great! Roads and shipping connect places where goods are made with markets.

activities.prompt: Modern infrastructure helps trade grow only within India.
activities.explanation: No need to worry. Trade can grow within India and with other countries too.

activities.prompt: Which statement correctly links each example to its benefit?
options: A canal and an electric water pump support defence access across different terrain.
Roads and railways support tourism but never help trade.
Better terrain access supports India's defence forces.
Solar parks and telecom towers supply water to farming fields.
activities.explanation: Well done! Better access to different terrain helps India's defence forces.

activities.prompt: Roads and railways connect goods makers with markets. What effect can better links have?
options: Goods can be made without markets.
Markets can close during the day.
Trade can grow in more places.
Villages can lose their roads.

This wrongly assumes that goods makers do not need markets.
This wrongly assumes that better transport makes markets close.
This wrongly assumes that better transport removes roads.

activities.explanation: Better links connect goods-making places with markets and help trade grow.

activities.prompt: A village had few transport links. Later, roads and railways improved. What could change?
options: More goods could reach markets.
More fields could lose water.
More homes could lose power.
More calls could stop working.

This confuses transport links with canals and pumps for irrigation.
This confuses transport links with the electricity utility.
This confuses transport links with communication networks.

activities.explanation: Improved roads and railways can connect more goods-making places with markets.

activities.prompt: A map shows roads, railways and water pipelines. What can we learn about them?
options: They are all tools used for communication.
They only make electricity for nearby homes.
They are places where people buy goods.
They are parts of a wider infrastructure network.

why.They are all tools used for communicatio: This mistake treats roads and pipelines as communication tools.
why.They only make electricity for nearby ho: This mistake treats water pipelines as energy-making structures.
This mistake treats infrastructure lines as markets.

activities.explanation: These structures show a wider network that keeps cities and villages working.

activities.prompt: The government has one rule: connect remote areas to markets. Which plan follows it?
options: Add internet and telephone lines.
Build roads and railway lines.
Build windmills and solar parks.
Add oil and gas pipelines.

Communication lines help communication, but they do not carry goods to markets.
Energy structures make energy, but they do not carry goods to markets.
Oil and gas pipelines carry energy, not goods to markets.

activities.explanation: Roads and railways connect goods makers with markets and link remote areas.

activities.prompt: A maker wants to sell goods in other markets. Why might the maker support better roads?
options: Roads can help windmills and solar parks.
Roads can carry water into nearby fields.
Roads can take goods to more buyers.
Roads can carry calls between telecom towers.

why.Roads can help windmills and solar parks: This confuses roads with energy infrastructure.
why.Roads can carry water into nearby fields: This confuses roads with water pipelines.
why.Roads can carry calls between telecom to: This confuses roads with communication networks.

activities.explanation: Roads connect goods-making places with markets, so this helps trade.

lessons.title: Roads, Highways and Living Root Bridges

activities.prompt: How do roads and living root bridges connect people, places, and daily life?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Roads help us travel
activities.body: Local roads help children reach school. Farmers carry crops, and ambulances reach hospitals on them. States build and maintain local roads, state highways and other state roads. Expressways are fast roads connecting cities across different states. Bridges and tunnels give easier access where highways cannot be built. Living root bridges use tree roots. Some take many years to mature but can last for hundreds of years.
keyPoints: Local roads help children, farmers and ambulances.
Expressways connect cities across different states.
Living root bridges use tree roots and can last for hundreds of years.
activities.explanation: Different roads and bridges help people and goods travel safely.

activities.prompt: How can a bridge help farmers sell fresh vegetables and fruits?
steps: The Dhola Sadiya Bridge connects Assam and Arunachal Pradesh across the Lohit River.
It provides year-round travel, so farmers can reach markets throughout the year.
It has reduced travel time, so vegetables and fruits can reach the market sooner.
Therefore, the bridge helps farmers sell their produce before it spoils.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Match each road or bridge with its description.
pairs: Give easier access where highways cannot be built
activities.explanation: Each description matches the road or bridge connected with it.

activities.prompt: Expressways are fast roads connecting cities across different states.
activities.explanation: Expressways are fast roads. They connect cities across different states.

activities.prompt: The Dhola Sadiya Bridge connects Assam and ______ Pradesh across the Lohit River.
activities.hint: The bridge links Assam with another state.
activities.explanation: The bridge joins Assam and Arunachal Pradesh across the Lohit River.

activities.prompt: What do bridges and tunnels do where highways cannot be built?
options: Remove the need for roads
Make every road fast
Give easier access
Change difficult terrain
activities.explanation: Bridges and tunnels provide easier access where highways cannot be built.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order.
items: Khāsi and Jaintia tribes craft bridges using tree roots
Some living root bridges take many years to mature
Some living root bridges can last for hundreds of years
activities.explanation: The tribes craft the bridges, and some take many years to mature before lasting for centuries.

activities.prompt: What can farmers now do with vegetables and fruits?
options: Keep vegetables away from markets
Reach market before vegetables spoil
Wait for vegetables to spoil
Carry vegetables only by trains
activities.explanation: Farmers can now take their vegetables and fruits to market before they spoil.

activities.prompt: Local roads help ambulances reach hospitals. Which road helps an ambulance most?
options: A local road that reaches the hospital
A railway line that passes nearby
An expressway that bypasses the village
A living bridge far from the hospital

why.A railway line that passes nearby: This confuses a railway line with a road for ambulances.
why.An expressway that bypasses the village: This connects cities across states, not a village hospital.
why.A living bridge far from the hospital: This is far away and does not help reach the hospital.

activities.explanation: This is right because local roads help ambulances reach hospitals.

activities.prompt: States build and maintain local roads. Which road should a state build for farmers carrying crops?
options: A local road for carrying crops
An expressway between distant cities
A living root bridge over a river
A railway station for waiting trains

why.An expressway between distant cities: This connects cities across states, not local crop carriers.
why.A living root bridge over a river: This uses tree roots, while local roads are built by states.
why.A railway station for waiting trains: This is a railway place, not a road for carrying crops.

activities.explanation: This is right because states build local roads that help farmers carry crops.

activities.prompt: Roads connect with railway stations, airports and ports. What does this suggest?
options: People and goods can travel smoothly between them
Only roads can carry people between them
These places have no links at all
Airports and ports replace all roads

why.Only roads can carry people between them: This ignores the links between roads, stations, airports and ports.
why.These places have no links at all: This mistakes connected places for places with no links.
why.Airports and ports replace all roads: This confuses different links with roads being useless.

activities.explanation: This is right because these links help people and goods travel smoothly.

lessons.sceneCaption: Double-decker living root bridges in Nongriat village, East Khasi Hills district, Meghalaya.

lessons.title: Railways and Metro Trains

activities.prompt: How do railways and metro trains connect people, goods, and cities?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Railways Changed India
activities.body: The British introduced railways in India in 1853. Railways moved British goods. Troops also moved quicker. This helped Britain control India more tightly. Indian Railways is a very large employer. It carries more than 20 million passengers daily and supports indirect work. Railway expansion encouraged trade and helped markets and settlements grow. Cargo trains carry goods. India aimed for electric trains by 2025. Metro trains reduce traffic in 23 cities.
keyPoints: Railways began in 1853 and strengthened British control.
Indian Railways employs about 1.21 million people and carries passengers.
Metro trains operate in 23 Indian cities.
activities.explanation: Railways affected British control, work, trade and travel in Indian cities.

activities.prompt: A British officer needs quicker troop movement. Why use railways?
steps: Railways allow quicker troop movement, so the officer can move soldiers sooner.
Faster troop movement helps the British control India more tightly.
Therefore, the officer would use railways to strengthen British control.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Moving British Goods
activities.prompt: How did railways help British goods?
options: Move across India
Move only within one city
Stay in one station
Travel only by road
activities.explanation: The lesson says railways helped British goods move across India.

activities.title: A Very Large Employer
activities.prompt: Indian Railways has about 1.21 million employees.
activities.explanation: Indian Railways is a very large employer with about 1.21 million employees.

activities.title: Match the Railway Details
activities.prompt: Match each railway fact with its detail.
pairs: Number of cities with metro trains
activities.explanation: These details show the size and development of India's railway system.

activities.title: Metro Trains Everywhere
activities.prompt: Metro trains operate in every Indian city.
activities.explanation: Metro trains operate in 23 Indian cities, not every city.

activities.title: Railway Expansion and Trade
activities.prompt: Put these effects of railway expansion in order.
activities.explanation: Railway expansion encouraged trade, and this helped new markets and settlements grow.

activities.title: Strengthening British Control
activities.prompt: Which pair shows two ways railways strengthened British control?
options: Growing markets and creating jobs
Reducing traffic and shortening travel times
Moving goods and troops
Carrying coal and running metros
activities.explanation: Railways moved British goods and troops more quickly. Both helped Britain control India more tightly.

activities.prompt: Adding metro trains will most likely change a city's road traffic how?
options: Road traffic may fall because some travellers will choose metro trains.
Road traffic may rise because metro trains carry goods daily.
Road traffic may stay because all trains must use roads.
Road traffic may rise because more taxis will serve commuters.

why.Road traffic may rise because metro trai: This mistakes cargo trains for metro trains and ignores metro effects.
why.Road traffic may stay because all trains: This wrongly assumes that all trains travel on roads.
why.Road traffic may rise because more taxis: This confuses indirect taxi jobs with less road traffic.

activities.explanation: Metro travel can be quicker, so fewer people may travel by road.

activities.prompt: An officer needs quicker troop movement. Which transport should the officer choose?
options: The railway system, because it moves troops more quickly.
The cargo system, because it carries goods across India.
The metro system, because it works in twenty-three cities.
The taxi system, because it creates indirect railway jobs.

why.The cargo system, because it carries goo: This confuses moving goods with moving troops.
why.The metro system, because it works in tw: Metro trains shorten travel times, but the need is troop movement.
why.The taxi system, because it creates indi: This confuses indirect jobs with the railway's military role.

activities.explanation: Railways move troops more quickly, which is what the officer needs.

activities.prompt: A map shows metro lines in twenty-three cities. What can we conclude?
options: Metro trains operate in every city shown on the map.
Indian Railways works only in the cities shown on the map.
Cargo trains work only in the cities shown on the map.
All trains work only in the cities shown on the map.

why.Indian Railways works only in the cities: This confuses all of Indian Railways with only the metro system.
why.Cargo trains work only in the cities sho: This confuses cargo trains with metro trains.
why.All trains work only in the cities shown: This wrongly treats every train as a metro train.

activities.explanation: The map marks metro lines, so those cities have metro trains.

activities.prompt: By 2025, all trains should use electricity. What must change?
options: Train power must change from non-electric to electric use.
Train power must change from passenger trains to cargo trains.
Railway work must change from paid staff to volunteers.
The number of metro cities must fall below twenty-three.

why.Train power must change from passenger t: This confuses changing train power with changing what trains carry.
why.Railway work must change from paid staff: This confuses the power target with the number of railway workers.
why.The number of metro cities must fall bel: This changes metro cities, but the rule concerns train power.

activities.explanation: The target requires every train to run on electricity.

activities.prompt: A trader sells cloth in distant markets. Why support railway expansion?
options: Railways can carry textiles and help new markets grow.
Railways can move troops faster and tighten British control.
Railways can create new metro jobs in twenty-three cities.
Railways can carry coal and help reduce road traffic.

why.Railways can move troops faster and tigh: This is the military effect of railways, not the trader's reason.
why.Railways can create new metro jobs in tw: Metro jobs and city numbers do not explain textile trade.
why.Railways can carry coal and help reduce: This mixes cargo transport with the effect of metro trains.

activities.explanation: Railways carry textiles, and expansion helps new markets grow.

activities.prompt: A railway station serves many more passengers. Which work may grow nearby?
options: Catering, vending and taxi services may need more workers.
Coal, grain and textile cargo may need more workers.
Metro lines and electric trains may need more new workers.
British control and troop movement may need many workers.

why.Coal, grain and textile cargo may need m: These are goods carried by cargo trains, not the listed station services.
why.Metro lines and electric trains may need: This confuses metro and electricity work with indirect railway services.
why.British control and troop movement may n: This confuses British control and troop movement with jobs around a station.

activities.explanation: More rail passengers can increase indirect work in catering, vending and taxis.

lessons.sceneCaption: Twin WDG3A locomotives haul a freight train at Sitaphalmandi station in Secunderabad.

lessons.title: Air Transport, Shipping and Ports

activities.prompt: How do airplanes and ships help people, goods, and communities connect?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Moving People and Goods
activities.body: Air transport is the fastest way to connect people and places. Passenger flights carry people, while cargo flights move valuable or perishable goods. Flights can deliver aid during floods and earthquakes. Aircraft can also reach difficult places, including mountains, deserts and forests. Ships carry heavy goods more cheaply over long distances. India’s long coastline helps trade with West Asia, Africa and Europe.
keyPoints: Air transport is the fastest way to connect places.
Flights carry people, goods and disaster aid.
Ships carry heavy goods cheaply over long distances.
activities.explanation: Different transport options help people, goods and aid reach different places.

activities.prompt: Floodwaters block roads to a far village. A shipment of medicine is ready to go. Should it travel by air or ship?
steps: Use air because it is the fastest way to connect places.
It fits because flights can deliver aid during floods and earthquakes.
Speed matters because the medicine is needed quickly.
Send it by air so the aid reaches the village sooner.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which transport is the fastest way to connect people and places?
options: Cargo flights
Passenger flights
Air transport
Ships
activities.explanation: Air transport is the fastest way to connect people and places.

activities.prompt: Flights can deliver ______ during floods and earthquakes.
activities.hint: People need help when disasters happen.
activities.explanation: Flights can quickly deliver aid to disaster areas.

activities.prompt: Passenger flights carry people, while cargo flights move goods.
activities.explanation: Yes. Each type of flight has a different main job.

activities.prompt: Match each transport option with its main job.
pairs: Carry heavy goods over long distances
activities.explanation: Each transport option has a useful job for people and goods.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order.
activities.explanation: The disaster happens first, and people receive the aid last.

activities.prompt: How many more minor ports than major ports does India have?
activities.explanation: India has 217 minor ports and 12 major ports. So, 217 - 12 = 205.

activities.prompt: Floodwaters block roads to a village. Medical aid must arrive quickly. Which transport should be used?
options: Air transport, because it is the fastest.
Sea shipping, because it is cheaper.
Road transport, because it avoids floods.
Rail transport, because it carries heavy goods.

This mistake values cheap sea travel more than urgent speed.
why.Road transport, because it avoids floods: This mistake ignores that floodwaters have blocked the roads.
why.Rail transport, because it carries heavy: This mistake focuses on carrying heavy goods instead of reaching quickly.

activities.explanation: Air transport is fastest, so it can reach the village soonest.

activities.prompt: A flower seller must send fresh flowers to another city. They can spoil quickly. Which type of flight should carry them?
options: A cargo flight, because it carries perishable goods.
A passenger flight, because it carries people.
A cargo flight, because it carries heavy goods.
A passenger flight, because it carries valuable goods.

why.A passenger flight, because it carries p: Passenger flights carry people, not the seller's flowers.
why.A cargo flight, because it carries heavy: This mistake mixes up cargo flights with ships, which carry heavy goods.
why.A passenger flight, because it carries v: This mistake mixes up passenger flights with cargo flights.

activities.explanation: Cargo flights move perishable goods, so they suit fresh flowers.

activities.prompt: A mountain village needs supplies. Its roads are hard to use. Which transport can reach it easily?
options: Air transport, because it reaches difficult places.
Sea shipping, because it reaches mountains easily.
Road transport, because roads are easy there.
Rail transport, because it reaches mountains easily.

why.Sea shipping, because it reaches mountai: This mistake wrongly assumes that ships can reach mountain places.
why.Road transport, because roads are easy t: This mistake ignores that roads in the village are hard to use.
why.Rail transport, because it reaches mount: This mistake wrongly assumes that trains can reach difficult places easily.

activities.explanation: Aircraft can easily reach difficult places such as mountains.

activities.prompt: India has the world's third-highest domestic air traffic. Its airports handled around 376 million passengers in 2024–25. What do these facts together show?
options: Domestic air travel is very important in India.
Domestic air travel is almost absent in India.
India's port traffic is higher than its air traffic.
India has fewer than three busy airports.

why.Domestic air travel is almost absent in: This mistake treats very high air traffic as very low use.
why.India's port traffic is higher than its: These facts give no comparison between port traffic and air traffic.
why.India has fewer than three busy airports: This mistake confuses third-highest traffic with having only three airports.

activities.explanation: High traffic and millions of passengers show that air travel is widely used.

activities.prompt: India's long coastline supports trade with Europe. It has 12 major ports and 217 minor ports. A company wants to send heavy goods cheaply. Which transport should it use?
options: Shipping by sea, because ships are cheaper.
Air transport, because it is the fastest.
Passenger flight, because it carries people.
Cargo flight, because it carries goods.

why.Air transport, because it is the fastest: This mistake chooses speed instead of the cheaper transport.
why.Passenger flight, because it carries peo: This mistake confuses carrying people with carrying heavy goods.
This mistake confuses moving goods with the cheapest long-distance option.

activities.explanation: Ships cheaply carry heavy goods over long distances, and ports support trade.

lessons.sceneCaption: A cargo aircraft transports valuable goods by air.

lessons.title: Communication Infrastructure

activities.prompt: How does your voice note travel to a friend’s phone?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Messages Travel
activities.body: Infrastructure includes cables, wireless devices, towers, satellites and data centres. It carries messages, images and videos. Mobile alerts help people respond quickly during natural disasters. Businesses sell products worldwide through e-commerce. E-governance helps citizens apply for documents, complain and find information. Jagadish Chandra Bose developed new ways to send information without wires. His experiments used microwaves in the millimetre range.
keyPoints: Communication infrastructure includes cables, wireless devices, towers, satellites and data centres.
It allows messages, images and videos to be transmitted.
Bose pioneered wireless transmission using millimetre-range microwaves.
activities.explanation: This card introduces communication infrastructure, its uses and early wireless work.

activities.prompt: Rani sends a voice note. How does it reach the other phone?
steps: Electricity powers the mobile tower, because the tower must receive Rani's voice note.
The message travels through fibre cables buried under fields and roads, because cables carry it onward.
It then passes through satellites and servers, because they continue the route to the other phone.
Therefore, communication infrastructure connects both phones and delivers Rani's voice note.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which items are part of communication infrastructure?
options: Roads, farms and shops
Books, pens and bags
Cables, towers and satellites
Buses, trains and cycles
activities.explanation: That is right. These are parts of communication infrastructure.

activities.prompt: Rani’s message travels through ______ cables buried under fields and roads.
activities.hint: Use the type of cable mentioned for Rani’s route.
activities.explanation: That is right. Rani’s message travels through fibre cables under fields and roads.

activities.prompt: Match each group or need to the service that helps it.
activities.explanation: That is right. Each pair connects a service with the people it helps.

activities.prompt: What helps Rani’s voice note reach the other phone?
options: Mobile tower, fibre cables, satellites and servers
Electricity, fibre cables, farms and roads
Satellites, servers, shops and buses
Buses, shops, farms and towers
activities.explanation: That is right. The tower receives the note before fibre cables, satellites and servers carry it.

activities.prompt: What did Jagadish Chandra Bose use in his wireless experiments?
options: Fibre cables under roads
Millimetre-range microwaves
Mobile tower electricity
Data centre servers
activities.explanation: That is right. Bose used microwaves in the millimetre range for his wireless experiments.

activities.prompt: Put the voice note’s journey in order.
activities.explanation: That is right. The tower receives the note first. The message then travels through fibre cables, satellites and servers.

activities.prompt: Rani's village loses electricity. What happens to her voice note first?
options: It will not reach the mobile tower.
It will travel only through fibre cables.
It will reach the other phone faster.
It will be received directly by satellites.

why.It will travel only through fibre cables: This assumes fibre cables can replace the tower's first step.
This mistakes a power loss for a faster connection.
why.It will be received directly by satellit: This skips the tower and fibre cable steps in the route.

activities.explanation: Without electricity, the tower cannot receive Rani's voice note.

activities.prompt: A map shows fibre cables under fields and roads. What can we infer about a message's route?
options: The message can pass through those buried cables.
The message must travel above ground by satellite.
The buried cables will power the mobile tower.
The message will stop at the first data centre.

why.The message must travel above ground by: This assumes cables carry no messages and satellites take over.
why.The buried cables will power the mobile: This confuses the cables' job with electricity powering towers.
why.The message will stop at the first data: This assumes the message stops before reaching the other phone.

activities.explanation: The map shows that messages can travel through buried fibre cables.

activities.prompt: A mobile alert warns people about a flood. Why can this help them respond quickly?
options: They learn of the danger and can act soon.
They must find buried fibre cables before acting.
They can act only after the flood has ended.
They will receive fewer mobile warnings after it.

why.They must find buried fibre cables befor: This confuses the warning system with cables carrying messages.
why.They can act only after the flood has en: This reverses the purpose of sending a quick disaster warning.
why.They will receive fewer mobile warnings: This assumes an alert reduces warnings instead of giving one.

activities.explanation: Mobile alerts and apps help people respond quickly during natural disasters.

lessons.title: Social Infrastructure and Collective Responsibility

activities.prompt: How can we make our shared spaces safer, cleaner, and kinder for everyone?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Caring for shared places
activities.body: Social infrastructure includes schools, hospitals, police stations, fire stations, parks and libraries. Damage to these public places makes life harder for everyone. Everyone must share responsibility for caring for them. Better waste, sewer and traffic management can improve services. New infrastructure should meet the needs of children, elderly people and disabled persons.
keyPoints: Social infrastructure provides places and services for everyone.
Damage affects everyone, so responsibility must be shared.
New infrastructure should meet different people's needs.
activities.explanation: Public places work better when everyone helps care for them.

activities.prompt: A town's library is damaged. How should the town rebuild and care for it?
steps: The library is social infrastructure, so damage makes life harder for everyone.
Collective responsibility matters, because everyone must care for social infrastructure.
Use cleaner energy and environment-friendly materials, because infrastructure should be clean.
So rebuild it, because children, elderly people and disabled people need it.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which services need better waste, sewer and traffic management?
options: Public schools and hospitals
Police and fire stations
Panchayat and municipal services
Roads and waterways
activities.explanation: The lesson says panchayat and municipal services need better management.

activities.prompt: Kautilya recommended punishments and ______ for people who damaged infrastructure.
activities.hint: Think about what people received besides punishments.
activities.explanation: Kautilya recommended punishments and fines to protect infrastructure.

activities.prompt: Match each place or choice with its role.
activities.explanation: Each pair links a place or choice with its role in the lesson.

activities.prompt: What were ancient road widths based on?
options: The punishments given
The energy used
The traffic expected
The roads maintained
activities.explanation: Ancient builders adjusted road widths to the amount of expected traffic.

activities.prompt: Good infrastructure supports other economic activities, ______ and ease of living.
activities.hint: Think of the work that infrastructure can support.
activities.explanation: Good infrastructure supports other economic activities, employment and ease of living.

activities.prompt: Who helped build and maintain roads and waterways?
options: The police, fire stations and parks
State, village and sabhās
The schools, hospitals and libraries
Clean energy and environment-friendly materials
activities.explanation: Kautilya's text names the state, village and sabhās as helpers.

activities.prompt: A park has broken facilities and damaged paths. What will happen to daily life in the area?
options: Life will become harder for everyone who lives there.
Only people who visit the park will face problems.
The park will have no effect on anyone else.
Only workers who clean the park will face problems.

why.Only people who visit the park will face: This wrongly limits the harm to park visitors.
why.The park will have no effect on anyone e: This wrongly thinks a damaged park affects nobody else.
why.Only workers who clean the park will fac: This wrongly limits the harm to park workers.

activities.explanation: Right, because damage to social infrastructure makes life harder for everyone.

activities.prompt: A source describes ancient roads with different widths. What does this show about road planning?
options: Road widths matched the traffic expected on each road.
Every ancient road had exactly the same width.
Road widths were decided without thinking about traffic.
Only busy roads received any planning at all.

why.Every ancient road had exactly the same: This wrongly treats different widths as evidence of one width.
why.Road widths were decided without thinkin: This wrongly says traffic was ignored when roads were planned.
why.Only busy roads received any planning at: This wrongly says only busy roads received planning.

activities.explanation: This is right because road widths matched expected traffic.

activities.prompt: A source says state, village and sabhās built and maintained waterways. What does this show?
options: Only the state was responsible for building and maintenance.
Different groups shared responsibility for social infrastructure.
Waterways were maintained without any group helping.
Each group cared for its own work and shared nothing.

why.Only the state was responsible for build: This wrongly makes the state the only group responsible.
why.Waterways were maintained without any gr: This wrongly denies the help described by the source.
why.Each group cared for its own work and sh: This wrongly treats separate help as no shared responsibility.

activities.explanation: This is right because several groups shared responsibility.

activities.prompt: A town plans a new public building. Which design should meet the needs of all users?
options: Only children should have suitable access to the building.
Only disabled persons should have suitable access to the building.
Only elderly people should have suitable access to the building.
Children, elderly people and disabled persons should have suitable access.

why.Only children should have suitable acces: This wrongly thinks only children need suitable access.
why.Only disabled persons should have suitab: This wrongly thinks only disabled persons need suitable access.
why.Only elderly people should have suitable: This wrongly thinks only elderly people need suitable access.

activities.explanation: This is right because new infrastructure must meet these groups' needs.

activities.prompt: A town improves roads and public services. What can this bring besides easier daily living?
options: More economic activities but less employment.
Less economic activity but more employment.
Support for economic activities and more employment.
Neither economic activities nor employment.

why.More economic activities but less employ: This wrongly thinks economic support must reduce employment.
why.Less economic activity but more employme: This wrongly thinks good infrastructure reduces economic activity.
why.Neither economic activities nor employme: This wrongly says infrastructure has no economic effects.

activities.explanation: This is right because good infrastructure supports activities and employment.
